PREFACE 

A study of what the authors choose to call Business Law and Procedure is appropriate at the present time, because business methods are becoming increasingly technical and involved. These changes in method are due largely to enactments by local, state, and Federal governing bodies, and also to precedents established by court decisions. The approach and the subjects included in this study are of special concern to teachers and students of business law. The topics most common to our business activities have been fully treated, therefore, in this text. 

Business Law and Procedure is, in the main, a study of our legislative and judicial systems and of the principles of law applicable to the contract situations that grow out of our varied business activities. This book not only presents the legal regulations of many kinds of contracts, but it also explains the processes involved in the business transactions from which these various contracts result. Experimentation in classes has disclosed that this method of presenting the subject helps students to acquire a better understanding of how business is transacted as well as of the laws and rules that govern contracts.

Since the organization of the material for teaching purposes is of major importance, attention is called to the various units in this book. 

1. The treatment of each main subject in the text is preceded by a glossary of technical and legal terms used, for the most part, in discussing that particular subject. 

2. The question or statement approach is commonly employed to introduce the different principles of law. 

3. An appropriate example is provided in cases where it will aid in illustrating or amplifying the principle of law that is being discussed. 

4. Following the complete treatment of each main subject the principles of law covered therein are summarized in brief form.

vi 

PREFACE 

5.

Two sets of questions follow the treatment of each main 

Text Questions are answered specifically in the text and are intended to serve as a review of the subject matter. 

General Questions may be used at the discretion of the teacher. 

These questions are answered generally in the text, but not so specifically as are the "text questions." The "general questions" can be used to advantage by the teacher in class discussions. 

6. Cases for Decision cover the important principles of law treated in connection with some particular topic, and they afford an excellent means of testing the student's understanding of the application of the principles of law involved. These cases require the student (a) to state the essential facts in the case, (b) to state the principle of law that applies, and (c) to give his decision. 

7. Following the cases for decision is a complete outline of the main subjects and subtopics in the particular unit of the text material. This outline may be used by the teacher in the development of the lesson or by both teacher and pupil in the review checkup. 

8. A significant feature of the text is the authors' comments on certain concepts of legal, social, or economic importance that should be brought to the attention of the student in his study of business-law procedure.

The material in this text is authentic, practical, and teachable. 

The authors have had business experience, teaching experience, and experience in preparing text material on the subject of commercial or business law for instruction purposes. This text reflects that experience. The last chapter of the book treats of labor and social legislation, such as the National Labor Relations Act and the Social Security Act. The last part of the chapter is devoted to recent changes in the statutes of New York that indicate a trend toward similar changes in other states. 

The authors wish to express sincere appreciation to their many friends who have given helpful suggestions in the spirit of providing a more teachable and authentic business-law text.

INTRODUCTION 

 has to do primarily with those rules and principles of law which apply specifically to business transactions and to the methods of transacting business. 

Business embraces all activities in which people engage for the purpose of gaining a livelihood or economic advantage and security and for ministering to the social needs of the people. The extent and multiplicity of these activities are such that rules and laws for the guidance and the control of those engaged in business are necessary to the well-being of everybody. 

A knowledge of business law is helpful. 

It is important that every individual who engages in a particular business or even transacts personal business affairs should have some knowledge of business law. The rights he acquires and the liabilities he assumes depend upon the rules of law applicable to the particular transaction into which he enters, and he should know enough about the rules to protect himself. However, a familiarity with this book, or any book on business law, will not be sufficient if the case is complicated or involved. The law is a broad, difficult, and highly technical science of which only the rudiments can be given in such a work as this, and the advice of a lawyer should be obtained on any question of importance. 

By what laws are we governed? 

Law and order are the foundations of our world. Without them there could be neither security nor progress. They are indispensable to our physical and social well-being. 

We are governed by and enjoy the benefits of different kinds of laws. The laws of nature control our relations with the natural world. They operate uniformly and inevitably and require no human agency for their enforcement. Moral laws control our personal conduct and are enforced only by the individual's sense of 1

right and wrong. Social laws control our social relations with our fellow men and are observed because of a general willingness to conform to accepted standards of conduct. 

The rules of law which apply to business transactions may be divided into two general classes-statute law and common law, sometimes described as written and unwritten law. 

Statute law.

Statute law is made by the legislatures of the several states or of the United States. When there is an evil to be corrected, or some rule of conduct to be prescribed, the desired result may be reached quickly by the enactment of a statute. If the new law does not work well in practice, or if changing conditions make an alteration necessary, the statute may easily be amended or repealed. The strength of legislation lies in its prompt response to immediate needs. 

Common law.

Common law has its origin in custom which is so long and well established that it has the force of law. The rules of common law are found in the decisions of the courts. It is called "unwritten law" because it is not based on any statute or other writing, but on custom. Common law changes slowly and tends to fall behind the requirements of our rapidly changing modern civilization. For that reason many statutes are passed which alter common-law rules.

This text is based on the common law, except as to subjects which are governed by generally accepted uniform statutes, such as Sales and Negotiable Instruments. It should be borne in mind that there may be other differences arising from local statutes which cannot be included in the compass of this book.

OUR LAWS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Constitutional. In agreement with the Constitution of a state or of the 

United States.

Executive. That branch of our government which carries into effect or executes our laws.

Judicial. That branch of our government which passes judgment and imposes penalties on those who violate our laws. 

Legislative. That branch of our government which makes our laws. 

Political. Having to do with governmental matters, particularly the machinery of government. 

Statute. A law enacted by a legislative body. 

Unicameral. Consisting of one house, as a single-chamber legislature. 

How may our laws be defined?

The kind of law with which we are presently concerned may be defined as a system of principles and rules which govern our dealings and relations with other persons. It differs from the other kinds of laws in two important particulars; first, it is made and established by a body of men designated for that purpose; and, second, obedience to the law is enforced by the state. 

What are the functions and departments of each political unit? 

The creation, interpretation, and enforcement of the law are among the principal functions of every governmental body, and for these purposes there are three departments in each political unit. The legislative department makes the laws. The judicial department interprets and applies the laws. The executive department enforces the laws by carrying out the judgments of the courts. The stability of state or national government depends largely on the enactment and enforcement of adequate laws. 3

The United States as a political unit. 

The United States is a single political unit. Its laws are made by the Congress, consisting of two houses, the Senate and the House of Representatives, subject to approval by the President. 

The United States or Federal Courts interpret and apply these laws, and they are enforced by the Executive Department, of which the President is the head.

The state as a political unit. 

Each state is a political unit, having its own legislature of two houses and its own judicial and executive departments. The Nebraska legislature now operates under the unicameral system. The process of making, applying, and enforcing state laws is similar to that of the United States. 

What are the political subdivisions of a state?

Within each state are further political subdivisions, such as counties, cities, towns, and villages, and usually other subdivisions for special purposes, such as school districts, fire districts, and drainage districts. These subdivisions have such governmental powers as may be conferred by the Constitution or laws of the state. 

How is a county governed?

A county is governed by a board of representatives, called supervisors, commissioners, or chosen freeholders. The county court deals with matters arising in the county or those in which the residents are involved. The sheriff is the principal official to enforce the laws, but he is not an executive like the President or Governor. 

How is a city governed?

A city has its own legislature, called the common council or board of aldermen, with power to enact ordinances for the government of the city. Its chief executive is the mayor, and it has its own courts. The commission plan of government has been adopted in some cities. Under this plan a small number of commissioners are elected by the people, and the commissioners choose a city manager and other administrative officials. This plan is thought

​Copyright by Harris & Ewing

PRESIDENT FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT ADDRESSING A JOINT SESSION OF CONGRESS

to promote efficiency and economy and to result in nonpartisan administration.

Example of direct government. 

The town meeting, still held in some states, is the only example of direct government of the people and by the people that we have. 

All qualified residents of the town are entitled to attend the meeting and vote on matters pertaining to the government of the town. 

Decisions of the voters at such meetings have the force of law. In other states town affairs are managed by a board of elected officials, whose duty it is to administer the affairs of the town and execute the laws.

Other political divisions, such as villages, school districts, and fire districts, may enact ordinances or regulations, which are enforced by their own officers.

Our laws are classified. 

International Law. Rules that result from agreements or treaties between nations and among nations and regulate the dealings of one nation with another, form what is known as international law.

Municipal Law. Rules prescribed by governmental authority of a state or any political subdivision of a state for the purpose of regulating the intercourse of the particular state or subdivision with its people or of the individuals with each other form our municipal law. The divisions of municipal law are Constitutional 

Law (national and state), Statute Law (law passed by legislative bodies), and Common Law and Equity (laws resulting from customs and precedents in practice).

What is Constitutional Law? 

The United States, and each separate state thereof, has a Constitution, which enumerates specifically the rights, duties, and powers of the particular unit of government and of the people governed. This Constitution might be considered as the framework of government. To say that a particular statute law is unconstitutional means that it conflicts in some way with the Constitution.

OUR LAWS 

7 Laws passed by the Congress which are in any way in violation of the Constitution of the United States are unconstitutional and not enforceable. Likewise, laws passed by the legislature of a state which violate the Constitution of that particular state or of the United States are not enforceable.

What is Statute Law? 

The laws enacted by a legislative body are statute laws. The laws passed by Congress or by state legislatures, and ordinances passed by a city common council or a board of aldermen are all statute laws, as are laws passed in a town meeting or on petition and vote of the people. All such laws and the constitutions of states and the Constitution of the United States are known as written law. Our lawmaking machinery is so complete and so flexible that the tendency is to reduce all regulations having the force of law to written law. 

What is Common Law and Equity? 

Written law cannot and does not cover every possible situation out of which a dispute may arise. When a civil case comes into court involving a dispute not governed by any statute, the judge must decide it fairly and equitably. In such a case, he looks for guidance to the principles of common law, which had its origin in the customs of the people and which has been developed by the courts through the centuries. Since common law is a body of principles and not of specific rules, it is flexible and can be applied to new situations as they arise, due to changing conditions of business life and the advancement of civilization. 

How are the principles of our common law developed? 

The principles of common law are set forth in court decisions. 

When a case is before the court for decision, the lawyers search the records for decisions in similar cases. When cases are found in which a principle is applied to a certain situation, those cases are precedents and guide the judge in deciding later cases involving similar situations. If no exact precedents can be found, the judge selects the principles which logically should control and applies them in such a way as to do justice to the parties.

What is the difference between common law and equity? 

The differences between common law and equity are in the methods of procedure and the kind of judgment awarded. A lawsuit is tried by a judge and jury, and the judgment is an award of money damages to the successful party. An equity action is tried by a judge without a jury, and the decree requires the defendant to do, or refrain from doing, some act. Injunctions, decrees of specific performance, and the sale of property under mortgage foreclosure are examples of equity decrees. Money damages may be awarded by an equity court as an incident of the principal purpose of the action.

Our laws are divided according to their nature and purpose. 

Criminal Law. We are members of a great social order. The preservation of this order and the protection of its members are absolutely necessary to the safety and the well-being of us all. 

Therefore, society has established rules for the regulation of its members in their conduct toward each other, and toward society in general. Certain acts which injure or tend to injure persons in their bodily health or safety, or in their property, are declared to be crimes and are punishable by fine or imprisonment, or both. 

In most states, very serious crimes, such as treason and murder, are punishable by death. The penalty imposed for breaking the law determines whether the forbidden act is a crime. Murder, assault and battery, burglary, larceny, and the violation of the speed laws are all crimes, although some are more serious than others. Because of the evil tendency involved, an attempt or a conspiracy to commit a crime is itself a crime, even though no actual injury is done to anybody.

In most states the legislature has passed statutes which constitute the entire criminal law of the state. 

Civil Law. Civil law differs from criminal law in the nature of the right protected and the nature of the penalty imposed for a violation. Civil law protects the rights of a person as an individual, as distinguished from his rights as a member of society, and the penalty is in the form of a judgment designed to recompense the injured person instead of punishing the wrongdoer. For example,

OUR LAWS 

9 if a thief steals your property, he commits a crime and may be imprisoned under the criminal law. He has also wrongfully deprived you of your property and is liable to a civil judgment requiring him to return the property or pay you its value. 

Thus all laws which protect the rights of a person in his individual dealings with other persons and which provide for specific recompense or protection to a person injured by violation of such rights are civil laws. 

Business Law. Business law is a branch of civil law. It includes all rules of civil law which govern business transactions, particularly contracts, and the rights and duties of persons engaged in trade or commerce.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Law and order are fundamental to human progress. 

2. Following is the order of authority on our laws: (a) Constitution of the United States (b) Laws of the Congress (c) Constitutions of the different states (d) Laws of the state legislatures (e) The common law and equity 3. Individual liberty is restrained only to the extent that it is repressed or controlled by some rule of law. 

4. The authority of law is confined to the boundary limits of the municipality responsible for the law. 

5. Laws increase in number as human needs become more varied and social and economic conditions more complex. 

6. Each political unit of government reserves to itself the right to make its own laws. 

7. The laws of a lesser political unit must not conflict in any way with the laws of a political unit of which it is a subdivision; i.e., the laws of a city in a particular state must not conflict with the laws of that state; likewise, the laws of a state must not conflict with the laws of Congress. 

8. Any law is unconstitutional and not enforceable if it conflicts with the Constitution of the political unit passing the law or with the Constitution of the political unit of which it is a subdivision.

TEXT QUESTIONS

2. How many different kinds of laws are we as a people subjected to? 

3. How are the laws which govern our dealings and relations with other persons made and enforced? 

4. Name three governmental bodies whose principal function is to create, interpret, and enforce laws. 

5. What are the three departments of any organized unit of our government and what are the functions of each department? 

6. How are our laws classified? 

7. How are our laws divided according to their nature and purpose, and what is the difference between them? 

8. What does that branch of civil law known as business law include?

OUR COURTS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Appeal. A proceeding by which a case is brought to a higher court for the correction of errors in the lower court.

Chancery. A name given to a court of equity. 

Circuit. The district within which the circuit or district court has jurisdiction.

Judgment. The decision, decree, or sentence of a court. 

Magistrate. An official having jurisdiction in criminal cases. 

Probate. Official proof of the last will and testament of a deceased person. 

Referee. An official to whom a matter is referred for settlement or who is to hear the evidence in a case and to report thereon to the court. 

Surrogate. A judicial officer who has jurisdiction over the probate of wills and the settlement of estates. 

What must be done when a person violates the law?

It would avail us little to have laws unless we had some means of enforcing them. Our courts are established to determine when a law has been violated and what the penalty or award of damages shall be. The judgments of the courts are enforced by the sheriff, marshal, or other executive official. 

When a person has violated the law, a court proceeding must be started against him. If a criminal offense was committed, the proceeding is brought by the people in the name of the state and is conducted by a public official called the district attorney, state's attorney, or prosecuting attorney. If a civil wrong is involved, the proceeding is begun in the name of the injured person and is conducted by his personal attorney. 

A court must have jurisdiction.

The power and authority of a court to hear and determine a case is called its jurisdiction. The jurisdiction of the court may 11

be limited by the law which created the court. Thus there are courts established to hear appeals, to decide criminal cases, to deal with wills and the administration of estates, to decide claims against the state, and various other special courts. Also some courts cannot decide cases which involve more than a certain amount of money, the limit being fixed by law. If a court should decide a case which was beyond its powers, the judgment would be worthless. Before a court can proceed legally with any case, it must have jurisdiction over the subject matter and jurisdiction over the person.

Jurisdiction over the subject matter. Jurisdiction over the subject matter means that the claim or thing in dispute must be within the power of the court. Thus a criminal court could not try a civil case; a probate court could not try an automobile accident case; a justice of the peace could not try a case involving a large sum of money. Also, there is a rule of law that a case involving the title to land must be brought in the judicial district where the land is situated. If the wrong court should attempt to hear such a case, it would have no jurisdiction over the subject matter. 

Jurisdiction over the person. Jurisdiction over the person means that all persons who are parties to the action must be brought within the power of the court, either voluntarily or otherwise. 

The plaintiff submits himself to the court by bringing the action. 

The defendant may voluntarily appear, either in person or by an attorney, or he may be made subject to the court by the service of process; i.e., a summons or any order of the court delivered to him personally. Elsewhere in this book "process" is treated. 

Our Federal Courts. 

United States courts are known as Federal courts. They have the power to hear all cases arising under the Constitution, laws, and treaties of the United States. According to the Constitution, the judicial power of the United States shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such lower courts as Congress from time to time shall establish. Federal judges are appointed by the President, with the approval of the Senate. 

Congress has established, in addition to the Supreme Court, a

OUR COURTS 

13 Circuit Court of Appeals, District Courts (one to four in each state), a Court of Claims, a Court of Customs Appeals, and Consular Courts. 

Supreme Court. In the Supreme Court there are one chief justice and eight associate justices. It has original jurisdiction in 

By Ewing Galloway, N. Y.

UNITED STATES SUPREME COURT BUILDING 

all proceedings brought against ambassadors, public ministers, and their families, and also in all suits between states. It has appellate jurisdiction to hear appeals from the circuit court of appeals, and in some cases, from the highest court of a state. 

Circuit Court of Appeals. This court has appellate jurisdiction to review final decisions of the district court. In a few cases appeals may be taken directly from the district court to the 

Supreme Court.

The United States is divided into ten circuits, in each of which there is a Circuit Court of Appeals. 

District Court. In each state there is at least one District 

Court, and in some states there are as many as four, depending upon the demand for such a court. Each District Court is presided over by a district judge.

The District Courts have original jurisdiction over all civil suits brought by the United States and over suits which arise under the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States, or between citizens of different states, or a citizen of a state and a foreign country. These courts also have original jurisdiction over cases arising under the revenue, postal, patent, copyright, trade-mark, and bankruptcy laws.

Other Federal Courts. The Court of Claims hears and determines claims against the United States. The Court of Customs Appeals hears all cases arising under the revenue laws of the United States. The Consular Courts hear cases affecting citizens of the 

United States who are in some foreign country and who might otherwise be subjected to the uncertain and barbarous laws of certain countries. There are also Local Courts for the District of 

Columbia, the Philippines, and Alaska.

Our State Courts. 

While there is some variation in the kind and number of courts in the different states, the usual local and state courts are a Justice Court, Municipal or City Court, Police or Magistrate's Court, County Court, Surrogate's or Probate Court, Circuit or District Court, Court of Claims, Appellate Division, and Supreme Court or Court of Appeals.

Justice Court. The Justice Court is the local village or town court. It is the lowest court and is presided over by the justice of the peace who is elected by the votes of the district which he is to serve. This court has original jurisdiction only, and it is not a court of record. It hears both civil and criminal cases and is of limited jurisdiction.

Municipal or City Court. In cities there is a court that hears both civil and criminal cases. It takes the place of the justice

OUR COURTS 

15 court, which is confined to small communities. The Municipal or 

City Court has only limited or special jurisdiction according to regulations fixed by statute, the same as our justice courts. 

Police or Magistrate's Court. In large cities the city court has two branches, one for hearing civil cases and one for hearing criminal cases. The jurisdiction of the Police or Magistrate's 

Court is confined to criminal cases arising out of crimes committed within the particular city.

County Court. The jurisdiction of the County Court, in those states and counties having such a court, is confined to those cases especially assigned to it by statutory regulations. In some states it is called the probate or orphan's court, and deals with the settlement of estates, the probate of wills, and the protection of the interests of minor children. In New York and some other states the County Court has jurisdiction over certain civil and criminal cases arising within the county. In a few states, New 

York among them, and particularly in large counties, there are two courts, one held by the county judge for civil and criminal cases, and one presided over by the surrogate, a judge of the probate court.

Surrogate's or Probate Court. This court, in states or counties having such a court, deals with the probate of wills and with the settlement of estates of deceased persons who left no will, in which case an administrator of the estate must be appointed by the court. When a will is left by a deceased person, the one named in the will as executor must execute the will according to its terms; nevertheless, the will is subject to the jurisdiction of the County or Surrogate's Court, and must be offered for probate. This court also administers the property affairs of orphans left with property. 

In such cases the judge of the court having jurisdiction appoints a guardian who is charged with the administration of the business affairs of the orphan.

Circuit or District Court. In every state there is a court having general jurisdiction to try all cases in law and equity, except those triable in the Federal courts or those assigned to special courts, such as the Probate Court or the Court of Claims. The state is divided into districts or circuits containing one or more counties,

and there is a court in each district. These courts are usually called Circuit Courts or District Courts. In New York they are called Supreme Courts.

In some states a separate tribunal, called the Court of Chancery, held by a Chancellor or Vice-Chancellor, exercises the equity powers of the court. In most states the Circuit or District Court has jurisdiction in both law and equity. 

Court of Claims. The Court of Claims has exclusive jurisdiction in the case of any claims by any individual, firm, or institution against the state. The state cannot be sued without its permission. The Court of Claims is presided over by judges appointed by the governor, and all claims against the state are heard and decided upon by this court.

Appellate Division. In many states there is a court having appellate jurisdiction only, which is intermediate between the lower courts and the court of last resort. It is called the Appellate 

Division or Court of Appeal. Its purpose is to relieve the highest court of some of the burden of appeals. Most cases may be appealed to the Appellate Division as a matter of right. In many instances its decision is final, and appeals to the high court are allowed only in important cases. The laws regulating the right to appeal vary in the different states. 

Supreme Court. In each state there is a court of final appeal, called the Supreme Court or Court of Appeals. It exercises appellate jurisdiction only, and its decision is final in all cases except those in which a right under the Federal Constitution or laws is denied, when an appeal may be taken to the United States 

Supreme Court.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Provisions for enforcing laws are necessary if they are to be effective. 

2. Courts are a necessary part of our governmental machinery, for the purpose of enforcing our laws and punishing offenders. 

3. A court can legally proceed with a case only when it has jurisdiction over both the subject matter and the person involved.

OUR COURTS 

17 4. Our courts are classified, first, according to the political unit which they serve, and second, according to their jurisdiction. 

5. The United States or a particular state cannot be sued by any individual, firm, or institution, unless permission to sue is granted.

COMMENTS 

The demand for simpler and more direct processes in suits at law is urgent, particularly where the amount involved is small, and in many places a different type of court is being established to meet this demand. 

In New York State it is possible to establish what is known as a small debtors' court in places (cities or communities) where it is needed. In 

New York City it is organized as a branch of the municipal court, and five branches have been established, one branch in each of the five boroughs. 

In this court, the injured party may appear and explain his case to the clerk of the court. If he has a case, the clerk writes down all the details, and a hearing is set for a particular day not less than five or more than eleven days later. On the day the clerk receives the case, notice of it is sent by registered mail to the defendant. When the case is called, both sides tell their story to the judge. Witnesses may be called to testify. 

The judge will decide the case. Persons having claims of $50 or less may avail themselves of this court, and the court cost is $1.25 for each case. 

Lawyers are not necessary.

Similar courts are in operation in Boston, Chicago, Cleveland, Philadelphia, and Spokane. Among the states providing for small debtors' courts are: California, Idaho, Massachusetts, Nevada, Oregon, and South

Dakota. Other cities and states will no doubt provide for the establishment of such courts as the need becomes more urgent and their value to the party who has a small claim is more fully understood.

CRIMINAL LAW TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Felony. A criminal act which is more serious than a misdemeanor. 

Misdemeanor. Misbehavior which amounts to a crime less serious than a felony. 

Prosecute. To seek to enforce by legal process. 

What is criminal law?

Criminal law is that branch of our laws which defines certain acts against individuals and society generally as criminal acts, and defines specifically what penalties shall be imposed on those who commit any of these acts. 

Our criminal laws are in the form of statutes passed by the state legislatures and certain common-law principles. Criminal law has no direct connection with business law except that many crimes are committed in connection with business transactions. Every criminal act is contrary to the peace and welfare of the public, and the offender is prosecuted by the proper officials of the state. The district attorney usually prosecutes criminals, and the case is usually tried in a county court or the supreme court of the state. Crimes.

The two general classes of crimes are felonies and misdemeanors. 

The most common crimes are further classified as follows: Felonies Misdemeanors 

1. Arson 

2. Conspiracy 

3. Embezzlement 

1. Disorderly conduct 

2. Drunkenness 

3. Disregarding traffic rules 

4. Creating a disturbance 

4. Forgery 

5. Larceny 

6. Obtaining something under false pretenses 20

CRIMINAL LAW 

21 

1. What is arson? Willfully and maliciously setting fire to another person's building, or willfully burning any property which results in a loss to some other person, is a crime of arson. A person who burns his own house that he may recover the insurance is also guilty of the crime of arson. In such case the insurance company would suffer an unnecessary loss. State laws with regard to the crime of arson and the penalties imposed for this crime vary greatly. 

2. When does a conspiracy result? A conspiracy results when two persons conceive of and carry out a plan or scheme to defraud or injure in some way another party who is innocent of the conspiracy. Whether a particular conspiracy is a felony or a misdemeanor depends upon the laws of the particular state where it is committed. 

3. What is embezzlement? A person who wrongfully appropriates for his own use money belonging to another person and entrusted to him is guilty of the crime of embezzlement. 

A person who holds a responsible position and is trusted with the handling of funds belonging to his employer is usually required to furnish a bond which protects the employer against loss resulting from embezzlement by an employee. There are bonding companies who make a business of bonding employees. They charge a fee for these bonds according to the amount. 

When an employee embezzles funds belonging to his employer, the bonding company makes good the loss to the employer, but the employee may be prosecuted as a criminal, and the penalty in case of a verdict of guilty is imprisonment for a term of years. 

4. What is forgery? Any person who without proper authority signs another person's name to an instrument or who alters a written instrument in such a way as to defraud another, has committed an act of forgery. Signing one's own name and passing it as the signature of another person of the same name is a forgery. 

Likewise, writing a statement over the signature of another person would be considered forgery in some states. 

5. What is larceny? Any person who unlawfully takes goods or money belonging to another person with the intent of converting such goods or money to his own use is guilty of the crime of larceny,

which is stealing. This is considered a serious offense against society, and the penalty is usually imprisonment. 

6. Obtaining something under false pretenses. Any person who represents himself as having authority and on the strength of it influences someone to give him money or goods is guilty of a crime. Such an act to amount to a crime must result from a misrepresentation with respect to some past or present fact. Representation regarding a future act would not be considered a false pretense, but it might be considered a warranty. 

Example 1. Wade fraudulently represented that he was the duly authorized agent of the Hornell Nursery Company, and took an order from Shaw for $250 worth of fruit trees, on which Shaw made a payment of $50. This is a false representation of a present existing fact, and amounts to a crime. 

Example 2. Long represented that a car he sold to Green for $300 would make a speed of 50 miles per hour. This representation on the part of 

Long is not a false pretense amounting to a crime, but instead it is a warranty. 

Certain offenses are misdemeanors.

Such offenses as infractions of traffic regulations, drunkenness, disorderly conduct, etc., are classed as misdemeanors. They are not considered so serious as are felonies, and the penalty imposed is usually a fine or imprisonment in the county jail, one or both. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A crime is an offense against the state (the people). 

2. A crime may be an act which the law forbids or the failure to perform some act which the law commands to be done. 

3. Criminal acts are considered to be against public policy, or against the public good. 

4. The state, through its duly elected or appointed officials, prosecutes criminals. 

5. Usually an act is not a crime unless a wrongful intent existed at the time it was committed. 

6. An intention to commit a crime may amount to a crime. 

7. A pretense as to some future event, though it proves to be false, does not amount to a crime. 

8. The offender, in the case of theft or embezzlement, cannot

CRIMINAL LAW 

23 rightfully keep the goods or money stolen, even though he pays the penalty imposed by law. 

9. Whether or not an act can be considered a crime depends upon the criminal laws of the particular state. 

10. Murder is a major felony, and is always punishable by death or imprisonment.

TORTS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Conversion. The wrongful appropriation of the goods of another. 

Deceit. Underhanded trickery; fraud.

Encroach. To enter into the rights of another; advance beyond rightful limits; intrude. 

Libel. A wrongfully published statement intended to expose another to contempt or ridicule, to his detriment. 

Slander. A false oral statement uttered with intent to injure the reputation of another.

Trespass. To wrongfully enter upon the property of another; to injure or offend another.

Unscrupulous. Devoid of principle; without moral integrity. 

What is a tort?

Tort is a French word which means the same as our word wrong. 

Any person who illegally encroaches upon the rights or security of another person is guilty of committing a tort. A tort may be further defined as a violation of any civic duty or obligation fixed by law that is not covered by a contract obligation. Contract obligations are treated later. Liability for torts arises from violation of the duty imposed by law, and not from violation of an agreement as in contracts. In a case of tort, the injured party brings suit, and the redress, if any, granted by the court is in the form of money damages. 

Common examples of tort.

The most common examples of tort are assault and battery, libel, negligence, slander, trespass, or any other act which illegally interferes with personal safety or security, such as deceit, and influencing another to break his contract, etc. 25

The same act may be both a tort and a crime. Thus assault and battery is a crime, because it disturbs the peace and security of people in general, and is punishable by fine or imprisonment. It is also a tort, because it is the unjustifiable infliction of actual and intended violence upon a person, and he may sue for damages in a civil action.

Assault and battery. Actually harming another person physically is considered battery, and threatening to harm another physically, provided the one making the threat has the apparent ability or power to carry out the threat, is considered an assault. 

The assault and the battery, which amount to an injury, are usually committed together, and for this reason such an offense is called assault and battery.

Libel. Any person who makes in writing and discloses false statements concerning another person or who prints and circulates concerning a person false reports which damage his reputation has committed a libel. All damaging statements in any written form are classed as libels, and the injured person may recover damages unless the defendant in the case proves that they are true. In case a newpaper prints false statements concerning a person, the author of the statement and the publisher of the paper are both liable.

Negligence. The tort of negligence results when a person is injured or his property damaged as the result of the carelessness of another person. The injured person may recover in a civil action the damages he has suffered.

The tort is committed in many ways. Negligent driving of automobiles is the most common example, and the annual loss of life and property because of this form of negligence is a most serious menace to society. Other examples are negligent handling of explosives, negligent construction, negligent operation of elevators or other machinery, and, in general, any careless act through which another is injured. When the act is intended to harm others, or is utterly reckless and heedless, and the injury results in death, the negligence may be a crime.

Slander. The tort of slander consists in uttering words injurious to the reputation of another. The distinction between

TORTS 

27 libel and slander is that libel results from written or printed statements or from pictures suggesting scandal or corruption detrimental to a person's reputation, while slander results from false statements made orally. It is easier to prove a case of libel because the evidence is in writing, and the exact language complained of may be submitted to the court and jury. In slander it is sometimes difficult to prove that the injurious statements were made.

Trespass. The tort of trespass results when one person unlawfully traverses the property of another or encroaches upon the rights and liberties of another in the use of his property, in such a way as to cause injury. Anyone, other than an officer of the law in the performance of his duty, who enters upon the property of another is guilty of trespass. In such cases, even though little or no damage results, the courts will usually impose a nominal sum as damages, thus establishing a precedent through which the rights of the individual are preserved. 

In some states a person who enters or passes over the real property (land) belonging to another is not guilty of trespass unless the property is "posted." This means that there must be notices posted on the property in full view: "No trespassing under penalty of the law." Then anyone who disregards such a notice may be prosecuted.

Deceit. The tort of deceit results where one person by trickery or false statements influences another person to perform some act to his injury. A sharper may represent a brick covered with gilt to be a bar of solid gold, or a cotton garment to be all wool. Such false statements, if made with intent to deceive or injure another, are fraudulent acts and are classified as torts. 

Influencing another to break his contract. Anyone who knowingly causes another party to break his contract is guilty of a tort for which he lays himself liable for damages. Such a case would result where one party entered into a contract to work for another party for a definite time at a certain salary, and a third party, with full knowledge of all the facts, offered the first party a larger salary, thus inducing him to break his contract. The third party is liable to the employer for damages.

Wrongful conversion of property. A person who wrongfully appropriates the goods of another and converts them to his own use is guilty of a tort, and the one whose property has been misappropriated has a right of action to recover the property and collect damages, one or both. Such conversion is also the crime of larceny or embezzlement.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A tort arises from the violation of a duty, and not from the violation of an agreement. 

2. Any act which interferes with a person's safety or security is a tort. 

3. A single act may amount to both a tort and a crime. 

4. True statements, even though injurious to the party about whom they are made, do not amount to slander or libel. 

5. Injury or death inflicted through reckless and wanton disregard of the safety of others is criminal negligence and punishable accordingly. 

6. Any act whereby one party traverses the property of another or encroaches upon the rights or liberties of another is an act of trespass. 

7. Fraudulent acts to deceive or injure another are classed as torts. 

8. Published pictures may give rise to the right of tort action of libel.

PROPERTY TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Devise. To give by means of a will. 

Joint. A kind of ownership in property when two or more persons have interests or shares.

Police Power. The power of the state to regulate private conduct or the use of private property for the benefit of the public. 

Several. A kind of ownership in property when only one person has an interest. 

What is property?

In general, property means things owned. It is something of value, and it may be in the form of a tangible asset such as furniture, buildings, land, or any articles of value capable of ownership; or, it may be in the form of an intangible right, such as a right to possess, use, enjoy, or dispose of. All kinds of property, both tangible and intangible, fall into two classes called real and personal.

Real property. Land and everything that belongs with the land, such as trees, fences, buildings, and all things which are permanently affixed to the land or are a part and parcel of the land are classed as real estate or real property. 

Personal property. All forms of movable property, such as furniture, books, clothing, portable machinery, stocks, bonds, livestock, cultivated crops, and all personal effects of any kind are classed as personal property. Leases of land, other contracts, and certain rights which may be enjoyed and owned or controlled by someone are classed as personal property.

Under certain conditions property may be classed as real property, and under different conditions the same property may be classed as personal property. For example, stones on the land 30

PROPERTY 

31 would be considered a part and parcel of the land, but when they are gathered and put in a pile for some purpose they might be classed as personal property. Likewise, trees while standing would be classed as real property, but if these same trees were cut down, they would become personal property just as soon as they were severed from the stump, and in any form thereafter, the classification would be personal property, unless in some form such as lumber or fittings they became permanently attached to the real property. Machinery while loose and portable may be considered as personal property, but should it be attached as a permanent fixture to the building in which it is used, it becomes real property. 

We may say, therefore, that real property includes the land and everything that goes with the land as part and parcel thereof, and personal property includes every kind of movable property; that is, such articles as are intended to be moved. 

What is meant by ownership of property?

Ownership of property means in general the right to use and enjoy it to the exclusion of everyone else. A person may have an interest in property or own property which he does not actually possess; that is, ownership of property does not necessarily mean possession of the property. The owner of a store building may lease it for a term of years to another party; in this case the lessee has possession of the building and the owner is bound to respect his rights. 

Two kinds of ownership.

The two kinds of ownership are several and joint. When one person owns the property outright, his ownership is several. When two or more persons together own the property, the ownership is joint. Their ownership may be a joint tenancy or a tenancy in common. In a joint tenancy, if the one owner dies, his interest in the property passes to the surviving owner or owners. In a tenancy in common, if one owner dies, his interest passes to his heirs. If there is more than one heir, they may agree among themselves on a division of the property, or they may ask the court to make an equitable division of the property.

On what does the value of property depend?

The value of any kind of property depends upon the demand for it, which is influenced by the desirability and usefulness of the property. The fact that property is useful and there is a demand for it is the reason why we must have well-defined rules and laws for the protection of ownership in property. There are many laws which have for their purpose the regulation of property rights, and the transfer and ownership of property, as a study of contract law will reveal. 1 

What limitations are imposed on rights of owners?

While the owner of property is said to have exclusive rights as to possession and use, there are certain limitations imposed upon him by law. 

1. No owner has a right to use his property in such a way as to injure others. In using his property, he is bound to respect the rights of others. 

2. Every owner of property must comply with the orders of the court with respect to his property, and his property may be taken by due process of law to pay his lawful debts. 

3. Property is subject to taxation, and taxes properly levied are a lien on the property. If they are not paid, the owner of the property may be forced to give up his right of ownership. 

4. Each state has the right to take possession and control of private property under certain extreme conditions, such as in the case of uprisings and riots. This is one illustration of the "police power" of the state. 

5. The United States, each state, and each political subdivision, such as counties, cities, etc., has the "right of eminent domain," which means the right to take private property for public purposes by paying the owner a just compensation for his property.

Thus while the owner of property enjoys certain rights and privileges, he at the same time is subject to many political, social, and economic regulations. For this reason most of our legal

PROPERTY 

333 difficulties result from disagreements regarding property rights, or from a misunderstanding of the rules and laws governing these rights.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The value of property depends upon its actual or potential use or the purpose it serves. 

2. All forms or kinds of property belong in one of two general classes, real and personal. 

3. Some kinds of property are convertible from one class to the other. 

4. Ownership implies exclusive right of possession or control, subject to governmental authority. 

5. Ownership of property may be vested in an individual, a group of two or more individuals, an organization, or a political unit. 

6. Ownership of property may be acquired by gift, grant, purchase, devise, or inheritance. 

7. Ownership of property is several when one person is the absolute owner, and joint or in common when two or more persons are owners. 

8. Ownership of property is subject to taxation, police power of the state, right of eminent domain, personal debts, and the legal rights of others.

THE ELEMENTS OF CONTRACTS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Agreement. The consent of both parties to a contract; the meeting of their minds.

Fundamental Elements. The necessary parts of a legally enforceable contract.

Implied. Something in a contract not fully stated, but understood from the nature of the agreement, or from the words, acts, or circumstances of the parties.

Offeree. The party to a contract to whom the offer is made. 

Offeror. The party to a contract who makes the offer. 

Promisee. The one to whom the promise is made. 

Promisor. The one who makes the promise. 

Tangible. Real; actually existing. 

What are the fundamental elements of a contract? 

Example 1. Green offered to sell a used Buick automobile to Mapes for $300, cash payable on delivery of the car. Mapes accepted the offer, saying: "All right. I will take the car."

This is a contract between Green and Mapes whereby, a used automobile is sold by Green to Mapes for $300. It resulted from an offer on the part of Green and its acceptance on the part of Mapes. 

In this case Mapes was in the market to buy a used automobile and Green's offer of his car for $300 induced Mapes to buy it at that price.

In this contract there are two parties, the offeror and the offeree; the agreement resulting from the offer on the part of one party and its acceptance on the part of the other party; the subject matter or the thing contracted about, the automobile; and the consideration, which is the promise to pay $300 for the automobile. The con- 35

sideration for the promise to sell is the promise to pay; therefore, there are two promises, each of which is the consideration for the other. 

This contract might have resulted from an offer on the part of Mapes to pay Green $300 for his car. If Green desired to sell his car, and if he felt that $300 was a good price, he would accept Mapes's offer, and a contract would result in the same way as it did in Example 1.

In every enforceable contract, therefore, there must be four elements, commonly referred to as the fundamental or necessary elements of a contract. They are: 

1. The two parties, the offeror and the offeree; 

2. The agreement, the offer and the acceptance thereof; 

3. The subject matter, the thing contracted about; 

4. The consideration, the thing given or promised by each party. Consideration may be any tangible or intangible benefit to the promisor or detriment to the promisee.

The term consideration is popularly used as meaning the price to be paid or other inducement to a sale of goods. This is not the technical legal meaning that is more fully explained under "Consideration," page 96.

No contract is complete and binding upon the parties thereto if any one of these elements is lacking. The legal requirements of the fundamental elements are discussed later. 

In some contracts the price does not have to be mentioned specifically. It may be implied from the terms of the contract that the price will be the usual charge or price, or what the thing contracted about is reasonably worth. 

A man may order a ton of coal from a dealer; if no price is mentioned, it will be understood that the dealer will charge the regular price.

Example 2. Nelson employed Martin to work as a truck driver during the absence of his regular driver. No mention was made of wages. From the nature of this contract it would be understood that Nelson would pay Martin the prevailing wage for this kind of work. 

Every business transaction is a contract in some form. 

Every business transaction which results from an offer on the part of one party and its acceptance on the part of another party,

THE ELEMENTS OF CONTRACTS 

37 regardless of how small the transaction may be, amounts to a contract and is subject to all the rules and laws governing contracts. The purchase of a daily paper at a newsstand; the purchase of any article in a store; the calling of a Western Union messenger; telephoning for a taxicab; stepping into a trolley car or bus and paying the fare; putting an automobile into a repair shop to be repaired; leaving one's shoes at a shoemaker's to be half-soled; or calling a doctor; all are contracts and all are in the same category as a contract to buy a locomotive for $60,000, except that buying a locomotive would include detailed specifications and agreements regarding payments and time of delivery, all of which would be in writing and signed by the contracting parties. 

A contract defined.

A contract is an agreement between competent parties, based upon legal consideration, to do or not to do some particular thing which is possible to be done and which is not prohibited by law. 

While a contract is an agreement, there are many agreements which are not contracts, because one or more of the necessary elements is lacking.

Example 3. Mr. Vincent agreed to meet Mr. Holden at the 9 o'clock train and take him to a meeting of the directors of the Dime Savings Bank. 

Mr. Vincent failed to meet the train and Mr. Holden did not reach the bank in time for the directors' meeting.

This was an agreement between Mr. Vincent and Mr. Holden, but it was not a contract. As Mr. Holden did not agree to pay anything to Mr. Vincent for his services, there was no consideration for Mr. Vincent's promise and he is not bound in a contract. 

His responsibility in this agreement is what would be termed a social obligation. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A contract is an enforceable agreement between two parties. 

2. An agreement is enforceable only when it contains all the necessary elements of a contract. 

3. All the essential elements need not be expressly stated if they are necessarily implied from the terms of the contract.

4. A contract results from an offer by one party and its unqualified acceptance by another party. 

5. A party who assents to a contract is bound by all the conditions contained therein. 

6. Each party to an enforceable contract becomes obligated to perform his part according to the terms of the agreement; failing to perform, he renders himself liable for damages suffered by the other party. 

7. As a general rule, if a contract is not enforceable against one of the parties, the other party thereto is released, the exception being in the case of a contract between an adult and an incompetent party. 

8. An agreement amounting to a contract results from mutual assent of the parties thereto. It may be oral, in writing, or indicated by action. 

9. Entering into a contract imposes an obligation on each party thereto, and every phase of the contract should be carefully considered before the agreement is finally reached.

INSTRUCTIONS FOR MAKING CASE DECISIONS 

Example: Hays made an oral agreement with Bates to act as superintendent on Bates's farm for two years at a salary of $1,200 per year, payable monthly. Hays worked and was paid for six months. Bates then discharged Hays without giving any reason. Has Hays a cause of action against Bates for damages? Has Bates any defense?

In reaching a decision in this and other cases proceed as follows: 

1. State the essential and operative facts of the case. 

2. State the principles of law that apply to the case. 

3. Decide the effect of each principle applicable to the facts and state the result. 

Apply this method to the example as follows: 

1. The essential and operative facts: 

a. An oral agreement was made. b. The agreement was to be performed for two years. c. Hays performed his part of the contract as long as he was permitted to do so. d. Bates committed a breach of contract.

There are other facts in the case, e.g., that Hays was to act as superintendent and that he worked for six months; but he might have worked in some other capacity and for a longer or shorter time without changing the principles to be applied or the result. 

2. The principles of law that apply: a. A party to a contract who is not in default has a cause of action for damages against the other party who has broken the contract, unless there is a legal excuse for the breach. b. A contract which cannot be performed within one year from the time it was made is required by the Statute of Frauds to be in writing. c. A contract which the Statute of Frauds requires evidenced by writing may be enforced unless the defendant asserts the statute as a defense. 

3. Applying these principles to the facts we conclude:

Hays has a cause of action under (a) because he was not in default and Bates had broken the contract. We must now determine whether 

Bates had a legal excuse. The agreement comes within (b), so it must be in writing. Under (c) Hays may enforce the contract, unless Bates asserts the statute as a defense, and in any event Hays has a cause of action and may sue for damages. We are now prepared to answer the two questions. Has Hays a cause of action? Yes. Has Bates a defense? Yes.

Notice carefully the difference between a statement of fact, a statement of a principle, and a statement of legal result. A fact is a specific circumstance in the particular case. A principle is a general rule applying to all cases on which it operates. A legal result is determined by the application of principles to facts. In our example: That an oral agreement for two years was made, is a fact; that an oral agreement not to be performed within one year is unenforceable, is a principle; the result is that 

Hays cannot recover if Bates asserts the Statute of Frauds as a defense, because the principle has that effect on the fact. 

A principle of business law is a rule of action which determines the legal rights of the parties to a business transaction. All principles do not apply to every case. A particular situation may call into operation one or more principles, but the principles which do apply are controlling. The principles to be applied are those which are established in the place where the transaction occurred. The principles of business law are substantially the same throughout the United States, but there are some local variations resulting from statute, judicial decisions, or even from local custom, and in all cases the local law controls, even though it is different from the generally accepted rule. 

1. State the essential facts in the case. 

2. State the principle of law that applies to the case. 

3. Give your decision according to the rights of the parties. 

1. Walter Howard entered into a contract with George White, whereby 

White is to paint Howard's house for $250. Are all the necessary elements contained in this contract? Explain. 

2. David Howe called a doctor to attend his child who was very ill. Is there a contract between Mr. Howe and the doctor? What is implied? 

3. Mr. Lamson offered a dealer in used cars $300 for a certain used car. 

The dealer replied, "I will think about it." Does this proposition on the part of Mr. Lamson obligate either party? Is either party bound by any form of a contract? Explain. 

4. William Mapes agreed to take a friend of his with him on a trip.

They were to meet at a particular place to start on the trip. The friend got ready and appeared at the place of meeting agreed upon. Mapes did not appear. The friend, after waiting some time, hired a car and made the trip himself. Was there a contract between Mapes and his friend? Was 

Mapes obligated in any way?

COMMENTS 

In analyzing a contract to see if it meets all the legal requirements necessary to make it enforceable, the first things to check are the essential or fundamental elements. It is not reasonable to assume that any person would fail to understand how necessary these elements are in a contract, but there are so many qualifying conditions that may affect any one or all of the elements, that the subject of contracts as a whole requires considerable study.

For one reason or another the parties to a contract may not be qualified; the agreement may fail because of some misunderstanding affecting the reality of consent; the subject matter for some reason may fail; or the consideration may not be sufficient. 

Then again, contract agreements are not only subject to certain laws which regulate the making of them, but they are also subject in certain cases to established practices which cannot be ignored at will. For example, you may purchase an article from a merchant, pay for it, and take it with you. To all intent and purpose, this is a completed contract; but, if the merchant makes a practice of exchanging articles purchased in his store, or of refunding the purchase price when an article is returned, he can make no exceptions in your case unless he does so at the time the sale is made, and with your consent.

Contracts are, therefore, subject not only to legal regulations, but also to established practices and methods of dealing.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Affirm. To sanction or approve.

Deferred. Postponed; put off until a later date. 

Disaffirm. To disapprove; to refuse to perform. 

Infant. A person who has not reached the age when he may be legally bound in a contract.

Necessaries. Those things needed by a human being, such as food, clothing, and shelter, that he may properly exist. 

Option. The right to choose or elect; a chance to decide. 

Ratify. To approve; to make valid. 

Repudiate. To refuse to comply with; to renounce.

Valid. Good in every respect; lawful and binding. 

Void. Worthless; not enforceable; having no value. 

Voidable. Can be avoided; does not have to be fulfilled. 

Who are the parties to a contract?

In every contract there are at least two parties, and after they have been named (individual or company names) in a written contract they are commonly referred to as party of the first part and party of the second part.

The party of the first part is the one who makes the offer, and the party of the second part is the one to whom the offer is made, or the one who accepts the offer as made. It is not uncommon in practice for several persons to have an interest in a particular contract and to be named therein as parties to the agreement. An individual cannot contract with himself; that is, one person cannot take the place of both parties to a contract. There are two or more parties to a contract, and there may be two persons or several persons identified therewith. That is, any one of the parties to a 1 42

contract may be composed of several persons; for example, Jackson, Harper, and Cooper may enter into a contract with King, or with King, Green, and Holcomb.

There are no restrictions as to the number of persons to a contract. One company or corporation may contract with another company or corporation. Companies act through their officers and agents in all business transactions resulting in contracts. 

May all persons enter into a contract?

There are legal regulations which have to do in general with the parties to a contract.

Competent parties. It is an accepted principle of law that every person has a right to contract, unless for some mental or legal reason he is disqualified from entering into a binding contract. 

Incompetent parties. Insane persons, drunkards, and spendthrifts are incompetent because they lack mentality. Infants and aliens are incompetent because of public policy. 

The laws of the different states vary considerably regarding capacity to contract. The following questions should be answered for each state: (Your state) a. When is a person an infant, and when does he legally become an adult? b. When may a person be considered legally insane? c. What are the legal rights of married women as to contracts? 

Who is an infant?

An infant is a person under twenty-one years of age. A person becomes legally of age on the day preceding his twenty-first birthday. The rule of the Common Law has been changed by statute in some states. The laws of your state on the subject should be examined.

Rules governing infants' contracts. Contracts entered into by infants are voidable at the option of the infant. 

Example 1. Harry Marvin, an infant eighteen years of age, entered into a contract with a manufacturer of airplanes whereby Marvin agreed to purchase an airplane. He paid $50 at the time of signing the contract and agreed to pay the balance of $700 as soon as the plane was delivered within sixty days.

Marvin had planned to draw $700 from his savings account and pay for the airplane; he found, however, when he presented his passbook at the bank with his signed voucher (check) for $700, that the bank would not permit him to withdraw the money without his parents' consent. His parents were opposed to his purchase of the airplane, and they would not assent to his withdrawing the $700; as a result, Marvin could not fulfill his contract with the airplane manufacturer. 

Marvin legally cannot be required to fulfill this contract or to pay any damages for (breach of contract) not fulfilling his part; and he can demand that the manufacturer return to him the $50 paid at the time of signing the contract. 

A contract is either valid, void, or voidable.

A valid contract is one that contains all the necessary elements and is enforceable. A valid contract must be fulfilled or, if one of the parties thereto fails to perform his part of the contract, he is liable to the other party, who may take court action against him for breach of contract, and the court may require him to fulfill the contract or pay damages.

A void contract is one that cannot be enforced against either party. It is for some reason absolutely worthless; its lack of validity is due to legal reasons which will be explained later. 

A voidable contract is one that may not be enforced against one of the parties. That is, one of the parties may avoid fulfilling the contract, or if he does fulfill the contract he may have the contract set aside and force the other party to return whatever he received under the contract. a. An infant's contract is voidable at the option of the infant. 

An apparent exception to this rule is where the infant has obligated himself in the purchases of necessaries such as food, clothing, shelter, medical attention, and education for his needs. The infant will have to pay a reasonable price for articles purchased by him which can be properly classed as necessaries. b. An adult's contract with an infant is binding upon the adult; that is, if the adult is legally competent to contract. c. An infant who seeks to avoid a contract and recover what he

has paid must return to the other party anything he has received or its value; but an infant who is sued on a contract may use his infancy as a defense even though he cannot return the benefits received.

Example 2. Genter, an adult, sold and delivered a set of books to Winn, an infant. Winn promised to pay $20 for the books. The books were destroyed by a fire before the $20 was paid, and Genter attempted to collect it from Winn.

Winn has a right to avoid this contract. When an attempt is made by the adult party to require an infant to fulfill his contract, the infant may repudiate the contract, returning any benefits that he received under the contract; but if he no longer has the benefits he received (goods or money), he may still repudiate the contract. 

If, however, the infant takes action to repudiate his contract and recover what he has parted with, he must return the benefits received. The principle of law is expressed: "Infancy is a shield, not a sword," and an accepted maxim of law that applies in the case of infants as in the case of adults is: "He who seeks equity must do equity." 

What are the rights of an infant who, at the time he entered into a contract with an adult, stated that he was past 21 years of age? 

Example 3. An infant nineteen years of age purchased a diamond ring from a jeweler for $150. At the time he purchased the ring he stated he was past twenty-one years old and the jeweler relied on his statement. 

A year later, the infant took the ring back to the jeweler, claimed he was but nineteen years old when he bought it, and demanded the $150 paid. 

Regardless of what the infant stated, the facts in the case prevail; the infant may require the jeweler to take the ring back, and the jeweler must refund to the infant the $150 he paid. In some cases an infant can be held liable in damages for fraud. In addition to this, the infant may be held for fraud and prosecuted under the criminal code of the state where he lives. 

Precautions. The safe course for an adult to pursue when entering into a contract with an infant is to have the infant's parent or guardian guarantee the contract and thereby assume responsibility for the infant's fulfilling his part of the contract; if he fails, the parent or the guardian becomes liable on his guaranty.

Example 4. A young man eighteen years old bought a fur coat for $150 on credit from a local merchant. Before the merchant would sell the coat to the young man, whom he knew well and whose parents were in comfortable circumstances, he asked the young man for a letter from his father addressed to the merchant, authorizing the purchase of the coat. This letter, which the father wrote to the merchant, committed him to the contract, and he is fully responsible for seeing that the merchant is paid for the coat.

Where an infant contracts for necessaries, he can be held to pay only a reasonable price for them.

Example 5. An infant bought an overcoat which he needed, for which he agreed to pay $45. The merchant regularly sold the same coat for $30, which was its reasonable value. 

The infant can be made to pay for the overcoat, but he is not liable for the price he has agreed to pay. He is liable for only $30, the reasonable value of the coat. 

Can an infant be held on a contract for borrowed money which he used to buy necessaries?

Example 6. An infant borrowed $40 from an uncle of his and used the money to buy food and clothes which he needed. 

The fact that the infant used the money to buy necessaries obligates him on the agreement he made with his uncle for the loan of the $40. Had he used the money for some other purpose, he could have avoided his agreement. 

What must an infant do on becoming of age if he wishes to be bound in an executory contract he made during infancy? 

Example 7. An infant twenty years and eleven months old contracted to buy a motorcycle from a dealer for $250, and to accept delivery and pay for it within ninety days. He failed to fulfill his agreement, and at the end of ninety days the dealer demanded that he take the motorcycle and pay for it. This is an executory contract, in that it has not been completed. 

The rule of law is very definite, that an infant must ratify his unperformed contract when he becomes legally of age, or within a reasonable time thereafter; otherwise, it is void. Keeping silent is not sufficient. There must be an act of ratification. This rule applies to executory contracts, but if the contract is executed, the infant must disaffirm; otherwise, he is bound.

What must an infant do if he wishes to avoid or disaffirm a contract he has already performed, and when must he disaffirm? 

Example 8. An infant, who was twenty years old on April 4, purchased on June 15 following his birthday a used automobile from a dealer for $300. 

On June 25, a little more than a year after the infant had purchased the car, he returned it and demanded of the dealer the $300 paid. 

The infant could disaffirm this contract only on or before April 4, his twenty-first birthday, or within a reasonable time thereafter, and then only by allowing the dealer to retain from the $300 an amount sufficient to reimburse him for the depreciation in the value of the car. Nearly three months after his majority is not a reasonable time, and he is bound by the contract. The dealer is not legally bound to take the car back or to return the $300, or any part of it, paid for the car by the infant. 

Example 9. An infant, twenty years and six months old, bought a radio for $75, on the deferred payment plan. He paid $5 down and agreed to pay $5 on the first of each month until the full amount was paid. He made eight payments and when the ninth payment became due, he sought to return the radio and repudiate his contract. 

The infant is bound by this contract. He continued to perform under the contract for two months after he became of age, and this amounted to an affirmance of the contract. 

An infant cannot disaffirm a part of the contract and affirm the rest. 

Example 10. An infant purchased a used boat and outboard motor from a dealer. He paid $200 for the outfit complete. The infant was not pleased with the motor. It was not speedy enough to suit him, and he returned it to the dealer and demanded of him that he return $125 of the $200 paid for the outfit.

The dealer cannot be made to take the motor back. The infant is not within his legal rights in disaffirming a part of his contract. He can disaffirm the whole contract during his infancy or within a reasonable time after his majority, and the dealer will have to take back the boat and the motor and return to the infant the $200 he paid for the outfit. The dealer is within his rights in claiming pay for the use or the depreciation of the articles.

The infant is responsible for his own malicious acts and torts. 

Example 11. An infant who was driving his own car, had a collision with another car, which resulted in serious injury to the driver of the other car. In this case the law does not protect the infant. He is personally liable and will have to suffer whatever penalty is imposed by the court. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Infants' contracts are voidable at the option of the infant. 

2. An infant is responsible to the extent of the reasonable value of the necessaries contracted for, which are suitable to the infant's station in life. 

3. The fact that an infant represented himself to be of age (twentyone years old) does not affect his right to avoid his contract. 

4. An infant has a right to contract, and he is protected by the law in that if he makes a poor contract he can get out of it; he can avoid it, but he must give back whatever he has in his possession that he received under the contract. 

5. An adult who contracts with an infant is bound on his contract, and he should protect himself in his dealings with an infant by requiring the sanction or authorization of the parent or guardian of the infant for all voidable contracts to which he is a party. 

6. An executory contract must be positively ratified by an infant at his majority, or it is avoided. 

7. An executed contract must be positively disaffirmed by an infant at his majority, or it is ratified. 

8. An infant cannot legally affirm a part of a contract and disaffirm the rest. 

9. An infant can avoid a contract any time during infancy, but he can ratify only after becoming of age.
