1. Arthur Moore, an infant eighteen years old, purchased a bicycle for $40 from a local dealer. After keeping the bicycle for four months, he decided it was too small for him, so he returned it to the dealer and demanded

the $40 he paid for it. The dealer refused to take the bicycle back or to refund the $40. What are the rights of the parties? 

2. An infant, nineteen years old, ordered an expensive rifle from a local dealer and paid a deposit of $10. The dealer placed a special order for the rifle, but when it arrived the infant refused to take it, and he demanded the return of the $10. What are the dealer's rights? 

3. An infant sold his motorboat to an adult for $80. The infant spent the $80 and then he demanded that the adult give back the motorboat. 

Is the adult legally bound to comply with the infant's demands? 

4. An infant, who was nineteen years old at the time, stated to the merchant from whom she bought a fur coat for $200, by paying $20 down and agreeing to pay $15 a month for twelve months, that she was past twentyone years of age. The infant made one $15 payment, and then nothing happened for four months, when the merchant demanded a settlement. Has the infant a right to avoid this contract? 

5. An infant called at a local music store and asked the proprietor to sell him a saxophone on the deferred payment plan (paying in installments). 

The infant agreed to pay $10 down and $5 per month for twelve months. 

The proprietor explained the proposal to the infant's father, who approved of the transaction. Is the father bound in any way by this contract? 

6. An infant, who was known to be somewhat of a spendthrift, bought a suit of clothes of a local merchant, who charged the infant $90 for a suit he had never sold before for more than $45. The infant was able to get conclusive proof of the facts as stated here. What are the infant's rights? 

7. An infant contracted for the loan of $25 with which he bought food and a few clothes. Can he avoid this contract? 

8. An infant, twenty years old, purchased a radio for $160. He paid $10 and agreed to pay $10 on the first of each month for fifteen months. Two months after making the last payment he returned his radio to the dealer, demanding that he refund the amount paid, on the ground that it was purchased during infancy. Must the dealer comply with the infant's demands?

COMMENTS Many infants of necessity, by reason of their connections and business activities, enter into contract relations with adults; and in the case of other infants it is highly desirable at times for them to be allowed contract rights and privileges, else they may at times suffer serious handicaps and possible hardships.

Before entering into a contract with an adult, an infant should think the whole transaction through, get advice from someone who is able to direct him, and proceed accordingly. When once he has entered into a reasonable contract in good faith, he should fulfill his part of the contract if it is possible for him to do so.

CONTINUED TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Decree. To decide what is to be done or not to be done; an order issued by a court.

Deranged. Mentally unbalanced; in a state of mental incompetency. 

Insanity. A mental condition which renders a person incapable of acting as a normal person. 

Lawfully Authorized. Given the right legally to act.

Negotiate. To deal with; to bring about through a proposition. 

Prodigal. A wayward and irresponsible person. 

Recourse. A source of help; a thing resorted to. 

Spendthrift. One who spends his money in a reckless manner. 

Status. The existing state or condition of some person or thing. 

When is a person insane?

It may be said that a person is insane when he acts strangely, when he is suffering from an apparent mental disorder which affects his judgment and his conduct, and it may be true that this person is mentally deranged to such an extent that he is incompetent to contract. He is not legally insane, however, until he has been examined and decreed insane by an authorized authority, and a guardian has been appointed to manage his property. After he has been lawfully decreed insane, he is without capacity to enter into a contract. Should he, however, enter into contracts, some of his contracts might be enforceable and valid, depending upon the circumstances, and he might avoid other contracts. 

Can a person mentally deranged enter into a binding contract? 

Example 12. Herman Stacy, who appeared sane but was mentally unbalanced, ordered an easy chair costing $35 from a local furniture dealer. 51

The chair was delivered to Mr. Stacy's home and accepted. At the end of the month a bill for the chair was sent to Mr. Stacy. 

This was a legitimate business transaction, and the dealer has a right to collect the $35 from Mr. Stacy for the reason that he had not been decreed insane by legal authority, and he was able to go about and transact business the same as a normal person. 

The contracts of an insane person are voidable, and after he has been judicially declared insane, his contracts are void. The exception is that (1) when the insanity was unknown and not apparent to the other party, (2) the contract was fair, and (3) the status quo ante cannot be restored (restored to the same position the parties were in before entering into the contract), then the parties may recover on the contract. However, an insane person is liable for necessaries the same as an infant. 

When a person avoids a contract on the grounds of insanity, he must return whatever he received under the contract to the other party. The same rules apply here that apply in the case of an infant who avoids his contract. 

Example 13. Bossert, who had been declared insane, ordered a valuable set of books through a sales representative of the publishers. Bossert signed the order for the books and paid $10 down at the time. 

This contract is void. An insane person who has been legally decreed insane has no legal right to contract. 

Any contract entered into with an idiot is void or voidable. 

An idiot is a simple-minded person who never had reasoning power. He was born mentally defective. A contract with an idiot is always voidable and in most cases it is absolutely void. 

A contract entered into while a person is intoxicated is voidable. 

Example 14. Sanders, while intoxicated, signed up with an automobile salesman for the purchase of a high-priced car and paid a deposit of $200. 

When he received notice that the car was ready for delivery, he did not know what it was all about. 

If Sanders can show he was intoxicated to that extent, he can avoid the contract, and demand that any money he paid on the contract be returned to him.

A prodigal or spendthrift may be denied the right to contract. 

Example 15. John Akins was a man of considerable means who was well known and highly esteemed in the community where he lived. He had a brother James who was such a spendthrift that he was rapidly squandering the large property interests left to him by his father. What could be done about it?

John, or any of his interested kin (relatives), can engage a lawyer and through him petition the court to subject his brother James to an examination as a means of determining his fitness to manage his own business affairs. If it appears from the examination that James is unfit to manage his affairs, the court may appoint a competent person to administer his property. After this has been done, any contract made by James is void. 

Married women, as a rule, are permitted to contract. 

At common law, married women were not permitted to make contracts. Statute laws of the different states, although they vary considerably, have largely removed this common-law disability. 

Now a married woman who owns property in her own name may enter into contracts that have to do with her property interests, and she may conduct her own separate business. In most states she is permitted to enjoy the same contract rights an unmarried woman enjoys, except in some states she is not permitted to enter into a contract with her husband or to assume responsibility for the obligations of another party. The wife can bind her husband in a contract for necessaries purchased for her use or for use in their immediate family.

Are contracts between an alien and a citizen of this country enforceable?

In times of peace a contract entered into between a citizen of this country and a citizen of a foreign country is a good contract if it meets all the legal requirements. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A person who lawfully (according to law) has been decreed insane is disqualified from entering into a contract.

2. A person who has not been decreed insane may be in such a state of mind as to make it possible for him to avoid a contract he has entered into. 

3. A person who is so intoxicated as not to know what he is doing can avoid a contract agreed to while in that condition. 

4. In certain cases a contract with a person mentally deranged or intoxicated may be enforced. It must be a reasonable contract; the other party must be innocent of fraud or sharp practice; the insanity must be unknown and not apparent to the other party; and the status quo ante cannot be restored. 

5. An insane person is liable for necessaries which have been furnished him. 

6. When a trustee or guardian has been appointed to administer the business affairs of an insane person, he is denied the right to act for himself in making contracts. 

7. An insane person who is known to have “lucid intervals” (periods when he is in his right mind) can, during such intervals, enter into a binding contract. 

8. Contracts entered into by prodigals or spendthrifts are binding upon them until such time as they have been decreed incompetent and a trustee appointed to look after their interests. 

9. A husband can, by legal means, restrain his wife from obligating him in contracts other than those for necessaries. This he can do by advertising in a local paper of general circulation that, from this time henceforth, he will not be responsible for debts incurred by his wife. 

10. Convicts are denied the right to contract. 

11. An ex-convict has no contract rights until his citizenship is restored to him by the governor of the state where he served his sentence; then he is permitted to contract the same as a normal person. 

A convict who is pardoned is automatically restored to citizenship.

COMMENTS 

The competency and responsibility of the parties to a contract are of vital concern in their contractual relations. 

The laws that deal with the competency and incompetency of the parties to a contract are fairly well defined. Certain legal restrictions have been imposed on certain incompetent persons with relation to their ability to contract and for very good reasons, as a study of these legal rules will reveal.

When a contract is contemplated by one party, very naturally his first concern is the competency and responsibility of the other party. Each party for himself must consider and pass judgment on the competency and responsibility of the other party. It is important for anyone transacting business to know the law with relation to parties to a contract. This is particularly so where the law limits or removes entirely the liability under a contract of certain persons who are incompetent.

THE AGREEMENT TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Counteroffer. An offer made by the offeree instead of accepting the original offer. 

Express. To state fully. 

Forfeit. To give up; to lose.

Inscribe. To write or mark in some way. 

Mode. Way of doing; manner or form. 

Mutual. Affecting all parties alike. 

Remuneration. A payment; compensation. 

Requisite. Something required. 

Revoking. Refusing to fulfill; annulling or taking back.

Stipulation. Something stated or agreed upon. 

Verbally. By word of mouth; orally.

From what does the agreement in a contract result? 

Example 1. Kingsley, who was moving to a distant city, offered to sell his radio to Cross for $100. Cross accepted the offer, gave Kingsley a check for $100, and agreed to call the next day for the radio. 

This is an agreement. This agreement resulted from an offer made by Kingsley and its acceptance by Cross. The radio belongs to Cross; if anything happens to it, through no one's fault, Cross must stand the loss.

There can be no contract without an agreement, and there can be no agreement unless all the parties express by words or actions an intention to be bound in a contract by mutual assent. This agreement, which is so fundamental in a contract, is reached by the contracting parties in certain definite ways and in accordance with certain rules and laws which we now shall learn about. 57

1. THE OFFER 

How may an offer be communicated by the offeror to the offeree?

An offer must be communicated to the offeree (the person to whom the offer is made). It may be communicated (1) orally, directly or over the telephone; (2) in a written communication sent through the mail or by messenger, telegram, or radiogram; (3) it may be published; (4) an offer in the form of an act may be communicated by seeing the act. An offer is not communicated until it reaches the offeree.

An offer must be definite. 

Example 2. Haller, the owner of a cheese factory, wrote a letter to the 

John Davis Company in which he offered to sell them fall cream cheese in any quantity at 21¢ a pound (F.O.B. packed 24 pounds in a carton).

An acceptance of this offer by the Davis Company would not make a contract, because the quantity is indefinite. If Haller had offered 500 pounds instead of any quantity, the offer would be definite, and an acceptance would make a contract. 

If the Davis Company had replied to the indefinite offer, "We will take 500 pounds," no contract would result unless Haller accepted the Davis Company's proposition. 

When the offer is indefinite in any particular, an acceptance, in any form, will not result in a contract until the offeror agrees to it. 

Offers are made in different ways.

A merchant displays his wares with the selling price plainly marked upon each article. In this way he is making an offer to sell any article displayed at the marked price. The buyer will select any article of his choice, pay the price, and the contract is complete. 

A dentist opens an office and displays his sign. This amounts to an offer of his services to anyone who sees fit to engage them at the price he may charge. When someone engages his services, there is a contract. 

An auctioneer may start to sell a certain article by saying: "How much am I bid for this article? Who will make it $10?" Some interested listener will say, "$10," or by a nod of his head or a sign he will indicate that he is willing to pay $10 for the article.

THE AGREEMENT 

59 The auctioneer will announce: "I am offered $10; who will make it $11?" If there are no bids higher than the $10 bid, the auctioneer will declare the article sold to the party who bid $10, and there is a contract, resulting from the offer by the bidder and its acceptance by the auctioneer. Putting the article up for sale is not an offer to sell, but an invitation to those within hearing range to make an offer to buy.

Advertising an article for sale in a publication or circular letter is not an offer, and even though it might seem to be an offer, a contract would not result from some person's accepting it as an offer. It indicates on the part of the sponsor of the advertisement a desire to sell and is considered an invitation to others to buy. A contract would not result, however, until seller and buyer negotiate and reach an agreement.

When a reward is offered for the return of a lost article, and notice of this reward is published in a local paper, it amounts to an offer to pay a certain sum of money to the person who finds the article and returns it to the owner. The person who finds the article and returns it, with full knowledge of the offered reward and with the intention of accepting the offer, can demand the reward, and the person who offered the reward is bound in a contract.

The person who finds and returns to the owner a lost article for the return of which a reward is offered, is not entitled to the reward if he does not know it is offered. 

Example 3. Bowers owned a valuable dog which strayed away, and he advertised in a local paper that he would pay a reward of $50 for the safe return of the dog alive. A farmer, who found the dog, discovered by the tag on his collar that he belonged to Bowers and returned him to his owner, not knowing a reward had been offered. 

In this case, the farmer has no legal claim to the reward, and it is optional with Bowers whether or not he pays it. 

How may an offer be terminated?

An offer may be terminated by the offeree's accepting or rejecting it; or, the offeror may revoke or withdraw his offer.

Example 4. Wilson offered a set of encyclopedias to his friend Hodge for $50. Hodge rejected the offer. Later he attempted to accept the offer.

Hodge's rejection of the offer terminated it, and accepting it later would not bind Wilson in a contract unless in some way he showed that he was willing to be bound. 

When may an offer be withdrawn?

An offer may be withdrawn at any time before it has been accepted, but the withdrawal does not take effect until it reaches the offeree. After an offer has been accepted, it cannot be withdrawn. 

Example 5. Grant wrote a letter to Moore in which he offered him $200 for a cement mixer which Moore had for sale. In the letter Grant stated that his offer was good for ten days. Five days later Grant bought a good mixer for $175. He wrote Moore at once withdrawing his offer. In the meantime and before Grant's letter withdrawing the offer was received by Moore, he had mailed a letter to Grant accepting his offer. 

According to the principle of law, a contract exists between 

Grant and Moore. Moore's acceptance of Grant's offer is binding as soon as made, but Grant's withdrawal of his offer was not effective until it reached Moore. It is circumstances such as appear in this case that cause trouble between contracting parties. Recalling or taking back an offer amounts to revoking it. 

How may an offer lapse?

An offer may lapse by the expiration of the time set, or, if no time is set, of a reasonable time. Death or insanity of either party before the offer is accepted will cause it to terminate. Dissolution of a partnership or a corporation will cause their unaccepted offers to terminate.

Example 6. The Globe Insurance Company offered Meriam $3,000 a year to give a sales talk each Saturday morning to a group of the company's salesmen. Meriam intended to accept the offer, but before he could do so, he was taken ill and died. His death caused the offer to lapse. 

In this case, had the Globe Insurance Company set a time limit for accepting their offer and Meriam failed to accept within the time set, or had they dissolved and discontinued business before Meriam accepted their offer, it would have lapsed. 

Example 7. Hall offered to pay Martin $500 if he would repair, according to specifications, a certain house belonging to Hall. Martin accepted the offer, but Hall died before the work was completed. There was a con-

THE AGREEMENT 

61 tract between Hall and Martin, and Hall's estate is liable for the $500. 

Had Hall died before Martin accepted his offer, his offer would have died with him, and no contract would have resulted. 

Can an offer be so worded that silence on the part of the offeree may be considered an acceptance? 

Example 8. Howard received the following telegram (night letter): "I am selling Grade A eggs at thirty cents a dozen. If I do not hear from you by tomorrow night I shall ship you twenty crates, of thirty dozen each, at this price. Signed, C. L. Coons."

Howard did not reply, and he is not bound in a contract. It is a principle of law that a man cannot be forced to reply to a communication or be bound in a contract. However, previous courses of dealing and other circumstances may create a contract in such a case. Had this been a mode of dealing followed by Howard and 

Coons in the past, Howard's failure to reply would bind him in a contract.

Example 9. Everts was in the habit of sending extra milk to a milk factory once or twice each week. The factory had always used the milk and paid for it, but on one occasion they did not use the milk, and they refused to pay.

Everts has a good claim against the owners of the milk factory, and he can collect for his milk which they did not use. As they had been taking Everts's extra milk regularly, they should have notified him in advance if they could not use it. This previous mode of dealing with Everts obligated them to pay him. 

2. THE ACCEPTANCE OF AN OFFER 

How may the acceptance of an offer be communicated?

An acceptance must be communicated by the offeree; it may be communicated in any way, provided the acceptance is actually received by the offeror.

When an offer is made by mail or telegram, an acceptance sent in the same way the offer was sent or according to directions accompanying the offer, is a valid acceptance, even though delayed or lost in the mail. 

When an offer is accepted in any way other than the way the

offer was made or not according to directions accompanying the offer, the acceptance does not become effective until it reaches the offeror.

Example 10. Mede, a local distributor of a well-known make of electric refrigerator, offered verbally to sell a used refrigerator to Downs for $40. 

Mede made this offer to Downs in the course of a conversation with him (a sales talk).

The offer was made orally, and it should have been accepted orally then and there by Downs, in order that a contract might result. It is not always done this way, and very often a contract will finally result from continued negotiations. 

Other modes of accepting an oral offer that might be used. 

1. Downs might keep absolutely silent, take out his purse, and pass $40 to Mede. Mede takes the $40, and the deal is closed. 

There is a contract. 

2. Downs might by some act, such as a nod of the head, indicate his acceptance of the offer. 

3. Downs might keep silent but write out a check payable to 

Mede. Mede accepts the check and the contract is closed. 

4. An acceptance may be in the form of a promise or an act. 

Example 11. Gedny offered orally, in the presence of several listeners, $100 to anyone who would get some valuable papers in his office in a burning building near by. A young man who heard the offer rushed into the building in the presence of Gedny and rescued the papers. 

This young man by an act in the presence of the offeror accepted his offer, a contract resulted, and he is entitled to the $100. 

An offer may be made by a written communication (letter, telegram, or radiogram).

Example 12. Thayer wrote a letter to Judson in which he offered to sell 

1,000 sixteen-quart baskets of first-grade peaches at 60¢ a basket. Thayer agreed to pick and pack the peaches and deliver them F.O.B., Thayer's home town, consigned to Judson via any available transportation line he might suggest.

This is an offer by letter. It can be condensed and sent by telegraph (telegram, day letter, or night letter), or it can be sent

THE AGREEMENT 

63 by radiogram if facilities are available at the place from which the communication is sent. 

If Judson wishes to buy these peaches, he must accept Thayer's offer within a reasonable time. When an offer is made by letter, there is a contract as soon as the letter of acceptance is mailed, and usually twenty-four hours after receiving an offer by letter would be considered a reasonable time in which to accept it. 

Thayer's letter contained a definite offer to sell 1,000 baskets of peaches at 60 cents a basket. Had Judson offered to buy 500 baskets or had he agreed to pay only 55 cents a basket, there would be no contract until Judson's counterproposition reached Thayer and he agreed to it.

It is the practice in cases such as the one just described, where a quantity of some commodity is offered for sale by letter, for the offeror to send out a statement, usually indefinite as to quantity or price, or incomplete in some particular. He might state his offer in this way: "While they last, I am offering first-grade peaches in any quantity, at 60 cents a basket." By stating his offer in this indefinite way, it matters not how the acceptance is made, the offeror is not bound in a contract against his will. His letter is simply an invitation to buy, and it may bring an offer from someone which he will accept; then he is bound in a contract. Most statements of this kind, even though quite complete as to terms, are construed as mere advertisements, and not as offers. 

When does an acceptance become binding?

The general rule is that an acceptance becomes binding as soon as it is made or started on its way in a communication. This rule holds good even though the offeror does not know that his offer has been accepted. Such is the case where an offer made by mail has been accepted by mail. Where the offeror states how the acceptance is to be made, he assumes the risk of the acceptance not reaching him.

Example 13. Adams wrote a letter to Kline in which he offered to sell him 100,000 ft. of sheeting boards at $28 per M. board foot, F.O.B. 

Adams gave the following directions: "Wire me your acceptance within twenty-four hours after you receive this letter if you wish to buy this lumber at the price named."

BUSINESS LAW AND PROCEDURË 

Kline wired his acceptance as directed, but delivery of the telegram to Adams was delayed, and in the meantime he sold the lumber to another party. 

As this case stands, there is a contract between Adams and Kline. Kline has purchased the lumber, and he can demand of 

Adams that he deliver it as he agreed to or pay damages. It is likely that the telegraph company could be held responsible for the delayed telegram.

An acceptance cannot be qualified in any way and be effective. 

Example 14. Arnold offered his motorboat for sale for $200. Howard agreed to pay $200 for the boat if Arnold would have it painted. 

This is a conditional acceptance of Arnold's offer by Howard, and there is no contract. Before a contract could result, Arnold would have to agree to Howard's counterproposition. In such a case, the contract would consist of Howard's offer to buy the boat if Arnold would paint it, and Arnold's acceptance of the offer. 

How can an offer be kept open?

Example 15. Wilson offered to sell his gasoline and service station to 

Knapp for $1,800, on the following terms: One half cash and $75 per month for twelve months.

Knapp was anxious to buy the service station, but he wanted a little time in which to consider the offer, and he asked Wilson to hold it open for thirty days, which he promised to do. 

Wilson's promise to keep the offer open is not binding, as nothing was paid for it. Wilson is morally, but not legally, bound to keep the offer open, and it remains open for the stated time unless withdrawn.

In the preceding case, Knapp should have paid Wilson $100 or any amount for the thirty-day option, with the understanding that if he (Knapp) did not buy the service station, he would forfeit to Wilson the $100 deposit, but if he bought the station within the thirty days, the $100 would apply as a part of the cash payment. 

This explains one way of taking an option or of making a payment or a deposit to bind an agreement to keep an offer open for a certain length of time.

THE AGREEMENT 

65 Example 16. The Powers Realty Company paid $1,500 to the Johnson 

Holding Co. for an option, for six months, on 100 building lots priced at $300 per lot ($30,000).

This is a straight option for which $1,500 was paid, and in case the Powers Realty Co. purchases these lots within six months, the $1,500 paid for the option cannot be applied on the purchase price.

The Johnson Holding Co. by reason of accepting $1,500 for this option are bound in a contract not to sell these lots for six months, and to sell them at any time within the six months to the Powers Realty Co. at the price named. This contract was in writing. 

It must be understood that the option contract is entirely separate from any contract to buy the lots which may result from this transaction, and if it does result, it will be the main contract. 

Can a party who made part payment on a contract which he failed to complete recover the amount paid?

Example 17. Wade contracted in writing to buy a certain building lot from Edmond for $1,200 and paid $200 down at the time of signing the contract. Wade did not complete this contract.

Unless it was agreed in the contract that the $200 should be the amount of damages, or that the deposit should be forfeited in case Wade did not complete his agreement, Edmond would have a right to claim only the amount of damage he actually suffered, which might be more or less than the $200. If Edmond could not show that he had suffered damage as a result of Wade's failure to complete his contract, Wade could recover the whole $200. 

A person cannot perform a service for another person without his knowledge or consent and bind him in a contract. 

Example 18. A man, who was away from his home all summer, decided he would not have his yard cared for in his absence. A gardener, who had worked some for this man before, discovered that his yard needed attention, and he took it upon himself to care for it. When the owner returned, he discovered that someone had cared for his yard during his absence and that it was in fine condition. Very soon thereafter he received a bill from the gardener who had cared for the yard. There was no contract between the owner of this yard and the gardener; therefore, the gardener cannot collect his bill unless the owner sees fit to pay it. The principle of law as stated applies in this case.

Had the owner of the yard known what the gardener was doing and allowed him to continue, the latter could collect his bill. It would be implied that the owner had accepted the gardener's services, and he would have to pay a reasonable price for them. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The offer must be definite. 

2. The offer may be communicated by words or by acts. 

3. An offer is not effective until it reaches the offeree. 

4. An offer may contain any number of conditions. 

5. An acceptance must be communicated, but it does not have to reach the offeror in every case to be effective. 

6. The acceptance must be complete, unconditional, and in accordance with the exact terms of the offer. 

7. When the directions for accepting an offer are given by the offeror and they are followed by the offeree, the offeror assumes the risk of not receiving the acceptance. 

8. A qualified acceptance is not effective until it is agreed to by the offeror. 

9. An acceptance is binding as soon as made. Intention to accept is not effective. 

10. An offer may be withdrawn at any time before it has been accepted, but a withdrawal of offer is not effective until it reaches the offeree. 

11. The contracting parties may agree on how long the offer will remain open. This is binding only when something is paid or an option contract is made. 

12. The offeror may withdraw his offer at any time before it is accepted unless he receives some remuneration for keeping it open a definite time. 

13. An offer lapses if not accepted within the time named, or, if no time is set, within a reasonable time or when there are no longer two parties living to complete the contract. 

14. An acceptance cannot be implied from an offeree's failure to answer; neither can silence be considered an acceptance, unless the previous course of dealing between the parties justifies the offeror in expecting a refusal.

THE AGREEMENT 

67 15. A proposition on the part of one party calling for an acceptance on the part of another party constitutes an offer. 

16. An advertisement or a circular letter by which means certain articles are offered for sale does not constitute an offer, but instead an invitation to make offers to buy. 

17. An offer made to the public, such as an offer of a reward, may be accepted by anyone who can meet the requirements of the offer. 

18. A person who finds a lost or stolen article and returns it to the owner is not legally entitled to any reward offered of which he has no knowledge. 

19. An offer addressed to a particular party is not effective if accepted by some other party. 

20. Stipulations printed on the front or back of money orders, telegrams, express company receipts, insurance policies, etc., are binding upon the person who contracts for any of these services. 

Few people ever read them. 

21. Previous modes of dealing may so influence negotiations as to result in binding the parties in a contract. 

22. A merchant who offers his goods for sale by displaying them cannot be forced to sell.

COMMENTS 

The most important element in a contract is the agreement which results from a bona fide offer and its acceptance in a way that meets all legal requirements. No one can study the fundamental legal requirements of the offer and its acceptance without being impressed with the necessity of having reasonably definite rules to follow when making a contract. 

It must be understood that there can be no contract without an offer and its acceptance and that the validity of the contract depends on whether or not the offer and its acceptance conform to the legal requirements; and also, that the relation of the parties, their previous mode of dealing, and the circumstances in the case will influence a decision in case the parties to a contract disagree and their case finds its way into court.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Burden of Proof. The obligation of proving by evidence something asserted to be true. 

Credit Rating. The rating given the financial standing of a customer debtor by his creditor or by some credit agency. 

Estop. To bar; to stop.

Reality of Consent. The nature of the consent, whether actual or affected by any conditions which would make the contract voidable. 

When is consent real or full consent?

Consent is real or full when it has been given willingly and there are no conditions existing such as the following which would affect its reality. There are qualifying conditions affecting consent to a contract which will make the contract voidable in some cases at the option of the party or parties affected by these conditions. 

They are: Mistake, Misrepresentation, Fraud, Duress, and Undue

Influence. 

A party to a contract cannot avoid it when a misunderstanding results from his own carelessness in not finding out certain things or failing to read certain statements in the contract before assenting to it. 

1. What is a mistake in a contract?

A mistake is a misunderstanding or a misconception regarding some material fact connected with a contract. A mistake may be common to both parties to the contract, in which case it is a mutual mistake, or if it is made by one party, it is a unilateral mistake.

A mutual mistake of fact may be made with regard to the existence, identity, or quality of the subject matter. 72

A mistake as to the existence of the subject matter. 

Example 1. A lumber dealer from Portland, Oregon, called on a Chicago lumber merchant and sold him a specific lot of lumber to be delivered within sixty days. Before the contract was made and unknown to either party, the lumber had been destroyed by fire. 

In this case there was a mutual mistake of fact as to the existence of the lumber, and the contract is voidable. In reality there was no contract, for there was no subject matter to contract about. 

Where a mutual mistake is made by the parties to a contract, it is voidable, but a contract is not voidable on account of a mistake unless it is mutual; that is, it must affect both parties. 

A mistake as to the identity of the subject matter. 

Example 2. Waters attempted to purchase a used car from Bowman.

Bowman showed him two cars which looked somewhat alike, one a fourdoor sedan, and one a coach. Waters agreed to buy the sedan, but Bowman misunderstood and thought he had sold the coach. 

This case indicated clearly that the parties had not agreed upon the same thing, and in reality there was no contract. 

A mistake as to the quality or value of the subject matter. 

Example 3. Wardell bought a very old clock from one of his neighbors for $10. He had it but a short time when he sold it to an antique collector for $1,000. The neighbor did not know the value of the clock, and as there is nothing wrong with the contract he made with Wardell, he is bound by it.

The contract would be valid in Example 3, if in the absence of any misrepresentation by his neighbor which would amount to fraud, Wardell had paid his neighbor $500 for this clock, believing it was very old and valuable when it was only an ordinary clock worth not more than $5.

How is the contract affected when a mistake is made by only one of the parties (a unilateral mistake)? 

A unilateral mistake may be a mistake regarding the subject matter of the contract, or it may be a mistake as to the identity of the other party to the transaction. 

Example 4. Danby lived at Number 40 First Street and owned the adjoining house, Number 42. He offered Horton $200 to paint "my

house," which Horton agreed to do. Danby intended to have No. 42 painted, but Horton did not know he owned that house, and his agreement was to paint No. 40.

This contract is binding. The mistake was unilateral, being on the part of Danby only.

How is the contract affected when one party makes a mistake in identifying the other party?

Example 5. A man by the name of Fenner had taken care of West's yard and shrubbery during April for a number of years. One evening during the last of March, a Mr. Tanner called Mr. West on the telephone and said: "This is Mr. Tanner. Would you like to have me clean up your yard and cut your shrubbery sometime in April?" Mr. West, thinking he was talking to Mr. Fenner, said, "Yes." He did not discover his mistake until he was told by Mrs. West that a Mr. Tanner had cleaned up their yard and cut the shrubbery.

In reality there was no contract; the consent of West was unreal. 

There was no actual meeting of the minds. But West actually made an agreement with the person to whom he was talking. He was mistaken as to the name, but not mistaken as to the individual.

This being the case, West is bound in a contract to pay Tanner. 

A mistaken identity by one party of the other party to a contract may render the contract voidable.

Example 6. Groves, who was formerly with the Union Oil Company, resigned and became a salesman for the Globe Oil Company. Harper, who had contracted through Groves for his oil, thought he was getting it from the Union Oil Company. When he discovered his mistake, he refused to accept the oil.

If Harper can show that this was a mistake of fact on his part as to the identity of the seller, he can avoid this contract. But if the mistake resulted from Harper's carelessness in not reading his contract, in case it was written, or in not finding out the facts, he cannot avoid it. 

What effect has a mistake of law on a contract?

Example 7. Taber leased from the Bowen Realty Company, a building to be used as a factory. The parties thought that a zoning ordinance forbidding factories did not apply to this building, but as a matter of law the ordinance did apply.

In this case there was a mutual mistake regarding the law applicable to the contract. A distinction is to be made between a mistake of law and a mistake of fact. A party who makes a mistake as to the legal effects of his statements or acts cannot escape from his contract on the grounds of a mistake of law. 

2. When is a representation misrepresentation?

Example 8. A person who has a watch for sale, may, in the course of his selling talk, make some exaggerated statements such as: "This is the best watch made; it keeps perfect time, etc."

Such statements do not amount to misrepresentation. They are simply expressions of opinion. This person's "puffing" about his watch, or his idle boasting, is not to be taken seriously by anyone.

Statements made in connection with, and to induce another person to make, a contract are called representations. False statements, or misrepresentations, as to existing facts are fraudulent, and a contract made in reliance on them may be avoided. 

Exaggerated or even false representations as to matters of opinion, value, and the like are called "puffing" or "selling talk."

A buyer has no right to rely on them and cannot avoid a contract. 

An innocent misstatement, while it may misrepresent, is about the same as a mistake; while a willful misstatement made with intent to deceive, if acted upon, amounts to fraud. 

Example 9. Jerome, who was trying to sell a used automobile, stated that the car had been driven but 4,000 miles, and that it had never been in a repair shop for repairs, when he knew all the time that the car had been driven over 30,000 miles, and that it had been repaired several times. 

This is a clear case of willful misrepresentation with intent to deceive, and if someone buys this car relying on these statements, he may avoid the contract when the facts are known by him. The burden of proof, however, is on the buyer. 

Any misrepresentation whatever, even though it was made innocently, will in certain cases affect the contract. 

Example 10. Mason was being examined physically for life insurance. 

He was asked if any of his family had died of tuberculosis. He replied, "No," believing his answer was correct, when his mother had died of the disease only a few years before.

This positive, unqualified answer, "No," becomes a part of the insurance policy contract, and the facts would give the insurance company grounds for avoiding the contract in case Mason developed tuberculosis and died. He should have answered: "Not to my knowledge," unless he knew for a fact. 

3. What is fraud?

Fraud is a willful misrepresentation of a material fact made with a full knowledge of its falsity, and with the intention of having it acted upon by another party in such a way as to damage him. It is artful deceit practiced to the extent of damaging someone. 

Where there is proof of fraud in the making of a contract, the contract is voidable, and the party guilty of committing the fraud can, in some cases, be prosecuted in a criminal court action. 

How does fraud affect a contract?

Example 11. Gross offered to sell a rug to Mrs. Ress for $350. He represented it to be a genuine "Persian" rug (oriental rug). Mrs. Ress, relying on this representation, agreed to buy the rug and paid $50 of the purchase price at the time. When she investigated, she learned that the rug she had bought was a "domestic oriental" worth no more than $75. 

These facts make it possible for Mrs. Ress to avoid her contract on account of the misrepresentation by Gross, which amounted to fraud. Gross will have to refund the $50. 

Example 12. Wilson purchased a trucking business which was represented to him as doing a business of at least $3,000 a month. The entries in the books which Wilson examined showed this amount of business. 

Wilson had operated the business but a short time when he discovered the business did not amount to $1,000 a month and that the entries in the books had been falsified, as an examination by experts revealed. 

Wilson brought action in the court against the former owners of this trucking business, and they were required to take it back, refund the amount paid, and pay some damages on the ground that fraud had been practiced. 

In what ways may fraud arise?

Example 13. Allen bought a used car from Mason, who represented it to be in good condition. The car had been damaged in a collision; the frame was badly bent, and one cylinder was cracked. These facts

known by Mason were concealed by him. Allen bought the car, depending on Mason's representation.

This is a clear case of fraud. Allen may require Mason to take the car back and refund the price. 

Fraud may arise where a material defect is concealed. 

In some cases it is a legal duty to disclose a material fact. 

Example 14. Bramley's son, then nineteen years old, came into possession of $10,000, willed to him by his grandfather. The father owned ten $1,000 foreign bonds which were worthless. He induced his son to buy these bonds from him at their par value, $10,000. 

The father in this case was guilty of fraud. The relation of father and son is such that it was the legal duty of the father to disclose any material fact that would affect the contract. 

In the absence of a legal duty to disclose a material fact, nondisclosure does not amount to fraud. Strangers dealing with each other may have the benefit of their knowledge. One does not have to disclose facts which the other is free to find out for himself. 

Had Bramley sold the bonds to a banker without misrepresentation, the contract would have been valid. The banker would be bound to find out about the bonds. He had no right to rely on 

Bramley, and Bramley was under no duty to him. 

Other situations resulting from misrepresentation and fraud. 

1. Nondisclosure does not make a contract voidable unless there is a breach of confidence as a result of the relation of the parties. But when the relationship is such as imposes a duty to disclose a material fact, then nondisclosure renders the contract voidable by the injured party. 

2. A contract is rendered voidable by a misrepresentation of a fact made with a knowledge of its falsity and with intent to injure the other party. An expression of opinion does not amount to a misrepresentation. To say a watch cost $100 is a statement of fact; to say a watch is worth $100 is an expression of opinion. 

3. Fraud does not always result from falsehoods. It may result from acts or devices intended to deceive such as those often discovered in games of chance or sales of stock.

4. When fraud has been practiced in connection with a contract that has been entered into, the injured party can take action against the other party to the contract, and, in order to avoid the contract, the injured party must prove that fraud resulted from a misrepresentation of a material fact on which he relied. 

Fraud results when: 

1. There was a misrepresentation of a material fact. 

2. The person making the misrepresentation knew it to be false, or he made it carelessly, without regard for its truth. 

3. The misrepresentation was made for the purpose of influencing the other party to act upon it. 

4. The other party actually relied upon the misrepresentation to his detriment.

The person who was influenced by fraudulent means to enter into a contract may avoid it as soon as he becomes aware of the fraud. By accepting any benefits under the contract, after he has learned of the fraud, he affirms it. He has a right to affirm the contract and sue in tort for fraud. 

4. What is duress?

Example 15. Rowe was forced to sign a note for $1,000 under a threat of unlawful arrest and imprisonment. 

This note is voidable on the grounds of duress, if the party making the threat has the apparent authority to carry it out. 

Duress is forcing a person to assent to a contract or to perform some act against his will through a threat to injure him, his property, or some member of his immediate family in some way. It is actual or threatened violence or imprisonment. 

What would be considered duress? 

1. There can be no duress without the apparent power to carry out the threat. 

2. A threat to destroy property. 

3. A threat of wrongful imprisonment. 

4. A threat of criminal prosecution for an improper purpose. 

5. A threat to do violence to the man himself, or his parent, wife, or child.

6. The injury must be inflicted or threatened by a party to the contract or someone acting for him with his consent. 

5. What would be considered undue influence?

Example 16. A wealthy man was ill in a hospital. The head nurse in the hospital cared for him at times, and as he grew gradually weaker, she influenced him to make a will giving a large portion of his property to the hospital. He made this will involuntarily, feeling that he was at the mercy of the nurse. This fact he revealed to a friend of his, who called on him in the hospital. When this man died, his will was contested by his near relatives on the ground that undue influence was used by this nurse. 

When one person is possessed of the power to control another person's acts, and he uses this power to induce assent to a proposition, he may be rightly accused of using undue influence. 

Undue influence arises where the parties to the contract are not possessed of equal capacity or knowledge, and the stronger party takes advantage of the other party's weakness. This was the case in Example 16, and the hospital cannot hold this property if the facts can be proved.

Cases of undue influence usually develop as a result of a promise made by a child to its parent, a patient to his physician, an orphan to his guardian, a person to his spiritual adviser, or a wife to her husband. Such promises entered into in good faith will not be set aside; but, on account of the relations of the parties, it must be clearly shown that the party benefited did not take advantage of his position. Undue influence, when used to gain assent to a contract, renders it voidable at the option of the injured party or someone claiming through him.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A contract is binding only when there has been real or full consent to it by the parties thereto. 

2. A party to a contract cannot avoid it when a misunderstanding has resulted from his own neglect or carelessness. 

3. A mutual mistake of fact may render a contract voidable. 

4. A mistake of law does not avoid a contract. 

5. As a rule a mistake will not make a contract voidable. It depends upon the nature of the mistake. Only mistakes that prevent reality of consent may make a contract voidable.

6. Misrepresentation on which the parties to a contract did not rely or which did not influence them in giving consent cannot be used as a reason for avoiding the contract. 

7. A willful misrepresentation of a material fact may be used as a reason for avoiding the contract only when the innocent party relied upon it and was influenced by it to his injury. 

8. Expression of opinion and idle jesting are not to be considered as misrepresentation. 

9. A definite answer to a question in an application for insurance becomes a part of the policy contract. Unless you are sure, a definite answer should not be given. It is better to say: "Not to my knowledge"; "I do not know"; "I am not sure"; etc. 

10. A misstatement, though innocent, is grounds for avoiding a contract calling for the utmost good faith between the parties thereto. 

11. In case of fraud, the burden of proof rests on the injured party who seeks to avoid the contract. He must prove that he was defrauded. 

12. Concealment is fraudulent only when there is a duty to speak. 

13. Duress, when used as a means of forcing assent to a contract, renders it voidable.

REALITY OF CONSENT: SUMMARY OUTLINE IV. Duress I. Reality of Consent 

A. Mistake 

1. How defined 

2. Effect in general 

3. Requisites a. Material b. Mutual c. Unilateral d. Of fact

V. Undue Influence 

COMMENTS In a comparative sense, mistakes, misrepresentation, fraud, duress, and undue influence are very uncommon practices today. 

It usually is better for one to consider the other person as being honest until he is proven dishonest. That "Honesty is the best policy" has never been successfully denied. Any person who has any business to transact or becomes a party to a contract should not sacrifice his reputation or damage his credit in an attempt, by unscrupulous means, to profit at the expense of the other party.

SUBJECT MATTER TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Defendant. One against whom legal action is brought. 

Economic System. The basis upon which business, finance, and credit rest, including the methods by which they are controlled. 

Franchise. Permit to operate some business such as public utilities within the limits of a city or town; a privilege granted. 

Injunction. An order issued by a judge restraining some person from doing a particular thing or requiring him to do something. 

Juryman. A person selected with others, usually six or twelve, to listen to a case tried in court and decide questions of fact. 

License. A permit issued by some authority giving a person a right to practice his profession or trade in a certain place. 

Litigation. A lawsuit; a case tried in court.

Monopoly. A right enjoyed to the exclusion of everyone else. 

Rescind. To revoke; to cancel; to make void.

Usurious. Bearing a higher rate of interest than the law allows. 

Wagering. Risking money on an uncertain event; betting. 

What is subject matter in a contract?

Example 1. Peters contracted with the Acme Heating Company to keep his oil-burning heater adjusted and in repair for one year for $25. 

The service to be rendered by the Acme Heating Company is the subject matter in this contract. This means that whenever 

Peters's heater is not working properly at any time during the year, he is to notify the Acme Heating Company, and they will send a man to adjust or repair it. 

The subject matter of a contract is that which was promised to be done or not to be done, or the object about which the contract is made. It is the service or thing to which the agreement relates. 84

SUBJECT MATTER 

85 It may be anything of value in the form of an act, a promise, or some tangible object. 

Example 2. Mrs. Gates rented a floor waxer and polisher from the 

Crown Paint Co. for two days at $3 per day.

The subject matter of this contract is the use of the waxer and polisher, which would be classed as service. It is machine service; while in Example 1, the subject matter is human or man service. 

Example 3. Quinn agreed to buy 100 bags of potatoes from Hart for $1.50 a bag. Quinn handed Hart $25 to bind the bargain.

The subject matter of this contract is the 100 bags of potatoes. 

Example 4. Stone borrowed $100 from Neves, which he promised to repay in thirty days.

The subject matter is Stone's credit, in the form of his promise to repay the loan.

There can be no contract without subject matter in some form. 

What three qualifying conditions affect subject matter?

The subject matter of a contract must be physically possible of performance, definite, and lawful. 

1. In case it is physically impossible to perform the subject matter of a contract, the contract is void. 

Example 5. Garvin entered into a contract with Collins whereby 

Garvin was to act as a night watchman at Collins's factory for 300 nights between January 1 and July 1 of the same year.

It was physically impossible to carry out this contract; therefore, the contract is void. 

2. Indefinite subject matter renders a contract void.

Example 6. An employer promised his clerk a satisfactory raise in wages if the clerk would work overtime to catch up on back work. 

The clerk cannot hold his employer on this promise. The proposition is too indefinite to be enforceable, since it is impossible for a court or jury to determine what is a satisfactory raise. 

3. Unlawful subject matter renders a contract void.

Certain contracts are declared to be illegal because they tend to cause injury to the state or the people. They are said to be

contrary to public policy. The following are illegal contracts: (a) Contracts in restraint of trade (b) Wagering contracts (c) Usurious contracts (d) Certain Sunday contracts (e) Contracts obstructing justice (f) Contracts affecting public service (g) Contracts affecting marriage relations (h) Contracts entered into by unlicensed practitioners in a profession, trade, or business calling for a license. 

How can a contract that was good when made be rendered void? 

Example 7. Burk, the owner of a nursery, in Rochester, N. Y., contracted in December to deliver to Hall in Providence, R. I., 1,000 rosebushes on or about April 15. During February, the Rhode Island 

Legislature passed a law prohibiting the movement of rosebushes in that state for one year on account of the spread of a rosebush blight. 

The contract is void. A contract not yet performed may be rendered void as the result of the passing of a law making the performance illegal, when as a matter of fact the performance was legal at the time the contract was entered into. 

What is restraint of trade?

Restraint of trade can be simply explained as a plan or agreement whereby someone is restricted from carrying on a particular trade or business within certain territorial limits for a period of time or indefinitely according to the agreement he has entered into. 

Contracts in simple or limited restraint of trade are usually binding if they are considered reasonable; while contracts in general or unlimited restraint of trade are never binding, for the reason that such contracts are against public policy. 

Example 8. Wise sold his fruit and vegetable store to Bantz and agreed not to open, buy, or operate a fruit and vegetable business of any kind within a radius of 2,000 feet of his former store, for five years. 

It is probable that this contract would be considered reasonable, and should Wise engage in a fruit and vegetable business in viola-

SUBJECT MATTER 

87 tion of his agreement with Bantz, he could be legally restrained from continuing. 

What would be considered unreasonable restraint of trade?

Example 9. The Seeley Furniture Co. sold its retail furniture business in Springfield, Mass., to the Bay State Furniture Co. of Boston and agreed not to engage in the retail furniture business at any time east of the 

Mississippi River.

This contract is in general restraint of trade, and the Seeley Furniture Co. is not bound by it, even though the Bay State Company has plans to open branch stores in many parts of the country. A contract as sweeping as this one would tend to foster monopolies and trade control which are considered against the general welfare of all the people. 

Other restraining agreements which are enforceable. 

Example 10. A manufacturer of electric light bulbs refuses to sell to retailers but instead lets them handle his bulbs on consignment with the understanding that they are to sell them at a stated price. 

Any retailer handling these bulbs is bound by this agreement, and should he sell at a different price, the manufacturer could refuse to allow him to handle his bulbs. This is a trade agreement which is enforceable.

A retailer who buys his goods outright, regardless of any retail prices the manufacturer may set, has a right to sell at his own prices. The manufacturer, however, is within his rights in refusing to sell his product to any particular retailer. Some states have by statute legalized price-fixing agreements in contracts between manufacturers or jobbers of trade-marked goods and retail dealers. 

Any person who is given employment and enters into an agreement with his employer whereby he will not divulge any trade secrets or process formulas is bound by this agreement, and he lays himself liable if he breaks it. 

Wagering contracts or gambling contracts are not enforceable.

Example 11. Gains bet Adams $100 that Bates would be elected to 

Congress. Bates was defeated, and Gains failed to pay Adams the $100.

Adams cannot collect the $100 from Gains. Such contracts are generally forbidden by law, and no court would entertain a case of this nature. Had Gains paid the $100, even though the contract was illegal, he could not recover it. In some states, New York for example, the loser is allowed by statute to recover the amount lost either from the stakeholder or the winner. 

Contracts calling for an interest rate in excess of the legal rate permitted in that particular state are not enforceable. 

Example 12. Wade lent Bowers $500 on his note for one year with interest at 10% per annum.

In any state where the legal rate is less than 10% this would be a usurious contract and subject to the laws of the state wherein it is to be performed. 

The laws of the different states vary considerably, as do the penalties imposed for a violation of these laws. In most states the legal interest rate is 6%; in a few states it is 7%, and in a very few states a higher rate is permitted. It is common to specify a minimum legal rate and a maximum rate that may be charged by agreement. A few states permit any rate to be charged by agreement. The most usual penalty is forfeiture of principal or interest, one or both.

A contract involving a rate of interest in excess of the legal rate may not be a usurious contract. 

Example 13. Kemp purchased from Grant for $90 Owen's $100 note due in three months.

This transaction amounts to Kemp's receiving $10 for the use of $90 for three months. In reality the interest rate is nearly 45%. 

This transaction is not usurious. The usury statutes are intended to protect the needy borrower against the exactions of a rapacious lender. Owen, the borrower, is paying only the legal interest and, since the note was good when issued, it is not usury for the payee to sell it at a discount. Likewise, when money is advanced to be used in a joint venture and is to be repaid with a share of the profits if any, the transaction is not usurious, because it is not a

SUBJECT MATTER 

89 loan in the usual sense. The share of the profits may largely exceed the legal rate of interest without making it illegal. In some states it is not considered usurious to charge a rate in excess of the legal rate if the interest is paid in advance. 

In a case where some device has been resorted to as a means of securing a usurious rate, the courts will, as a rule, impose the penalty for usury. This is true in New York and in most states. 

When a usurious contract has been executed, as a general rule the penalty will not be applied, and the debtor cannot recover his money. This rule is modified by statute in some states. 

When the note or contract states "with interest" and no rate is mentioned, the legal rate may be charged. When the interest rate is mentioned, it may be any rate not in excess of the rate allowed by law. The lender has a right to charge the borrower, in addition to the interest, for any expense incurred in making the loan. 

Some exceptions to usury laws. 

By special legislation some organizations and kinds of businesses are not subject to the usury laws: 

1. Personal loans made by an organization duly chartered in the state to make such loans. 

2. Loans made by pawnbrokers. 

3. Call loans of $5,000 or more made by banks and secured by collateral (stocks and bonds). 

4. Loans made to corporations. A corporation cannot plead usury on any loan. New York State has such legislation and so have many other states, with some modifications. 

What contracts made on Sunday are illegal and void? 

Example 14. Harmon agreed to trim Jameson's shrubbery on Sunday for $6.

Under the statutory laws of most states, if not all of them, this contract is illegal. In some states contracts entered into on Sunday to be performed on a weekday are lawful. Many contracts are negotiated on Sunday and finished on a weekday. Such contracts do not come under statutory regulations. Many states do permit, by special statutes, various games and entertainments to be performed on Sunday.

Contracts entered into which are to be performed on a legal holiday are valid. A note falling due on a legal holiday is payable on the day following. As a rule, where the date of performance of a contract falls on a holiday, it may be performed on the next business day. 

What contracts made on Sunday are enforceable?

Example 15. A nurse was called for service on Sunday. Can she collect for her services?

The law recognizes the necessity of permitting certain work on 

Sunday. Nurses, doctors, policemen, firemen, railroad men, hotel employees, and many others, by reason of the work that must be done and the economic system under which we live, find it necessary to carry on every day in the week. They can collect pay for services performed regardless of the day. 

What contracts may obstruct the course of justice? 

Example 16. The defendant in a case for damages resulting from an automobile accident said to a possible juryman, "If you are drawn on the jury for my case, I will pay you $50 if you will hold out for no damages.' 

This man was drawn, and he held out for no damages to the point where the jury agreed to disagree.

Both parties are guilty of a criminal act, and they may be prosecuted. Any contract that has for its object the bribing of witnesses, the influencing of jurymen, the intimidation of the judge, or that would in any way obstruct the legitimate and regular course of justice is void and illegal. Likewise, agreements to conceal a crime, to refrain from prosecuting a criminal, and to refrain from testifying as a witness have illegal objects and are void. 

What contracts affect public service adversely?

Example 17. A wealthy man owned an estate a short distance from the main highway. When the state highway engineers surveyed for the state road, he agreed to pay them $2,000 if they would bring the state road past his place. By some maneuvering, the engineers carried through the wealthy man's desire at an additional cost of several thousand dollars to the state.

SUBJECT MATTER 

91 Any contract that has for its object the influencing of legislation for the benefit of some special interests as against the public welfare is void. Influence and special privileges which have a market value for improper purposes, or which are used to further the interests of unworthy individuals or organizations, too often result in agreements injurious to our public service. 

All agreements of an official to pardon a criminal or to make an appointment for pay, or of someone to pay an officer for special favors, are illegal and void. 

What contracts affecting marriage relations are void? 

Example 18. A father, fearing that his daughter would get married and leave him, gave her $10,000, and she signed an agreement never to marry.

This contract is not binding upon the daughter. She can keep the $10,000 and also get married if she has a chance. It is a void agreement.

Contracts which interfere with the freedom or security of marriage, as a promise not to marry, and any agreement to pay someone for bringing about a marriage, or a mutual agreement between husband and wife to obtain a divorce, are all void as interfering with marriage relations and against public policy. 

Other agreements that are against public policy. 

1. Any agreement that has for its object the promotion of litigation. 

2. Any agreement contrary to good morals. 

3. Any agreement to break a law of another state. 

4. All price-fixing agreements for the purpose of controlling prices unless by governmental authority. 

5. Any agreements that would result in a control of prices or of the supply of certain commodities to the point of being a monopoly. 

Monopolies are forbidden by statute in most states. The antitrust laws of the United States are aimed at the same evil. Refer to (a) The Sherman Antitrust Act, passed in 1890; (b) The Federal 

Trade Commission Act, passed in 1914; (c) The Clayton Act, passed in 1914; and (d) The Webb-Pomerene Act, passed in 1918.

A license to practice or to operate is required in some professions and in certain trades and lines of business. 

Example 19. Bender, a local real-estate broker, sold a house and lot for Jordon on a commission of 5%. Bender had failed to secure his license which was required, and Jordon refused to pay the commission. 

Bender cannot legally collect his commission because he is not a licensed operator, and by acting as a broker he lays himself liable to any penalty which the state law may impose for so operating. 

Doctors, dentists, lawyers, and certified public accountants are not permitted to practice until they secure a license through the license bureau of the state in which they are to practice. In many states real-estate brokers and insurance brokers are required to secure a license to carry on their business. Some states extend the license requirements to include other professions, businesses, and trades. Many cities require that plumbers and electricians secure a license before they can operate in that city. 

What laws apply when the subject matter of a contract is illegal? 

1. A contract in which the subject matter is illegal and has not been performed, cannot be enforced. It is void. 

2. A contract in which the subject matter is illegal but has been performed, cannot be set aside, and the parties restored to their former positions.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The subject matter of a contract may be any act or thing which can be given a value. 

2. No contract is valid if the subject matter is an illegal act to be done. 

3. The subject matter of a contract must be definite and possible of performance. 

4. Any contract classed as illegal is void. 

5. Any contract against public policy is illegal. 

6. Any illegal contract that has been performed cannot be rescinded. 

7. Contracts in reasonable restraint of trade are usually binding.

SUBJECT MATTER 

93 8. Contracts in general or unreasonable restraint of trade are not binding. 

9. All gambling contracts are unenforceable. 

10. All usurious contracts are unenforceable. 

11. The usury law does not apply in the case of certain transactions permitted by law. 

12. Sunday contracts are subject to special legislation. Many are void; others are enforceable. Legal holiday contracts are valid. 

13. Contracts which obstruct the course of justice are void. 

14. Contracts interfering with the public service are void. 

15. Contracts interfering with marriage relations are void. 

16. When an illegal contract has been executed, the courts will not interfere to aid either party. 

17. Price-fixing agreements and agreements to limit or control the supply are void unless under governmental control.
