E. Rules of Law Applicable 

1. When subject matter is illegal COMMENTS

This study of "subject matter" makes it clear that illegal contracts are void. Courts will not lend their aid to enforce an illegal contract, nor will they help a person who has parted with money, property, or services in reliance on such contracts. Consequently, everybody should be careful that any agreement he makes is legal and enforceable. It must not only be legal under the statute law of his state, but it must not have an immoral, fraudulent, or other improper tendency, because courts will declare any such contract void.

Illegal contracts are infrequent, but the principles of law applicable must be understood in order that such contracts may be avoided.

CONSIDERATION TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Abducted. A person secretly taken away by force. 

Bonds. Written promises under seal to pay interest and principal when due. 

Deeds. Written instruments under seal to convey real property rights from one person to another. 

Detriment. Inconvenience or loss.

Mortgage. An instrument under seal used to conditionally transfer title to property to secure a debt. 

Presumptive Evidence. Something presumed or understood from the nature of the case.

Under Seal. Bearing the impression of the seal or its equivalent. 

What is consideration in a contract? 

Example 1. Reed sold an electric washer to Mrs. Pierce for $150 cash.

The $150 is the consideration in this contract. It was the price paid by Mrs. Pierce for the washer.

Consideration is that essential element of a contract which each party gives in exchange for the obligation of the other party. It may be something of value he has, or a promise to do or to refrain from doing some possible act. 

Is an unperformed agreement in which there is no consideration enforceable?

Example 2. Weeks agreed in writing that just as soon as he sold a large tract of land he was trying to sell, he would give his nephew, John Weeks, $1,000. Weeks sold the land, but John did not get the $1,000. 

Weeks cannot recover it from his uncle. There was no consideration to support this agreement, and it is not enforceable. 96

CONSIDERATION 

97 

Of what may consideration consist? 

1. It may be an act or something of value given in exchange for a promise. 

2. It may be a promise given in exchange for another promise. 

To be sufficient consideration, the promise must impose an obligation to do an act which will or may be a legal detriment (loss or inconvenience) to the promisor, or a legal benefit to the other party.

The question that must be raised in connection with every contract is whether there is a consideration for the promise of each party.

Example 3. Bentley, whose wife had died recently, said to a niece of his, "If you will agree to keep house for me for one year, I will pay all your expenses for three months' travel in Europe." The niece promised to keep house for her uncle.

This case illustrates a promise for a promise. The niece suffered a detriment by promising to devote time and effort to keeping house, and thus furnished consideration for the uncle's promise. 

The uncle suffered a detriment by promising the trip to Europe and thus furnished consideration for the niece's promise. Each promise is consideration for the other.

A promise to give up a legal right is sufficient consideration. 

Example 4. Eberle said to his son, "Jack, if you will never play in a game of football again while you are in high school and college, I will give you $1,000 when you graduate from college." Jack promised his father he would not play football, and he kept his promise.

Jack's promise to refrain from doing something which he had a legal right to do is sufficient consideration to make his father's promise binding.

If a person has a legal right to do or refrain from doing some act, a promise to give up that right at the request of another is consideration for the other's promise. The act need not be actually beneficial to the other party. Promising to name a child at the request of the promisor, or a promise not to smoke until twentyone, are examples coming under this principle of law. Any legal act may be consideration.

Does the consideration have to equal in value the value of the article sold? 

Example 5. Morley was left a valuable ring by his mother. Not knowing the value, he sold it for $50. Later he learned the ring was worth $600.

In the absence of fraud, Morley can do nothing about this contract. A person may sell any article he owns at his own price. If he makes a bad bargain, he has no redress. The courts will not hear cases that would require them to pass on the adequacy of the consideration, unless fraud has been practiced; otherwise they would be kept busy passing on the merits of bargains. 

A contract is not affected by the inadequacy of the consideration. 

In many written contracts, "one dollar" is mentioned as the consideration, or "one dollar and other valuable consideration."

Such agreements are enforceable. 

Would an agreement to perform an illegal act be sufficient consideration in a contract?

Example 6. A divorced father promised an irresponsible fellow $500 if he would abduct his small son from his mother. The son was successfully abducted.

The father is not bound by this contract. The consideration for his promise, being an illegal act, is not sufficient consideration. 

Distinction between subject matter and consideration. 

Example 7. Grey said to Bates, "If you will agree to look after my home during my absence this summer, I will pay you $50." Bates agreed. 

The subject matter on the one side is the thing contracted about, while consideration on the other side is the thing given or done, or promised to be given or done. An agreement may result from mutual promises. In such an agreement one promise is consideration for the other promise, and the subject matter is the thing about which the promises are made. 

The subject matter is Bates's services. The consideration for 

Grey's promise to pay $50 is not the services themselves, but Bates's promise to render them. The consideration for Bates's promise is Grey's promise.

CONSIDERATION 

99 6 A promise to do an impossible or vague act is not sufficient consideration.

Example 8. Quade offered Lentz $25 if he would pick and pack 500 bushels of apples, in one day of eight hours, without help from anyone. 

If Lentz were foolish enough to accept this offer, the agreement would not bind him in a contract. For one man to pick and pack 

500 bushels of apples in eight hours is a physical impossibility. 

The promise must be definite to be sufficient consideration. 

What is the distinction between present consideration and what is termed past consideration?

Example 9. Harris gave Nolte $10 for a picture. The $10 is present consideration. It was given at the time the agreement was made or at the present time. Had Nolte purchased the picture from Harris and promised to pay him $10 on the first of the next month, the consideration (the promise) would still have been present, even though the payment was to be made in the future.

Present consideration is anything of value given at the time of the promise, or a promise given at that time, even though the thing promised is to be done in the future. 

Example 10. Morrow was some distance from home when he met with an accident. A family living near where the accident occurred took him into their home and cared for him for three days. When Morrow was able to leave, he assured Mr. Borden, with whose family he had stayed, that as soon as he reached home he would send him a check for $50. 

Where the supposed consideration was given or performed before the promise is made it is past consideration and is not sufficient to support a contract.

Morrow is not legally bound by this promise. The consideration which prompted it was performed before the promise was made. This is an example of past consideration. Past consideration, which is in reality no consideration, is not sufficient to support an agreement.

Had Morrow requested Mr. Borden to help him and the result was what happened in Example 10, then there would have been an implied promise on the part of Morrow to pay, and Mr. Borden could collect a reasonable amount.

Is the effect of lack of consideration the same in a performed contract as it is in a contract to be performed? 

Example 11. Greer promised to give a trustworthy employee $1,000 on the fifth anniversary of his employment. The employee worked five years, and Greer made good his promise. Later Greer wanted his money back. 

This promise on the part of Greer was not enforceable for lack of consideration. Greer performed his promise, but for some reason he desired to recover the $1,000 given to his employee. This he could not do. Lack of consideration will not make a performed contract void.

If a contract has been performed, it will not be set aside because of lack of consideration, while an agreement to be performed is not enforceable if the consideration is lacking.

Has a promise to make a gift sufficient consideration to support it as a contract?

Example 12. An aunt said to her niece, "Mary, I promise you now that 

I will give you $1,000 when you get married."

Mary may get married, but her aunt's promise is not enforceable because of lack of consideration to support it. Had the aunt paid the $1,000, even though consideration was lacking, she could not recover it.

A promise by someone to do something which he is already legally bound to do is not sufficient consideration. 

Example 13. Bader contracted with the Suburban Oil Co. to supply him with oil for the season. During a severe storm his oil ran low and he thought deliveries would be delayed, so he promised the Suburban company $10 extra to make a delivery. 

There is no consideration for Bader's promise to pay $10 extra. 

By delivering the oil, the Suburban company is doing no more than they contracted to do. They cannot legally require Bader to pay the $10.

When are mutual promises sufficient consideration? 

Example 14. Boyers and Gilbert owned adjoining properties. There were two vacant lots between the two properties. Boyers owned the one

CONSIDERATION 

101 next to his property, and Gilbert owned the lot adjoining his property. 

They agreed between themselves not to sell the vacant lots or build on them while either one owned the adjoining property. 

In this case the promise of one party is sufficient consideration to support the other party's promise; therefore, each promise is consideration for the other. Their promises are mutual promises, and should either party break his agreement, he is liable to the other party for any damages he may sustain as a result of the agreement's being broken.

A promise that does not impose a legal liability on the promisor is not sufficient consideration to support a promise; therefore such a promise is not binding on the promisor.

Example 15. Harper, a coaldealer who thought he might sell oil as a side line, agreed to buy from the Union Oil Company, at 4¢ a gallon, all the oil that he might sell to the trade, and the Union Oil Company agreed to sell him the oil at this price. Harper's promise is not binding upon him for the reason that he may not need any oil; therefore he would not have to buy any. If Harper were in the oil business and needed oil, then his promise would impose a legal liability on him, even though the exact quantity he would need is uncertain, and would be sufficient consideration to support the Union Oil Company's promise to sell. 

What is the effect of a seal on a contract? (Refer to the law in your own state for definite information regarding the effect of the seal on a contract.) 

Written contracts such as leases of land, deeds, mortgages, bonds, etc., are under seal, which means that the seal has been affixed to the instrument, or the letters L. S. have been written thereon, following the signature of the maker. The use of the seal is fully explained under "Formal Contracts," page 117. 

The exact amount of consideration in a contract under seal is rarely given. The statements "for good and sufficient consideration," or "for valuable consideration," or "for $1 and other valuable consideration," are commonly used. The fact that the contract is under seal is presumptive evidence that consideration was given. The lack of consideration may become an issue, however, if it is proved.

Are voluntary subscriptions made by individuals or firms to a fund being raised for a purpose enforceable?

Example 16. A project was under way to start a country club, and subscriptions were being solicited for the purpose of buying the land. 

Slater, Morley, Hessler, and Dwyer agreed to contribute $1,000 each.

Their subscriptions with those of others made it possible to buy the land. 

Court decisions indicate that the promise on the part of the organization to carry out the project is sufficient consideration to support the promise on the part of the subscribers to contribute to the fund. The promises are mutual and the carrying out of the project imposes a binding obligation on all who subscribed. Had the project failed, no one would have been obligated; and had any money been collected, it would have to be returned. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Consideration is necessary in every enforceable contract. 

2. An example of consideration is where the promisee passes something to the promisor at his request in return for his promise. 

3. Consideration may exist in three forms: (a) A benefit to the person making the promise or to someone for him. (b) A loss or detriment to the person to whom the promise is made or to someone for him. (c) Mutual promises exchanged between the parties. 

4. A performed contract cannot be set aside because of lack of consideration. 

5. Doing or promising to do an illegal act is not sufficient consideration to support a contract. 

6. Consideration must be definite and possible of performance. 

7. It is not necessary that the consideration benefit the promisor. 

8. Consideration must be present. Past consideration will not support a promise. An act previously performed is past consideration. 

9. A moral obligation is not sufficient consideration. 

10. A promise to make a gift is not enforceable because of lack of consideration. 

11. A promise from the promisee to perform a present act or an act in the future may be a sufficient consideration.

CONSIDERATION 

103 12. A promise to do what one is already legally bound to do is not sufficient consideration. 

13. The seal on a contract is presumptive evidence that consideration is given. 

14. Consideration may consist of: (a) Performing an act one is not already bound to perform. (b) Refraining from doing something one is free to do. (c) Giving of something of value (property or money). (d) Mutual promises (a promise given in consideration for another promise). 

15. A promise is not sufficient consideration to support a promise unless it imposes a legal liability on the promisor.

In the large mass of contracts consideration is money or a promise to pay money. The man who sells his goods or his services receives the cash or its equivalent or a promise to pay cash at some future time. The man who works for wages receives his pay in cash. When the sales of goods and services and the wage agreements are eliminated from the whole mass of agreements there are but comparatively few left to consider, and they form the exceptional cases reviewed in this chapter. 

There are certain rules and well-defined principles of law that apply to agreements in general, and to certain specific agreements where there is some question as to what is lawful and what rights the parties have. An understanding of all these helps the businessman to manage his affairs more efficiently and to protect his interests.

SPECIAL CASES OF CONSIDERATION TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Accord and Satisfaction. An agreement to settle a disputed claim (the accord) and the performance of the settlement agreement (the satisfaction).

Bankrupt. In a state of being legally decreed unable to pay one's debts. 

Chattels. Movable articles as furniture, livestock, machinery, etc. 

Moral Obligation. An obligation morally binding, but not legally enforceable.

Prima Facie. What is first apparent on the surface or face. 

When is a debt discharged?

Example 1. Elrod owed Clary $500 which was much past due. One day Elrod appeared at Clary's office and offered to pay him $350 if he would accept this amount in full satisfaction of the debt. Clary accepted the $350 and gave Elrod a receipt in full. 

This $500 debt is not fully canceled. There is still $150 unpaid which Clary has a right to collect. The reason is that there is no consideration for deducting the $150. Had Elrod paid the whole $500, he would have been doing no more than he was already bound to do.

A debt is not legally canceled after it becomes due by paying in cash or its equivalent a smaller amount than the original debt. 

One way to cancel a debt is to pay it in full when it is due. 

Example 2. Edmunds had loaned $300 to Harry for one year. Three months before the year was up, Edmunds needed money, and he offered Harry a receipt in full if he would pay $250 at this time. Harry paid the $250, and Edmunds gave him a receipt for $300. 

In this case, the full amount of the debt ($300) is canceled. Accepting a smaller amount in full satisfaction of a debt not yet due, if 107

agreed to, cancels the debt. Paying this debt before it is due is the consideration for the $50 discount, because it is something Harry was not bound to do. 

Example 3. Dunn had an account against Morel amounting to $480. 

It was long past due, when one day Morel drove his car up in front of Dunn's store, called him out, and offered him the car and $200 in full satisfaction of his $480 store bill. Dunn accepted Morel's offer. 

Morel's store bill of $480 is paid. The accepting of an article (chattel) of uncertain value in full payment or as part of the payment of the debt not yet due, or past due, if agreed to by the parties, cancels the debt. It matters not whether this car is worth $500, $50, or what it is worth, the debt is canceled by this agreement, because the debtor was not bound to give up the car. 

By accepting something else than money in full payment of a debt, even though the thing accepted is much less in value than the amount of the debt, it is canceled. 

Example 4. Miller and Hensel had some business dealings. Miller claimed that Hensel owed him $560. Hensel claimed that he owed Miller only $360. Miller finally compromised with Hensel and accepted $460 in full satisfaction of all claims. 

By this compromise agreement, Miller's claim, even if it was $560, is settled in full by Hensel.

Whenever the amount of a debt is disputed in good faith, a compromise agreement on any sum accepted in full satisfaction of the debt is binding. The consideration for the surrender of part of the debt by the creditor is the debtor's promise to pay more than he believed himself bound to pay. Whenever the parties concerned with the settlement of a debt are in a dispute regarding the amount and they reach an agreement whereby the debtor agrees to give or perform, and the creditor agrees to accept in satisfaction of the debt, a lesser sum or payment in other than money, and the compromise agreement is actually performed, the result is a settlement by accord and satisfaction. This means that the debt which was in dispute was settled by compromising the amount or by accepting in payment something other than money.

SPECIAL CASES OF CONSIDERATION 

109 Example 5. Powers entered into an agreement with Groves, whereby 

Powers was to pay Groves $900 in full settlement of a debt of $1,200 which was several months past due. Powers paid Groves the $900, and required him to give a release under seal for the whole debt. 

The courts have held that where a part payment is made and accepted, and a release under seal is given for the whole debt, the debt is canceled.

In a case where a settlement is made to avoid litigation, the agreement entered into by the parties involved is binding. 

Example 6. Hapner fell in Sprole's store and injured his hip. He threatened to sue Sprole for $500. Sprole felt that he might be liable, and to avoid the expense of defending a suit, and being short of cash, he offered Hapner his note for six months for $200, with interest at 6%, which Hapner accepted. 

Both parties in this case are bound by the terms of the settlement to which they agreed. Even though Hapner might not have won his case, nevertheless, as Hapner's claim was made in good faith, Sprole will have to pay his note to Hapner when it becomes due. Hapner's promise not to sue Sprole on an honest claim is sufficient consideration to support Sprole's promise to pay $200. 

An agreement to extend the time of payment of a debt already due is not valid unless it is supported by some consideration. 

Example 7. Kline held a note for $1,000 made by Bidwell. When the note was due, Bidwell asked for an extension of time of six months, and 

Kline promised him the extension.

Kline is not legally bound by his promise to extend the time of payment on Bidwell's note. There was no consideration given by 

Bidwell for this extension of time. Kline is only morally bound to keep his promise.

Had Bidwell given some consideration, such as some security, paying the interest in advance, or making some concession, the extension-of-time agreement by Kline would have been binding upon him. As the case stands now, Kline could take action at once on this note, and Bidwell would have no redress.

How can a debt be discharged by a compromise agreement with creditors?

Example 8. Hendricks, who was insolvent, entered into an agreement with his creditors whereby they were to accept 50 cents on the dollar in payment for their several claims and give receipts in full, this agreement to become binding when all the creditors assented to it. 

This is a valid mutual agreement, and all parties to it are bound by it. The agreement of each creditor to accept less than the full amount of his claim is consideration to the others who might lose the whole. By this agreement Hendricks's debts are fully discharged by his paying 50 cents on each dollar he owed. Had it not been possible for Hendricks to settle with his creditors through a compromise agreement, he would have been forced into bankruptcy.

Under the Federal Bankruptcy Act an insolvent debtor may give up all his property, and through court action, by which his property is divided among his creditors in proportion to their claims, he is relieved from further liability on all his debts. 

What is good consideration?

The phrase good consideration, as distinguished from valuable consideration, is sometimes used. Good consideration is that which results from the natural love and affection one has for a near relative. Good consideration is not sufficient to make a promise enforceable at law.

Example 9. A father promised his son, who was about to get married, that when he got married, he would deed to him the "Winn" farm. The father owned this farm.

In this case the father's promise is supported by good consideration, and that is not sufficient to make it enforceable at law. The son has no legal rights in the "Winn" farm as a result of his father's promise; however, the father has a moral obligation to meet, and if he did convey the farm to his son, the son would have a good title, not because there was any consideration, but because a completed transaction is valid without consideration. Moral obligations are no longer considered as being sufficient consideration in an agreement of any kind.

SPECIAL CASES OF CONSIDERATION 

111 1 Example 10. The parents of a well-to-do son became dependent on charity or public funds for support. The son did not provide for them. 

The case found its way into court at the instigation of the commissioner of welfare, who brought suit against the son to recover money spent by the county for the parents' support, and the judge issued an order requiring the son to contribute $25 per week for the support of his parents. 

The son is only morally bound to care for his parents, and his moral obligation does not make him liable. Many states compel an adult child to contribute to parents' support. 

Is a receipt in full conclusive evidence that a debt has been paid? 

Example 11. Judson owed Hobert $250. At one time Judson paid $100 and took a receipt; at another time he paid $50 and Hobert gave him a receipt for $150, the total amount paid. Judson held receipts aggregating $250 and he would pay no more. 

Hobert can take court action against Judson and compel him to pay the $100 still unpaid. A receipt is only prima-facie evidence that the debt was paid, and Hobert could easily prove how the receipts of $100 and $150 respectively were obtained by Judson. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Paying less than the full amount of a debt already due, even though accepted in full satisfaction, does not bar action to recover the balance unpaid. 

2. Paying less than the full amount of a debt not yet due, if an agreement is made to cancel the debt, bars action to recover the unpaid portion. 

3. When a chattel of uncertain value is accepted in full payment of a debt, it is canceled. 

4. When a compromise agreement is reached in the settlement of a debt, and the compromise is performed, the debt is canceled. 

5. When part payment is made and accepted and a release under seal is given for the whole debt, it is canceled. 

6. A settlement agreement made to avoid litigation is binding upon the parties thereto. 

7. An agreement to extend the time of payment of an obligation is legally binding only when supported by consideration.

8. Debts may be legally discharged as a result of a compromise agreement with creditors. 

9. Good consideration will not legally support an agreement. 

10. Moral obligations are not enforceable, except in some cases. 

Certain moral obligations are enforceable by statute law, such as an obligation of an adult child to support his parents. 

11. A receipt given for full payment of a debt only partially paid does not bar action to recover the balance.

In the discussion of "Special Cases of Consideration," some rather significant cases affecting the integrity and credit standing of individuals have been used as examples. These are not unusual cases; however, there are times when those who are known to be honest and reliable are forced to liquidate their assets and effect a settlement with their creditors. This forced liquidation and settlement may be caused by a severe depression, by changing business conditions, or by some other misfortune unforeseen. 

Under such conditions the unfortunate debtor should not be unjustly blamed. Nevertheless, where credit is used, it is in many cases abused. 

For this reason we have these cases involving settlements of accounts continually before us in our business relations with others. 

Integrity is the basis of the individual's credit standing, and from a business standpoint, the value of his credit cannot be overestimated. Every person who has any business dealings should strive at all times to maintain good credit ratings. Good credit is stock in trade.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Bilateral. Affecting two sides; promises by two parties, each to the other. 

Bill of Sale. A written instrument by which the title to goods or chattels is transferred from one party to another. 

Executed. Fully performed. 

Executory. Not yet performed; to be performed. 

Solemnity. More than ordinary formality, seriousness, or gravity. 

SS. Scilicet; to wit, namely.

Unilateral. Requiring performance of a contract by only one of the parties thereto, the other party having performed. 

Contracts may be oral or written. 

Example 1. A customer said to his grocer, "How much are potatoes?”

The grocer replied, "Potatoes are 30¢ a peck." The customer picked up a bag containing one peck of potatoes and walked out of the store. The grocer charged the customer's account with 30 cents.

Oral contracts result from a spoken (word-of-mouth) offer, a proposition, and a spoken acceptance of the offer as made. The offer and acceptance are usually made simultaneously unless there is some other agreement or understanding between the parties. An oral contract may result where words and actions combined are used to bring about a contract. The agreement in Example 1 resulted from words and actions. In many oral contracts there are actions which take the place of words. 

Agreements entered into over the telephone. 

The telephone is so commonly used for purposes of transacting business today that contracts entered into over the telephone are numerous. A contract made by telephone is as good as any other 1 115

oral contract, but one question that might be raised in connection with contracts entered into over the telephone is the question of the identity of the parties. Where this question is raised and the identity of the parties cannot be proved, the contract will not be enforced because its existence has not been proved. It is recommended where contracts of importance are entered into over the telephone that they be confirmed by letter. 

Why are written contracts desirable in some cases?

Written contracts may result from letters passing between the parties or from agreements reduced to writing in which all the conditions and stipulations are fully stated. In cases where there are many details mentioned in the agreement, it is usually in written form.

In an oral contract, when a dispute arises, the testimony of witnesses or the circumstances in the case must be relied upon to determine the rights of the parties, while in a written contract all that is necessary to produce the evidence is to produce the written form signed by the parties. Oral testimony cannot be permitted to change or contradict that which is written. 

A SIMPLE WRITTEN CONTRACT 

This agreement made this first day of November, 19.., between Homer 

C. Radkin of the city of Albany, county of Albany, and state of New York, party of the first part, and John F. Terry of city, county, and state aforesaid, party of the second part.

Witnesseth, that the party of the first part, for and in consideration of the agreement hereinafter contained, to be performed by the party of the second part, agrees to and with said party to give him employment as a traveling salesman for two years at a salary of $3,000 per year, 2% commission on all sales, and $60 per week for expenses from the first day of 

November, 19... And the party of the second part, in consideration thereof agrees to represent the said party of the first part for a period of two years as a salesman of hosiery; and to devote all his time and his best efforts to the selling of hosiery to the trade in the state of Massachusetts. 

Signed in duplicate on this first day of November, 19... 

Homer C. Radkin

John F. Terry

What is an acknowledgment?

An acknowledgment is an act by which a party (or parties) who has executed an instrument declares or acknowledges it before a competent officer to be his or her act or deed. The following is the usual form of an acknowledgment: SS 

On the first day of November, one thousand nine hundred and before the subscriber personally appeared Homer C. Radkin and John F. 

Terry, to me personally known to be the persons described in and who executed the foregoing instrument, and they severally acknowledged to me that they executed the same. 

O. D. Harmon 

Notary Public for Albany County, New York

Any written contract may be acknowledged. It is for the parties thereto to decide. The purpose of an acknowledgment is to do away with the necessity of proving the signatures to a contract. 

When an instrument has been acknowledged, the signatures are considered to be genuine, unless the contrary is proved. An instrument to be recorded, such as a deed, must be acknowledged. 

Contracts may be express or implied.

An express contract is one in which all the conditions and specifications are fully stated. It may be either oral or written. Written contracts are express contracts, with now and then an exception. 

Oral contracts are rarely ever express, for the reason that in an oral contract there is usually something not mentioned that is understood from the nature of the contract or circumstances. 

An implied contract is one in which the conditions or terms are not fully stated but are implied from the nature of the contract. 

Contracts may be simple or formal. 

A simple contract is one not under seal. It may be oral or written, express or implied, and its validity depends upon the presence of all the essential elements of a contract. 

A formal contract is always written and under seal. It is used mostly for the purpose of transferring interests in some kind of property from one person to another. It may be in the form of a

lease, deed, mortgage, or bill of sale. Many municipal and corporation contracts are under seal.

At the present time the seal in the form of an impression made by a metal die upon wax or a wafer attached to the instrument or on the instrument itself is little used. In its place the scroll is used, and within the scroll are written the letters "L. S.," the initials of the Latin words locus sigilli, meaning "the place of the seal." 

The use of the seal is a very old practice, dating back to the early ages; the purpose of its use now, as then, is to attach greater solemnity to the agreement, and at the present time it creates the presumption of consideration. Also, under the Statute of Limitations, contracts are enforceable for a longer period of time, usually twenty years, when under seal.

A FORMAL CONTRACT 

This agreement made in duplicate this first day of November, one thousand nine hundred and ..... by and between John C. Weston of the city of Albany, county of Albany, and state of New York, of the first part, and William H. Hobart of the city, county, and state aforesaid, of the second part.

Witnesseth, that the said party of the first part for and in consideration of the agreement hereinafter contained, to be performed by the party of the second part, agrees to and with said party to sell his hardware business located at 372 South Pearl Street in the city of Albany together with the good will of said business. It is further agreed that the assignment of the lease to the building now occupied by the business and the passing of title to and possession of the business shall take place as of January 1, 19.., and that the said party of the first part shall not within a period of ten years, establish or in any way identify himself with the hardware business within a radius of 1,500 feet of the present location. And the party of the second part, in consideration thereof, agrees to pay the party of the first part for the same the sum of ten thousand dollars, lawful money of the United States, as follows: the sum of one thousand dollars at the time of signing this contract, the receipt whereof is hereby acknowledged, and the balance of nine thousand dollars on January 1, 19.., when the transfer of title and possession is completed.

In Witness Whereof, the parties named herein have hereunto set their hands and seals the day and year first above mentioned. 

In the presence of 

C. R. Clayton

John C. Weston (L. S.) William H. Hobart (L. S.)

State of New York 

County of Albany

SS 

On the first day of November, one thousand nine hundred and before me, the subscriber, personally appeared John C. Weston and 

William H. Hobart, to me personally known to be the persons described in and who executed the foregoing instrument, and they severally acknowledged to me that they executed the same. 

C. R. Clayton 

Notary Public for Albany County, New York

Contracts may be either executed or executory. 

Example 2. Judson buys a table from Wilmont, pays for it, and takes it away with him.

This is an executed contract. Neither party has anything more to do, and neither party has any redress in case the contract might have been void or voidable before it was performed. An executed contract will not be set aside for reasons that might have rendered it void or voidable before it was executed; for example: lack of consideration, illegal subject matter, against public policy, etc. 

An executed contract is one that has been fully performed on both sides; that is, each party to the contract has performed his part. 

Example 3. Paden ordered a bill of goods from Shaw, who shipped them to Paden at once. Paden has not paid for the goods yet. 

This contract is executed on the part of Shaw and executory on the part of Paden. Executory contracts are subject to all the rules and regulations affecting the validity of contracts generally. 

An executory contract is one which has not been completed. It may be executory on the part of both parties or it may be executory on the part of only one of the parties, the other party having fulfilled his part. Its validity depends upon the presence of all the essentials of a contract.

Contracts may be bilateral or unilateral. 

Example 4. Dowd contracted with the Glow Oil Company for his season's supply of furnace oil, the oil to be delivered as needed and to be paid for within thirty days after delivery.

ARA This is a bilateral contract, as both parties are bound by promises and both have something to do in connection with the agreement.

The Glow Oil Company must deliver the oil, and Dowd must pay for it. A bilateral contract is one in which both parties have something to do in connection with it, since they are bound by promises they have made to each other.

Example 5. Wade offered to pay Morton $5 if Morton would deliver a load of sand to Wade's place within the next five days. Morton delivered the sand.

This is a unilateral contract. Morton was never bound to do anything. When he delivered the sand he both accepted the offer and performed his part of the contract, whereupon Wade became bound by his promise to pay.

A unilateral contract is a one-party agreement; only one party is bound by the promise. The offer is in the form of a promise, and the acceptance is an act.

Contracts may be divisible or indivisible. 

Example 6. Gardner bought a lamp for $16, an easy chair for $30, and a couch for $150 from the Modern Furniture Co. When the articles were delivered, the lamp was broken and had to be returned. 

As this is a divisible contract, the lamp may be returned and the $16 refunded. Gardner will have to keep the chair and the couch. 

In any case, where the contract is made in such a way that partial performance of the contract will not destroy the whole purpose of the agreement it is a divisible contract. 

A divisible contract is one in which the parts are independent of each other, and any one of the parts may be performed and pay can be had for the part performed. 

Example 7. A painter made a contract to paint a house for $200 and a barn for $100. The barn was struck by lightning and burned. He may paint the house and collect the $200. This is a divisible contract. 

In Example 7, had the painter agreed to paint the house and the barn for $300, destruction of the barn would have made the whole contract unenforceable.

Example 8. Grant purchased a plow, a harrow, and a mowing machine from Long for $200. Before they could be delivered, Long's team ran away with the mowing machine and ruined it.

This is an entire contract, and if part fails, it all fails. Grant cannot be required to take the plow and the harrow. Where articles are priced together or where acts are dependent one on the other, the contract is indivisible. 

An indivisible or entire contract is one that has only one act or promise on one side and only one on the other. There is one thing to be done on each side.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. An oral or verbal contract has the same legal effect that a written contract has unless the law requires a written contract. 

2. An oral contract may result from spoken words and from acts. 

3. A contract entered into over the telephone is binding. It is best to confirm it by letter. 

4. A contract that results from letters passing between the parties is a written contract. 

5. An express contract is one in which the terms and specifications are fully stated. 

6. In an implied contract some parts are understood from the nature of the contract or from the circumstances. 

7. A simple contract may be oral or written not under seal. 

8. A formal contract is always written and under seal. 

9. An executed contract is one that has been performed. 

10. An executory contract is one that is to be performed. 

11. In a bilateral contract both parties agree to do something. 

12. In a unilateral contract only one party has promised to do something. 

13. In a divisible contract the parts are independent of each other. 

14. In an entire contract the parts cannot be separated.

COMMENTS 

People are entering into contracts continually without much thought about the particular kinds or classes of contracts they are making. By far the larger number of contracts are oral; however, written contracts, both simple and formal, exist in large numbers. Insurance policies, leases, deeds, mortgages, contracts resulting from letters, and many other types of agreements in written form are all classed as written contracts, and whenever the seal is used, the agreement becomes a formal contract. 

It is a safeguard for the contracting parties to have the contract in written form. It would not be practical or even possible to have every contract written, but the written form should be used for every important contract in which there are many specifications, conditions, or terms.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Beneficiary. One who receives a benefit or something as a gift. 

Joint and Several Obligation. An obligation assumed by two or more persons, any one of whom is individually liable for the whole obligation or all of whom are liable together. 

Joint Obligation. An obligation assumed by two or more persons. 

Operation of Law. Procedure according to the provision of the law. 

Proportionate Share. Sharing according to the various interests of the parties.

Several Obligation. An obligation assumed by one person. 

Subcontractor. A contractor who contracts with the general contractor to perform some part of the general contract. 

Who may acquire rights under a contract? 

Example 1. Weber owed Haden $180. Weber agreed to paint Gordon's house, and Gordon agreed to pay Weber's debt to Haden. 

By the agreement between Weber and Gordon, Haden acquired a right against Gordon and may enforce the payment of the $180. 

It is a general principle of law that only the parties to a contract acquire rights under it. There are, however, some exceptions to the rule. The courts of most states hold that the third person, for whose benefit a promise is made (Haden), may sue at law to enforce the promise, provided the promisee (Weber) then owed a debt to the beneficiary (Haden). 

Can one person pay another person's debt and thus make himself a creditor?

Example 2. Hooker voluntarily paid a debt of $200 for a relative of his. 124

The relative is under no obligations to pay Hooker, and should Hooker attempt to collect, he could not succeed unless the relative saw fit to pay him.

One person cannot, of his own volition and without being asked to do so, pay another person's debts and by doing so make himself a creditor of this person. 

When is liability under a contract joint and when several? 

Example 3. A note is worded we promise to pay and signed by H. E. 

Downs and C. L. Kress. 

This is a joint undertaking or agreement. Downs and Kress have agreed to act on one side of this agreement as a single person. 

The effect is that neither Downs nor Kress can be held individually by this agreement, and in case action is necessary to recover on this note they cannot be sued individually for the whole amount nor each one for his share. They are jointly liable, and they must be sued jointly; they are liable as one person. 

The wording of an agreement and the number of parties who have made promises to be fulfilled determine whether an agreement is a joint or several undertaking.

An agreement worded "I promise," or "We promise jointly and severally," or "We or either of us promise," or any other wording that clearly indicates the intention of each party to be wholly responsible is a several agreement. 

Example 4. Worth and Myers jointly and severally agreed to pay 

Sanderson $400 for the standing timber in a certain wood lot belonging to Sanderson. They removed the timber, but Sanderson has not been paid. 

This is a joint and several agreement. Either Worth or Myers is individually liable on this promise. Sanderson has the privilege of taking action against either one or against both of them. 

Should either Worth or Myers pay Sanderson the full $400, the one paying in full would have a good claim against the other for his proportionate share. 

What contracts are assignable?

Certain contracts are assignable; that is, third parties may acquire right in a contract by assignment. A contract is, in most

cases, a property right which is transferable like other property. 

Any contract calling for the delivery of goods to a particular person may be assigned by him so that these goods will be delivered to another person. The person making the assignment is known as the assignor, and the person to whom the right is assigned is known as the assignee. 

When a contract is assigned, it is still subject to all the defenses that might have been brought against it in the hands of the assignor. The assignee gets no better title or no more rights than the assignor had. He can enforce the contract in his own name. 

Example 5. Hart contracted to buy 100 bales of cotton from the Cotton 

Sales Company of Savannah, Georgia. Before this cotton was delivered, Hart sold and assigned this contract to the Eastern Mills Company. 

This contract is assignable, and the Eastern Mills Co. acquired the same rights under it that Hart had. The principle back of this assignment is that it makes no difference to the Cotton Sales Company to whom they deliver the cotton. The contract is not changed in any way, and the money from one source is as good as that from another.

It must be understood that the assignor cannot avoid his liability by assignment. After Hart had assigned his contract in Example 

5, if the assignee did not perform, Hart would be liable. 

Permitting the assignment of such a contract makes possible the sale and transfer of goods from one person to another without actually handling the goods, as Example 5 illustrates. 

Any contract calling for the payment of money is assignable. 

Example 6. The Central Garage Company sold a used car to Martin 

Quinn for $300. He paid $25 down and agreed in writing to pay $25 on the first business day of each month for eleven months.

The party to whom the money is payable can assign his contract so that the money will be payable to someone whom he names in the assignment.

This contract was assigned to the General Finance Company by the following assignment: 

Albany, N. Y., August 15, 1934

For a valuable consideration We hereby assign and transfer to the General Finance Company of Albany, N. Y., our full interest in our contract

with Martin Quinn of 228 South Pearl Street, Albany, N. Y., whereby he is to pay the sum of $275 in installments of $25 each on the first business day of each month. 

Central Garage Co.

Per Otis Powers 

President

The assignment may be written on the contract itself, or it may be on another sheet of paper and attached to the contract. On some contracts blank assignments are printed in part to be filled in when the assignment is made. 

In Example 6, the General Finance Co. would send notice to

Martin Quinn to the effect that his contract with the Central Garage Co. had been assigned to them. They would do this to make sure that Quinn received his notice, rather than depend on the assignor to give the notice. The notice may be given in any form, oral or written. It is usually given in writing. Finance companies handling assigned contracts have regular notice forms which they send out.

An assignment does not become effective against the other party to the contract until he has received notice that it has been made.

Example 7. Thomas bought an oil-burning heater from the Arcade 

Heating Engineers, Inc., for $950 on the following terms: $50 down and $75 to be paid on the first of each month for twelve months from the date of the contract, or the privilege of paying all cash, less 6% discount, within thirty days after installation.

The heater was installed, and Thomas's contract was assigned to the General Finance Company. Thomas, .who had received no assignment notice, sent his check for the full price less the discount to the Arcade Heating Engineers, Inc., before the thirty days had passed.

This assignment would not concern Thomas in any way until he received notice of it. By paying cash he completed his contract with the Arcade Heating Engineers, Inc., and any adjustments in this transaction would have to be made by them with the General 

Finance Company.

Contracts may be assigned by operation of law. 

Example 8. Baden contracted in writing to pay Woods $5,000 for a trucking business which Woods owned and was operating at the time. 

Before the sale was completed, Woods died. The administrators or executors of Wood's estate will have to see that this sale is completed and that the $5,000 is collected according to the contract. 

Had Woods been under a contract to install a new accounting system in the Union Bank and he died when his contract was about half completed, his contract would have died with him. 

The difference in the two contracts is that one calls for performance which need not be personal, and the other calls for personal services, which cannot be performed under the contract by another person.

Contracts are assigned as a result of bankruptcy. 

Example 9. Worden was indebted to the Higgins Coal Company to the extent of $125 for his winter's supply of coal. 

The Higgins Coal Company was forced into bankruptcy. They had many outstanding accounts, both receivable and payable. 

The court appointed a trustee, whose duty it was to wind up the business activities of the Higgins company as speedily as possible. 

As soon as the trustee was appointed, all contractual rights of the bankrupt firm passed to him. 

This unperformed contract of Worden's is, by operation of law, assigned to the trustee in bankruptcy for the Higgins company, and Mr. Worden will be required to settle his account with this trustee. All other debtors and creditors of the Higgins company will likewise have to make their settlements with the trustee, and any other unfinished contracts in which the Higgins Company is a party will have to be adjusted or settled by him under court regulations. 

What contracts are not assignable?

Example 10. An agreement was entered into between Larson and Goddard whereby Larson was to paint Goddard's house for $250. Larson was not able to paint the house, so he assigned his contract with Goddard to another painter by the name of Nelson.

As this case stands, Nelson had no rights under this contract. 

Goddard cannot be required to accept Nelson's work in the place of Larson's, for which he contracted. The only way Nelson could acquire any rights under the contract would be for Goddard to assent to its assignment by Larson to Nelson. In reality, this would amount to Goddard's entering into a contract with Nelson. 

While this contract was to paint the house, this does not mean that Larson would be expected to do all the work himself; the nature of the work would imply that he might employ others to help him; nevertheless, this is his contract, and he is individually responsible for seeing that the work is done in a workmanlike manner. His workmen, so far as the kind of work done is concerned, are in no way responsible to the owner of the house. 

It is a well-established principle of law that a person who has assumed contractual obligations of a personal nature cannot assign his personal obligations to another to fulfil; that is, he cannot compel the party to whom he is obligated to accept performance from some other party. A person agreeing to accept performance from some person has a reason for so doing, and he has a right to know with whom he is dealing. The principle of law is that contracts requiring personal services cannot be assigned without the consent of the parties affected. 

Example 11. Barker contracted to paint a picture for Long.

This contract is not assignable. Long cannot be required under this contract to accept a picture painted by any other artist, for the reason that the services are of a personal nature requiring a particular kind of skill.

Example 12. Hobson contracted with Lent to build a brick house for him according to certain plans and specifications agreed upon. 

Hobson has a right, under his contract, to employ workmen to help build this house, and to subcontract for the construction of any portion or for the installation of any equipment or fitting ineluded in the specification. He cannot, however, assign this contract and avoid his liability without Lent's consent, and he is the one person who is wholly responsible for performance.

Example 13. On July 1, a well-known singer contracted with the owner of a music hall in Chicago to appear in a concert role for six performances a week during October and November. In the meantime the music hall changed hands, and the former owner assigned his contract with this singer to the new owner.

This singer's contract cannot be assigned without her consent. 

Should she refuse to appear, the new owner would have no redress. 

The only course open to him, not having secured her assent to the assignment, is to enter into a new contract with her. Had she appeared in accordance with her agreement which was assigned, then she would have, by her own actions, assented to the assignment, and she would be bound.

The principle of law works both ways. A person cannot be required against his will to accept the personal services of one with whom he did not contract; nor can one to whom services are due assign his right and thus require the services to be rendered to a third party. This applies only when the obligation involves personal qualifications.

Example 14. Allen contracted in writing to sell 100 tons of coal to Bass to be delivered within thirty days. Allen assigned the contract to Cragin, who agreed to deliver the coal.

In this case Bass can be compelled to accept delivery from Cragin and to pay him the contract price, since there is nothing personal in the contract and it makes no difference to Bass who delivers the coal. However, if Cragin fails to carry out the contract, Allen is liable to Bass. 

What is a novation?

Example 15. Howe entered into an agreement with Mason for the purchase of his office furniture, for $200. Howe decides that he cannot use this furniture, so he interests Ordway in the purchase of it, and all concerned agree among themselves that Ordway shall take Howe's place as the purchaser of this furniture on the terms to which Howe agreed. 

This is an example of a novation. A novation is the substituting of a new contract for an existing contract. This may be done by substituting different parties or different terms for the original parties or terms.

Example 16. Curtis had a contract with the Phelps Lumber Co. for the purchase of 50,000 feet of lumber at $34 per M. A new agreement is made whereby Curtis is to purchase 100,000 feet of lumber at $33 per M instead of 50,000 at $34 per M. This new agreement is substituted for the old agreement, and the old agreement is canceled. 

This is another example of a novation in which different terms were substituted for the original terms, which amounts to a new contract in the place of the old contract.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Only parties to a contract acquire rights under it, except in a case where a third party becomes a beneficiary. 

2. Rights under a contract of a personal nature cannot be assigned. 

3. Contracts calling for personal services where special skill, knowledge, or judgment are required cannot be assigned. 

4. Many contracts can be assigned by consent of the parties thereto that could not otherwise be assigned. 

5. One person, without being asked to do so, cannot pay another person's debts and establish himself as a creditor of that person. 

6. When the liability under a contract is joint, the two or more persons obligated are bound as one person. 

7. When the liability under a contract is joint and several, the persons obligated are individually as well as jointly liable. 

8. "We" in a promise indicates a joint obligation; "I" or "We jointly and severally" in a promise indicates an individual obligation. 

9. Where the nature of the contract permits, others may be employed to help perform, or parts to be done can be parceled out to subcontractors. 

10. A contract right to collect money or receive goods can be assigned without consent. 

11. Assignments of a contract may be oral or written. They are usually written. 

12. The notice of an assignment may be given orally or in writing. 

It is not effective until actually received by the party whose obligation was assigned. 

13. Contracts may be assigned by operation of law in the case of death or bankruptcy of one of the contracting parties.

14. An assigned contract is subject to all the defenses that might have been brought against it in the hands of the assignor. 

15. A novation is where new parties or new terms are substituted for old parties or old terms, which results in a new contract in the place of the old contract.

C. By Operation of Law III. A Novation COMMENTS 

The content of the chapter on "Operation of Contracts" is important for everyone engaged in any kind of business. It is one thing to enter into contracts and quite another thing to know how contracts operate and what rights one has under them. Innocent mistakes due to a lack of understanding cause much trouble.

Many contracts are assigned. The business of different finance companies is to handle assigned contracts. As a result of the popularity of the deferred payment plan of purchasing certain articles such as household appliances and automobiles, the business of assigning contracts has increased rapidly in recent years. In case anybody's contract is assigned, he should know what are his rights and obligations.

WRITTEN AGREEMENTS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Administrator. A person named by the probate court to settle the affairs of a deceased person.

Concurrent. Happening or becoming effective at the same time. 

Estate. A person's interest in land; his property possessions. 

Evidence. Anything offered to prove the existence of an alleged fact. 

Executor. A person named in a will to administer the estate of a deceased person.

Goods. Articles, wares, merchandise which are bought, sold, and exchanged.

Guarantee. To assume legal responsibility for an obligation or the performance of some act by another person. 

Intestate. Leaving property without leaving a will.

Legal Obligation. An obligation which can be enforced by law. 

Memorandum. Written evidence of any fact, usually a business transaction.

Statute of Frauds. A statute to prevent fraud by requiring that certain agreements be in written form. 

Contracts requiring written evidence. 

An act requiring that written evidence should be supplied in proving certain contracts was passed in England in 1676. It was entitled "An act for the prevention of frauds and perjuries." This act, commonly referred to as the Statute of Frauds, has been reenacted by nearly every state of the United States. It provides that certain contracts, or some memorandum of them, "shall be in writing" and signed by the party against whom action might be brought to enforce the contract or by his authorized agent. The contracts that generally come under this statute are as follows: 135

1. A promise that amounts to a guaranty by one party to pay a debt or assume a legal obligation contracted by another party must be written and properly signed. 

Example 1. Wassen asked a local merchant for credit. The merchant replied that he would give him credit if some responsible party would guarantee that the account would be paid. Wassen solicited his employer, who wrote a letter, addressed to the merchant, in which he stated that, in case Wassen failed to pay, he would pay for all purchases on account made by him up to and not exceeding $100. 

This letter from Wassen's employer to the merchant meets all legal requirements, and if Wassen fails to pay his account, his employer will have to pay it. A promise such as this must be in written form and signed by the party who assumes the responsibility for seeing that the debt is paid, and must be given to the prospective creditor before the debt is contracted. 

The consideration is the furnishing of goods to Wassen. This is also the consideration for Wassen's promise to pay. One consideration will support any number of promises if they are concurrent. A promise of this kind (a collateral promise), to be enforceable, must be given before or at the time the debt is contracted; otherwise, there will have to be some new consideration for the guaranty. A promise to pay a debt already contracted by 

Wassen is not enforceable without new consideration. 

2. Any contract that, by its terms, cannot be performed within one year from the making thereof must be in writing. 

Example 2. Zeller entered into a contract whereby he is to spend six weeks in each of twenty-four European cities as named, in the interest of the Empire Importing Company. 

This contract, by its terms, cannot be performed within the space of one year; therefore, to be enforceable it must be in written form, and in this case signed by both parties. 

Example 3. Willard contracted to build a stone wall, 800 feet long, for 

Jordon. This was an oral contract, and no time was stated except that 

Jordon mentioned fifteen months as being the time limit. 

A written contract is not necessary in this case. While it may take fifteen months or even longer for Willard to build this wall,

WRITTEN AGREEMENTS 

137 it would be possible to complete it in much less time by employing more men. It is only in a case where it is clearly impossible to complete the contract within one year that the written agreement is necessary.

A promise to furnish a particular person board and lodging, for a consideration as long as he lives, does not have to be written. 

He may not live a year. While this is a general principle of law, New York State, and possibly others, has a law requiring that such contracts be written.

Anyone who engages his services for a full year and is to start work on a future date, must have a written contract to be legally protected. 

3. Any contract for the sale of land or any interest in land (real estate) must be in written form.

Example 4. Howard contracted to buy four building lots on a particular street in a certain city, from the Home Development Company, at a certain price.

This contract containing full details and a complete description of the lots would have to be reduced to written form, and signed by Howard and an authorized representative of the Home Development Company. When the contract is for the sale of land, for obvious reasons a contract should be made and signed by all the parties concerned. In New York State and most other states, leases of real property (building and land) for one year or less need not be in writing.

In most cases, where written evidence of a contract is required, a memorandum signed by the party who is responsible for its fulfillment is all that is necessary, and letters may serve as written agreements. 

Example 5. Dwyer leased a house from Bates for one year from October 1.

This agreement was entered into between Dwyer and Bates on August 15. 

An oral agreement is binding in this case. The fact that the agreement dates from August 15 and the lease proper from October 1 does not affect its legality. The lease dates from the time the tenant starts to pay rent and not from the time the agreement was

made. While this oral lease is legally enforceable, leases for a year almost without exception are in written form and signed by the owner or his representative and by the tenant; the exception being mostly in villages and country places where rentals are lower and the mutual rights and obligations of landlord and tenant are less complicated and are well understood by the parties. 

4. A promise to perform some special act or to transfer some property rights in consideration of marriage must be in writing. 

Example 6. Worth promised Miss Hemming orally that, if she would marry him, he would deed her his home (house and land) and give her $10,000 in cash.

This oral promise, made by Worth and agreed to by Miss Hemming, is a good contract. That is, it is not void or illegal but merely unenforceable under the statute, and she cannot enforce the performance of the contract. Without the written agreement, even if Miss Hemming furnishes the consideration by marrying Worth, he cannot legally be required to fulfill his promise.

Promises of the kind illustrated in Example 6 must be performed or reduced to correct written form and properly signed. 

All that is necessary to satisfy the statute is written evidence. It need not be made at the time of the agreement, nor need it be given to the promisee. It is sufficient if the promisee can show a signed written promise. 

5. The promise of an executor or administrator to pay from his own private funds any of the debts of the estate he is administering must be in writing. 

Example 7. Knapp was administrator of his deceased brother's estate.

Among the many bills against the estate, the doctor's bill seemed the most urgent. Knapp promised the doctor that, if the funds of the estate were insufficient to meet all bills, he would pay the doctor's bill from his own private funds.

Knapp is not legally bound by his oral promise. For the doctor to collect from Knapp, this promise of his would have to be written and signed. In an attempt to enforce a written promise in this case, the question of consideration might be raised. It must be

WRITTEN AGREEMENTS 

139 understood that consideration in some form is necessary to make an agreement of this kind enforceable. 

6. Contracts for the sale of goods (any form of personal property) at a price of $50 or more, must be in writing, or there must be some memorandum thereof properly signed, unless some part or all of the purchase price is paid at the time the purchase is made, or some part or all of the goods are delivered and accepted by the buyer, or the sale is at public auction. 

Example 8. Lowden stepped into the office of his coaldealer and ordered twenty tons of coal at $12 per ton to be delivered before October 1. 

Lowden is to pay for this coal when he receives the bill from the dealer. 

To make the agreement in Example 8 legally binding it will be necessary for the dealer to have Lowden sign a memorandum of sale, or for Lowden to pay some part or all of the purchase price, or for the dealer to deliver a part or all of the coal and have it accepted by Lowden. 

The statutes of some of the states place the amount of the sale at more or less than $50 ($35 to $200). 

When a sale is made at public auction, a record of the sale is made, and what transpires in connection with making the sale is sufficient to meet the requirements of a sales memorandum. The sales memorandum, which must be signed by the purchaser to meet the requirements of the law, may consist of letters passed between the parties or a sales slip signed by the purchaser. It is a common practice, when goods are ordered and not paid for, to have the one ordering, the buyer, sign the sales slip.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. An oral contract is not legally enforceable when a written contract is required by law. 

2. A written memorandum containing the essential facts, and signed by the party liable for performance, will in most cases suffice for a written agreement. 

3. An agreement resulting from letters passing between the parties is a written contract. 

4. A promise by one person to answer for the debt of another

person, if made after the debt is contracted, is not enforceable unless some new consideration is given to support the promise. 

5. A promise by one person to pay for goods supplied to another, if made before or at the time the goods are delivered, need not be in writing. This would be an original promise. 

6. When a promise not to be performed in a year is in question, the time is computed from the making of the promise to the completion of performance, except leases for one year, which run from the beginning of the tenancy, regardless of when the lease was made. 

7. It must be clearly impossible to perform the contract within the year to necessitate the written form. 

8. Sales-of-land contracts should be formal written contracts containing complete terms and a full description of the property according to a survey. 

9. Written contracts are necessary when the promise is in consideration of marriage. 

10. An administrator or executor is responsible for any debts of the estate to which he personally commits himself in writing for a consideration.

COMMENTS 

Many contracts are entered into orally and fulfilled without any thought of whether or not they were legally enforceable under the statutes requiring that certain contracts be in written form. It is only when a disagreement results that one of the parties to a contract may decide to test its validity. It is for this reason that it is best to make sure at the time of entering into a contract that it conforms in every way to the provisions of the law affecting such contracts. 

A safe course to pursue, where the contracts involve a number of details or the payment of a considerable sum of money, one or both, is to have them in written form. Do not sign any agreement unless you understand fully what you are signing. Each party to a written contract should have a copy of it. One party has no right to make any change in a written agreement without the consent of the other party, and any change made in a written contract after it is signed by the parties should be properly initialed by each one to make sure that it was done with full knowledge and consent of all the parties to the original agreement.

WRITING CONTRACTS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Attested. Signed as a witness.

Circumstantial Evidence. Evidence of the circumstances in the case offered to prove other facts.

Controlling Circumstances. Circumstances which govern the decision in a disagreement over a contract.

Technical Meaning. The meaning given terms according to their use in a certain trade or profession. 

What advantage has the written contract over the oral contract?

Sometimes when the parties to an oral contract disagree, it is difficult to determine their real intention or purpose. In reaching a decision as to the rights of the parties in disagreement over their contract, the court, at the best, must rely upon the circumstances and the testimony of witnesses to determine how the case should be decided. When a contract is in written form, the terms and stipulations therein cannot be contradicted or changed by oral evidence. The court, however, may admit oral testimony for the purpose of determining the real intentions of the parties concerned. 

Example 1. Hays contracted to buy from the Arco Refining Co. various grades of sugar, the price stated being "base 4.2." The contract did not explain the meaning of "base 4.2.” Oral evidence was offered to show that it means $.042 a pound for granulated sugar, and a differential for other grades.

In this case oral testimony would be permitted to show the intention of the parties and the meaning of the statement "base 4.2." Neither party could escape responsibility under this contract because it can be explained. 144

WRITING CONTRACTS 

145 

What should the written contract contain?

Certain parts of all contracts conform to the same general plan, 

1. The date (at the beginning or at the end) 

2. The names and addresses of the parties 

3. A statement of the purpose of the contract 

4. The consideration 

5. Stipulations and conditions affecting the parties 

6. Time allowed for performance 

7. Signature of the parties 

In preparing a written contract great care should be used to state every part of it fully and clearly so that any possibility of a misunderstanding may be avoided. There is less chance of a misunderstanding where all details are fully stated than where an attempt has been made to make the contract short and concise.

This agreement made in duplicate the twentieth day of 

July, 19.., by and between Herman J. Black, of the village of Depew, state of New York, party of the first part, and John T. Haws, of the city of Buffalo, state of 

New York, party of the second part. 

Witnesseth: that the party of the first part agrees to construct for the party of the second part a two-story, four-door garage on his home premises in Buffalo, according to certain plans and specifications which accompany and are a part of this agreement. 

The party of the second part, in consideration thereof, agrees to pay the party of the first part the sum of $5,500 as follows: $1,500 when the foundation is completed; $2,000 when the roof is on; and, $2,000 when the building is completed and ready for occupancy.

The party of the first part agrees to commence work on the foundation not later than August 15, 19. ., and to have the building completed and ready for occupancy not later than December 15, 19...

In Witness Whereof, the parties herein have hereunto set their hands in duplicate the day and year first above written.

Herman J. Black John T. Haws

This is a simple written contract prepared in duplicate and signed by the two parties concerned. The specifications for the building furnish a complete guide for the builder, and the details of the written contract are sufficiently complete to meet all requirements. 

The main difference between a simple written contract and a formal contract is the use of the seal on the latter. A formal contract may be signed, witnessed, and sealed as follows:

In Witness Whereof, the parties have hereunto set their hands and seals the day and year first above mentioned.

Witnesses: 

John C. Hall for both parties

If the parties to this contract wish to acknowledge it, they go before a notary public, who will record their acknowledgment on the contract as follows: 

State of New York 

County of Erie On the twentieth day of July, one thousand nine hundred and 

Herman J. Black (L. S.) John T. Haws (L. S.) 

SS before me personally appeared Herman J. Black and John T. Haws, to me personally known to be the persons described in and who executed the foregoing instrument, and they severally acknowledged to me that they executed the same.

The purpose of an acknowledgment, as stated before, is to do away with the necessity of proving the signatures. 

Witnesses: 

David C. Crane 

Notary Public for Erie County, New York 

Observe the following suggestions: 

1. No one should sign a contract until he has read every part of it carefully.

2. A contract should be worded as simply as possible to insure clearness. 

3. All details and terms should be fully stated. 

4. No blank spaces should be filled in or any change made after the contract has been signed, unless the parties concerned initial the same.

147 Someone who can write will insert William D. Roberts's name, and he will make his mark just below or in some conspicuous place on the instrument, and then someone will write just below, "his mark." Signing an instrument in this way meets every legal requirement. Serious illness may make it impossible for a person to write.

Any important instrument so executed should be witnessed and properly acknowledged. Forgery is too easy. The Federal government and the laws of some states require that such signatures shall be witnessed by one and sometimes two witnesses. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Written contracts are not desirable or possible in every case. 

2. Written contracts are desirable in case the terms or stipulations are involved, and in many other cases they are required by law. 

3. The written contract supplies tangible evidence that cannot be varied or denied by testimony. 

4. Oral evidence may be introduced to show the meaning of the language used in a written contract when it is uncertain, technical, or otherwise unintelligible. 

5. A written contract should contain all details and all fact information which will make possible a correct understanding and interpretation of it. 

6. The untrained and unskilled individual should not attempt to prepare an important written contract. 

7. A simple written contract is signed by the parties thereto; while a formal contract is not only signed by the parties, but is sealed by them and usually is acknowledged before a notary public or other officer.
