COMMENTS 

The content of this chapter reveals how important it is to prepare carefully written contracts and at times to have the contract drawn up by an attorney. A large transaction containing many specifications involves so many details and legal requirements that it is not advisable for an inexperienced person to attempt to prepare the contract required. 

The parties who sign a written contract should study every part of it before signing, question every part that is not fully understood, and make sure that the stipulations and terms are correctly stated. These precautions very often will save trouble for all parties concerned later on.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Abrogate. To annul; to revoke or repeal. 

Automatically Discharged. Discharged as a result of some provision or condition, or because of something happening. 

Confidential Relations. Close intimacy; secret; communicating in confidence.

Contingency. Something unforeseen that may possibly happen. 

In Statu Quo. In the same condition they were before making the contract. 

Material Alteration. An alteration or change in a contract after it was made that affects some important element of the contract. 

Merger. The absorbing of one contract in another, resulting in a new contract in the place of an old contract.

Prerequisite. Something necessary to be done before. 

Subsequent Costs. Costs that accrue after an accepted settlement of a debt.

Subsequent Impossibility. An impossibility that developed after the contract was made. 

When is a contract discharged by performance?

Example 1. Ryan contracted to build a cement sidewalk in front of 

Judson's home for $180. Ryan completed the walk in accordance with the contract, and Judson paid him the $180. 

This contract was discharged by performance. Each party fulfilled his part of the agreement. When Ryan completed the walk, the contract was executed on his part, and when Judson paid the $180, the contract was fully executed. 

A contract is discharged by performance when the terms of the contract are fully carried out as to time, place, and conditions. 

Performance is the usual way of discharging a contract, but it is 149

not the only way; some contingency may make performance impossible, or for some legal reason the contract may be discharged. 

When is a contract substantially performed? 

Example 2. Robbins installed a heating system in Matthews's home under a contract whereby he guaranteed that every part of the house could be heated to 70 degrees in zero weather. The test showed that the temperature in one bedroom could not be raised above 68 degrees. 

Should Matthews refuse to accept this heating system or pay Robbins, and should Robbins take action to recover the contract price, it is probable that the court would declare this contract substantially performed and that Matthews would have to pay the contract price, less such damage as he could show for the defective performance.

A contract is considered to be substantially performed when the work has been done honestly and in good faith; and even though there has been some deviation from the exact stipulations or terms specified therein, it did not materially affect the contract. 

Substantial performance of a contract can be claimed only where the thing contracted about is of a mechanical nature or is work or labor not involving personal taste. 

What happens when the contract involves personal taste?

Example 3. Piper, an artist, contracted to paint a picture of Mrs. 

Hardman for Mr. Hardman. The picture was to be copied from a photograph, and Piper guaranteed that the reproduction would be satisfactory to Mr. Hardman.

When this picture is completed, Mr. Hardman is the sole judge as to whether or not it is satisfactory to him. If he is not satisfied with it, he does not have to accept it or pay the contract price. 

This contract involves the question of personal taste and it must be performed to Mr. Hardman's satisfaction. 

Is a contract discharged when a note or a check is accepted in payment?

Example 4. Good built a house for Avery. When the house was completed, Avery lacked $600 of having money enough to make the last payment. Good filed a mechanic's lien on the house and finally accepted 

Avery's $600 note for six months, at 6% interest.

This contract called for the payment of money, and Good did not have to accept Avery's note. But he did accept it; now the question arises as to whether the original contract is discharged or whether this note is to be regarded as a conditional payment. 

If it is a conditional payment, it does not discharge the contract until it is paid. The rule is that a debtor's note taken in payment is always conditional payment, unless it clearly appears that it was accepted in full discharge. When a third party's note is taken, it is in full discharge, but if it is regularly endorsed, the endorser assumes responsibility for its payment. If Good canceled his mechanic's lien, it would appear that he intended to accept Avery's note and discharge the contract. If he allowed his lien to stand, it would appear that he had accepted the note only as a conditional payment; and if it is not paid when due, Good can ignore it entirely and take action on his lien to recover the $600 unpaid. Or, he can sue on the note, which is usually done because it is simpler, and if he is paid, both the contract and the note are discharged.

It is generally held that a note or a check accepted in payment of a pre-existing debt is taken conditionally, and that the debt or contract is not discharged until the note or check is paid. 

Is a contract discharged where some contingency makes it impossible for one of the parties to perform? 

Example 5. The Penn Coal Co. entered into a contract with the 

Western Fuel Co. of Chicago on April 1, 19—, whereby the Penn Coal Co. 

was to deliver to the Western Fuel Co., in Chicago, 100,000 tons of hard coal before November 1, 19—. A strike in the mines of the Penn Coal Co. kept them from fulfilling their contract. 

The Penn Coal Co. are liable on their contract with the Western 

Fuel Co. They could have provided for unforeseen contingencies at the time of entering into this contract; but failing to do so, they cannot escape responsibility. They should have inserted a clause in their contract to the effect that their agreement is subject to unforeseen contingencies over which they have no control, and which may make it impossible for them to fulfill their contract; such a clause would have relieved them of responsibility.

When is a contract discharged by impossibility of performance? 

We have already learned that no contract exists if, at the time it was entered into, it was clearly evident that performance was impossible; this is termed prior impossibility. 

Where impossibility of performance arises after the contract is made, the promisor is not excused from performance, and he is liable to an action for damages if he fails to perform. As explained under Example 5, he should protect himself against contingencies or subsequent impossibility of performance by a clause in the contract. An exception exists in the case of personal service contracts. 

Example 6. Martin contracted to drive a taxicab for six months for

The Green Taxicab Company. After working for three months, he was taken ill and could not serve under his contract. 

In this case Martin is not liable under his contract. In contracting for personal services the uncertainties of life and health have to be taken into consideration, and the law considers continued ability to perform as an implied term of the contract. Had either party become legally barred from operating taxicabs, the contract would have been automatically terminated as a result of legal impossibility.

Example 7. The Ladden Shoe Company contracted to sell 10,000 pairs to be made in a particular factory on special machines. Within six weeks thereafter and before the shoes could possibly be made, the factory and its contents were destroyed by fire. 

The performance of this contract depends upon the continued existence of this factory and the special machines. There is in the contract an implied condition that if anything happens to the factory or machines making performance impossible, the contract is automatically discharged.

Where the performance of a contract depends upon the continued existence of a special thing, the destruction of this thing discharges the contract.

How may a contract be discharged by agreement of the parties? 

Example 8. Lawrence leased a house from Bates for one year. After living in the house for five months, circumstances made it necessary for Lawrence to move to another part of the country, and he asked Bates to

30 arte sary Bate release him from his lease. Bates agreed to the release to take effect in thirty days.

A contract is created by the agreement of the parties, and if they choose, they may terminate and discharge it by agreement. 

If the contract has not been performed, each party may waive his rights under it, and the waiver of the rights of one is the consideration for the waiver of the rights of the other. 

Has one party to a contract a right to break his promise and then enforce the contract against the other party? 

Example 9. Grey agreed to deliver goods to Sayer on May 1. He failed to deliver them on this date, but finally delivered them on May 15. 

Sayer refused to accept them, and Grey sued for damages. 

Grey has broken his contract; therefore, he cannot enforce it against the other party, who is in no way at fault. 

When one party has performed his part of the contract, he must receive consideration for his release of the other party. 

Example 10. Hood purchased a camping outfit from Doner for $95, and agreed to work for him for thirty days to pay for it. After the outfit was delivered, Doner decided he did not want Hood to work and released him. 

Doner's promise to release Hood does not bind him unless Hood gives a new consideration or the release is in writing and under seal. Otherwise, Doner could still legally require Hood to work even though he had agreed to release him. 

A contract may be discharged by a provision therein. 

Example 11. An insurance policy provided that the insured building should be used as a warehouse, but that no explosives should be stored in it, and the policy also provided that a breach of warranty avoided the policy. A ten-gallon can of gasoline which was placed inside of the warehouse until it could be used in the trucks caught fire, exploded, and the warehouse burned.

Under the terms of the policy, the presence of gasoline in the building automatically avoided the policy. It would make no difference whether it was the cause of the fire, or whether it was in the building at the time of the fire. The violation of these restrictions automatically discharged this contract by its own provisions.

A contract may be so worded that it provides for its own discharge. For example, it may contain a provision that one party may terminate it by giving a certain notice or performing certain conditions. 

What is the meaning of legal tender?

Under our monetary system legal tender is money which Congress has declared must be accepted if offered in payment of such obligations as are to be discharged by the payment of money. 

Section 43 (b) of the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 provides that "All coins and currencies of the United States (including Federal Reserve notes and circulating notes of Federal Reserve banks and national banking associations) heretofore or hereafter coined or issued shall be legal tender for all debts, public and private."

Tender is an offer to perform an obligation, with the present ability to perform it, so that acceptance of the tender by the other party will then and there be complete performance. A tender may be made of any contract duty, such as to pay money, deliver goods, render services, etc.

Proper tender, to be legal, must be exactly according to the contract, at the proper time and place, to the proper person, and there must be a present ability to perform. If money is due, legal-tender money must be offered. If goods are due, goods meeting the requirements of the contract must be tendered. 

What is the effect of tender?

If a tender is accepted, the obligation of the party making the tender is discharged. If a tender of money is refused, the debt is not discharged, but interest from that date and any subsequent costs are not recoverable. If any other tender is refused, the person making it is excused from performing his obligation, and he may sue for breach of contract.

How are the conditions affecting the discharge of a contract classified?

In every contract there are definite conditions imposed upon one or both of the parties to the contract which must be fully per-

formed before the contract is discharged. These conditions are classified as precedent, concurrent, and subsequent.

Example 12. The officers of a closed bank offered to its depositors a three-point plan for opening. One of the points provided for the sale of a certain number of shares of stock in the reorganized bank. Anyone who subscribed for this stock would not be obligated to pay for it until all three points provided for in the reorganization plans had been consummated. 

The three points to be realized are conditions precedent to the payments for the stock.

A precedent condition in a contract is one which must be fulfilled or realized by one of the parties before the other party is under any obligations to perform his part of the contract. 

Example 13. Haines purchased a used car from the City Garage Company for $600. The City Garage Company is to give Haines a bill of sale for the car at the time he pays the $600. The two conditions in the agreement are to be performed concurrently by the parties. 

A concurrent condition is one which must be fulfilled by one party at the same time another condition is fulfilled by the other party. That is, both conditions must be complied with at the same time in order that the contract may be performed according to its terms.

When a contract contains a condition precedent or concurrent, the liability of one or both parties is suspended until the happening of the condition. 

Example 14. Bowen agreed to sell and Green agreed to buy Bowen's horse for $500; delivery and payment to be made on May 1. It was agreed that if the horse did not trot a mile in 2:10 before November 1,

Green could return the horse and get his money back. 

The failure of the horse to trot a mile in 2:10 is a condition subsequent. It does not prevent or postpone the obligations to deliver and make payment on May 1; but, if it happens, the contract may be entirely abrogated.

A condition subsequent is one which does not suspend liability but, if it happens, may abrogate a contract already made. 

How is a contract discharged by operation of law?

The law operates to discharge a contract when its performance is made unlawful; when a written instrument has been materially

altered; when death or disability of one of the parties occurs; when an old agreement is merged in a new agreement; and when one of the parties becomes bankrupt. 

Example 15. The Merchants Dress Company rented from Begbee a loft in an old building in a congested part of the city, for a term of ten years, and therein established their factory. Five years later this building was condemned by the authorities as being a fire hazard, and the occupants were given ninety days in which to vacate. The contract between the Merchants Dress Co. and Begbee, whereby the Dress Company had the use of the loft in this building, was discharged by the operation of this law which gives the authorities the right to condemn any building within the city limits that is unsafe or unfit for use. 

How is a contract discharged by a material alteration? 

Example 16. Sloan endorsed Dart's note as surety. The note was dated July 15, and was given for six months after date. Before Dart delivered the signed note, he changed the time to nine months and inserted "with interest at 6% per annum." Sloan knew nothing of these changes.

This is a material alteration made with intent to defraud or deceive Sloan, and he is relieved from liability on this note which he endorsed.

When a material alteration is made by one of the parties to a written instrument, or by someone else with his consent, and without the consent of the other party to the instrument, the contract will be discharged, provided the alteration was made with intent to defraud.

When an alteration is innocently made without intent to defraud, the contract is not necessarily discharged, but may be enforced as originally made. For instance, in Example 16, had the payee added "with interest at 6% per annum" after he received the note, believing that it was overlooked and that it should be added, it is not likely that this alteration, made in good faith, would discharge the original contract. It is not good practice, however, to change a written agreement after it is signed by the parties. All modifications, corrections, or changes should be made before the agreement is finally signed.

When is a contract discharged by the death of one of the parties? 

Example 17. Graham entered into a contract with the Proof Paint

Company to act for them as general sales manager for one year from January 1, 19—. He served for about five months when he was taken sick and died.

Death in this case discharged this contract. Any executory contract for personal services, in which skill, taste, and judgment are required, or where there is a confidential relation between the parties, is discharged by the death of either party. But a contract between parties, not requiring personal services, is not discharged by the death of one of the parties, and his estate may be held for its performance.

In case of the death of one of two joint contractors, the contract is not discharged, and the surviving joint contractor will be held to complete the contract.

Can a contract be discharged by an act of one of the parties? 

Example 18. Weaver agreed to build a retaining wall for Holbart for $200. Holbart was to furnish all the material. He never made any provisions for the material; as a result Weaver could not build the wall. 

Weaver's obligation to build the wall is discharged, but Holbart is liable on the contract for damages. The furnishing of the material was a condition precedent to Weaver's liability. The breach of contract by Holbart excused Weaver. One party cannot discharge the contract; he can discharge his own liability by performing, or discharge the other party by his own breach. 

How is a contract discharged by a merger?

Example 19. Loomis was owing Ball $240 on an open book account. 

Ball agreed to accept Loomis's secured note for $240 for one year at 6% interest and cancel the book account. 

This is a novation or merger by agreement. By this agreement the contract involving the open book account is merged in the new agreement and is thereby discharged. 

Example 20. Bryan sued Jassen to recover $300 which Jassen owed him on account. The result of the suit was a judgment for $300 against 

Jassen in favor of Bryan, and by this operation of law the open book account became merged in the judgment.

A simple contract may be merged in a new contract under seal, thereby discharging the simple contract; or, an unsecured obligation or open book account may be merged in a judgment for the same amount, thereby discharging the old contract. 

How is a contract discharged through bankruptcy?

Example 21. Gordon, as a result of a court action, was declared a bankrupt, and a trustee was appointed to settle his business affairs. The trustee found that Gordon's gross assets made it possible for him to pay 

65¢ on a dollar. Gordon owed the Home Baking Co. $312, and the trustee settled this amount by paying them $202.80. 

This obligation was legally discharged in bankruptcy by the trustee's paying the Home Baking Company the $202.80. Gordon is legally relieved from this obligation; and all his obligations to pay money will be discharged in the same way as a result of the bankruptcy proceedings. While a discharge in bankruptcy makes the obligation unenforceable if the debtor pleads his discharge as a defense, a new promise to pay the discharged debt is enforceable (if in writing, in New York). The consideration for the new promise is the moral obligation remaining after the discharge. "Bankruptcy" is explained in the following Unit of this text. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Performance is the usual way of discharging a contract. By performance according to the terms of the contract, either party discharges his obligation under the contract. 

2. Substantial performance can be claimed only in a contract not involving the element of personal taste or satisfaction. 

3. A contract involving personal taste, that by its terms is to be completed to the satisfaction of the party paying the bill or for whom the work is done, makes him the sole judge as to whether or not the work is satisfactory. 

4. The acceptance of a note or a check in payment discharges the contract only when the parties thereto intend that it shall be discharged and there is evidence of such intention. 

5. An unforeseen contingency will not discharge a contract unless a clause is inserted therein which would relieve the party who is

宣言 ​affected by the contingency from performing, in which case the other party would be released and the contract would be discharged. 

6. A prior impossibility renders a contract void. 

7. A subsequent impossibility discharges a contract only when protected against by a clause therein, except in the case of a contract for personal services requiring taste or skill, or in the case of the destruction of something necessary to the contract. 

8. A contract results from an agreement and, while executory, it may be terminated and discharged by an agreement of the parties. 

9. One party who has broken a contract can never enforce it against the other party. 

10. A contract may provide for its own discharge by a provision therein for giving a notice, or performing a condition. 

11. A tender is an offer to pay or perform an obligation. 

12. Legal tender is money which the law states shall be acceptable for the payment of debts. 

13. Precedent, concurrent, and subsequent conditions affect the discharge of a contract. 

14. The law will operate to discharge a contract in case it is or becomes unlawful, in case of a material alteration, in case of death or disability of one of the parties, in case of a merger, and in case of bankruptcy. 

15. Death of one of the parties will discharge an executory contract for personal services only when skill, taste, or confidential relations are a factor. 

16. Breach of the contract by one of the parties not only discharges the other party to the contract, but makes the one who committed the breach liable in damages.

IX. Discharge in Bankruptcy

COMMENTS 

Bankruptcy proceedings against a man mar his business record. Regardless of how justifiable they may be, a critical public is inclined to treat him with a degree of skepticism for some time thereafter; for this reason many bankrupts seek a new location for a fresh start. 

Bankruptcy serves an important purpose, however, by making it possible for a debtor who is hopelessly involved financially to settle with his creditors under the provisions of the Federal Bankruptcy Act, and as a result be freed from his debts so that he can start again from the beginning. 

Another purpose which the bankruptcy act serves is to make it possible for the creditors to proceed against a debtor who is not meeting his financial obligations and force a settlement so that they may not be required to suffer any further losses.

Experience has shown that an equitable bankruptcy law is very necessary, and there is no doubt that the present bankruptcy law is serving an important purpose, in many cases, in the interests of both debtors and creditors.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Court Proceedings. The action of the court in hearing a case. 

Economic Activities. Occupational activities in which people are engaged for a livelihood. 

In Default. Not fulfilling promises; not meeting obligations.

Quasi Contract. Not in reality a contract, but as if a contract did exist. 

Right of Action. Right of the injured party to avail himself of the services of the court to collect damages. 

Subsidiary Terms. Terms in a contract that explain, qualify or add to the principal terms. 

What is a breach of contract? (1) Any act or omission, by one or both of the parties to a contract, which violates the terms of the agreement is a breach of contract. (2) The contract obligation of one party to a contract is discharged by a wrongful act of the other party which constitutes a breach of contract. The wrongful act may be his failure to perform some act which he has contracted to perform, or it may be his commitment of some act which, according to the terms of the contract, he should not have committed. 

In case there is either failure or refusal of one of the parties to fulfill the agreement, the contract is broken and in its place a new obligation is imposed on the party in default. This new obligation is in the form of a liability for damages which must be paid by the defaulting party to the injured party. The new right which the injured party acquires is called a right of action. 

How may a contract be broken? 

1. A party may refuse to be bound by the terms of a contract he has entered into. 174

2. A party may commit acts which will make it impossible for him to fulfill the terms of his contract. 

3. A party may fail to perform, wholly or partially, what he promised. 

Example 1. Lance contracted to furnish the Garden Hotel with 30 dozens of eggs each day throughout the year for 45¢ a dozen. During December, when eggs were worth 60¢ a dozen, he delivered only about 15 dozen a day.

The Garden Hotel management refused to continue to take the eggs from 

Lance under their contract with him.

The refusal of the Garden Hotel management to continue to take the eggs from Lance was justified because they had been discharged from their contract to take eggs. 

When a contract is broken by one of the parties, the injured party not only has a right of action for damages, but he is also discharged from his obligations under the contract, unless the violation of the particular term did not defeat the main purpose of the contract, or the contract is divisible. 

Example 2. Garris sold 1,000 bushels of Burbank potatoes to Bender, and agreed to deliver them not later than October 31. When Garris delivered the potatoes he found it necessary to put in two bags of White 

Mountain Potatoes to make up the 1,000 bushels.

This act on the part of Garris by which he deviated slightly from the terms of the contract is not enough of a breach to make it possible for Bender to cancel the entire agreement. It is substantial performance. Had Garris put in 200 bags of White Mountain potatoes and said nothing to Bender about it, this act on the part of Garris would have amounted to a breach of contract that would have given Bender the right to refuse to accept or pay for any of the potatoes and also a right of action for damages. 

How is a contract broken by one of the contracting parties renouncing his liability thereunder? 

Example 3. On July 7 Wade contracted to purchase 100,000 yards of woolen goods from the New England Woolen Company and to accept delivery during October. On August 10, Wade wrote a letter to the New 

England Woolen Company stating that he would not accept delivery of the goods in October. At the time the New England Woolen Co. received 

Wade's letter they had more than 50,000 yards ready for delivery.

Wade has broken his contract with the New England Woolen Company by declaring in advance that he would not accept delivery of the goods purchased, and they may bring action against him at once to collect damages. A breach of contract arises when one of the parties refuses to perform his part, even though such refusal is before the time of performance, and the injured party may institute court proceedings at once. This is called anticipatory breach. However, the innocent party may refuse to accept the breach and thus keep the contract alive.

A party to a contract may start to perform but refuse to continue; in which case the other party is excused from further performance.

Example 4. Bond, a second hand furniture dealer, bought from a hotel 

300 used mattresses which he intended to rebuild and sell as rebuilts. He agreed to pay at the rate of $3 a piece for these mattresses and to accept delivery within one week from the time of making the agreement. Bond accepted delivery of 100 mattresses when he learned that a sanitary code would not permit him to sell rebuilt mattresses. He could sell them only as second-hand mattresses, so he notified the hotel that he would not accept any more mattresses. Under the circumstances, the hotel is excused from further performance. 

Bond broke his contract with the hotel, and they are entitled to the contract price for the 300 mattresses or to damages for breach of contract. This is an indivisible contract. Whether a contract is entire or divisible does not depend solely on how the price is stated. The intent is to be determined from the whole transaction. 

A party may commit acts which will make it impossible for him to fulfill the terms of his contract.

Example 5. Warren secured a contract from Ross to deliver orders for one year for the Globe Department Store owned by Ross. He bought a small delivery truck for the purpose. Within six months Ross sold the 

Globe Department Store, and the new owners refused to continue Warren's delivery service.

Ross, by selling out, put it out of his power to perform fully his part of the contract, and Warren may consider the contract broken. Ross is responsible to Warren for whatever damage he suffered by the breach of contract.

The party who seeks to recover damages for a breach of contract through nonperformance must show that the other party's promise was not dependent upon his act. 

Example 6. Harder agreed to pay Law $50 if he would find purchasers for a touring car and a light truck belonging to Harder. Law succeeded in finding a purchaser for the truck, but he could do nothing with the touring car.

The finding of a purchaser for both cars was a condition precedent to any liability on the part of Harder. In order to recover the $50, Law would have to show complete performance on his part, and since he cannot, he has no claim. 

Where there are two or more promises in a contract independent of each other, a breach of one does not discharge the other. 

Example 7. Evans leased a building from Thomas for three years with the privilege of renewing for another term of three years at the same rental. When the three years were up Evans was in arrears for two months rent, and Thomas refused to renew the lease. 

In this case, payment of the rent is not a condition on which the renewal of the lease depends. The promise to renew the lease and the promise to pay the rent are independent of each other. 

Evans can demand a renewal of the lease. However, failing to pay the rent according to the terms of the lease would amount to a breach of contract. 

What rights has the injured party in the case of a broken contract? 

1. The injured party may seek to recover damages resulting from the breach of contract. 

2. He may have a right to enforce performance. 

3. He may be discharged from his own obligation. 

Whether the injured party may take action to recover damages, or to enforce performance, or whether he may be discharged from his own obligation depends upon the nature of the terms violated by the other party.

To recover damages caused by another's violation of the terms of a contract the injured party must show (1) that the breach which he acted upon occurred before the time of performance (an

anticipatory breach), or (2) that the breach occurred at the time fixed for performance and that he was then willing, ready, and able to perform his part of the contract. 

In addition to showing one of the conditions mentioned, he must show proof of being damaged.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A contract is broken when one of the parties refuses or fails to perform his part or by an act makes it impossible to perform. 

2. A breach of a contract by one party gives the injured party a right of action for damages and also discharges him from the contract. 

3. A breach of an unimportant term in a contract (a subsidiary term) or a slight deviation from a major term may not amount to a breach of contract. 

4. An entire contract calls for full performance and anything less than complete performance amounts to a breach of contract. 

5. In a divisible contract the failure to perform a part of the contract does not amount to a breach of the whole contract. Recovery can be had for the part performed. 

6. A right of action in favor of the injured party arises at once when one party to a contract refuses to perform. 

7. Where one party refuses to perform, in advance of the time for performance, it is called an anticipatory breach. 

8. The injured party has a right of action for damages against the other party to a contract who makes performance impossible. 

9. A contract is divisible when one part can be performed independent of another part, or when the consideration is divisible.

COMMENTS 

In the course of our numerous economic activities many contracts are entered into and fulfilled according to their terms, but many other contracts are entered into and broken in some way. 

This unit on Breach of Contracts explains the ways contracts are generally broken. When a contract is broken as a result of circumstances over which the parties have no control it is a legal breach, but fair dealing requires an amicable settlement so that there may be little or no loss suffered by either party. But, if the contract is deliberately broken by one of the parties, the injured party must defend his interests, and very often he is forced to suffer a loss. For this reason any one entering into a contract should know what acts by one of the parties amount to a breach of the contract which would discharge the other party from performing, and at the same time give him a right of action for any damage he has suffered.

REMEDIES TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Counterclaim. A claim asserted by the defendant against the plaintiff who has brought action to collect a claim from the defendant. 

Demurrer. A pleading by the defendant in an action, admitting that all the facts alleged by the plaintiff are true, but still claiming that they do not entitle him to recover.

Jury Trial. A trial of a case in court before a selected group of persons who will render a verdict based on the facts brought out by evidence. 

Legal Remedies. The remedies which are available to the plaintiff through court action.

Lien. A legal claim upon real or personal property for the satisfaction of some debt.

Outlawed Claim. A claim that has run so long that it is barred by the 

Statute of Limitations. 

Question of Fact. Question which has to do only with the facts in the case and which must be decided by the jury. 

Question of Law. Question in a suit of law which must be decided by the judge according to legal principles. 

Reciprocal Agreement. One party agrees to do something in consideration for which another party agrees to do something. 

Setoff. One claim that offsets another claim. 

Statute of Limitations. A statute that limits the time during which action may be started.

Statutory Period. The period during which a debt may run without becoming outlawed under the Statute of Limitations. 

Testimony. The oral evidence of the witnesses in a suit at law. 

What is a right of action?

The breaking of a contract by one of the parties thereto gives the injured party a right of action through the courts to recover 181

any damages he has suffered. The injured party may bring suit against the party who has defaulted in his contract in an attempt to force him to pay damages. 

How may a right of action be settled out of court?

A right of action may be settled and discharged without resorting to legal proceedings, if the parties agree upon a sum of money to be paid by the party in default to the injured party and it is actually paid in settlement of the dispute. In connection with such a settlement the injured party will give the other party a release under seal, which generally is sufficient to discharge the right of action even without payment. 

How may a settlement be made by arbitration?

When the parties are in disagreement about the terms of a contract or the performance or lack of performance by one of the parties, they may agree to submit their case to arbitration. This is usually carried out by each party to the contract selecting a man, and the two men selected will select a third man to act with them. 

The three men selected will hear both sides of the case and give their decision. The agreement of two of the three will amount to a final decision and parties must adjust their differences accordingly.

The courts will sustain agreements to arbitrate, and when a case has been settled by arbitration the parties thereto or one of the parties should have the decision of the arbitrators confirmed by the court; then it is equivalent to a judgment and is enforceable in the usual way. Arbitration is a speedy and inexpensive method of settling disputes. 

What effect has the lapse of time on a right of action?

Where the right of action is allowed to run beyond a certain time, usually six years from the time action might have been taken, it is made unenforceable by the Statute of Limitations if the defendant pleads the statute.

The statute varies in the different states. In most states the statutory period for action of debts or contracts is six years. In some states real property (real estate) actions are allowed to run

REMEDIES 

183 for a longer period, and in most states judgments and contracts under seal are allowed to run twenty years. 

When the defendant in the case is absent from the state for any part of the statutory period the time is extended to cover the time of absence.

If the plaintiff is under a legal disability such as infancy or insanity at the time the right of action arises, the time will be extended. This disability, however, will have no effect if it did not exist at the time the statute begins to run. 

How can a right of action which has lapsed be renewed? 

A right of action that has lapsed under the Statute of Limitations may be renewed by an acknowledgment or by a new promise, which under some statutes must be in writing, or by a payment on account. The statute begins to run anew from the time the payment is made. The time under the statute varies in the different states; therefore, the laws of one's own state should be consulted.

Remedies which injured parties may avail themselves of in case of breach of contract.

The remedies provided by our laws to furnish redress to the injured party who has suffered loss as a result of a breach of contract are called civil remedies. These remedies are secured through the courts by means of a "suit at law." In case the wrong committed is against society, such as murder, robbery, kidnaping, etc., it is a public wrong, and is called a crime. In cases of crime, the penalty is provided by our criminal law. This study is confined to civil remedies and the ways in which they are secured. 

What are the usual formal steps in a "suit at law”?

The first step is for the party who takes action in a suit at law (the injured party) to procure the issuance of a summons, either by an attorney or by the clerk or other court officer, and have it served upon the party whom he wishes to sue. The party who brings action is called the plaintiff, and the party against whom action is brought is called the defendant. 

The following are the usual steps in a suit at law: The injured

party will engage the services of an attorney who will secure the summons, and serve it or have it served on the named defendant. 

The summons, when served, is notice to the defendant that he is being sued. The summons specifies the time within which the defendant must appear and answer, or judgment will be taken by default. The trial may be averted by a settlement outside of court. Following the summons, the steps in order are: 

1. The attorneys for the opposing parties prepare and present their pleadings to each other and to the court. 

2. The court trial before a judge or before a judge and a jury. 

3. The judgment which results from the verdict or decision of the judge or of the jury. (When the case involves questions of facts, the trial is generally before a jury.) 

4. The taking of defendant's property under execution. 

5. The levy and sale to satisfy the judgment. 

What are the pleadings in a suit at law?

The pleadings are formal statements of both the plaintiff and the defendant by which they present to the court and to each other their respective versions of the question in dispute. The attorney for the plaintiff prepares the complaint against the defendant, and the attorney for the defendant prepares the answer to the complaint.

After the summons has been served the parties are required to have their pleadings ready within a certain definite time, prescribed by statute or the rules of court. In some lower courts, such as justice of the peace court, oral pleadings are allowed. 

What is the complaint and how is it entered?

The complaint, which in some states is called the petition or declaration, contains a statement of the cause of the action which the plaintiff sets forth as his reason for bringing suit against the defendant. It is prepared by the plaintiff's attorney and signed and sworn to by the plaintiff.

The complaint is usually served on the defendant with the summons, but it may be served later. The complaint (a copy) must always be served upon the defendant or his attorney and generally the original must be filed in the court.

REMEDIES 

185 

What is the answer and how is it made?

The answer, sometimes called the plea, is a brief statement of the defendant's reason for not complying with the plaintiff's demands. It is prepared by the defendant's attorney and signed and sworn to by the defendant. The answer may deny the claim of the plaintiff, or it may admit it and set up a counterclaim or set-off. 

When a counterclaim is set up it is necessary for the plaintiff, if he wishes to deny it, to reply. This reply is in reality the plaintiff's answer to the claims or new facts set forth by the defendant. 

The defendant is given a certain number of days, usually twenty, to file his answer to the complaint. If his answer is not filed, the plaintiff is given judgment against the defendant by default. The defendant's answer to the plaintiff's complaint may be in the form of an answer or a demurrer. The demurrer is not used in the 

New York courts. The same result is reached by motion for judgment on the pleadings. 

What is the trial and how is it conducted? 

The second step in the progress of a suit at law is the trial before the judge or before the judge and the jury. A jury is a body of 

A COURTROOM SCENE P. & A. Photos

persons, usually twelve, who are drawn by the clerk of the court from a selected list of citizens who are available for jury duty. 

The jury is brought together when a case is to be tried, and after qualifying for service on the particular case, they are required to take oath to decide the case according to the evidence brought before them. 

What questions are to be decided?

The questions which are to be settled by a suit at law may be questions of law or questions of fact. Questions of law are decided by the judge without a jury, when the facts of the case are admitted, and the question to be decided is how to apply the law to the facts in the case. When the testimony of the witnesses differs, the facts remain to be determined. Questions of fact in the case are generally tried before a jury. Points of law must be decided by the judge, but the facts in the case must be decided by the jury. 

In civil cases a jury trial may be waived by the parties and questions of fact as well as questions of law left to the decision of the judge.

In some minor courts a jury trial is not had unless the defendant demands a jury at the commencement of the proceedings. 

How is the evidence in the case secured?

In the process of trying the case, all written documents and papers pertaining to the case may be offered as evidence. Persons who know something about the case are subpoenaed as witnesses and sworn to tell the truth. The evidence in any suit at law is the testimony of witnesses, and the written documents and papers pertaining to the case.

Evidence is not admissible in the case unless it complies with the rules of evidence, which are intricate and technical, but are all designed to secure a fair and impartial trial. 

What is the subpoena and how is it served?

A subpoena is an order issued under authority of the court commanding that the person named therein appear at a certain time to give testimony in a certain case. A person who, after being subpoenaed as a witness, fails to appear or refuses to testify is subject to a fine for contempt of court.

REMEDIES 

187 It is not within the power of the court to compel the attendance of a witness who lives outside the jurisdiction of the court in which the case is to be tried. In the high court the jurisdiction is statewide. In lower courts it is limited to a particular district, such as a city or county.

Therefore, the law provides that his testimony may be taken in a certain prescribed way before a notary public or other officer who will reduce the testimony to writing and return it to the court. Taking testimony in this way is called a deposition. The attorney for the opposing party must have notice of the deposition and an opportunity to question the witnesses. 

What part has the lawyer in a suit at law?

Lawyers for both the plaintiff and the defendant conduct the suit. They prepare the pleadings, each lawyer for his side, present the case to the court, question the witnesses, and sum up the case before the court.

If the trial is before a jury, the judge will give his charge to the jury, to instruct them on points of law in the case before they prepare to give their decision. The jury will not be dismissed until it gives a verdict or agrees to disagree. Each party may conduct his own case without a lawyer, but it is almost always unwise to attempt to do so. 

What is a verdict and how is it rendered?

The decision by the jury is called the verdict. The jury listens to the testimony given by the witnesses for both the plaintiff and the defendant, considers the evidence on both sides, and then decides, according to their judgment, which party is in the right. There can be no verdict unless all the jurors agree. In case they disagree, the one elected foreman of the jury will report a disagreement, and the judge will dismiss them, and a new trial will be ordered to be held before another jury. 

What is the judgment and by whom is it given?

The jury decides from the facts in the case which party is in the wrong. After the jury has given its verdict, the judge decides upon the legal rights of the successful party, and what shall be

the judgment against the defeated party. If the suit is for damages, judgment will include the amount of damages as found by the jury, and a certain allowance for costs, which are awarded to the successful party for his expenses in conducting the suit. 

In a criminal case the decision of the jury is either that the defendant is guilty or not guilty. In case he is guilty the judge names the penalty or punishment, otherwise he is discharged. 

How is the judgment executed?

If the debtor does not pay voluntarily the amount of a judgment, an execution is issued (by the attorney for the creditor plaintiff) to the executive officer of the court (sheriff, constable, or marshal) directing him to levy upon (take into his possession) sufficient property of the debtor to satisfy the judgment. The officer will actually take possession of chattels. He does not take possession of real estate, but may sell it to satisfy the judgment. 

The process is as follows: After a judgment is rendered by the judge it is filed in the office of the county clerk of the county where it was rendered and is indexed (docketed) against the name of the judgment debtor. It may also be filed and docketed in any other county in the state where the debtor has property. The docketing of the judgment constitutes it a lien against any real estate of the debtor in the county, not exempt. After a judgment is docketed the creditor may have an execution issued, under which real estate may be sold and personal property seized and sold by the sheriff to an amount sufficient to satisfy the judgment. If execution is not issued, the judgment remains a lien against the real estate for twenty years. 

What are exemption laws?

The exemption laws provide that the sheriff or officer cannot levy upon any property belonging to the judgment debtor which is exempt under the law. Exemption laws differ in the various states, but the exemptions, as a rule, consist of a homestead, wearing apparel, household furnishings up to a certain value, usually $250, and such tools and instruments as would be used in gaining a livelihood. Married men, or one who supports a family, are dealt with more liberally than are single men.

REMEDIES 

189 1 

Under what conditions may a case be appealed?

If the defeated party is dissatisfied with the judgment of the trial court, he may take an appeal to a higher court on questions of law. The lower court's decision on the facts is usually final. An appeal involves additional expense for printing and fees and should not be undertaken unless counsel advises it. The higher court (appellate court) hears the arguments of the lawyers on each side and then decides to affirm the decision of the trial court or to reverse it and send the case back for a new trial. 

What are supplementary proceedings?

The officer whose duty it is to collect the money or to find sufficient property to satisfy the judgment may find it necessary to return the execution with his certification that it is unsatisfied, which means that he cannot find sufficient property of the judgment debtor to pay the amount of the judgment. The party in the case who obtained the judgment (the judgment creditor) may apply to the judge for an order to examine the judgment debtor in reference to his property. If this order is secured, the judgment debtor must appear before a referee appointed by the court and answer questions in reference to his property. The referee has the authority to subpoena other witnesses and to adjourn the case from time to time. The referee reports the evidence to the judge and in case any property is found which is not exempt, the judgment debtor is ordered to turn it over to the proper officer. Such proceedings are in aid of or supplement the execution and are therefore called supplementary proceedings. 

What is an attachment?

An attachment is a procedure taken under court order to seize certain property belonging to the defendant and hold it as security for any judgment that may be obtained. 

The attachment is used principally in the cases where the debtor may attempt by fraudulent means to escape the execution of the judgment. In some states it is issued in every case at the time action is begun. It is issued also in cases where the goods to be attached are in the state where the action is pending and the defendant lives in another state. When the attachment is executed,

the court gets jurisdiction of the property attached, which it may dispose of to satisfy a judgment resulting from the suit. 

What is a replevin and when is it used?

A person who has an interest in certain articles of personal property which have been wrongfully taken, or, having been rightfully taken are being wrongfully withheld, may bring an action to recover possession of them. This action is called replevin. The plaintiff in this action can, by giving a bond to protect the rights of the defendant, have the property taken from the defendant and held in the custody of an officer until the action is determined. 

What is garnishment and when may it be used?

In some states it is possible by a process of law to require a third person owing money to the defendant not to pay this money over to him, but instead to pay it into court that it may be applied toward his indebtedness. This is called garnishment, or garnishee process, or trustee process. When a person who is employed for wages is in debt, his creditor may take action to recover and, judgment having been obtained and execution returned unsatisfied, the court will issue an order to his employer to pay over a part of his wages to the court, or retain a part specified to apply on the judgment. This is called garnisheeing a wage earner's wages to satisfy a judgment against him. Only a portion of his wages can be taken, depending on the amount he is paid. If his wages are too small, nothing can be taken. 

How are damages awarded?

Where one party to a contract fails or refuses to perform his part, the injured party has a right of action through the courts to compel him to pay damages. The court has it in its power to compel the party in default to make good the loss suffered by the other party, that is if the party in default has any property which can be legally levied upon. 

The judgment secured through the court, except in a case of extraordinary remedies (see page 192), is for damages which the plaintiff has suffered at the hands of the defendant. Seek legal advice before bringing suit for damages.

REMEDIES 

191 

How is the amount of the damages determined?

The amount of the damages which the plaintiff in the case is entitled to receive is determined by the jury. The decision is reached according to well-defined rules after the evidence and the circumstances in the case have been carefully considered. 

A law suit very often results in a loss for both the plaintiff and the defendant. The plaintiff may win the suit, but he cannot show that he has suffered much loss by the defendant's breach of contract, and the court will award him only nominal damages. The amount of nominal damages may be as little as six cents. To this amount will be added the cost of the action, which the defendant will have to pay. 

What are liquidated damages and when are they recoverable? 

Liquidated damages are damages agreed upon at the time the contract is entered into, which shall be paid according to the agreement or in a lump sum in case of a breach of the contract. The agreement may be so worded that either one or the other of the parties to the contract will be affected by it, or so it will affect only one party.

Example 1. The Haden Construction Company entered into a contract with the board of education of a certain city, to erect a school building for $250,000. The contract provided that the building is to be ready for occupancy for school purposes within twelve months from the time of signing the contract, and for every day of delay beyond that period the Haden Company agreed to pay $200 as damages. 

The damages agreed upon which shall be paid for delay in this case are liquidated damages. But whether or not the board of education could collect the agreed amount of the damages in case the Haden Company required several days beyond the twelve months to complete the building will depend on whether or not they can show that the amount agreed upon bears some reasonable relation to the damage they would suffer by delay and that the actual damage would be difficult to prove. When liquidated damages are specified in the contract they cannot be collected if they are so excessive or unreasonable as to amount to a penalty. 

Courts will not impose penalties in contract cases.

Extraordinary remedies. 

In certain cases the decision of the court may make available to the plaintiff a remedy in the form of an injunction or in the form of a specific performance. 

Example 2. Deitz, a ballplayer, contracted to play with the Union

League for the season of 1937. Shortly after signing the contract with the manager of the Union League, Deitz notified him that he could not play this season. Later Deitz signed a contract with the manager of the White 

Sox League and started to play when the season opened. 

The manager of the Union League can, through his attorney, ask the court for an injunction restraining Deitz from playing in the White Sox League. If he was able to play, he should fulfill his contract with the manager of the Union League. Although Deitz would be liable in damages for breach of contract, damages would not be an adequate remedy, since Deitz's services are special. So he may be enjoined from breaking his contract, which in effect will result in his performing it.

An injunction is an order of the court restraining the party named therein from committing some act which would injure the party securing the injunction. After a person has been enjoined by the court from committing some act, should he persist in violating the injunction, he will be "in contempt of court," in which case the court could fine or imprison him. A person cannot, as a rule, be enjoined from breaking his contract, but, when the subject of the contract is personal services of a special nature, an injunction may be issued.

What is specific performance and when is it available as a remedy? 

Example 3. Davis contracted to sell a site for a factory to the Acme 

Manufacturing Company. Before the time came for closing the contract,

Davis was offered several thousand dollars more for this site by another company, and he refused to complete his contract with the Acme Manufacturing Company.

If this case were taken to court, the court would decree, without doubt, that Davis must complete his contract and convey by deed this piece of real property to the Acme Manufacturing Company. 

Money damages would not compensate the purchasers of this

REMEDIES 

193 property for their loss for the reason that they are entitled to the property contracted for and money damages would not enable them to buy it if Davis refuses to convey it. This does not apply to an ordinary contract for goods, because money damages will permit the buyer to go into the market and buy the goods. 

If the Acme Manufacturing Company defaulted on their contract with Davis, he would still hold the property which was the subject matter of the contract. He could then sue for damages, in which case he would have to prove how much he had lost; or he also could sue for specific performance and compel the Acme Manufacturing Company to take the property and pay for it. 

Specific performance, when decreed by the court, means that the defendant in the case will be ordered to do the thing he contracted to do. It is available, in case of a breach of contract, when money damages would not be considered an adequate remedy. It is made use of principally in contracts calling for the conveyance of land (real property) which the owner fails or refuses to convey as agreed.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A breach of contract by one party gives the injured party a right of action through the courts to enforce performance or collect damages. 

2. A right of action may be discharged by agreement of the parties or by arbitration and thereafter a suit may not be maintained. 

3. The Statute of Limitation bars action unless begun within a certain time after the cause of action has accrued. 

4. The remedies for a breach of contract available to the injured party as a result of a suit at law are called civil remedies. 

5. Property belonging to the defendant which is subject to a properly recorded judgment may be sold at auction by an officer to satisfy judgment. 

6. In a civil case the defendant, if he loses his case, is made liable either for damages to be paid in money as a result of a judgment, or, in some cases, to an injunction, or a specific performance order. 

7. A judgment may be entered up against a judgment debtor and becomes a lien on any real estate he owns in the county, and any

property he owns, which is not exempt, may be levied upon to satisfy the judgment. 

8. Any property listed under a statute law in a particular state as being exempt cannot be taken for debt in that state. 

9. An appeal to a higher court may be made on a question of law, but the party making the appeal must agree to pay the costs if the case is decided against him. 

10. Supplementary proceedings may be resorted to on request of the plaintiff when no property belonging to the judgment debtor càn be found to satisfy the judgment. 

11. The court must issue an attachment in a proper case when property belonging to the defendant is to be taken and held as security for any judgment that may be obtained. 

12. Property that was wrongfully taken from the owner or rightfully taken but improperly withheld may be replevied (recovered) through due process of law, by a party who has rights or an interest in the property. 

13. A garnishee order requires a creditor or an employer to pay a portion of any sum due the judgment debtor over to the court to satisfy a judgment. 

14. Specific performance is a remedy for a breach of contract only when the damage could not be compensated for with money.

COMMENTS 

The discussion of Remedies indicates that action through the courts to collect money due, or for damages suffered, or to redress a civil wrong is an intricate procedure. The procedure followed, however, has been worked out through centuries as being the best way to protect the rights of all parties and to reach a fair result. Any person who suffers an injury at the hands of another person will find a remedy available through a legal

process. Court action, because of the volume of litigation, is slow, and because of the technical nature of legal processes, it requires experts and is expensive; therefore, arbitration or settlement is sometimes preferred to court action.

Group I. 

1. Adams offered to sell an air compressor to Baily for $200 cash on delivery at Baily's factory. Baily agreed to buy the compressor if Adams would agree to deliver the compressor within a reasonable time and would guarantee that it would work satisfactorily for six months. Was there a contract? 

2. On October 1, Gorton, in New York, wrote Shaw, in Kansas, offering to sell Shaw 100 barrels of Grade A Baldwin apples for $4 a barrel and requested an answer by return mail. The usual time for letters between 

New York and Kansas is two days. Shaw received the offer on October 3 and immediately wrote and posted a letter accepting the offer. The letter never reached Gorton. On October 8, Shaw telegraphed Gorton accepting the offer and Gorton received the telegram the same day. Was there a contract, and, if so, when was it made? 

3. Palmer, an infant, bought a used motorcycle from Riggs for $120 

He paid $20 down and $10 a month for ten months. Three months after making the last payment and before he became of age, Palmer returned the motorcycle to Riggs and demanded the return of $120. The motorcycle was then worth $70. What are the rights of Palmer and Riggs? 

4. John Doe was of unsound mind but appeared sane. He bought a diamond ring from Tiffany & Company for which he agreed to pay $1,000, a reasonable price. Doe gave the ring to his fiancée. When sued for the price he defended on the ground that he was insane when he made the contract. Should Doe be obliged to pay for the ring? Would it make any difference if he had been judicially declared insane before he bought the ring? 

5. Meriam offered to sell his gas engine to Hopkins for $200. Hopkins asked for 10 days in which to decide, to which Meriam agreed. Two days later Meriam sold the engine to Weaver for $225 and wrote Hopkins that he had done so. After Meriam's letter was mailed, but before Hopkins received it, Hopkins wrote Meriam that he would buy the engine. What are the rights of the parties? Would it make any difference if Hopkins had received Meriam's letter before mailing his acceptance? 

6. Poor, à nurseryman, offered to sell fruit trees to Marvin. They talked about 300 in all, 100 of each of three varieties, and also 900 in all, 300 of each variety. Poor prepared a written contract for 900 trees. Mar-

199 vin signed the contract without reading it, supposing it was for 300 trees. 

On a later occasion Poor and Marvin discussed a purchase of shade trees.

AGENCY TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Auctioneer. A person who makes a business of selling by auction. 

Authorized Act. An act by which one person gives another person permission to perform for him. 

Corporation. An artificial person, created by law, composed of individuals whose interests are represented by shares of stock. 

Factor. An agent, who, as a regular business, sells goods entrusted to him for that purpose by the owner. Also called a commission merchant. 

Servant. One employed by another to perform mechanical tasks or menial duties.

Unincorporated Associations. A group of persons acting as a unit, but not under authority of law to be a corporation. 

What is an agency?

An agency is the relationship between two parties, resulting usually from a contract, whereby one party is to act for and in the place of the other party in the performance of certain acts which he has a legal right personally to perform. These acts generally have to do with business transactions. As a rule, whatever one person has a legal right to do for himself, he may have another person do for him. 

What are the parties to an agency contract?

Example 1. Lowden was engaged by Watt, who owned and operated a creamery, to call on the grocers in a certain section for the purpose of advertising and selling his creamery products. 

In this example Watt is the principal and Lowden the agent. 

The parties to an agency contract are the principal and the agent. 

The principal is the party for whom another acts as agent. Any 203

person who is legally qualified to make a binding contract may appoint or employ another to act for him. 

The agent is the person appointed or employed by another to act for him in his behalf. Any person who is capable of following directions is legally qualified to act as an agent. Therefore, a person may act for another as agent, yet he may not be legally qualified to make a binding contract for himself. 

How are agents classified?

Agents are generally classified as general, special, and public. 

This classification is on the basis of the extent and nature of the authority of the agent to act for the principal. 

Example 2. Case was employed to manage Small's store, with full authority to buy and sell goods for cash or on account, collect and pay bills, and perform other necessary acts peculiar to the management of the business.

Case is a general agent. A general agent is one whom his principal has authorized to transact all of his business of a particular kind or in a particular place. Within the limits of his authority he may perform all acts necessary or customary to carry out the purpose for which he was appointed, without special authorization, but he cannot represent the principal in other respects. 

A general agent's authority, though limited, is much greater than that of a special agent.

Example 3. Weaver was employed by the Continental Steamship Company as their booking clerk and ticket agent at a particular place. 

Weaver is a special agent. His authority is limited to the performance of those acts or duties for which he was engaged. In 

Example 1, Lowden is also a special agent. 

One who is employed to transact a particular piece of business or for a special purpose is classed as a special agent. Inasmuch as a special agent's authority is limited, his principal is not bound by his acts should he exceed the scope of his authority. 

Any public official or employee of the government is a public agent. An agent generally is individually responsible if he exceeds his authority in any transaction for his principal. But public

AGENCY 

205 agents are an exception to this rule. Every one is assumed to know what authority a public agent has, and should he exceed his authority, he is not liable. 

Not all employees are agents.

Example 4. Havens was employed by the Matison Store, Inc., as a packer in their packing and shipping department, and Moore was employed as a salesman.

Havens is an employee of the Matison Store, Inc., but he is not an agent. He was employed to perform only mechanical duties in business transactions. Moore is also an employee, but he is also an agent, with authority to do such things as salesmen customarily do and, within the limits of that authority, can bind the principal in business transactions. 

Who are classed as agents?

Auctioneers, brokers, factors or commission merchants, attorneys, or any special representative of some person are classed as agents. In certain cases an employee who was not employed as an agent may be considered as such. A chauffeur may be instructed by his employer to perform some business transaction for him, such as buying gasoline and oil, or having the car repaired. In such transactions the chauffeur is acting as an agent. A domestic servant may be instructed by her mistress to place orders with local tradespeople for household supplies. In this capacity she is acting as agent. The business of corporations is managed exclusively through agents, and the directors and all officers are agents of the corporation. Each member of a partnership is a general agent for the firm. Unincorporated associations, such as clubs and societies, transact their business through officers and appointees who serve in the capacity of agents. 

Who is a "del credere agent"?

Example 5. Mead, as agent for Wilmont, sold goods to Goddard on credit. Mead guaranteed to Wilmont that Goddard would pay for the goods. By making this guaranty, Mead became a del credere agent. 

The agent who sells goods for his principal on credit and guarantees that the party to whom he sold the goods will pay for them is a del credere agent.

Mead's guaranty in this case does not have to be in writing to be enforceable. In reality the principal sold the goods to the agent, who in turn sold them to Goddard on credit. Should Goddard fail to pay for the goods, Mead will have to settle with Wilmont. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Any person physically capable of doing as directed is legally qualified to act as agent. 

2. Only a person who is legally qualified to make a binding contract may assume the role of principal. 

3. An agent acts for his principal in business matters requiring knowledge and judgment; a servant performs for his master routine duties. 

4. A person may employ another to do for him whatever he himself has a right to do. 

5. An agency exists when one party authorizes a second party to act for him in his dealings with third parties. 

6. The principal may be liable in a transaction in which his general agent assumed to have authority that he did not have. 

7. Partnership firms, societies, and business organizations may act in the capacity of an agent or a principal. 

8. An employee whose major duties are not those of an agent may at times act as an agent.

COMMENTS 

Business enterprises which are so small as to be conducted entirely by the owner are comparatively few in number and of minor importance. 

A corporation, being an artificial person, can act, however, only through agents. Consequently, all business done with large organizations such as the national and state governments, banks, insurance companies and railroads, and other corporations, involves dealing with an agent for the corporation as the principal. Even when a business is owned by an individual, he usually has salesmen, clerks, and other employees who represent him to some extent and for whose acts he may be responsible. 

As a result, almost every contract, sale, or other business transaction may bring up questions of agency law, such as the powers, duties, and liabilities of the agent and the rights and liabilities of the principal and the third person. It is of great importance that those who transact business through agents for themselves or with agents acting for others understand the rules of law applicable to such relations.

Estoppel. A rule of law which stops a person from denying a fact which he in some way previously admitted. 

Irrevocable. Cannot be revoked or set aside.

Premises. A piece of real estate.

How is an agency created?

The relation of principal and agent may be created by any one of the following ways: agreement (either oral or written), ratification, estoppel (conduct of parties), or necessity. 

How may an agency be created by agreement? 

The usual way of creating an agency is for one party to appoint or employ another party to act for him in a certain capacity or to represent him in a certain transaction. When an agency is created in this way the principal and the agent are under a contract and are subject to the laws and rules applicable to contracts in general, and also to those laws and rules that govern the relations of principal and agent between themselves. The one exception is in the case of a gratuitous agent. A gratuitous agent is one who is to serve without pay; and, there being no consideration, there can be no enforceable contract.

What form of agreement is necessary? 

Example 1.

Addison was employed by Young as a district sales 209

manager for one year. The contract specified that Addison was to begin work thirty days following the date of contract.

According to the terms of this agreement, Addison could not possibly perform his part of the contract within one year, and it would have to be in writing, therefore, to comply with the Statute of Frauds. See page 136.

An agent may be appointed by oral agreement, which is as effective as a written agreement, except in those cases where a written agreement is required by law. 

When must the agent's appointment be under seal?

When the agent is required to execute instruments under seal with third parties for his principal, his appointment must be in writing and under seal. The exceptions to this rule are: 

1. When the instrument is signed by the agent in the presence of his principal. 

2. When the agent signed an instrument under seal on which the seal was not required. 

3. When the agent signs as a member of his firm. 

4. When the agent is authorized to sign for a corporation. 

While any contract may be written and the seal attached, the laws of the different states specify that only certain contracts are to be under seal, and usually those contracts that have to do with real property, such as mortgages and deeds. In some states the agent must have authority in writing to lease or sell real property. 

How is the agent's appointment made formal?

Any written contract creating an agency may be executed under seal, thereby making it a formal contract. The usual way of appointing an agent who has to execute instruments under seal for his principal is by an instrument known as a power of attorney. 

An agent without formal authority may negotiate a contract which, when executed, would have to be under seal, but his principal would have to sign and seal it in person. If the agent is to sign sealed instruments in his principal's name, his authority to do so must be under seal. ?
