In some places a power of attorney authorizing the conveyance of real property by an agent is filed in the office of the county clerk. 

How may an agency be created by ratification?

Example 2. Ward, a tenant on Curtis's farm, acting in behalf of Curtis, but without authority, placed an order with a local dealer for a pump. 

The dealer installed the pump and sent the bill to Curtis, which he promises to pay.

The principal may assent to the act of an agent either before or after the act is performed. If he assents before the act is performed, an agency is created by agreement, but if he assents after the act is performed, then an agency is created by ratification. An agency created by ratification is just as effective as one created by agreement.

In Example 2, had Ward said to Curtis, after the pump had been installed, "I found it necessary to have a new pump installed," and 

Curtis had replied, "I am glad you did. Have the bill sent to me," this statement would have amounted to a ratification of 

Ward's act.

Any statement on the part of the one for whom the act was performed, which indicates clearly that he intends to be bound by the act, amounts to ratification.

Again in Example 2, if Curtis, after learning what Ward had done, allowed him to continue to use the pump without repudiating his act, he would have ratified the act by acquiescing in it. The principal, failing to disaffirm the agent's unauthorized act within a reasonable time after learning of it, is presumed to have ratified it. 

By remaining silent after he has full knowledge of the fact that the agent exceeded his authority, the principal has acquiesced and has thereby given assent to the contract. Curtis would have to see that the pump, in Example 2, was returned to the dealer within a reasonable time; otherwise, it would be assumed that he had ratified by accepting the benefits. Acceptance of the benefits resulting from an act of the agent's shows clearly that the principal is willing to be bound in the contract and amounts to ratification. 

Ratification, if made under a misunderstanding or through a misrepresentation, will not bind the principal. If Curtis saw the pump, but thought Ward had paid for it himself, approval or acquiescence in purchase would not be ratification. The principal is not permitted to accept part of the benefits and reject the remainder. He must ratify the act as a whole or not at all. 

How is an agency created by "estoppel"?

Example 3. Jordon, a boarder in Mead's family, was employed in a near-by city. Mead raised vegetables for the market and Jordon frequently contracted to sell Mead's products to Nye, a city dealer. Although Jordon had no authority to do so, Mead had always carried out the contracts. 

On one occasion Jordon contracted to sell 10 bushels of potatoes for Mead to Nye for $1 per bushel. Mead refused to deliver the potatoes for this price, claiming that Jordon had no authority to act for him.

Mead's acts constituted a representation that Jordon was his agent, and, Nye having relied on the representation in buying the

CREATING AGENCY 

213 potatoes, Mead will be estopped from denying that an agency existed and is bound to deliver the goods. 

An agency by estoppel is not a true agency, since there is no contract relation between principal and agent. It is created by law to prevent injury to third persons who have justifiably relied on acts or representations of the principal. 

How is an agency created by necessity?

Example 4. Mrs. Ballard purchased necessary clothing for herself and three children from a local dealer on her husband's credit. Mr. Ballard refused to pay the bill, claiming that his wife was without authority to pledge his credit.

If it could be shown that Mr. Ballard failed to provide his family with necessary clothing, he would be held to pay for necessary articles of clothing purchased by Mrs. Ballard on his account. In this case, Mrs. Ballard acted as Mr. Ballard's agent, and an agency was created by necessity. The relationship existing between husband and wife is such that the wife has implied power by law to buy necessaries on her husband's credit. The creditor in such a case, in order to collect his bill, must prove that the articles purchased were necessary and that the husband failed to provide them.

Another example of an agency created by necessity is in the case of the master of a ship when on a voyage. He would have authority in case of necessity to purchase supplies for the ship or have repairs made and pledge the credit of the owner.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The contract of agency is subject to the law of contracts in general. 

2. A true agency exists only in case the agent received prior authority to act or there was subsequent ratification of his acts on the part of a party qualified to act as principal. 

3. An agency is created by estoppel when the principal by his acts or representations leads third persons to believe an agency exists. 

4. An agency is created by necessity when the relations of principal and agent and the conditions are such as to justify such an agency. ין

5. Only one having authority, express or implied, may legally act as agent. 

6. When an agent is required to execute written contracts under seal his appointment must be in writing and under seal. 

7. A formal appointment of an agent is by power of attorney. 

8. An agency may be created by ratification as well as by agreement. 

9. The principal is bound in an agency created by necessity.

Later the maid ordered a large quantity of groceries from the same dealer. Can Mrs. Wade be held to pay the bill? 

5. Dallas was away from his home for three months and in his absence 

Mrs. Dallas purchased the necessary food and fuel for the family and had it charged to Mr. Dallas's account. When he returned he refused to pay the bills. (a) Did an agency exist? (b) Under what conditions can the creditors collect from Mr. Dallas?

RELATION OF PRINCIPAL AND AGENT TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Compensate. To make amends or supply an equivalent; to pay or reimburse.

Fiduciary. Having the nature of a trust; bound to act in good faith in relations with another. 

Indemnify. To settle for loss or damages. 

Reimburse. To pay back or repay a person. 

Subagent. A person appointed by an agent to transact some of the business of his agency. 

What are the obligations of principal to agent? 

1. To compensate the agent for his services. 

2. To reimburse the agent for necessary expenses incurred in the performance of his duties, unless his salary covers these expenses. 

3. To indemnify the agent for any loss or damage to him, caused by following his principal's instructions. 

The principal is also required to provide the physical protection for his agent that his position or work requires. 

How may the compensation be determined?

Example 1. Deitz employed Udell to work for him as a salesman. No mention was made of the wages Udell was to receive. In this case, it would be implied that Deitz would pay Udell what other salesmen in his employ were receiving, or, if the wages could not be determined in this way, that he would pay what Udell's services are reasonably worth. 

The principal is obligated to pay his agent the wages, salary, or commission agreed to by both parties. When the compensation is fixed by the agreement, this will control. If no mention is made of compensation at the time the agency is created, the law will imply an agreement to pay what the services are reasonably worth, unless it was clearly intended that the services were to be gratuitous. 216

RELATION OF PRINCIPAL AND AGENT 

217 

Can an agent recover for unauthorized services?

Example 2. Hood was employed by the Wilton Publishing Company to sell sets of books for $60 per set, or $10 down and $5 for 12 months. 

Hood contracted to sell several sets for $5 down and $5 per month for 12 months. The Wilton Publishing Company accepted these contracts. 

By accepting these contracts unconditionally, the Wilton Publishing Company ratified Hood's acts and he is entitled to his full compensation.

In the event the principal subsequently ratifies unauthorized services or accepts the benefits resulting therefrom, the agent can usually recover for his services the same as though he had received prior authority. Otherwise, an agent has no right to claim pay for his services.

What claims of the agent against the principal are usually collectible? 

1. The principal who discharged the agent without the right to do so may be held to pay the agent his full compensation agreed upon. However, the principal, if he can show that the agent wilfully remained idle for the unexpired time when he might have been profitably employed in a similar occupation, may be required to pay less accordingly. 

2. When the agency is terminated by impossibility of performance, the agent may recover reasonable compensation for the services performed. 

3. An agent who breaks his contract of employment cannot, as a rule, recover any compensation except that in some cases he may recover reasonable compensation for services rendered, less any damages sustained by his principal. Laws of the different states vary in respect to such cases. No compensation is ever recoverable for services known by the agent to be illegal. 

4. Any agent who is required to have a license to operate as an agent cannot require his principal to pay for services rendered unless he has the necessary license. Insurance agents, real estate agents, solicitors, and auctioneers in some states or cities are examples of agents required to have a license. 

5. An agent who has suffered any loss in consequence of having

performed lawful acts which were authorized by his principal is entitled to indemnity from his principal to cover such loss. 

Example 3. Condor was employed by Weaver to operate a truck between Erie and Pittsburgh. On one trip the truck broke down and Condor paid $50 of his own money to have it repaired. Condor can require 

Weaver to reimburse him for this necessary expense. 

What are the obligations of agent to principal? 

1. The agent must obey his principal's instructions. 

The agent's most important obligation to his principal is to obey his instructions and so long as he does he is protected. An agent who disregards his principal's instructions can be held liable for any damage resulting in consequence thereof. The obligations of general and special agents are the same. 

2. An agent must use the necessary judgment and skill. 

Example 4. Wagner was employed by Green, a wholesale fruit dealer, to buy, pack, and ship apples for him according to instructions. Wagner, having undertaken to act in this capacity, must possess the necessary judgment and skill to buy the apples according to instructions, and also the necessary skill to securely pack and ship them. If he fails to possess and exercise such judgment and skill, he is liable for any damage resulting to Green.

An agent who undertakes the performance of some act must exercise the judgment and skill a prudent and careful person would be expected to exercise in the performance of such an act. 

The judgment and skill necessary in a particular case depends upon the nature of the act to be performed. The judgment, experience, and skill required of an agent employed to adjust losses in a claim department of a railroad company is quite different from that required of a regular ticket or freight agent. 

3. An agent must show good faith.

The relations existing between principal and agent are said to be fiduciary, which means that they must show good faith in their dealings. An agent, therefore, cannot act for himself contrary to his principal's interests, or for his principal and the third party in the same transaction without their consent.

RELATION OF PRINCIPAL AND AGENT 

219 Example 5. Bohn put his house in Miller's hands to sell for $6,000. 

Huber engaged Miller to act as his agent in the purchase of a house for about $6,000. Miller negotiated the sale of Bohn's house to Huber and collected $300 commission from each party. 

The facts in this case would bar Miller from collecting any commission. He had no right to serve two principals, without the consent of both, and without this consent he is not entitled to compensation from either. 

4. The agent must make an accounting to his principal. 

An agent is usually engaged to transact business for his principal; which means that he must handle property and money belonging to him. This being the case, he must make a complete accounting to his principal for all property or money with which he is entrusted. If the principal's belongings should become mixed with those of the agent, they are all deemed to belong to the principal until his claim is met. 

Example 6. Haden placed his automobile in Jordon's sales rooms to sell for $500 on a commission of 10%. Jordon sold the car for $600, and retained the $100 extra, plus the commission of $50, and gave Haden $450. 

In the absence of any agreement to the contrary, Jordon must account to Haden for the full proceeds of the sale ($540). An agent must account to his principal for all profits from any transaction to which he is a party, and this is the law, even though the transaction was illegal. 

5. The agent must act in person, unless he has the right to appoint a subagent.

An agent without the authority of his principal or an established custom to appoint subagents must act in person. It is reasonable to assume that a principal who employs a person as agent, because of the faith and confidence he has in him, would not be required to accept the services of someone else. 

Example 7. A local bank accepted for collection a draft payable in a distant city. It is necessary that this draft be sent to a bank in the city where it is payable. This bank to which the draft was sent will act as a subagent for the local bank in making the collection.

It is the custom for banks to handle out-of-town collections in this way; therefore, the local bank is within its rights in appointing a subagent to collect this draft. 

It sometimes happens that the nature of the transaction or the business to be transacted is such that the agent is required to appoint subagents. A general agent to sell insurance would be expected to appoint subagents to serve under him. When it is necessary to appoint subagents, an agent who uses due care in making his appointments is not liable for the acts of his subagents. 

What are the obligations of a gratuitous agent?

A gratuitous agent is not liable for refusing or failing to act, but should he act, he is bound to exercise prudence and skill in what he does, the same as would be expected of any agent in a similar situation. He cannot escape responsibility because he served without pay.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The principal's obligations to his agent have to do with compensation, reimbursement, indemnification, and protection. 

2. The agent, in the absence of definite stipulations, may demand such compensation as is customary in similar situations, or what is fair and reasonable. 

3. An agency created by ratification obligates the principal to the agent the same as one created by agreement. 

4. Only reasonable expenses and actual loss suffered in performing his authorized duties can be claimed by the agent. 

5. An agent who violates his instructions or does not act properly is liable to his principal for resulting damages or loss. 

6. A gratuitous agent who attempts to perform is held responsible for proper performance, but should he refuse or fail to act, he is not liable. 

7. An agent without the authority or the right to appoint subagents must act personally. 

8. The rule is that an agent cannot serve two principals in the same transaction. 

9. An agent has no right to use his position or authority for his own benefit.

RELATION OF PRINCIPAL AND AGENT 

221 10. An agent must account to his principal for all profits from the agency. 

11. An agent who acts without the necessary legal authority, such as a license, has no lawful claim against his principal for compensation. 

12. An agent cannot be held responsible if the undertaking fails through no fault of his.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Collusion. Secret agreement between two or more people to defraud or deceive another.

Concession. Act of yielding or granting; a thing yielded. 

Controlling Factors. Those conditions or elements that chiefly contribute to producing a result. 

What are the obligations of principal to third party?

Example 1. Small was authorized by Denman to sell the produce from 

Denman's farm. Small sold not only the produce but also the live stock on the farm. So far as third parties are concerned, the circumstances might be such as to make it appear that Small had authority to sell the stock. If so, it would be the same as though he had actual authority, and regardless of his instructions to the contrary, Denman is obligated to the third parties in the transactions for Small's acts. 

A person who transacts his business through an agent is responsible to the third party in the transaction. It is a rule of law that the principal is bound by the acts of his agent so long as the agent acts within the scope of his authority, and it matters not whether the identity of the principal is disclosed or undisclosed. If the principal succeeds in keeping his identity a secret, third persons with whom he has dealt through his agent could not exercise their rights to hold him liable, but in that case the agent would be liable. 

Some controlling factors.

When the authority of an agent must be in writing, as authority to convey real estate, or when the third person knows the agent has written authority, he is bound to examine the writing and discover the limits of the agent's authority, and cannot hold the principal on a contract in excess of the authority granted. 223

Any authority conferred upon the agent carries with it implied authority to do anything reasonably necessary to carry out the actual authority. Therefore, a power of attorney conferring authority to sell and convey real estate would carry with it implied authority to have all necessary papers executed and filed, and to deposit all moneys received. In case an emergency arises, the agent may perform unauthorized acts for which his principal will be liable.

Example 2. Davies, a salesman employed by Harmon, was left to close the store Saturday night. He discovered that water was coming into the cellar where a quantity of goods were stored. Harmon was out of town, so 

Davies employed two men to move the goods from the cellar. Harmon is bound by Davies's act, and he will have to pay the men for their services. 

In some cases an agent has authority other than that conferred upon him by his principal. Commission merchants, stockbrokers, bankers, and others who act as agents are subject to laws, established usage, and customs which apply specifically to these agencies, and an agent is justified in following custom even without specific authority to do so.

When an agent acts for an undisclosed principal. 

An agent who makes a contract on behalf of his principal, but who does not disclose that fact and appears to be acting on his own account, becomes personally liable on the contract, but the undisclosed principal has a right to enforce it against the third party. 

An undisclosed principal, when discovered, is liable to third parties, provided the agent acted within the scope of his authority, even though the third party may have thought he was dealing directly with the agent.

An agent who acts for an undisclosed principal is liable to third parties so long as the principal is unknown, but when the real principal is disclosed, the third party may elect to hold him on the contract rather than the agent. Should the agent sign a written agreement for an undisclosed principal, even though he signed as agent, without adding the name of his principal, he is liable on the contract. The fact that the principal was not disclosed by his agent does not bar him from claiming the benefits resulting from the agency.

PRINCIPAL, AGENT, AND THIRD PARTY 

225 How is the principal affected by notice to the agent? 

A third party who sends notice to the agent regarding anything within the scope of the agency has given notice to the principal. 

This being the case, the principal is assumed to know of everything in connection with the agency about which notice was given by a third party. An agent who acts in good faith keeps his principal informed regarding the affairs of his agency. A principal who could avoid his responsibilities by claiming ignorance would be inclined to avail himself of this privilege whenever he might wish to do so. 

What are the obligations of the agent to third parties?

Example 3. Dwier was employed as a special agent by the manager of a hotel to purchase vegetables in the market for use in the hotel. Once 

Dwier purchased a quantity of linen, which his principal refused to accept. 

Dwier will have to pay to the linen dealer such damages as he may have suffered.

A person who acts for another as agent warrants impliedly that he has authority so to act, and that the one for whom he acts is competent to give such authority. By acting without authority, he relieves his principal from responsibility, and the agent alone is liable to the third party for damages suffered, not on the contract which he seemed to make for his principal, but for breach of his implied warranty of authority.

When a contract negotiated by the agent is written and made out in the name of the principal, who signed it in person, the agent is not liable to third parties.

An agent who acts for a minor or any other incompetent persons becomes liable to third parties, for the reason that he warrants the competency of his principal. 

What are the obligations of third parties to the principal?

Example 4. Hurd was purchasing agent for an insurance company. 

Sparks, a pen and pencil jobber, got Hurd to agree to buy pens and pencils through him, with the understanding that he would bill the insurance company for twice the quantity supplied and divide the overcharge with Hurd. 

Sparks is guilty of practicing fraud, and the insurance company has a right of action against him for damages and also against 

Hurd, who was implicated with Sparks.

In general, a third party is liable on a contract in which the other party was represented by an agent in the same way and to the same extent that he would be liable on any other contract. 

A third party who is guilty of duress or fraud in his dealing with an agent is liable to the principal for any loss resulting therefrom. 

A third party who enters into an agreement with the agent to take advantage of the principal in business deals is guilty of collusion with the agent and can be held liable by the principal. The agent is also liable to his principal for breach of good faith. He may be discharged and made to pay damages. 

For what torts or wrongs of an agent is the principal liable? 

Example 5. Ward, who was authorized by the Model Garment Company to sell clothes for it, represented to a customer that the clothes were handmade from imported materials, which was untrue. 

The Model Garment Company is bound by the false statements made by Ward, even though they were unauthorized, and any purchaser of one of these garments has a right of action against them for damages from the fraud.

It generally is held that the principal is liable for fraud practiced by the agent for the principal's benefit. 

Example 6. Quade, who was employed as a salesman for the Cooper 

Stove Company, carelessly parked the company's car on a hill while calling on a customer. The car started to move and finally crashed into a store building at the foot of the hill, doing considerable damage. The 

Cooper Stove Company is liable for the damage to the building. 

The principal is also liable to the third party for any damage suffered by him as a result of the agent's negligence or carelessness. 

The principal is not liable for malicious wrongs or crimes committed by the agent unless it is evident that he authorized them. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Third parties may hold the principal liable on contracts made by his agent with his consent and for his benefit. 

2. Third parties dealing with an agent who has a power of attorney cannot hold the principal for acts of the agent beyond his authority.

PRINCIPAL, AGENT, AND THIRD PARTY 

227 3. Some agents have implied powers by law, usage, or custom, and limitations on such powers, imposed by the principal, are not effective as to third persons unless actually made known to them. 

4. A principal is bound when the agent acts within the scope of his apparent authority. 

5. An undisclosed principal has the same rights as a disclosed principal. 

6. Notice to the agent regarding agency matters is notice to the principal. 

7. One who acts as agent warrants that his principal is competent to contract and that he has authority to represent him. 

8. An agent who fails to disclose the name of his principal or who assumes to act as principal is personally liable to third persons having dealings with the agent. 

9. A third party who contracts through an agent is bound in a contract with the principal. 

10. The principal is generally liable for the negligence and fraud committed by the agent in transacting the business of the agency. 

11. The principal is not liable for malicious wrongs committed by the agent of his own free will.

TERMINATION OF AN AGENCY TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Irrevocable Agency. An agency that cannot be terminated at the will of the principal.

Mutually Agreeing. The principal and the agent agreeing between themselves.

Renouncing the Agency. The agent refusing to continue in the employ of the principal.

Revoking the Agency. The principal notifying the agent that he is not to continue in his employ. 

How may an agency be terminated?

The relation of principal and agent may be terminated by 

1. The terms of the agreement. 

2. The acts of the parties (principal and agent). 

3. A change in condition of parties. 

4. Impossibility of performance. 

5. Operation of law.

When is an agency terminated by the terms of the agreement? 

Example 1. The agreement between Lance as principal and Waters as agent provided that Waters should act as agent for Lance during the time Lance remained in Europe, which was indefinite. 

In this case the agreement provides for termination of the agency as soon as Lance returned from Europe. 

Termination of the agency stops the agent's authority and the principal's liability to third parties, except that the principal may be estopped from denying the existence of an agency in the case of a third party who did not receive notice of the termination. Therefore, notice to third parties is necessary. 229

The terms of an agency created by agreement may be such that termination of the agency is provided for in the agreement; or an agency may be created for a particular purpose or for a definite time. When the purpose is fulfilled or the time expires, the agency is terminated. In general, rules that apply to the termination of contracts apply also to the termination of an agency. How may an agency be terminated by the acts of the parties? 

The agency may be terminated by 1. The principal and the agent mutually agreeing to terminate the agency 

2. The principal revoking the agent's authority 

3. The agent renouncing the agency

Example 2. Gordon entered into an agreement with Hempy whereby 

Hempy was to work for Gordon one year as a salesman. The contract was enforceable in every respect and Hempy served for six months when 

Gordon discharged him.

Gordon had the power to terminate his contract of employment with Hempy, and thereby terminate Hempy's authority to bind Gordon in further contracts, but he did not have the right to terminate it within the year, and by doing so he laid himself liable for damages. Had Hempy renounced the agency and left the service of Gordon, he would have been liable to Gordon for damages. 

This agreement between Gordon and Hempy could have been terminated by mutual agreement; that is, both parties could have agreed between themselves to terminate it. It would have terminated automatically at the expiration of the year. If Hempy continued to act as agent after the year was up, and Gordon accepted his services, the agency would be extended by implied agreement either for another year or indefinitely until terminated by notice, depending upon the circumstances. 

As between principal and agent, the principal may revoke the agency by giving oral instructions or a written notice to the agent. 

In a case where conditions are such that it is implied or understood that the agency is terminated, notice to the agent is not necessary. 

As to third parties, notice of revocation is binding only upon those who receive it; therefore, the principal must give notice to

TERMINATION OF AN AGENCY 

231 those with whom he had dealings through the agent. Notice is not the revocation, but a means to stop the apparent authority; otherwise, the rules of estoppel may apply, and the principal might be held for the acts of the agent after revocation. 

When is an agency irrevocable by the principal? 

Example 3. Webb put his furniture in an auctioneer's hands to sell. The auctioneer advanced Webb $100, with the understanding that he is to deduct this amount from the proceeds of the sale. 

In this case Webb is without the right to revoke the agency at will. The auctioneer has an interest in the subject matter of the agency because it is security for the $100 he advanced to Webb. 

This is an example of an agency coupled with an interest. When the agency is coupled with an interest, it is irrevocable by the principal. Any expense incurred by the agent in an effort to sell the furniture would not serve to make the agency irrevocable. 

Change in condition of parties will terminate an agency. 

Example 4. Reems, the owner of a nursery, employed Carter to sell nursery stock for him in a western state. Reems died, but Carter did not learn of his death for three days, and in the meantime he had sold several lots of fruit trees to be delivered later. 

All contracts made by Carter for Reems after his death are void. 

In all probability Reems' estate would see that the trees were delivered to those who had contracted for them in good faith. But, as a matter of law, after Reems' death no agency existed, and Carter was without authority to act.

The death of either the principal or the agent terminates the agency, and the estates of neither the deceased nor the survivor can be held. In this case, notice to third parties need not be given. 

Any contract made by the agent for the principal after his death is void.

If either the principal or the agent becomes insane, the agency is terminated. The reason is obvious. But if the principal has not been decreed insane by the proper authority, persons dealing with the agent, not knowing of the principal's insanity, are protected. 

Illness of the agent may render him incapable of acting for the

principal, thereby terminating the agency. Illness of the principal would not ordinarily terminate the agency. 

Bankruptcy of either the principal or the agent will terminate the agency for the reason that a bankrupt is without the right to control his own property. In the case of a bankrupt agent, his authority ceases, but he may still perform certain formal acts not involving the transfer of any property.

Change in condition of the parties, caused by death, insanity, or bankruptcy will automatically terminate an agency.

How may an agency be terminated by impossibility of performance?

Example 5. Quinn was employed to sell a quantity of lumber from a certain lot stored in a lumber camp in Washington. Fire destroyed the camp and all lumber stored therein before Quinn sold any. 

Destruction of this lumber made it impossible for Quinn to perform his part of the contract, and the agency is terminated by impossibility of performance. 

Example 6. Davis, a wholesale dealer, employed Wade to buy sweet corn in a certain county and ship it to him in the city. An insect was discovered working in the corn, and a law was passed prohibiting any shipments of corn out of the county. This law terminated Wade's right to buy or ship sweet corn, and the agency is thereby terminated. 

Operation of the law may terminate an agency. An agent may be employed for a particular purpose and it may become illegal for him to act.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Any agency, regardless of how it is created, may be terminated by the parties, by law, or as a result of uncontrollable conditions. 

2. The principal may revoke the authority of an agent at any time, thereby terminating the agency. 

3. The agent may renounce the contract of agency at any time, thereby terminating the agency. 

4. An agency coupled with an interest cannot be terminated by the principal. 

5. A contract made by the agent after his principal's death is void.

TERMINATION OF AN AGENCY 

233 6. Notice to third parties of the termination of the agency is necessary in all cases except when terminated by death of the principal. 

7. A principal who fails to give notice of the termination of the agency to third parties may be estopped from denying that an agency still exists.

A few weeks later Wheeler decided to take up farming again and as the machinery had not been sold, he demanded of Dowd that it be returned to him. What are the rights of the parties? 

4. Paden, who owned and operated a mill for the production of poultry food, employed Slater as his agent in California. Paden became insane

and was put in an asylum. While he was in the asylum, but before he was legally decreed insane, Slater made several contracts with dealers to handle Paden's poultry food. (a) How would these contracts be affected before and after Paden was legally decreed insane? (b) Certain contracts were entered into by Slater after Paden was decreed insane. How would these contracts be affected? 

5. McCabe was employed by Fitch to sell and install electrical appliances in homes. In the city where McCabe was employed, the common council passed an ordinance requiring anyone who installed electrical appliances to have a license, the same as electricians. How would McCabe be affected by this ordinance?

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Contributory Negligence. Negligence that helped to cause the accident. 

Fellow Servant Doctrine. The doctrine of the Common Law that a servant has no claim against his master for injury caused by the negligence of a fellow servant.

Interstate Commerce. Commerce or business extending beyond the border of a single state.

Mandatory. Made compulsory by legal authority. 

Master. One who has another person subject to his will. 

Servant. One who is employed by another.

Technical Defenses. Defenses to lawsuits, based on legal technicalities and not on the merits of the case. 

What are the relations of employer and employees?

We have learned that an agent is generally an employee (except a gratuitous agent or an agent by necessity) but that not all employees are agents.

The relations that exist between the employer and his employee are very similar in many respects to the relations that exist between the principal and his agent. There are, however, some laws and regulations that apply specifically to the relations existing between employer (master) and employee (servant) that do not apply to the relations of principal and agent. 

There are many employees who are classed as servants in a legal sense, such as shop foremen, factory superintendents, production engineers, accountants, bookkeepers, stenographers, file clerks, or any employee who has duties to perform other than those that have to do with the actual transacting of business; and the employer is classed as master. 236

For what is an employer liable to his employees?

In case an employee, in the course of his employment, meets with an accident causing his physical injury or death, the employer may be held for damages. Under the common-law regulations, the employer could claim that the accident was caused by the employee's own negligence (contributory negligence), or by the negligence of a fellow employee (fellow servant doctrine); or, that the employee assumed the risk of the occupation (assumption of risks). 

These doctrines proved to work to the disadvantage of the employee in many cases. In recent years, as a result of concerted effort, legislation more favorable to the interests of employees has been enacted. The Federal government has passed the employer's liability act which provides that every common carrier by railroad engaged in interstate commerce shall be liable for the injury or death of an employee caused by its negligence or any defect in its equipment or appliances. Since about 1910, practically all states have passed workmen's compensation laws, which are in force. 

What are workmen's compensation laws? 

Example 1. Willis was employed by Sanderson Brothers to operate a machine in their mill. Willis lost his right arm in the machine. Sanderson 

Brothers are liable to Willis for compensation. The only two exceptions that might be considered are intoxication or willful intention of Willis. 

The laws of different states vary considerably, but in general they contain the following provisions. 

1. All employees engaged in certain specified occupations which are considered hazardous are protected by the laws. An exception is made in the case of farm laborers and domestic servants, who are not, as a rule, protected. 

2. Occupations are classified and every employer of labor in certain occupations is liable for compensation for an employee who is accidentally injured or killed in the course of his employment, without regard to the cause of the accident, unless it was caused by willful intent or intoxication of the injured employee. 

3. This liability of the employer has preference over any other liability whatsoever.

4. The compensation to be paid the employee during his disability is based on his wages. He is usually paid his wages for a certain time, as provided in a schedule of different injuries and disabilities. The employer is also required to furnish medical, surgical, and hospital facilities for a certain period after the accident. 

5. The employee is required to notify his employer of his claim for compensation, and if they cannot agree on the amount to be paid, the matter is referred to a commission for determination. 

This commission is appointed according to the provisions of the law. 

6. One provision of the law requires the employer to carry compensation insurance or to satisfy the commission of his ability to pay compensation and damages in case an employee meets with an accident causing his disability or death. An employer who fails to meet compensation payments is liable to a penalty, and the injured employee may elect to take compensation under the law, or he may sue for damages. An employer who is sued in such a case may not avail himself of the fellow servant doctrine, assumption of risk, or contributory negligence as defenses.

Where workmen's compensation laws do not apply. 

Example 2. Graham employed Snyder to wash windows. Snyder fell from a ladder and broke his leg. He is not entitled to compensation for his injury, but he might take action against Graham for damages. It is possible that Graham might be held in damages for the injury suffered by Snyder. If Graham carried liability insurance covering this risk, he could pass this liability on to the insurance company in which he is insured.

Workmen's compensation laws, as a rule, do not apply to employers who employ domestic service or workmen to do odd jobs, such as putting up screens or washing walls and windows. This is so, first, because it is domestic service; second, because it is casual employment; and third, because the employer is not likely to have the statutory number of employees. However, anyone who owns real property assumes some risk for injury that may befall anyone in or about his property. He can insure against this risk.

Example 3. Warren was employed as a farm hand on Wright's farm. 

During the threshing season Warren, while working about the threshing machine, accidentally injured his right arm so that he could not use it for some time.

Whether or not Warren could collect any compensation would depend upon the laws of the particular state. If working about a threshing machine is the duty of a farm hand and is so considered, he might not be protected, while if the law specified anyone working about a machine, he would be entitled to compensation. 

Sometimes the workmen's compensation laws apply to hazardous occupations only, sometimes to all industries, and sometimes to all kinds of labor except farm work and domestic services. Most laws provide that the injured party is not entitled to compensation unless his disability continues for from six days to three weeks. In case the injured employee or his representative is not satisfied with the compensation offered by the employer, the case may be brought before the State Commission. After hearing the case, the commission will decide how much the employer is to pay. Usually the employer is required to pay for a certain period a portion of the employee's weekly wages.

Employers are, in some states, required to carry compensation insurance, but as conditions are today, most large employers consider the employment risks so great that they voluntarily carry insurance.

What is the Federal Employer's Liability Act? 

This act provides that common carriers engaged in interstate commerce shall be liable for the injury or death of any employee caused by its negligence or any defects in its equipment or appliances. The provisions of this act include liability of the common carrier for the negligence of its officers, agents, or employees. 

A common carrier may not offer contributory negligence as a defense. But in case the employee was negligent, the amount of negligence directly attributable to the cause of the injury may result in the damages being diminished in proportion to the negligence.

The act further provides that the railroad must comply with

the statute and also with the Federal Safety Appliance Act, and failing to do so, carelessness or negligence on the part of an employee who is injured or killed will not reduce the amount of damages recoverable. It matters not in what place the accident occurred; if the common carrier is engaged in interstate commerce, the case is subject to the Federal acts. 

Congress has also passed a compensation act known as the Federal Workmen's Compensation Act, which protects all civil employees of the Federal government. 

What is the liability of the employer to third persons?

Example 4. Otis, in the usual course of his duties as an employee in 

Mattison's store, carelessly left a trap door open leading to the cellar. A customer fell through the opening and was injured. The employer is liable in this case for any damages recoverable by the injured customer. 

The employer is liable to a third person who was injured as a result of the carelessness or negligence of his employee in the usual course of his duties.

Example 5. Men employed by a contractor piled building material in the street, and complied with the city ordinance by putting red lights on it and observing all other regulations. Weston, failing to observe the red lights, ran his automobile into a pile of material, damaging both material and car. Weston's contributory negligence bars him from recovering damages, and he may be held for damaging the building material. 

A third party whose injury resulted from his own negligence cannot hold either the employer or employee liable. 

Is the employer liable for the willful acts of his employee? 

Example 6. Gibson, who was employed by the Star Taxi Company, willfully ran the taxi he was driving into a taxi driven by Deso for the Red Taxi Company, doing considerable damage to the Red Taxi Company's Gibson deliberately planned to do this damage because of a disagreement he had with Deso over a particular stand. car.

The Star Taxi Company is liable to the Red Taxi Company for 

Gibson's tort. Gibson is also personally liable.

An employee who willfully or intentionally commits a tort in the course of his employment imposes a liability on his employer for damages.

How may the relation of employer and employee be terminated? 

1. By completion of the contract. When the agreement has been fulfilled by both the employer and employee, their relations are terminated. 

2. When the employee breaks his contract of employment. The employee has the power to refuse to carry out the terms of his agreement with his employer; but, if he is without the right to do so, he may be liable to his employer for damages he has sustained as a result of the breach of contract. 

3. The employer may discharge the employee. When the employee, who has a contract, is discharged by his employer without cause, the employer is liable for the damages sustained by the employee by reason of his employer's breach of contract. The employer may discharge an employee for cause and not render himself liable for damages. The causes that may justify the action of the employer in discharging an employee are disobedience, showing bad faith, incompetency, and neglect.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. In the absence of controlling laws or organization influences, an employer is free to employ whom he wishes to employ. 

2. In the absence of controlling circumstances, the employee is free to decide for whom he will work. 

3. Anyone who performs services for another for hire is an employee. 

4. Employers are required to provide for the physical security of their employees. 

5. Statute laws in most of the states make it mandatory for an employer to pay compensation in case of injury or death of an employee in the course of his employment. 

6. Intent to be injured, or intoxication may bar an employee from collecting compensation. Under some statutes contributory negligence may lessen the amount recovered. 

7. Compensation acts generally provide that the employer shall carry compensation insurance or satisfy the authorities that he is abundantly able to pay compensation for injury or death of an employee.

8. The Federal Employer's Liability Act applies to railroads and other common carriers engaged in interstate commerce. 

9. An injured person can hold an employer liable if his injury resulted from the negligence or tort of his employee. 

10. An employer can discharge an employee for justifiable causes. 

Otherwise, a violation of his agreement may render him liable for damages.

II. Obligations of Employer to Employee

The most significant lesson to learn here is that between the employer and the employee there is a relationship existing which requires that they deal fairly and honestly with each other.

The employer and the employee have interests in common in whatever enterprise they are engaged, and the interests of both are served by the success of the enterprise. Therefore, it behooves every employee to serve his employer honestly and faithfully in the interests of their mutual success; and the employer should foster the economic, social, and physical well-being of his employees in the interest of efficient service. When the relationship between the employer and his employees is what it should be, there is little chance of serious disagreements or legal difficulties. 

On the assumption that honesty, good faith, and ability are present, the rules of law and statutes discussed in this chapter furnish adequate protection for the rights of principal and agent, employers and employees, and persons dealing with them.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS-PROMISSORY NOTES 245 

A negotiable instrument is an unconditional promise or order in writing to pay a certain sum in money to order or to bearer at a fixed or determinable future time. It may be transferred from one party to another by endorsement and delivery (in some cases by delivery only), and the legal title becomes vested in the party to whom it is transferred.

The principal negotiable instruments in common use are checks, drafts or bills of exchange, trade acceptances, notes, and bonds. Other instruments in common use that have certain characteristics similar to those of negotiable instruments are warehouse receipts and order bills of lading.

What is the Negotiable Instruments Law? 

The Negotiable Instruments Law is a statute embodying a code of rules enacted to regulate the use of negotiable instruments. It is in force in every state and territory of the United States. The law is a uniform law, and the fact that the same rules apply to negotiable instruments throughout the country has made them a much safer and more convenient medium for the transaction of business than they were when the rules and usage varied in different states. 

What are the essential requirements?

The Negotiable Instruments Law does not specify any set form which must be used, or any particular order of arrangement of the required essentials, but, because of the nationwide use and circulation of negotiable instruments, the practice is to use forms that are very similar in make-up.

The differences between a negotiable and a nonnegotiable instrument are many and have important consequences. The former passes by endorsement and delivery, or by delivery only; the latter passes only by assignment. Consideration is presumed for the former, and must be proved for the latter. The rights of the holder in due course of a negotiable instrument are often better than those of the transferor. The rights of the assignee are only those of the assignor. Because of the importance of negotiability, the law prescribes certain essential requirements to which every instrument must conform if it is to have the characteristic of negotiability.

In studying each essential, refer to the specimen instrument on page 244, and see if it fulfills these legal requirements. 

1. The instrument must be in written form.

It stands to reason that a negotiable instrument could not be oral, for it would be impossible to transfer an oral order or promise. by endorsement. It may be either written or printed, or both. The writing may be done with either lead pencil or ink; however, ink should be used. Every part of an instrument may be printed or written on a typewriter, except the signature, which must be written.

Printed forms with blank spaces in which to fill in on the typewriter or in writing the varying elements, such as date, amount, and names of parties, are in general use. 

2. Must contain an unconditional promise or order.

Example 1. Walsh promised to pay Heath $200 as soon as he sold his automobile. The payment of the $200 depends upon a contingency which may never happen.

No one would take an instrument unless he felt sure he would get his money; therefore, any condition or stipulation in the instrument which qualifies the promise to pay renders the instrument nonnegotiable. 

3. Must be payable to order or bearer.

Since the instruments are to pass from hand to hand, they must show on their face that such was the intent of the signer. This means that the instrument must be worded in such a way as to make it negotiable in form. The following wording may be used: "I promise to pay to the order of D. O. Waters"; "I promise to pay D. O. Waters or order"; "I promise to pay D. O. Waters or bearer"; "I promise to pay the bearer"; and (in the form of an order) "Pay D. O. Waters or order"; "Pay to the order of D. O. 

Waters"; "Pay D. O. Waters or bearer"; or "Pay the bearer."

The forms most used are: "I promise to pay to the order of" and "Pay to the order of." This wording is necessary that the instrument may be transferred by endorsement from one person to another.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS-PROMISSORY NOTES 247 

An instrument may be made nonnegotiable by making it payable to a particular person only, or omitting the negotiable words. Such an instrument may be a good contract between the immediate parties, but it is not transferable by endorsement. 

4. Must be payable to a definite payee or to bearer. 

In an instrument payable to order, the payee must be named or definitely indicated. See note, page 244. This note becomes negotiable as soon as it is endorsed by A. Student. 

The Negotiable Instruments Law provides that an instrument payable to the order of one or any number of several payees is negotiable; therefore, it may be negotiated as soon as it is endorsed by any one of the several parties. 

The Negotiable Instruments Law also provides that it will be sufficient if the payee is not definitely named, but indicated in such a way as to make his identity certain. For example, "Pay to the order of the Treasurer of Bondell & Company."

Any instrument payable to a fictitious payee is payable to bearer. 

Examples are checks payable to Cash, Petty Cash, Current Funds,

Pay Roll, etc. This applies only where the drawer knows the payee is fictitious. The reason is that, knowing such facts, the drawer could not expect the payee to endorse, but having issued the instrument, he must have intended it to circulate. The only instruments that circulate without endorsement are bearer instruments. 

Therefore, a fictitious payee makes it a bearer instrument. 

5. A negotiable instrument must be payable on demand or at a time that is certain.

When an instrument is payable on demand, it rests with the payee to decide when he shall demand payment; otherwise, the time the instrument is payable must be definitely stated at a determinable future time. An instrument payable on the happening of some event is not negotiable unless the event is sure to happen. 

This precludes about every happening except death. 

A note payable "six months after date" or "six months after death" makes the time of payment determinable. A note payable "five days after I sell my wheat" is not negotiable. The wheat may never be sold.

6. The instrument must be payable in money only.

An instrument payable in grain, coal, lumber, or any commodity other than money is not negotiable; the reason being that the value of the commodity might not be definite. 

Example 2. A note dated and payable in Detroit calls for payment in

Canadian money. This note is not negotiable, but it may be a good contract between the immediate parties. 

Money means the legal tender of the United States, and, if payable in any other kind of money, it is not negotiable in this country. 

7. The sum to be paid must be definite and certain. 

Example 3. A note dated August 1, 1935, contained a promise to pay $450 and any increase in the price of 500 bushels of wheat before November 1, 1935. This note is not negotiable. The exact sum to be paid is uncertain.

A promise to pay money and something else is not negotiable. 

The sum is considered to be definite even though the face of the instrument contains a statement, such as "with interest," or "in stated installments," or "with exchange.” 

8. The instrument must be signed by the party executing it. 

The maker or the drawer of the instrument must sign it in person or through the medium of someone duly authorized to sign for him. A person who cannot write may make his mark in the place of the signature, and someone who can write may add “his mark," followed by his name. 

X (his mark) 

James Holcomb

The signature may be placed anywhere on the instrument if it is plainly understood to be the signature, unless the law requires that it be subscribed. It usually is placed at the end or close of the writing. The federal government and the laws of some states require that a signature of this character be witnessed by one or two persons whose addresses must be given. 

A negotiable instrument should bear the signature of the maker if he is an individual, or of the makers if there are two or more.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS-PROMISSORY NOTES 249 

Signing an instrument as treasurer or agent, "W. R. Wade, Treasurer," or, "W. R. Wade, Agent," binds only the one signing. The terms treasurer and agent are considered descriptive. The following are correct signature forms to use when signing for someone else and a firm or company:

H. R. Harper by W. R. Wade, Agent The Oliver Machine Company by W. R. Wade, Treasurer

An instrument signed in this way, or in any similar way, indicating that the signer was acting on behalf of another, is not binding on the signer but on the one for whom he signed, provided he was authorized to make the signature. If he signed without authority he is liable on the instrument, and not merely for breach of warranty as in ordinary cases of unauthorized acts of an agent. 

9. Delivery of the instrument is essential. 

Example 4. A promissory note for $500, payable to W. J. Browning or order, was completely made out by Hood and left on his desk to be delivered later.

If Browning should come into possession of this note without its being delivered by Hood or his authorized agent, he would not have a valid right to it. But if he did get possession of it irregularly and transferred it by endorsement to Snell, who became a holder in due course, and who is innocent of any defects in the instrument, it would be a valid instrument in Snell's hands and he could recover against Hood. Browning, however, would be liable for any illegal acts in this connection. In case this note had not been completely made out and Browning had taken it from Hood's desk; and, without authority to do so, completed it and transferred it to Snell, it would not have been a valid contract. 

A negotiable instrument does not serve its purpose unless it is delivered by the maker to the party to whom it is made payable; therefore, delivery is essential to its validity. 

An instrument made payable to bearer may be transferred by anyone who comes into possession of it, and the transferee gets a good title, even though it was stolen; for this reason, "to bearer" should not be used in negotiable instruments.

Nonessentials that may be omitted. 

The statement "for value received" usually appears on certain negotiable instruments, but unless required by special statute, it is unnecessary. The assumption is that consideration was given, and this statement adds nothing to the validity of the instrument. 

The validity of a negotiable instrument is not affected by the omission of either the place or date or both. If the holder acts in good faith and the insertions are according to the original agreement, it is permissible for him to insert correctly any omissions that are classed as nonessentials, such as "for value received," the place and the date, and the place where payable. A holder in due course may recover, even if the omissions are not filled in according to agreement.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. An order-negotiable-instrument contract is transferable by endorsement and delivery only. 

2. A negotiable instrument must be in writing, payable to a designated payee, properly signed, negotiable in form, payable in money of a definite sum, payable unconditionally, and it must contain a promise or order to pay on demand or at a fixed or determinable future time. 

3. The negotiability of an instrument is not affected by giving the payee the privilege of accepting in payment something other than money. 

4. An instrument payable in anything but money is not negotiable. 

5. Consideration and delivery are presumed in a negotiable instrument in the hands of a holder in due course. 

6. A maker who delivers an incomplete instrument assumes full responsibility to an innocent third party who acquires it for value. 

7. An incomplete instrument not delivered does not bind the maker, even though an innocent third party should acquire it. 

8. A check made payable to a fictitious payee is payable to bearer. 

9. An instrument payable to a certain person only or lacking the negotiable words is not negotiable. 

10. A negotiable instrument payable to bearer gives any innocent third party who acquires it for value a good title.

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS: SUMMARY OUTLINE

A. Defined

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Bank Clearings. The total amount of all negotiable paper passing through the clearinghouses or a particular clearinghouse in a certain day or during a certain period. 

CHECKS 

Clearinghouse. A place where bankers meet to exchange checks and bills and settle balances.

Countersign. To sign in another place on an instrument to authenticate the signature already affixed.

Dishonor. To refuse to accept or pay a negotiable instrument. 

Exchange. The process of transmitting funds from one party and place to another party and place by means of check, draft, etc.

A CHECK A check is an order issued by a depositor on his bank to pay on demand to the party named in the check or to his order a definite sum of money. This order must bear the exact signature of the depositor. The use of the check is subject to strict regulations. 253

Who are the parties to a check?

There must be three original parties to every check and there may be a number of subsequent parties, depending on the number of hands it passes through before it is finally cashed at the bank on which it is drawn. The three original parties are: the drawer, the one who signs the check and against whose bank account it is to be charged; the payee, the party to whom the check is made payable; and the drawee, the bank on which the check is drawn. The drawer and payee may be the same party; that is, a check may be made out payable to "Myself," or, in case of a firm's check, to "Ourselves." 

What does the drawer of a check guarantee?

Any person who draws a check guarantees that the bank will pay the check to any rightful holder who presents it for payment; and that if the bank for any reason refuses to honor the check and he is duly notified of the refusal, he, the drawer, will pay it. The one who accepts a check assumes responsibility for presenting it within a reasonable time.

A person who issues a check knowing that he has no funds in the bank is guilty of a crime in New York State. Some other states have laws intended to regulate the issuing of checks. One should consult the laws of his own state. Any bank should be able to furnish the desired information regarding the legal status of checks or any other negotiable instrument. 

Presentment for payment. 

Example 1. Sweeney, a sailor stopping in Galveston, received a check for $50 on a Galveston bank. He did not cash the check at the time, and when he returned nearly a year later, he presented the check and it was dishonored. In the meantime, the bank had closed, reorganized, and finally opened again, and the drawer of the check had lost heavily by the closing.

If this check was good at the time it was given, Sweeney has no claim against the drawer, who suffered loss through the bank's closing. If it could be shown that the drawer had suffered no loss by reason of the check being carried for a year, Sweeney could recover from him.

CHECKS 

255 NO. 3. Jl.... 

It is understood that, in order to hold the drawer responsible, a check must be presented within a reasonable time. While circumstances and conditions control to a great extent, a reasonable time is considered to be the time it would ordinarily take a person in the usual course of business or events to present the check. Holding a check for an unreasonable length of time before attempting to cash it relieves the drawer from liability in case the bank fails and the drawer loses thereby. In the absence of a special statute, the law allows only a reasonable time to present a check for payment, usually twenty-four hours in the same city.

A CERTIFIED CHECK 

A certified check is a regular check issued by a depositor and taken to the bank either by the drawer or the holder, where the cashier of the bank or a teller or some other official will stamp across the front of the check the word "Certified," together with the date and the name of the bank, followed by the signature of the official who certified it, which means that the drawer has sufficient funds on deposit to cover the check, and the bank warrants that it will be paid when presented.

As soon as the bank certifies a check it deducts the amount from the drawer's account and places it to the credit of the certified check account. The bank assumes responsibility for paying a

check it has certified whenever it is presented. While it is the practice of banks to certify checks when asked to do so they are not legally required to certify any depositor's check. 

Who loses if the bank certifying the check fails? 

Example 2. Keith received a check from Holbrook. Not desiring to use the money for some time, Keith had it certified. Before he decided to present the check for payment the bank failed. 

Keith must bear any loss that may result from this transaction. 

Had Holbrook secured the certification of this check before delivering it to Keith, he would be liable in the same way that he would be liable for his check if not certified. 

If the payee, before accepting a check, requests the drawer to have it certified and he complies with this request, the drawer is not discharged from liability until the check is finally cashed. 

If the payee should have the check certified instead of having it cashed, he will have to stand any loss to him resulting from the bank's failure. By having the check certified he accepts the bank as his debtor and thereby discharges the drawer. But, if the drawer should of his own accord have his check certified before delivering it, he is not released from liability until the check is honored and canceled. 

What other kinds of checks are in common use?

Other kinds of checks in common use are: Cashier's checks, bank checks, voucher checks, and traveler's checks.

A cashier's check is no different in form from a depositor's check. 

It is issued on authority of the bank by the cashier, directing his bank to pay the party named therein or to his order a certain sum of money. These checks are handled through a special account and the bank assumes full responsibility for their payment. They are issued to people who want bank credit or exchange for some purpose. A cashier's check may be endorsed to anyone and sent to any distant place; any bank will readily cash it for a holder who is known or properly identified. 

A bank check or draft is an order by one bank on a bank in another place, in which it has funds on deposit, directing it to pay a certain sum of money to a party named in the draft. It is

CHECKS 

257 used as a medium of exchange by those who have accounts in distant places to settle. It is payable only at the drawee's bank, but it is probable that the owner could get it cashed anywhere after it is properly endorsed. Its use is very limited today on account of the general use of the depositor's check.

CASHIER BANK CHECK OR DRAFT 

A voucher check is a regular check to which is attached a memorandum of the account the check is to pay. 

An ordinary check when canceled serves as a receipt for the payment of a certain sum of money, while a voucher attached to a check shows the particular account paid by the check. It serves as memorandum to the payee, and if it is signed and returned, as sometimes requested, it serves as a memorandum to the drawer. 

What is a traveler's check?

Any person who plans to travel in this country or in foreign countries may purchase from a bank or express company traveler's checks in denominations from ten dollars up. The purchaser must sign each check in the space provided at the time of purchase. 

The checks may be cashed at any bank or express company office, the payee being required to countersign the check in the presence of the party cashing it. This signing and countersigning by the purchaser is a protection for the one who cashes the check; and if a check is lost, the finder could not cash it because of the difficulty he would have in forging the signature. What is a letter of credit?

A letter of credit is not a negotiable instrument itself or any form of one. It is a medium of exchange against which negotiable drafts are drawn by the holder of the letter of credit in favor of the bank paying any part of the amount for which the letter was given, and it serves the same purpose as traveler's checks. The bank paying any part of a letter of credit, endorses the amount on the back of it and draws a draft for this amount against the bank issuing the letter. When the final draft is drawn, the canceled letter is attached to the draft and both are sent to the bank issuing the letter. The person or persons to whom the letter was issued signed it at the time it was issued and must sign each draft in the presence of the one in the bank who handles the transaction. The signature on the draft must correspond with the signature on the letter. This is the bank's safeguard against fraud.

CHECKS 

259 

Money orders are transferable by endorsement.

Money orders, which may be purchased at the office of an express company or at the post office, are used to transmit funds from one place to another. Either express or post-office money orders are permitted to be transferred by endorsement only once. 

They are always payable on demand at an office of the issuing company in the case of an express money order, or at a post office in the case of a post-office money order. Banks will usually accept them on deposit, and some banks will cash them. Telegraph money orders are not transferable by endorsement. 

Is it possible to stop payment on a check? 

Example 3. Briggs gave his check, No. 814, to Walton in payment of a used automobile. A few hours later Briggs learned on good authority that the car had been stolen and sold to Walton. Briggs stopped payment of his check, which he had a right to do. In case of an action by Walton to hold Briggs for the check, Briggs will have to prove that Walton did not have a good title to the car. 

The drawer may stop payment of his check any time before the bank on which it was drawn has cashed it. This he does by giving notice to the bank to which the check is addressed not to pay it when presented. Banks may require that the notice be written and that it contain the number and date of the check, the name of the payee, and the amount, so that the tellers can detect it when it is presented for payment and refuse to pay it. Should a notice be telephoned in, someone in the bank will fill out the "stop payment" blank for the tellers.

If a bank pays a check, after receiving due notice not to pay it, the drawer who has suffered loss thereby has a right to hold the bank liable for the amount of the check. 

The drawer of a check is not relieved of liability on the check by stopping payment of it, but he retains the money in his account in the bank. When sued on the check he may use any defense available. In Example 3, Briggs has a valid defense of failure of consideration against Walton. But if the check is negotiated to a holder in due course, the drawer's defenses are cut off, except the absolute defenses. (See pages 295-297.)

What is meant by postdating a check?

Example 4. Mager, while away on a pleasure trip, had a chance to buy a consignment of furs at a very reasonable price. Not having a sufficient balance in his checking account at the time, he arranged with the fur company to accept a check postdated fifteen days. In the meantime, Mager returned from his trip and deposited funds sufficient to meet his check when presented.

This is a legitimate transaction, but should Mager fail to make the necessary deposit and his check be dishonored, he would be liable in an action against him by the fur company. A check that bears a date later than the day on which it was made out is postdated. It is permissible to postdate checks, and under certain conditions the practice can be justified. 

Is a person who issues a worthless check liable?

For anyone to issue a check when he has no checking account is, by statute law in most of the states, a criminal offense punishable by a fine or imprisonment, one or both. Some states have laws making it a criminal offense to issue a check when the maker has insufficient funds in the bank to cover it. 

What is the relation of the bank to its depositors? 

A bank, for good reasons, may refuse to accept money on deposit from anyone, but in accepting a deposit for a checking account, it agrees to handle it according to the regulations of the bank and the controlling banking law. 

1. A bank is responsible for paying a check on which the signature was forged. The depositor, in order to hold the bank liable, must notify it of the forgery within a reasonable time after discovering it. 

2. The bank paying a check that has been altered in any way is usually held liable for any loss sustained by the drawer. However, if the drawer carelessly made out the check and the alteration could not be detected, the bank paying the check may be relieved from liability. Anyone altering a check by raising the amount is guilty of a criminal offense. 

3. Should the amount of a check expressed in figures not agree with the amount expressed in writing, the bank is protected in paying the amount expressed in writing. 

4. Should a bank for no reason refuse to honor a depositor's check, it is liable to him for any damage he suffered because of its action. 

5. In case a depositor dies, the bank is not permitted to cash any of his

CHECKS 

261 outstanding checks issued before his death. However, if the bank cashed a check not knowing of the depositor's death, it is not liable. 

6. It is considered that banks render valuable services to their depositors and they are permitted to require that depositors conform to certain regulations, and that they pay reasonable service charges. 

7. In case a check is lost, the drawer should give the bank on which it is drawn a "stop payment notice" before he issues another check in its place. 

Otherwise the bank will not be liable if it pays both checks. 

8. The bank sends each depositor a statement of his account at regular intervals, usually each month, or on request. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A check is a negotiable instrument in the form of an order addressed to a particular bank. 

2. Only depositors who have checking accounts are privileged to issue checks. 

3. There must always be three parties to a check, but there may be only one person and the bank, as in the case of a check made payable to "myself." 

4. Space on the back of a check is the only thing that limits the number of endorsements it may bear. If more space is needed, a piece of paper may be attached. 

5. A check is always a conditional payment until it is honored by the bank on which it is drawn. 

6. Unless a statute law gives the payee of a check a certain length of time in which to present it, he should not delay presenting it. 

7. The bank certifying a check assumes full responsibility for its payment. 

8. The person who identifies another person is in no way liable if the one identified is the right person. 

9. Any negotiable instrument in the form of an order that is payable on demand in cash at a bank is considered a check. 

10. The drawer may stop payment on any check. His liability to the third party will depend on whether or not he had sufficient reason for stopping payment. 

11. Should a bank pay a check on which the drawer stopped payment, it is liable for any loss resulting up to the amount of the check. 

12. Issuing a worthless check is a criminal offense under the laws of most states.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Acceptance. A time draft which has been accepted by the drawee; the act of accepting a time draft. 

At Sight. To be acted upon as soon as seen. 

Bill of Exchange. An order addressed by one person to another to pay a certain sum in money to a third person at a fixed or determinable future time. 

Domestic Exchange. Negotiable credit instruments, the use of which is confined to boundaries of one's own country. 

Sight Draft. A draft payable at sight or when presented. 

Virtual Acceptance. A written agreement to accept, that is not a part of the draft proper, amounts to an acceptance of the draft. 

What is a draft?

A draft is a written order by one party, the drawer, addressed to another party, the drawee, directing him to pay the party named therein (the payee) a certain sum of money according to the terms specified in the order (draft). If the drawee honors the draft, he becomes the acceptor and payer. 

Drafts and checks are similar, in that both are order negotiable instruments. A check is an order on a bank, and a draft may be an order on an individual, a firm, or a bank. Both are in reality drafts. 

What is a bill of exchange?

A bill of exchange is the same as a draft, and they are used in the same way and for the same purpose. Draft is the term in common use, and the inclination is to use the term "draft" when referring to instruments used inland or between different parts of the United States, and to use the term "bill of exchange" when referring to drafts used between different countries. Drafts and bills of ex- 264

change are usually negotiated through banks; however, they may be negotiated by individuals exclusive of any bank. 

How are drafts classed?

As to time, drafts are classed as time drafts and sight drafts. As to place of payment, bills of exchange (drafts) are classed as foreign and inland. A draft may be made payable "at sight," or a $40000

What is a foreign exchange?

Foreign exchange usually refers to the exchange between this country and some foreign country. A draft drawn by a bank in 

New York City and payable in London would be classed as foreign exchange. It was the general practice not so long ago, and still is when requested, to issue foreign bills in sets of two or three. Each bill is sent out by a different ship, to make sure that at least one will reach its destination. The bills are all payable at the same bank, and when one is paid, the others are canceled. Principally banks in seaport cities or in large commercial centers where foreign trade is carried on deal in foreign exchange. Smaller banks and banks in other sections selling foreign exchange, deal through banks that carry a foreign exchange account. 

What is a trade acceptance?

A trade acceptance is a two-name draft drawn by the seller of goods upon the one to whom the goods are sold. It is made payable to "Myself" or "Ourselves."

The trade acceptance is restricted to the settlement of accounts between the buyer and the seller of goods. After it is accepted, it may be offered by the drawer, who is also the payee, at a bank for
