BY WW. Bruce A TRADE ACCEPTANCE TREAS. 

discount. Various forms of trade acceptances are met with, but they serve the same purpose. In this country the trade acceptance is not used so generally as in England and the European countries. 

The trade acceptance proves itself in a court of law. 

What are the drawer's obligations?

In a three-party draft the drawer is liable to the payee until the draft is accepted and finally paid. He warrants that the drawee will accept it or pay it if proper presentment within a reasonable time and demand be made upon him. If the drawee refuses to accept the draft, the payee must send notice of refusal at once to the drawer, who becomes liable to the payee for the amount of the draft. Should the accepted draft be dishonored, the drawer is liable in the same way, if he is properly notified. 

What are the obligations of the acceptor?

A draft drawn upon a definite party is not binding upon him in any way until he accepts it either by paying it or writing on the face of it, usually across the face, the word "Accepted," together with any directions or conditions permitted, the date if necessary, and his signature. A drawee who accepts a draft unconditionally agrees to pay it according to its terms. Drafts are usually accepted in this way. This is called a general acceptance. Other forms sometimes used are qualified acceptance and virtual acceptance.

Forms of acceptance: 

General Acceptance 

Accepted 

May 12, 19Walter T. Loomis (Date may be omitted if draft is payable after date)

Acceptance with Directions 

Accepted 

June 15, 19 

Payable at First National Bank 

Walter T. Loomis

Qualified Acceptance 

Accepted 

January 6, 19Payable in 60 instead of 30 days 

Walter T. Loomis

The acceptor may qualify his acceptance in any way he sees fit. He may specify a condition of payment; he may change the time or place of payment; or he may accept to pay only a part of the amount. 

Example. A draft may be made out for $500, and accepted to pay only $300. Any differences resulting from a qualified acceptance will have to be adjusted between drawer and acceptor.

The holder of a draft is not bound to take a qualified acceptance. 

He has a right to consider the draft as dishonored and to hold the drawer liable. In case the holder takes a qualified acceptance without the consent of the drawer and prior endorsers, they are released from liability, and he and all subsequent holders are bound thereby. 

Any sight or time draft is transferable by endorsement either before or after acceptance.

The acceptor of a draft warrants to the transferee that the signature of the drawer is genuine; that he had a right to draw the draft; that the payee exists; that he is qualified to endorse the instrument; and, that he will honor the draft according to the terms of his acceptance. The warranties are not merely to the transferee, but to the payee, if there is no transfer. The acceptor of a draft does not warrant that the payee's endorsement or any subsequent endorsement is genuine. 

Must the acceptance be written on the instrument?

The acceptance does not have to be written on the instrument itself to be binding upon the acceptor, and when it is written on

another paper apart from the instrument, it is called a virtual acceptance, which is a written unconditional promise to accept a draft. This promise may be in the form of a written agreement to accept a draft described as already drawn or as one to be drawn in the future; or, the promise to accept a certain draft as described may be in the form of a letter. This agreement or promise to accept, which is written apart from the draft itself, is binding upon the one agreeing to accept in favor of the one who saw the promise to accept and took the draft on his faith in this promise. A promise is good to accept a draft to be drawn, in favor of one who took the draft on his faith in the promise. Seeing it is not necessary. The promise to be enforceable must describe the instrument fully and be absolute in its terms.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The drawee cannot be required to accept the draft. 

2. The drawee who chooses to accept a draft may use a general acceptance or a qualified acceptance. The holder is not bound to take a qualified acceptance; doing so, he assumes full responsibility. 

3. A promise to accept a draft may be written on a piece of paper apart from the draft or in a letter, and if properly executed it amounts to a "virtual" acceptance. 

4. The distinction between inland and foreign bills of exchange is not in the instruments themselves but in the places where issued and payable. 

5. A draft is dishonored by a refusal to pay a sight draft, and by a refusal to accept, or having accepted, to pay a time draft. 

6. Acceptance of a draft payable after date is unnecessary but advised. Dating the acceptance is unnecessary. Such a draft would be dishonored by the drawee's refusing to accept it. 

7. The drawer of a draft is liable to the payee in case the drawee fails to accept and pay. 

8. Should the drawee accept a draft on which the drawer's signature was forged, he is fully liable. 

9. The holder assumes responsibility for presenting the draft and notifying the drawer in case it is not paid or accepted.

PROMISSORY NOTES TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Collateral. Security attached to an obligation, to insure its performance. 

Compound Interest. Interest paid or charged upon interest that is not paid or collected when due. 

Coupon. A certificate of interest, that when due is to be clipped from a coupon bond and cashed.

Debenture. A negotiable certificate of indebtedness serving as a credit instrument or bond.

Transferee. The person to whom something is transferred. 

What is a promissory note?

A negotiable promissory note is an unconditional written promise made by one party to pay to another party or his order or bearer at a fixed or determinable future time a certain sum of money. It is a contract, subject to the laws and regulations governing contracts and also to those governing negotiable instruments. See illustration, page 244. 

Who are the parties to a note?

There are only two original parties to a note: the maker or the party who signs the note, and the payee, the party to whom the note is made payable. There may be one or more subsequent parties, depending upon the number of endorsers. A subsequent party may endorse a note as security or for the purpose of transferring it to another party. In either case he is liable for payment of the note if the maker fails to pay. Notes are frequently sold at a discount before maturity. A note that is sold or discounted at a bank must be endorsed by the holder before delivery. 

The parties to a note may be individuals, societies, partnership firms and incorporated companies. Two or more persons may be 272

PROMISSORY NOTES 

273 named in a note as payees or as makers. A note may be payable to 

Crane and Cooper and signed by Hill and King, either as partners or as comakers. 

What does the maker of a note promise?

The maker and signer of a negotiable note promises that he will pay the face of the note when properly presented, together with any accrued interest, in full, to the payee or to any rightful holder on the day it is legally due, or any later date. His promise cannot be qualified in any way without destroying the negotiability of the note. The note does not have to be presented for payment to hold the maker liable to the holder.

When is a note several and when joint and several? 

A note signed by one party is a several note; that is, only one original party has promised to pay it. A note worded, "We or either of us promise to pay," and signed by two or more parties, is a joint and several note. The note on page 244 is a several note. 

A note worded, "I promise to pay," and signed by two or more parties, is also a joint and several note. This wording indicates that each signer has promised to pay the full amount of the note. Regardless of how a promise is worded, if the note is signed by two or more parties and each party endorses the note before it is delivered, it is in effect a joint and several note. The form "We jointly and severally promise to pay" is sometimes used. 

What is a joint note?

A note worded, "We promise to pay," and signed by two or more parties, is a joint note, which means that each party is liable for the full amount, but they have to be sued jointly. When a note is payable to or endorsed to two or more persons jointly, and they transfer it by endorsement, they are liable as endorsers jointly and severally. A note signed by more than one maker, unless the wording clearly indicates their liability, is usually interpreted by the courts to be a joint and several note. 

What are the different forms of notes?

The different forms of notes in use are regular or simple (see illustration on page 244), collateral, and judgment. Bonds and ין

certificates of deposit are negotiable in form; and while they are promissory notes in effect, they are not considered as such. 

A collateral note is a note, the payment of which is secured by stocks, bonds, or other assets convertible into cash. It is a regular note to which is added a descriptive statement of the securities pledged by the maker to insure the payment of the note. The note usually contains a stipulation as to how the security is to be disposed of to satisfy the note in case the maker fails to pay it when it falls due. Usually the securities must be sold and the proceeds applied to pay the note.

A judgment note is a regular promissory note with an additional clause by which the maker confesses judgment in case he fails to pay the note when due. This means that the judgment can be entered up against the maker in court without the usual action at law and a trial. The advantage of this type of note, which is in general use, is that judgment can be entered up quickly without the expense of a lawsuit. After the judgment is entered up, it runs for the full time under the statute in the particular state, usually twenty years, unless it is paid off. $450.00

What is a certificate of deposit?

A certificate of deposit is issued by a bank at the request of a person who has deposited in the bank a sum of money he does not wish to use for a time, and does not want to carry about or keep unprotected, and which he does not want to carry in a regular checking account. A certificate of deposit is issued sometimes to corporations or groups of individuals who wish to deposit a certain sum in "escrow." Many large banks do not care to issue certificates for amounts less than ten thousand dollars. Interest is usually Teller

allowed on money so deposited, provided it is not withdrawn within a stated time, because the bank can count on the use of the money during that time. A certificate of deposit may be issued for a definite period stated in the certificate, or it may be issued for no definite period, in which case it is payable on demand. It may be made payable to the person making the deposit, or to him or his order. In the latter form it is negotiable and may be transferred by endorsement and delivery. A certificate of deposit is substantially a promissory note, made by the bank, promising to pay to the depositor or order the sum deposited at a stated future time or on demand. 

What is a bond?

Bonds in denominations of from $10 up are negotiable promises signed by the proper officials and issued under seal by a corpora-

tion, government, or a political division of government, such as a village, city, or county, whereby they are to pay the holder a certain sum at a certain time, and during the time the bond is in force, to pay at regular intervals the interest at the rate specified therein. 

They usually are issued for long periods of time, varying from five to fifty years, and the interest is payable quarterly, semiannually, or annually; frequently semiannually. Bonds are either registered or coupon. Both forms are in general use. Registered bonds may be transferred by endorsement and registration. Coupon bonds may be transferred without endorsement. 

A registered bond is issued to a first purchaser, whose name is registered on the books of the issuing corporation or government. 

Any subsequent purchaser to whom the bond is transferred by endorsement must see that the transfer is made on the books, to make sure that the interest check is sent to the real owner. The transfer of ownership is complete only when the name of the transferee is on the books.

A coupon bond has small, interest coupons attached to it-one for each interest period, and as the interest comes due, the owner of the bond detaches the coupon and cashes it at the issuing office or at a bank. The corporation or government issuing the bond is not concerned about who owns the bond; the coupons are cashed for the person presenting them. The bond is payable to bearer, and when it is due, it will be paid to the party presenting it. 

How is the payment of bonds secured?

Bonds are issued for the purpose of borrowing money. Bonds issued by any political division of our government, by reason of its power to tax property, are liens upon all the taxable property in that particular political division. Bonds that are issued by corporations, secured by a mortgage or deed of trust of the property of the corporation, are called mortgage bonds. Bonds that are issued solely on the credit of the corporation are called debenture bonds. 

What is interest?

Interest at a certain rate per cent per annum is an allowable charge regulated by law for the use of money. It is paid on bor-

PROMISSORY NOTES 

277 rowed money, and the sum on which it is paid is called the principal. The rate charged is referred to as the legal rate or the contract rate.

The legal rate is the rate allowed by law. It is payable in the absence of an agreement to the contrary.

Any rate 10 10 12 12 12 10 10 The contract rate is the rate specified in the contract, which cannot exceed the legal contract rate. Any rate higher than the contract rate, which is the maximum rate allowed by law, is illegal and is called usury. The penalty for charging a usurious rate of

interest varies in the different states, as does the rate that may be charged, but it is forfeiture of interest or principal, or both. 

Compound interest is not collectible by legal means. It is permissible to charge compound interest only when by agreement interest due and unpaid is added to the principal, or when the original contract calls for such a plan. 

Example 1. Mason borrowed $500 on his note for one year at 6% interest. When the note came due, he could pay neither interest nor principal, so he arranged with the lender to accept a note for $530 at 6% interest, in payment of the old note. Compound interest in this case is legally permissible. 

On what claims can interest be legally collected?

Interest at the legal rate can be collected on a noninterest-bearing note from the date it becomes due until it is paid; and, on a note which contains the words "with interest" or "with use," interest may be collected from the date of the note. Interest at the legal rate can be collected on an overdue account. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A note is an evidence of indebtedness and a promise by the debtor to pay the amount of the debt at a future time. 

2. The holder of a note does not have to present it to the maker when due to hold him liable. 

3. A note signed by one person is a several note; a note signed by two or more persons is a joint note or a joint and several note, depending upon how the promise is worded. 

4. A collateral note is a secured note which contains a description of the property pledged as security. 

5. A judgment note permits the entry of judgment by the court without a suit at law. 

6. Coupon bonds are negotiable in form and are payable to bearer; registered bonds are negotiable and may be transferred only by being reregistered in the name of the transferee on the books of the issuing corporation. 

7. The purchaser of a registered bond must see that it is regis-

PROMISSORY NOTES 

279 tered in his name on the books of the corporation or municipality issuing it. 

8. Mortgage bonds are secured by a mortgage or a trust deed of the corporation's property, made to a trustee, usually a bank, in the interests of the bondholders. 

9. Debenture bonds are issued on the credit of the corporation. 

10. All taxable property within a municipality is security for its bonds. 

11. The law of each state and territory specifies a legal rate of interest which may be charged, and in most cases a contract rate permitted which is the maximum rate. 

12. The lender may legally agree to accept a rate lower than the legal rate.

NEGOTIATION TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Allonge. A piece of paper fastened to a negotiable instrument, on which to write additional endorsements. 

Counterclaim. A claim that offsets another claim. 

Endorsee. The party to whom an instrument is transferred by endorsement.

Restrictive Endorsement. An endorsement that restricts the transfer of a negotiable instrument to a certain purpose, and it is no longer negotiable.

Without Recourse. Relieving the endorser from liability for payment in case the maker fails; cannot run back to him. 

What is meant by negotiation? 

Example 1. A promissory note made payable to the order of Charles E.

Gile was endorsed and delivered by him to John W. Elton. Now Elton is the holder and he may transfer it by endorsement to another party, or he may demand payment from the maker when the note becomes due. 

Had this note been payable to Charles E. Gile or bearer, it could have been transferred by delivery only, any number of times. The one holding it at the time it is due has a right to present it to the maker and demand payment.

Negotiation of a negotiable instrument means the act of transferring it from one person to another in such a way as to make the transferee the holder of the instrument in the place of the original payee or any former holder. 

What is the principal characteristic of a negotiable instrument?

A negotiable instrument may be transferred from one person to another by endorsement and delivery, if it is payable to order; or by delivery only, if it is payable to bearer. In the hands of an innocent 281

transferee who gave value for it in the usual course of business before it is due, it is enforceable, when possibly the original holder could not enforce it, for the reason that the maker had a good defense or a counterclaim against him. It is this characteristic that makes a negotiable instrument pass freely as a substitute for money.

What is the meaning of negotiability as applied to negotiable instruments?

I Negotiability as applied to all negotiable instruments means that the instrument is capable of being transferred or assigned by one party to another by endorsement and delivery, or, if payable to bearer, by delivery only. A negotiable instrument that is negotiated from one person to another passes free from certain defenses that the maker might have entered against it while it was in the hands of the original holder; in the transferee's hands, however, it is collectible. Defenses are explained later. 

What is the difference between assignability and negotiability? 

We have learned that any contract to pay money or deliver goods may be assigned, but any assigned contract passes subject to all the defenses which might be brought against it in the hands of the original owner, while any negotiable contract negotiated before it is due to an innocent purchaser for value in the usual course of business passes free from such defenses. 

Example 2. Sixty days after date I promise to pay to John C. Miller 

Two Hundred and 00/100

Dollars 

S. E. Powers 

This is not a negotiable note, but it may be assigned by Miller to another person. The assignee would have no better title, however, than Miller had. In case no consideration had been given for the note, or Powers had a counterclaim (a claim against Miller), neither Miller nor the assignee could enforce collection. But, if the note was negotiable and was transferred regularly to a purchaser, Powers would have to pay it, regardless of the defenses mentioned.

How are negotiable instruments endorsed by the payee?

The payee may endorse a negotiable instrument by writing any statement called for by the desired kind of endorsement, and signing his name; or he may sign only his name on the back of the instrument. If there is not sufficient room on the back of the instrument for the required endorsement, it may be written on a paper called an "allonge" and attached to the instrument. Endorsements may be stamped or typewritten.

Where the endorsement is made by the payee for the purpose of transferring title to the instrument to another party, the payee becomes a regular endorser. 

What does a regular endorser warrant to the transferee? 

1. That the instrument is genuine in every respect. 

2. That he has a good title to the instrument and a right to transfer it. 

3. That all prior parties thereto had capacity to contract. 

4. That he has no knowledge of any facts that would impair the validity of the instrument. 

5. That he will become responsible to the endorsee or rightful holder of the instrument for payment in case the maker fails. The endorsee can hold the endorser liable only under certain conditions. 

Under what conditions can the endorsee hold the endorser liable? 

1. The endorsee must duly present the instrument when due to the acceptor or maker for payment, or in case of a sight draft, to the drawee for acceptance, and later for payment. 

2. If the instrument is dishonored, the endorsee must notify the endorser of that fact at once. 

3. If the instrument is a foreign bill, it must be duly protested. 

There is a difference between the contract to pay and the warranties. The contract is conditional on demand and notice. The warranties are absolute and are broken, if at all, at the time of negotiation and can be sued on at once. 

It is important for anyone handling negotiable instruments, and particularly any endorser, to understand the legal effect of the different kinds of endorsements. 

What are the kinds of endorsements? 

The endorsements in use are (1) blank, (2) full or special, (3) qualified, (4) conditional, (5) restrictive. Blank and full endorse-

ments are used mostly. Qualified and restrictive endorsements are little used.

In case the payee's name is incorrectly spelled, the name as spelled should be endorsed on the back and the name correctly spelled should be written just below it.

A blank endorsement makes the instrument payable to bearer. Any holder has a right to change a blank endorsement to a full or special endorsement by writing "Pay to the order of" and the holder's name over the endorser's name.

CORRECTED SPELLING 

It is not wise to accept an instrument endorsed in blank, for the reason that, being payable to bearer, it can be claimed and possibly collected by anyone stealing or finding it. A blank endorsement may be safely used if the instrument is to be cashed at once. 

A full or special endorsement makes the instrument payable only to the endorsee or to his order, which means that if he wishes to transfer it to another, he must endorse it. Should he hold the instrument until it is finally paid, no other endorsement is necessary. Faber is protected in case this instrument is lost or stolen. 

Anyone finding or stealing an instrument endorsed in full could not transfer a good title to it, as against the true owner. While the words "or order" are generally used in an endorsement of this kind, they are not necessary. If the words "or order" were omitted, Faber could still transfer this instrument by any endorsement he saw fit to use.

A QUALIFIED ENDORSEMENT(2) 

Qualified endorsement has very limited use, for the reason that if the payee does not believe that the instrument will be paid when due and is not willing to assume responsibility for its payment, no one else would want it. There are circumstances, however, which merit the use of a qualified endorsement. 

Example 3. Welsh, a member of the firm of Welsh & Snyder, received a partnership note payable to James E. Welsh. He endorsed it to Welsh & Snyder "without recourse," for the reason that he did not wish to become personally liable on this note to his firm. 

Example 4. A father wishes to make one son a present of a note signed by one L. W. Wilson without involving the father's estate, so he endorses it "without recourse." 

A conditional endorsement may be used on any negotiable instrument. If an instrument bears a conditional endorsement, the maker is not bound to comply with it. The payee has no right to add to the maker's burden unless the maker agrees to it. Conditional endorsements are used only rarely. 

The endorser who used a qualified endorsement simply transferred whatever right or title he had in the instrument to the endorsee, and in doing so he assumed no responsibility for paying it in case the maker failed.

Who is an irregular endorser?

Example 6. Miles agreed to buy an automobile from Bowers if he would accept a note for six months for $500 at 6% interest. Bowers agreed to accept Miles's note if he would get some responsible party to endorse it. 

Miles secured E. H. Land's unqualified endorsement on his note, and 

Bowers accepted it.

Land is an irregular endorser. He endorsed the note before the payee endorsed it, and he is fully responsible for payment in case Miles fails to pay. By endorsing this note as he did, Land lent his credit to Miles so that he could purchase the car. Land, in this case, is what is termed an accommodation endorser, because he endorsed for the purpose of lending his credit to Miles. He is also an irregular endorser, because he is not in the chain of title, and his endorsement was not necessary to a transfer. He is not liable to 

Miles in any way, but to all subsequent holders he is liable the same as a regular endorser. The consideration for Land's endorsement is the automobile which Bowers sold to Miles and for which he accepted Miles's note endorsed by Land in part payment. 

What is the order of the endorsers' liability? 

Example 7. A note signed by Shirley was made payable to Dorsey, and was transferred to Pender, who in turn transferred it to Deitz, and Deitz finally endorsed it to L. M. Keller. When the note became due and Keller presented it to Shirley for payment, he refused to pay it. 

Keller may collect from any one of the endorsers. Each one is liable to him for the full amount of the note. If Deitz had paid it, he could hold both 

James W. Dorsey 

H. E. Pender 

F. O. Deitz

Pender and Dorsey, or either one. If Pender had paid it, he could hold 

Dorsey. Should Dorsey have to pay it, he will have to look to Shirley for payment, and the other endorsers are released. 

In case of two or more endorsers, when it can be shown that they are joint endorsers, each one can be held for the full amount, but he can get only proportionate contribution from his co-endorsers. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. An instrument is negotiated when it is transferred from one to another to make the transferee a holder. 

2. Negotiation is accomplished by delivery or by endorsement and delivery, depending on whether the instrument is payable to bearer or to order. 

3. An endorser may be the payee or any subsequent holder, or he may be a third party endorsing as a means of lending his credit as security for the instrument. 

4. A regular or unqualified endorser warrants that the instrument is genuine, that he has a good title to it, that prior parties are competent to contract, that the instrument, at the time of endorsing it, is a valid and existing obligation, and that he will be responsible for its payment in case the maker fails. 

5. A qualified endorsement relieves the endorser from liability for payment in case the maker fails. He is liable, however, if the instrument is not a good contract. 

6. The full endorsement is preferred to a blank endorsement when an instrument is transferred from one holder to another. 

7. A blank endorsement should be used only when the instrument is not likely to be passed from one to another. 

8. An instrument bearing a restrictive endorsement is no longer negotiable. 

9. The endorser's warranties are absolute, and any breach of them occurs at the time of negotiation. 

10. An infant in rightful possession of a negotiable instrument may transfer it by endorsement. 

11. A bearer instrument can be negotiated without endorsement; an order instrument can be negotiated only by endorsement. 

12. Where there are two or more endorsers on an instrument, all and each are liable to the last holder, but to each other they are liable in the order in which they endorsed, unless they are joint endorsers.

TEXT QUESTIONS

A. HOLDER IN DUE COURSE TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Holder in Due Course. A holder of a negotiable instrument whose title to it is free from any of the personal defenses that might have been used against it while in the hands of the original holder. 

Material Alteration. Any alteration in a negotiable instrument that changes the legal effect of the instrument. 

Personal Defenses. Defenses to a negotiable instrument available against any holder except a holder in due course. 

Prior Parties. Parties who were holders of the instrument before the present holder. 

Real or Absolute. Actual; genuine. Applied to defenses in a negotiable contract that the maker may use against any holder. 

Who becomes a holder in due course?

The Negotiable Instruments Law provides that a holder in due course is a holder who has come into possession of the instrument under the following conditions: 

1. The instrument must be complete and regular upon its face. 

If there are any noticeable irregularities such as erasures, or the instrument is not fully made out, or statements therein disagree, such as the time and the due date or any other known or noticeable irregularity which shows that the instrument does not conform to accepted customs or was not issued in the usual course of business, the one taking the instrument under such conditions cannot qualify as a holder in due course. 

2. He must become a holder of the instrument before it is overdue.

A holder who takes an instrument after it is due, or after having notice that it was dishonored, if such is the fact, as might be in the 291

case of a demand note, is not a holder in due course. The due date of a negotiable instrument is certain, even in the case of a demand note, which is due on demand a reasonable time after it is issued. An instrument transferred on its due date is not considered to be overdue.

A holder in due course has greater protection under the law than one who is not, as we shall learn later. 

3. The holder must take the instrument in good faith and give value for it.

Example 1. Hains held a note for $500 signed by Davis. This note was given by Davis for what Hains fraudulently represented to him to be an exclusive agency right to sell in a certain state a new kind of vacuum cleaner. Hains was to ship to Davis 100 cleaners at once. The cleaners were never shipped, and Hains endorsed the note to Sims, a colleague of his, who fully understood the circumstances. When the note became due, Sims tried to force Davis to pay it.

These facts would bar Sims from collecting this note. He did not take the instrument in good faith nor give value for it; therefore, he is not a holder in due course. Actual knowledge of a defect in the holder's title destroys the claim of good faith. The payment of a consideration much less than the face of the note is a suspicious circumstance. Any conditions surrounding the transfer which must have caused the holder to suspect that there was something wrong with the instrument are to be considered in determining his good faith. Such circumstances may cause the court to declare that the holder is not a holder in due course, and therefore he has no more rights in the note than the original holder had. 

4. The holder must not at the time the instrument was negotiated to him have notice of any defects in it or in the title of the person negotiating it.

The statement that a holder in due course must have innocently taken the instrument for value in the usual course of business and before maturity summarizes the provisions of the Negotiable Instruments Law. Emphasis is placed on the holder's being ignorant of any defects, or of any facts that would indicate bad faith, such as illustrated in Example 1. Sims was aware of the facts in this

case at the time this note was endorsed to him by Hains. A negotiable instrument that changes hands in a legitimate business transaction is almost certain to have been taken in good faith and without notice of defects, and if taken before maturity and for value, the taker will be a holder in due course. 

A successive holder becomes a holder in due course. 

The holder in due course has a good title to the instrument and he can transfer a good title to another; therefore, the one to whom he properly transfers the instrument becomes a holder in due course unless he was a party to the fraud or illegality whereby the instrument was originally secured and he does not have to comply with the requirements to get the benefits. Therefore, a holder after a holder in due course may take the instrument, knowing of defenses that might have been used against the original party, and his rights are not subject to such defenses. 

The holder in due course is the rightful owner of the instrument and he may enforce payment of it against the maker and all other parties in any way liable upon it free from personal defenses available against prior holders. 

What defenses may be asserted against an instrument?

Defenses are divided into two classes: personal defenses which are good against parties not in due course, and real or absolute defenses which are good against any holder. 

Personal defenses 

1. Fraudulent inducement 

2. Duress 

3. Lack of consideration 

4. Counterclaim 

5. Nondelivery 

6. Payment 

Real or absolute defenses 

1. Incapacity of parties 2. Illegality 

3. Fraudulent execution 

4. Forgery 

5. Material alteration 

6. Nondelivery of an incomplete instrument 

Personal defenses.

Personal defenses relate to the conditions under which the instrument was executed and certain facts surrounding it, rather than to the instrument itself. They are available to the maker of the instrument to be used against the payee, or any holder not in due course, but they are not good against a holder in due course.

1. Fraudulent inducement.

Example 2. Dursey fraudulently represented stocks to Wedover, who purchased them on Dursey's representation and gave a note in payment. 

Dursey transferred this note to Grant, an innocent purchaser for value. 

Wedover is liable to Grant, a holder in due course, but he could have defended against Dursey had he attempted to collect the note. Wedover should have investigated before accepting the stocks and giving his note. 

When a person has been induced by fraudulent means to sign a promissory note carelessly which reasonable judgment and foresight should have prompted him not to sign, he can defend against the other original party, but as against a holder in due course he has no defense. 

2. Duress.

The same rule with regard to duress that applies to other contracts applies to negotiable contracts. Duress is a good defense as between the original parties to the instrument, but it is not available as a defense against a holder in due course. 

3. Lack of consideration.

Example 3. Bates was willing to loan $500 to Green, but not having the ready cash, he gave Green his note for $500. Green endorsed the note and discounted it at a bank. The bank becomes a holder in due course and can collect from Bates. Bates is an accommodation maker, and Green could not collect from him directly or through someone to whom he might endorse the note for collection.

The payee of a negotiable instrument for which he gave no consideration cannot collect from the maker, but he can transfer the instrument to an innocent third party for value in the usual course of business, and this third party could hold the maker liable. Lack of consideration is a defense as between the immediate parties (maker and payee) and holders not in due course but not as against a holder in due course. 

4. Counterclaim.

Example 4. Wassen secured a loan of $100 from Grover on his six months' note at 6% interest. In the meantime Wassen worked for Grover until he had earned $80, which was unpaid. When Wassen's note became due, it was presented for payment by Denton, a local merchant, to whom Grover had transferred it. Wassen is liable for the full amount of the note.

even though Grover owes him $80. Had Grover presented the instrument, Wassen could have deducted the $80 and paid the difference. 

While a counterclaim is a good defense as between the immediate parties to a negotiable instrument and holders not in due course, it is not a good defense against a holder in due course. 

5. Nondelivery.

An instrument may not be delivered, or delivery may be made conditionally, for a special purpose and not to transfer title to the instrument. Whatever the conditions are, as between the original parties or a transferee not a holder in due course, the lack of delivery, or the failure of the conditions on which or the purpose for which delivery was made, is a defense to the maker. But should the instrument in some irregular way fall into the hands of a holder in due course, the maker is liable to him for its payment. 

6. Payment.

Any maker, at the time of paying his note, should take it up and deface it or detach his signature so that there would be no chance that he would ever have to pay it a second time. 

Should a maker pay his note before it is due without taking it up, and in some mysterious manner it finds its way into the hands of a holder in due course, he might have to pay it again. Any note that is paid and not canceled may cause the maker trouble later. 

Real defenses. 

Real defenses affect the instrument differently than do personal defenses. A personal defense is available only between immediate parties, the maker and the one whom he names in the instrument as payee, or a later holder not in due course, but if the instrument is in the hands of a holder in due course it is of no avail; while a real defense is available regardless of whose hands the instrument is in. Real defenses may be used against any holder of negotiable paper. They relate to the instrument itself rather than to the acts or conditions surrounding it. 

1. Incapacity of parties.

A negotiable instrument signed by an infant, a lunatic, or any other incompetent person is not a valid instrument; therefore, in-

capacity of parties is an absolute defense and is available against any holder. However, an infant who receives a valid negotiable instrument may transfer it to another in the usual way. 

2. Illegality. 

Example 5. Bell borrowed $500 on his ninety-day note from Gilman and agreed to pay 10% interest in a state where the legal contract rate is 6%, and usury is forbidden by statute. Bell has an absolute defense in this case.

An absolute defense does not arise from the mere fact that a negotiable instrument contract is illegal. A note may be given to pay a wager or bet which may be an illegal contract in that particular state. As between the immediate parties the contract is illegal and not enforceable, but a holder in due course can collect from the maker. Illegality is an absolute defense only in case the contract is made illegal and void by statute. 

3. Fraudulent execution.

Example 6. Barns was asked to sign a paper. He did not have his glasses and could not read it, but he was told it was "the usual receipt,' and he thought he was signing a receipt, as he had done on similar occasions before, for 500 advertising circulars which had been delivered to him. He really signed what turned out to be a note for $500, due in one year. In this case, Barns has a good defense against any holder. 

Fraud is generally a personal defense only, but when it makes the whole contract ineffective, it is available as an absolute defense, if the person defrauded can show that he was not negligent in allowing it to happen. Barns had no reason for thinking that he was signing any instrument other than the usual receipt, and as he was in no way negligent he could not be held. 

When a person signs a negotiable instrument, believing he is signing some other document, he cannot be held liable on the instrument, regardless of whose hands it is in. 

4. Forgery.

A negotiable instrument on which the signature has been forged is void and unenforceable in the hands of any holder who acquired title through the forgery. But if the payee endorsed the instrument to another, he is liable to the endorsee, for the reason that an

endorser warrants that the instrument is genuine, that he has a good title to it, and that all prior parties have capacity to contract. 

The person whose name was forged has an absolute defense. 

5. Material alteration. 

An alteration, to be material, must affect the rights of the parties to the instrument. Raising the amount, extending the time of payment, or increasing the rate of interest are material alterations. The alteration must be made intentionally by a party to the instrument or by one in lawful possession of it, and without the consent of the maker or acceptor. If an instrument that has been materially altered is in the hands of a holder in due course, not a party to the alteration, he may enforce payment thereof according to its original provisions. 

6. Nondelivery of an incomplete instrument. 

An incomplete instrument that is taken possession of wrongfully by someone, completed by him and transferred to an innocent party, cannot be collected from the supposed maker, for the reason that the party transferring it did not have a good title to the instrument; therefore, he could transfer none, even to an innocent purchaser. Nondelivery of an incomplete instrument is an absolute defense, regardless of who is the holder.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. To make the endorsee a holder in due course, the instrument must be complete and regular on its face, it must not be overdue, he must have taken it in good faith and given value for it, and he must not know of any defects or defenses that might operate against the instrument. 

2. A holder in due course may have a better title to the instrument than the original holder had, for the reason that he is not subject to certain defenses that might be used between the original parties. 

3. Personal defenses are available as between the original parties to the instrument. 

4. Real or absolute defenses are available against any holder of the instrument.

5. The term "for value" does not mean that full face value must be paid for the instrument. 

6. A negotiable instrument is incomplete and revocable as between original parties until it is delivered. 

7. Nondelivery of an incomplete negotiable instrument relieves the supposed maker from all liability. 

8. A holder in due course is sometimes called a bona fide holder. 

9. The endorsee of a holder in due course is likewise a holder in due course, unless he was a party to the illegal or fraudulent execution of the instrument.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Business Day. That portion of the twenty-four-hour day during which business is regularly transacted. It varies in the different communities. 

Certificate of Protest. The certificate prepared by the notary public, whereby he declares that a certain instrument was presented and dishonored.

Legally Due. The time when a negotiable instrument may be legally collected.

Presentment. Exhibition to the acceptor or maker of an instrument that is due and demanding payment.

Waiving Protest. Giving up the right to have a negotiable instrument presented when due and notice of dishonor sent to payee and endorsers. 

How important is presentment?

Presentment is necessary to fix the liability of the drawer or endorser. The drawer of a check or draft and the endorser of a check, draft, or note agree to pay only if the drawee or maker fails to pay. Under the law they are entitled to proper presentment, demand, and notice of dishonor, and such proceedings are absolutely necessary before they can be held liable. 

When is presentment for payment necessary? 

Presentment for payment is always necessary to fix the liability of secondary parties. The acceptor of a draft and the maker of a note are primarily liable, and presentment is not necessary to hold them liable, but the drawer of a draft or check and all endorsers are secondary parties, and unless the instrument is properly presented for payment to the acceptor or maker, they are discharged. 

It must be understood that an instrument on which no drawer or endorser is liable does not have to be presented. The debtor should 300

seek the creditor, but to hold subsequent parties (endorsers) and drawer liable, presentment must be made. 

A draft made payable at sight must be presented for payment, and if someone other than the drawer is the holder, he must notify the drawer and endorsers at once in case payment is refused. A draft made payable at a certain number of days' sight must be presented for acceptance. This is necessary that the holder may know what the drawee intends to do. Should he refuse to accept the draft, the holder must notify the drawer and endorsers at once. A draft made payable a certain number of days after date or on a certain day need not be presented for acceptance; it is sufficient to present it for payment on its due date. However, the holder may present it if he wishes to do so, and acceptance by the drawee is reasonable assurance that he will pay it when due. Twenty-four hours is allowed the drawee in which to decide whether to accept the draft; should he keep it for more than twenty-four hours, he is presumed to have accepted it. 

How is presentment made?

The holder or someone authorized by him must exhibit the instrument to the payer or hand it to him. The payer will understand that he is to accept or pay it, depending upon what the instrument requires. For the person presenting to state that he has the instrument to present is not sufficient. 

When an instrument is payable at a bank and is held by the bank at maturity, presentment and demand are deemed to have been properly made and, if the maker has no funds at the bank, the instrument is dishonored. Notice of dishonor must be given by the bank as in other cases. 

Where must presentment be made?

Presentment must be made at the place designated in the instrument. If no place is designated, then presentment should be made at the maker's or drawee's office or known place of business. If he has no place of business or it is not known, presentment may be made at his place of residence. In case no place of business or residence is known, the presentment may be made wherever the drawee or payer can be found.

When and to whom should presentment be made? 

Presentment must be made at a reasonable hour on the due date, or if the due date is a holiday, on the first business day following. 

An instrument due on Saturday need not be presented that day, but it may be presented for acceptance or payment if the holder desires. Presentment at an office or bank must be made during office or banking hours.

Presentment must be made to the party or parties who are named in the instrument as maker or drawee, or to his authorized agent. If two or more are named jointly, then presentment must be made to each person. 

Failing to present an instrument is excused in case of a serious accident, a legal obstacle preventing, or if the drawee is dead or is known to have left the country or he cannot be found after a diligent search. Presentment should be made to a deceased person's personal representative, if he is known to have one. 

When is an instrument legally due?

A negotiable instrument is legally due on the last day it has to run, and it may be paid any reasonable hour during that day. A note payable sixty days after date is due on the sixtieth day following, but a note made payable four months after date is due on the same date four months later, and it may run for 122 days, more or less, depending upon the particular months. An instrument falling due on a holiday or on Sunday would become legally due on the first business day following. Days of grace are now abolished by statute in most states, but where in force, they simply extend the time for the period of grace. Any interest has to be paid for the period of grace. 

What is a notice of dishonor?

When an instrument is presented to the drawee or payer and he refuses to pay or accept it, he has dishonored it, and notice of this dishonor must be sent to all parties who are in any way liable on the instrument (drawer or endorsers). If the instrument is a foreign bill, it must be protested. Any drawer or endorser not receiving this notice is discharged.

How may the notice be given?

The notice may be given orally or in writing, unless a protest is required; then a written notice must be given. The notice must be complete enough to describe the instrument and make known that it was not accepted or not paid. Notice may be sent by mail, by a messenger, or it may be delivered in person. The fact that the letter was mailed, even though it does not reach the party to whom it was addressed, is considered to be sufficient notice, if it is properly addressed. 

By whom and when should notice be given?

Notice should be given by the holder or by his authorized agent; but when an instrument is protested by a notary, he is often employed to send out the notices also. Notice may also be given by any person liable on the instrument to any other person to whom he can look for payment.

Under the Negotiable Instruments Law, if the parties live in the same place, notice must be given not later than the day following the dishonor, but if they reside in different places, notice must be mailed in time to go out not later than the day following. If given in any other way than through the mail, it must reach the addressee as soon as the mail would have reached him. 

Where should notice be sent?

The address of the parties who are responsible for the payment of an instrument or are liable in any way on it is important for the holder at the time it is due and payable. Notice should be sent to the known address of the party affected by the dishonor. If his address is not definitely known, it should be sent to the place where he is supposed to get his mail. The one mailing the notice should use his best judgment, and if he can show that he made every reasonable effort to reach the endorser, the endorser is not relieved from liability. However, failure to give notice will discharge the drawer or endorser on the dishonored instrument unless a satisfactory excuse can be offered or the instrument was endorsed with a waiver.

What is a waiver?

A waiver is giving up a right, and as applied to an instrument endorsed with a waiver, it means giving up a right to be notified in case the instrument is dishonored. The waiver may include the protest in case of an inland bill, and it would read: "Protest and notice is hereby waived." The waiver may be written, printed, or stamped, on the face of the instrument, or it may be written or stamped, following or above the endorsement. A waiver makes the endorser liable without the performance of the particular thing waived; it may be the formal protest or presentment and notice. 

A waiver may apply to all endorsers if it is so stated. If a waiver is given by one endorser, it applies to him only, and prior and later endorsers are fully entitled to notice. 

What is a protest?

A protest is a formal declaration in the form of a certificate and under seal made by a notary public, certifying to the demand and dishonor of a particular instrument described therein. 

A certificate of protest contains the following information: 

1. The time and place of presentment 

2. The fact that presentment was made and how 

3. The demand made and the answer given or the fact that the payer (drawee, acceptor, or maker) could not be found 

4. The reason for protesting the instrument

After attaching the instrument to this certificate of protest, the notary will mail a notice of protest to all endorsers. 

The notary usually mails the notices, but this may be done by the holder or his agent. When a notary public is not available, protest may be made by a resident of the place in the presence of two reputable citizens as witnesses of the act of presenting. 

The cost of the protest and notices must be paid first by the holder of the instrument, but finally by the party liable for the payment of the instrument. The fees for the certificate of protest are fixed by statute, and are in most states $1.25 or $1.50 ($.75 in 

New York State). To this sum is added the charge for postage on the notices mailed. Accrued interest from the due date of the instrument until payment is finally made, can be collected also.

How are negotiable instruments discharged?

The usual way of discharging a negotiable instrument is by payment. When the maker or acceptor pays the instrument, it should be taken up by him. This will release all parties to the instrument and close the transaction. 

The promise of the maker of a note or the acceptor of a draft is absolute, and he can be discharged only by performance or through certain of the defenses which may be available to him. See defenses, pages 293-297.

A holder who has lost the instrument can as a rule compel the maker to pay, but the maker has a right to require of the holder a bond to indemnify him in case the instrument should be found and a later demand for payment be made. 

Payment of a dishonored instrument by one of the endorsers does not discharge it. Any prior endorser and the maker or acceptor are still liable. The instrument is not discharged until paid by the party primarily liable. 

How may an endorser be discharged? 

Example 1. Lutz held Hood's note which was endorsed by Waverly.

When the note became due, Hood made a partial payment thereon and Lutz, without Waverly's consent, accepted a new note from Hood for the unpaid portion, and canceled the old note. This act on the part of Lutz discharged Waverly from liability.

Any act that discharges the instrument discharges the drawer or endorsers. They are also discharged in case a prior party is discharged, for the reason that their right of recourse is destroyed. 

This being the case, a second endorser would be discharged by any act that would discharge the maker or the first endorser. 

Lack of presentment, demand, and notice, or any one of them, will discharge an endorser.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The liability of the drawer or endorser to the holder of a negotiable instrument is fixed by demand and notice. 

2. A drawee who holds a draft more than twenty-four hours in deciding whether or not to accept it is presumed to have accepted.

3. Presentment must be made on the due date at appropriate time of day, and it should be made to the one who is primarily liable for payment. 

4. Failing to present an instrument discharges from liability the drawer or endorsers, unless a reasonable excuse for not presenting it is offered by the holder. 

5. Notice of dishonor must be sent to all parties who are liable on the instrument in case the maker, drawee, or acceptor fails to pay. 

6. Under the Negotiable Instruments Law, notice must be given to a party in the same place not later than the day following dishonor, or if sent by mail it must be sent out not later than the day following. 

7. An endorsement with a waiver relieves the holder from sending notice in case it is an inland bill that is dishonored. 

8. Negotiable instruments are discharged by payment and by any act that would discharge a simple contract.

1. Why is presentment made (a) for acceptance, (b) for payment?

COMMENTS 

Guaranty and suretyship have to do primarily with credits. Credit serves to postpone cash payments for a period of time, and, in such cases, it is good business to require some reasonable assurance that the debt or obligation will be discharged according to the terms in the agreement. One means of doing this is for the creditor to require the debtor to have some responsible party guarantee his account or obligation or sign with him as surety.

The different classes of credit common to our activities are: personal credit, business credit, banking credit, and investment credit.

GUARANTY AND SURETYSHIP 

327 Personal credit is the credit anyone extends to an individual. It is generally given through loans and charge accounts. Sometimes the individual has sufficient resources or credit standing so that he can secure credit without assistance, but in many cases the creditor will ask for security. 

Business credit results from various business transactions in which purchases are made on account or short-term bank loans are made. Here again in many cases the account or the loan must be secured in some way acceptable to the creditor. 

Banking credit is the credit which banks extend to business firms and individuals by means of short-term loans on notes secured and unsecured, depending upon the conditions, the financial standing, and the credit rating of the borrower.

Investment credit is the credit extended to a business organization through secured loans made to it or through the purchase of its credit instruments, such as mortgages on its property, its own bonds if it is allowed to issue bonds, and its long-term notes, which are issued against the fixed assets of the organization. The main source of this credit is the individual, either directly or indirectly, for the reason that all money invested ultimately comes from individuals, either by direct investment or through investing agencies, such as banks, to whom the individuals have entrusted their money. Banks lend the depositors' money, and in doing so they act independently and not as agents for depositors, and if loans are not paid, the bank is still bound to repay its depositors. Unsound loans were the cause of so many bank failures in the past that now, as a result of federal legislation, all banks qualifying under the Banking Act of 1933 may provide deposit insurance for each depositor's account up to $5,000; this they do through the purchase of stock in the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation. This purchase of stock must equal a certain per cent of the total deposits; then the corporation assumes the risk of the bank's failing and the depositors' losing thereby.

All the credit activities involve an element of risk on the part of the creditor, and for this reason he seeks to protect his interest by every reasonable means. Those extending credit or using credit in any form should be thoroughly familiar with the laws that regulate credit instruments. 

Anyone who is asked to enter into a contract of guaranty or suretyship should satisfy himself that the principal is honest and reliable, that it is a reasonably safe risk, and that there are justifiable reasons why the contract should be entered into. 

The one who enters into a contract of guaranty or suretyship must expect to assume full responsibility for the credit risk according to the terms of the contract in the event the principal defaults; for this reason, therefore, the one assuming this responsibility should use every precaution to protect his own interest. The risk is assumed without any direct return except in the case of bonding companies, who make a business of assuming such risks for a definite fee.

SALE OF PERSONAL PROPERTY TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Ownership. The exclusive right to possess and control property, subject to the law.

Title. That which gives a right to possess and to hold property; the right one has in property that amounts to ownership. 

Vendee. One to whom something is sold; the buyer. 

Vendor. One who sells something; the seller. 

What is a sale?

Example 1. Barns, a storekeeper, displays goods on counters, shelves, and in windows in his store. A customer comes into the store, calls for a certain article which Barns has for sale, pays the price requested, and takes the article with him.

This is a complete sale. By a very simple process this contract of sale was negotiated and performed. A sale is an agreement whereby the ownership of goods is transferred from one party to another for a price. It is in reality the carrying out of a contract whereby one party has agreed to sell something which another party has agreed to buy at a certain price.

Every sale, regardless of how large or how small, results from a contract in some form. The sale and purchase of a five-cent article is a contract in every sense, the same as the sale and purchase of a railroad locomotive for $100,000, and is subject to all the rules and laws that regulate sales contracts. The difference is in the degree of importance and the type of sales contract used. 

What is a contract to sell? 

Example 2. Craig contracted with the Benson Auto Sales, Inc., for the purchase of a new car for $995. By the terms of the agreement, Craig was to be allowed $250 for his old car which he traded in, and to pay $745 in cash when the new car was delivered within thirty days. 328

SALE OF PERSONAL PROPERTY 

329 This is a contract to sell. The price is agreed upon, but a part of it is paid by trading in an old car at an allowance price of $250. It is not a sale, because the transfer and payment are to be made in the future.

A contract to sell is an agreement whereby the seller (vendor) is to transfer certain goods to the buyer (vendee) at a future time for a price paid or promised to be paid, which is the consideration for the seller's promise to sell. Although the price is named in money, if the parties agree to it, any personal property may be given for part or all of the purchase price.

What is the difference between a barter and a sale? 

A barter is an exchange of one article of personal property or certain goods for another article or certain other goods. In a sale the price is named in money, even though some part or all of it is paid with other personal property at an agreed allowance price, as in Example 2. Price is a necessary element of a sale. The laws that apply to sales apply also to barter. 

Title and possession need not pass together. In a sale transaction, title may pass to the buyer without a change of possession or possession may pass to the buyer without a transfer of title. In the first instance the buyer may leave the article purchased in the possession of the seller until such time as it is convenient for him to take it. In the second instance the article may be purchased on the deferred payment plan whereby the seller retains the title until the last payment is made.

What is the Uniform Sales Act? 

The Uniform Sales Act is an act which has been adopted by most of the states for the purpose of regulating sales contracts and making them reasonably uniform throughout certain states where it is in force. It is sometimes referred to as the "Sales of Goods Act." 

Under this act the term "goods" is used to mean any form of personal property.

Some provisions of the Uniform Sales Act: 

1. The rights and duties of the seller and the buyer are clearly set forth. 

2. The sale of goods is defined as an agreement whereby the seller trans-

fers the property or title in the goods to the buyer for a consideration called the price. 

3. Property in the goods means the ownership therein or the title thereto, and it applies to all kinds of personal property, including money, and claims such as liens, mortgages, and promissory notes. 

4. A contract to sell is defined as one whereby the seller agrees to transfer the property or title in the goods to the buyer for a consideration called the price. 

5. The sale is executed when the seller transfers the property or title in the goods to the purchaser and receives the price of the goods. 

The discussion of Sales hereafter is based on the Uniform Sales Act, and provisions thereof are mentioned incidentally. 

When is the sales contract completed?

Example 3. Harlow sold Weston a portable building that was on 

Harlow's land. It was agreed that Weston was to pay $200 for the building and move it from Harlow's land within thirty days. As soon as Weston pays the $200, the sale is completed. 

The delivery in this case is constructive. Whenever the article sold is accessible to the buyer and he is to take it from where it is, delivery is said to be constructive. When the seller has delivered the goods to the purchaser, and the purchaser has accepted them and paid the price to the seller, the sale is completed. These acts are concurrent unless there is an agreement to the contrary. Delivery is not to be understood as meaning that the article itself must be passed from the seller to the buyer in every case, but instead that the ownership or title is passed. The delivery may be actual or constructive. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A sale is a contract subject to laws and rules governing contracts in general. 

2. A price in money is the consideration in a sale. 

3. In case no price is named, a reasonable price is presumed. 

4. In a barter, one article is exchanged for another article, and no price is mentioned. 

5. In a sale transaction, the title and possession may pass together, or either may pass without the other.

SALE OF PERSONAL PROPERTY 

331 6. The price agreed upon in a sale can, by agreement of the parties, be paid in any kind of personal property. 

7. "Goods" is taken to mean any kind of personal property, including claims to be paid in money. 

8. A sales contract is enforceable only when it contains the necessary elements of a contract.
