SALE OF PERSONAL PROPERTY: SUMMARY OUTLINE I. Sale Defined II. Contract to Sell III. Barter Distinguished from a Sale IV. Passing of Title and Possession V. The Uniform Sales Act A. Some Provisions of VI. When Sales Contract Is Completed COMMENTS 

A sale of personal property is the most common form of business transaction. Property of every kind may be the subject of a sale, including not only tangible articles, called chattels, but intangible rights, such as concessions, interests in corporations represented by shares of stock, and such things.

All sales, regardless of how small or how large may be the amount involved, are governed by the same rules of law, and a knowledge of at least the most important of these rules is essential for every person in the business world.

The development of easy and rapid methods of communication and transportation has made possible a wide distribution of commodities. 

Frequently, buyers and sellers live in different states. To avoid possible conflicting rules of law, a Uniform Law of Sales has been proposed and has been adopted in many states. The treatment of the subject "Sale of Personal Property" just discussed is based on this uniform law.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

By-bidding. Bidding on an article offered for sale at an auction by prearrangement with the seller, for the purpose of running up the price. 

Market Value. A value determined by the price at which similar goods sell in the market.

Pledge. To temporarily transfer the title of goods to another as security for an obligation. 

Pledgee. A person who lends money and receives the security. 

Pledgor. A person who borrows money and furnishes security for the faithful performance of his obligation. 

Who may sell goods?

Example 1. Drake borrowed a land roller from Poole and used it at times for three years.

An innocent prospective purchaser might be led to believe that Drake could convey a good title to this roller, but he could not. 

Poole, the owner, could demand the return of the roller from the borrower or the purchaser, had the borrower sold it. 

The general rule is that no one other than the owner or his duly authorized agent can sell goods and convey to the purchaser a valid title to the goods sold. The exceptions to this rule will be discussed later. It is not necessary that the owner be in possession of the goods sold; ownership at the time of the sale is enough to give him the right to sell. Possession of goods does not insure ownership on the part of the one possessing them. 

A factor or commission merchant may sell. 

A sale made by a factor or a commission merchant binds the original owner, the principal, even though the factor or the commission merchant exceeds his authority and sells the goods when 333

he is not authorized to do so. This is the law in most states, but a commission merchant cannot give a good title to the goods sold unless he has them in his possession at the time of making the sale. 

This statute is limited to mercantile transactions and applies only to commission merchants. 

A pledgee may sell.

A pledgee who lends money and accepts the custody of some form of personal property to secure the loan has a right, in case the borrower defaults, to sell the property pledged, and to apply the proceeds of the sale to the payment of the debt. Any surplus from the sale over the amount of the debt and the expenses belongs to the pledgor. In some states the pledgee must sell the goods not redeemed at public auction and return to the pledgor the proceeds of the sale in excess of the amount of the loan. This right of a pledgee is an exception to the rule that only the owner or his authorized agent may sell. 

An auctioneer may sell.

An auctioneer is a person engaged by the owner of goods or any kind of property to sell certain articles to the highest bidder. He acts as agent for the owner, and sales made by him are binding on the owner. 

How are auction sales regulated?

An auction sale is advertised and held for the purpose of offering certain specific goods for sale and giving all persons who learn of it a chance to attend and bid for the purchase of any of the goods or articles offered. Goods are sold to the highest bidder. However, certain reservations may be made by the owner of the goods, but they must be made known to prospective purchasers before any goods are sold. 

Who may contract to sell goods? 

Example 2. Powers contracted to sell 1,000 bushels of apples of a certain variety and grade to Miller for $1.25 per bushel and to deliver them to Miller's cold storage plant not later than November 1, following.

At the time of making this contract, Powers had no apples to sell, neither did he own or control an orchard from which they

might be harvested, but should he fail to procure the apples and deliver them according to his contract, Miller would have a right of action against him for damages for breach of contract. 

The law does not restrict anyone who is competent to enter into a binding contract from contracting to sell goods of any description, the sale of which is not prohibited by some special law, and it matters not whether the one agreeing to sell has the goods in his possession or even owns them at the time of making the contract, or whether or not the goods exist at the time. A contract to sell simply provides for the transfer of the title to certain goods at some future time, according to the terms therein. The party who contracts to sell goods which he does not own at the time, but which he expects to procure from some source, can be held for a breach of contract, should he fail to complete the sale. 

What are future goods? 

Example 3. On July 1, Kingman contracted to sell his crop of potatoes to Irwin for 90c per bushel. The potatoes were growing in a field belonging to Kingman, and they are to be dug and delivered by him not later than the following October 15.

This is a contract to sell an indefinite quantity of potatoes. 

When the potatoes are delivered and the price paid, the sale is completed, and it matters not whether there be one bushel or one thousand bushels. Should the crop completely fail, the seller is not liable in damages, because it is implied in such contracts that failure of the crop excuses delivery. 

Goods which are not in existence at the time the contract is entered into, but which must grow or be produced are called future goods. Such goods only can be the subject matter of a contract to sell, for the reason that title to them cannot pass until they actually exist, and passing of the title is necessary to a complete sale.

The seller must have a good title. 

The general rule is that the seller cannot give a better title than he himself has. This rule applies to every case involving the sale and transfer of property except in the case of the transfer of negotiable instruments, which is fully explained under "negotiable

instruments," page 293. Therefore, an innocent purchaser of goods does not acquire, as a rule, a good title from the seller who did not have a good title to begin with. The exceptions to this rule are as follows: 

1. A conditional vendee having possession but not title, may give good title.

Example 4. The Household Appliance Company sold a refrigerator to 

Mrs. Cole on the deferred payment plan. They failed to have the contract recorded as required by law. Mrs. Cole made two payments and then sold the refrigerator to Mrs. Horton. The purchaser in this case got a good title as against the true owner, for she was ignorant of the reservation of title.

Had this contract been recorded, the Household Appliance Company could have re-claimed this refrigerator from Mrs. Horton by proper legal proceedings. The buyer, in such a case, should look up the records, which are available to anyone, before making such a purchase. In a state not requiring the recording of such contracts the purchaser in this case would not get a good title. 

When goods are sold on the deferred payment plan and by the agreement that the title is not to pass until the last payment is made, the innocent purchaser of such goods from the vendee in possession gets a good title in states requiring that such contracts be in writing and recorded in some public office, usually the office of the town or city clerk, in cases where the seller failed to have the contract recorded. 

2. A buyer who acquired title by trick or fraud may give good title. 

Example 5. Webb inherited a very valuable clock over a hundred years old. A dealer who knew its real value told Webb that it was worth little or nothing, but finally offered $5 for it, which offer Webb accepted. Webb learned later that the clock was very valuable, but he did not attempt to recover it on the ground that the dealer had intentionally misrepresented its value. Later the dealer sold this clock to Foster for $1,000. 

While Webb could have re-claimed the clock from the dealer on the ground that he was defrauded, the dealer had a voidable title and was able to give good title to Foster, an innocent purchaser.

3. A seller in possession after a sale may give good title.

Example 6. Huber bought a mowing machine from Graft in October but did not call for it until about the middle of May following. On May 1 

Graft sold the machine to Demerst, who removed it at once. 

Demerst has a good title as against Huber, who made it possible for Graft to commit this fraud. Huber, however, has a right of action against Graft. 

4. A person who is permitted by the true owner of goods to hold himself out as the owner may give good title. 

Example 7. Weldon hired a motor truck from Harlow for $20 per month to use indefinitely. Weldon secured the license and insurance in his own name, and after using the truck for some time he sold it to Ayers. 

Ayers got a good title to this truck as against Harlow, the true owner, for the reason that Harlow made it possible for Weldon to hold himself out as the owner, by allowing him to register the truck in his own name.

An innocent purchaser gets a good title when the owner of goods allows another who is in possession thereof to hold himself out to anyone and everyone as the true owner or to use the goods in such a way as to mislead innocent third persons into believing him to be the owner.

Can a thief convey a good title to stolen goods? 

Example 8. Slater discovered that Waldo was using a watch that had been stolen from him over a year ago. When he questioned Waldo about the watch, Waldo claimed he bought it from Bryce, who had purchased it a short time before from a dealer in secondhand jewelry.

Slater is still the owner of this watch, and if he can prove his ownership, he can re-claim it from Waldo, who did not acquire a good title from the seller. The purchaser of stolen goods does not acquire a good title to them, and no matter how many times the goods are sold and transferred, the title is still vested in the true owner. The reason is that the thief acquires no title and can convey none.

Voidable title distinguished from no title. 

In Example 5, preceding, the dealer had a title transferred to him by Webb, the owner. The title was voidable because of the

dealer's fraud, but it was some title. If he sells the goods to an innocent purchaser who has no knowledge of the fraud, such purchaser may retain the goods as against the true owner. In 

Example 8, Waldo acquired no title to the watch for the reason that the seller did not have even a voidable title to begin with. 

Can the finder of lost property transfer a good title to it? 

Example 9. A stray pig found its way into Waldo's yard. Waldo put it into the pen with his own pigs, and after keeping it for six months and using every effort to find the owner, he finally advertised the pig for sale and sold it to the highest bidder.

The finder who takes certain property into his possession and in an effort to find the owner goes to some expense to advertise the property or to care for it, may after a reasonable time advertise and sell it at public sale in order to reimburse himself for the cost of care and advertising. The purchaser in this case gets a good title against anybody else except the owner.

The same rule applies to the sale of lost property that applies to stolen goods. The finder by merely taking possession of the goods does not acquire a good title to them as against the true owner, and he cannot transfer a good title, except in the case of certain negotiable instruments, which have been explained. See page 249. 

What are the rules governing the price to be paid? 

1. Under the Uniform Sales Act, the price named in a sale and also in a barter need not be payable in money, but it may be payable in any personal property.

Example 10. Wade bought a cow from Hager for $55 and gave fifty bushels of wheat at $1.10 per bushel in payment. 

While this transaction amounts to Wade's exchanging fifty bushels of wheat with Hager for a cow, it is a sale. In any transaction in which a price is named for either article exchanged, it is a sale. 

2. The price to be paid does not have to be fixed by the contract. If the contract is sufficiently complete so that the price can be determined, this is all that is necessary.

Example 11. Lent bought 100 bushels of potatoes from Garish, for which he agreed to pay the market price at the time of delivery within thirty days.

This is a good sales contract even though the price is not fixed. 

The price may be left to be determined by the market price or by a third party. A sales transaction in which a third party determines the price is called a sale at a valuation. Price is the amount agreed upon by the parties; value is what the goods are worth in the market. 

3. The price does not have to correspond with the value of the article sold. In the absence of fraud a sales contract is binding upon the parties thereto regardless of how much more or less is paid for an article than its true value.

Example 12. Devon offered and paid Myers $50 for a chair believing it to be very old and valuable. The chair was a copy of a very old chair and was worth not over $10.

If no fraud was practiced in this case, Devon is bound by this contract. 

What is a bill of sale?

Example 13. Herb, who was insolvent, gave a bill of sale of all his store fixtures and delivery trucks to Worth, who agreed to pay Herb's other creditors.

This is a valid contract of sale, and title to the goods passed to Worth. If the bill of sale were given to Worth without consideration, for the purpose of defrauding Herb's other creditors, it would be of no avail and Worth could not claim title. A bill of sale is evidence of the transfer of title resulting from a contract of sale, but it is not valid unless the contract itself is valid under the rules requiring consideration, capacity to contract, absence of fraud and mistake, etc.

Any document which is effective to transfer the title to goods is a bill of sale. The formal bill of sale is not used as a rule unless the amount is large enough to warrant, or the law requires that a bill of sale be given, as is the case in some states particularly when an automobile is sold. A bill of sale is used sometimes to show the transfer of the title to personal property when evidence of such transfer is desired for some purpose. A person can prove his ownership if he has a good bill of sale. A bill of sale must be recorded in some states.

Storage receipts may be used to transfer title to goods sold. 

The warehouse receipt is issued sometimes in two forms. One is the straight receipt which calls for the delivery of the goods stored only to the person named therein, and it is nonnegotiable. The other form is a negotiable receipt and may be transferred by endorsement so that the goods listed therein will be delivered to the endorsee upon presentation of the receipt and demand if all charges are paid. Goods stored may be sold and the title transferred to the purchaser by the owner's properly endorsing either receipt, but if a nonnegotiable receipt is used, it may not be possible to negotiate it in such a way as to give the endorsee a right to claim the goods from the warehouseman. The warehouse receipt is not negotiable in all states.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The true owner or his authorized agent may sell property. 

2. The factor or commission merchant and the pledgee may sell goods and transfer a good title. 

3. The seller must have a good title to the goods sold, or the circumstances surrounding the purchase must be such that the buyer can defend his title. 

4. The price does not have to be named if it is to be determined in some way. 

5. In the absence of fraud the price does not have to be adequate. 

6. The Sales of Goods Act applies to every exchange transaction where a price is named. 

7. The assumption in an auction sale is that the goods will be sold to the highest bidder and any restrictions or limitations must be made known to prospective purchasers before the sale. 

8. Lost goods not claimed by the owner may be advertised and sold by the finder to reimburse him for any expense incurred. 

9. The use of the bill of sale is optional except in states where by statute its use is made mandatory in certain sales transactions, such as the sale of a used automobile. Bills of sale must be recorded in some states. 

10. Anyone who offers goods for sale warrants that he has a lawful right to sell them.

11. The title to goods sold, while in storage or in transit, may be transferred by the owner endorsing the order warehouse receipt or the order bill of lading for the goods and transferring them to the purchaser. 

12. No sale is complete until the title to the goods sold is transferred from the owner to the purchaser.

THE WRITTEN CONTRACT OF SALE TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

In Earnest. Money or something of value paid on a purchase to bind the bargain.

Memorandum. A written statement of the essential facts of a sales agreement.

Personalty. All forms of personal or movable property. 

Realty. Land and all that is attached thereto as a part and parcel thereof. 

Statutory Minimum. The smallest amount specified in a statute requiring that certain sales contracts be in writing. 

What sales contracts are required to be in writing?

The seventeenth section of the English Statute of Frauds provides: "No contract for the sale of goods, wares, and merchandise, for the price of ten pounds sterling or upward shall be allowed to be good except: 

1. The buyer shall accept part of the goods sold, and actually receive the same; or 

2. Give something in earnest to bind the bargain or in part payment; or 

3. That some note or memorandum in writing of the said bargain be made and signed by the parties to be charged by such contract or their agents thereunto lawfully authorized."

When a sale is at auction, no written agreement is required. The memorandum of the auction sale is sufficient. 

Similar statutes have been adopted in most of the states in the 

United States. Alabama, Kansas, Louisiana, North Carolina,

Texas, Virginia, and West Virginia do not have such statutes. In 

Florida and Iowa, it matters not how little the price is, the sale must conform to the Statute of Frauds. All other states have statutes conforming to the requirements of the English statute, except that the prices in the different states vary from $30 and up- 345

ward to $500 and in Ohio the price is fixed at $2,500 and upward. 

Price in this connection means the actual sum agreed upon to be paid by the purchaser.

Goods, wares and merchandise are taken to mean any article of personal property which may be the subject matter of a sale, and according to the Uniform Sales Act and the provisions of most statutes for regulating sales claims of different kinds, contracts, bonds, and shares of stock are considered personal property. 

1. The buyer shall receive and accept a part or all of the goods. 

Example 1. Dugan contracted orally to buy 500 yards of gravel from

Posner at $3 per yard delivered. Posner delivered two yards of the gravel at the time the agreement was made and Dugan accepted it. 

This contract does not have to be in writing to satisfy the statute. Regardless of the amount of money involved in a sale of goods, the contract need not be in writing if the goods or any part of them have been delivered to and accepted by the buyer. The goods may be actually or constructively delivered by the seller, and the acceptance may be in the form of an act or a statement by which the buyer shows conclusively that he has accepted the goods or some part of them. In Example 1, the acceptance was by an act. If no part of this gravel had been delivered, received, and accepted, this contract, to be enforceable in a state having adopted a Statute of Frauds, would have to be in writing. 

2. The buyer shall pay and the seller shall accept a part or all of the purchase price. 

Example 2. Atkins contracted with Snyder for the purchase of 1,000 boxes of oranges at $3 per box, F.O.B. Orlando. Atkins paid Snyder $300 or 10% of the purchase price at the time of making the contract. 

Should Atkins fail to complete his contract by refusing to accept the oranges, Snyder could hold him in damages, but he could not keep any part of the $300 in excess of the damage allowed. There is a distinction between part payment and taking an option. See page 64-65. The party to whom the sale is made may not receive the goods or any part of them, but he may pay part or all of the purchase price at the time the sale is made or at any other time. The stat-

THE WRITTEN CONTRACT OF SALE 

347 ute is satisfied if something in earnest is paid on the purchase price, and the contract does not have to be in writing. In this country, it is the practice to allow the part payment to apply on the purchase price. In England, any amount paid as "earnest" is no part of the purchase price.

A note or memorandum of the sale signed by the party to be charged is sufficient. 

Example 3. Wessel, a coal dealer, placed an order with a mining company for 300 tons of stove coal to be delivered F.O.B. Carbondale, Pa., by 

November 1 following, at $5.50 per ton. The coal dealer prepared a memorandum containing the necessary details and Wessel signed it. 

This signed memorandum meets all the requirements of the usual Statute of Frauds provisions, and it might be signed by Wessel's authorized agent, as such, instead of Wessel signing it in person.

This memorandum, which is required unless provisions 1 and 2 of the Statute of Frauds have been complied with, may be a sales memorandum such as is illustrated in Example 3, or it may be a paper, a letter, or a telegram, or two or more of either if all the papers when read together, contain the necessary facts and amount to a sales contract, and it may be printed or written. It must contain the names of the parties, a list of the articles, the price if agreed upon, and the terms of the sale; and it must be signed by the party to be charged, or by his authorized agent. Although it is not required, nevertheless, it is best to have the memorandum signed by both the seller and the buyer; then neither party can avoid the contract without becoming liable to the other party. 

When the amount of the contract is less than that specified in the law of the particular state, the written memorandum or contract is not necessary. In all such sales the oral contract is valid. 

It must be understood, however, that when the sale includes articles, each of which is priced less than the minimum amount specified by law, and the value of all the articles is greater than the amount specified, the contract must be written. 

An executed contract of sale for any amount above the minimum price in the statute stands, even though it was not in writing.

A contract for labor and materials may be oral. 

Example 4. Mason gave an oral order to a manufacturer of furniture to make for him according to his own design a couch to match certain period furniture which Mason had in his home. 

The cost of this couch was more than the minimum amount specified in the statute, but as the contract is for work, skill, and material, the statute did not apply and it did not have to be in writing. The general rule as applied under the Uniform Sales Act in states having adopted statutes modeled after the seventeenth section of the English Statute of Frauds, is that if the contract is essentially one for labor and materials it may be oral. 

Under the Uniform Sales of Goods Act, the Statute of Frauds section applicable to sales as adopted by the state applies to all contracts for the sale of goods, "notwithstanding that the goods may be intended to be delivered at some future time, or may not at the time of such contract or sale be actually made, procured, or provided, or fit or ready for delivery, or some act may be requisite for the making or completing thereof, or rendering the same fit for delivery; but if the goods are to be manufactured by the seller especially for the buyer and not suitable for sale to others in the ordinary course of the seller's business, the provisions of this section shall not apply."

This is the test generally applied to determine whether the contract is one of sale or for work and material, and any contract involving work and material in the production of some article which the seller does not produce regularly for sale and which would be unfit for his regular trade does not have to be written, even though the amount exceeds the statutory minimum. 

Examples are a suit of clothes made to order; a metal smokestack built to order for a particular boiler; or an order for any article differing in plan or design from those regularly offered for sale by the one making the article. Sale of personal property contrasted with sale of real property. 

Contracts for the sale of land or any interest in or concerning land must be in writing, under one of the provisions of the fourth section of the Statute of Frauds. This section in some form has

THE WRITTEN CONTRACT OF SALE 

349 been adopted so generally by the states of the United States that it is an accepted practice to reduce to writing all contracts that have to do with the sale of land or any interest therein. We know what the provisions of the seventeenth section of this same statute are with regard to the sale of personal property. But our real problem at times is to determine whether certain commodities or articles are real property or personal property. Personal property is defined as movable property, and real property is defined as fixed or immovable property. It includes the land and whatever is affixed thereto as part and parcel of the land, such as buildings, fences, growing trees, and all plants and shrubs that grow naturally on the land, as well as the substances beneath the surface, as coal, minerals, and oils. Crops raised, natural products of the soil, products of a mine detached and made ready for market and portable buildings are generally treated as personal property. A contract to sell any article, regardless of its value, must be in writing if it is treated as realty. If it is treated as personalty the contract does not have to be in writing if the price is below the statutory amount, or if part payment is made, or part of the goods are received and accepted. The statutes of your own state should be consulted. 

Example 5. Webb contracted to sell to Muller the crop of wheat growing on his farm for $250. Muller paid the purchase price in cash and agreed to remove the wheat as soon as it was ripe enough to harvest. 

Growing crops are personal property, and as this is a sale of personal property in which the price was paid and accepted at the time the agreement was entered into, no written contract or memorandum is necessary. The contract is good, and liability cannot be avoided.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The contract of sale in which the price specified is less than the statutory minimum need not be in writing. 

2. If the buyer receives and accepts part of the goods, or pays a part of the purchase price at the time the purchase is made, regardless of price, the written contract is not required. 

3. A written contract or memorandum of the sale setting forth the

essential facts and signed by the party to be charged is required in sales at or above the price specified in the statute, unless some part of the price is paid or some part of the goods delivered and accepted at the time. 

4. The sales memorandum may be a sales slip, order form, a paper, a letter or a telegram, and if it contains the necessary facts and is properly signed it will satisfy all legal requirements. 

5. The facts called for in a sales contract or memorandum are: names of parties, list of articles, price if agreed upon, and the terms. 

It must be signed by the purchaser or his agent. 

6. A contract made principally for labor and material used in making the article, which is to be delivered under the contract, is not required to be in writing, regardless of the price. 

7. The distinction between what is realty and what is personalty is important in determining what sales contracts must be written and what ones may be oral. 

8. When in doubt regarding a contract of sale, the safer plan is to use the written contract.

THE WRITTEN CONTRACT OF SALE: SUMMARY OUTLINE I. Seventeenth Section of the English Statute of Frauds II. Sales Contracts Required to Be in Writing Unless: 

A. Part or All of the Goods Are Delivered and Accepted 

B. Part of the Price Is Paid and Accepted

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Bulk Sale. The sale of an entire stock of goods. 

Common Carrier. One who transports goods for hire.

C. O. D. (Cash on delivery). Goods to be paid for when delivered. 

F. O. B. (Free on board). Goods delivered free to the carrier at shipping point or at their destination.

Fungible Goods. Goods all of the same kind or variety in bulk quantity.

Passing of Title. Change of ownership of goods from the original owner or seller to the buyer.

Specific Goods. Goods in existence and actually selected and agreed upon by the parties to a sale. 

Unascertained Goods. Goods not in existence or actually selected and specifically indicated by the parties to a sale. 

What are the two classes into which goods are divided? 

The Uniform Sales Act divides all goods into two general classes or groups. All goods in group 1 are referred to as ascertained or specific goods; and all goods in group 2 are referred to as unascertained goods. In this connection two sets of rules are given for determining when the title passes from seller to buyer. The rules for determining when the title passes in the case of specific goods are different from those which are given for determining when title passes in the case of unascertained goods. 

What are specific goods? 

Example 1. Darby offered for sale and Hensel selected and agreed to buy one day bed for $90. This day bed is classed as specific goods for the reason that it is ready for delivery, selected and offered for sale and definitely agreed upon by both parties. 362

Any existing goods selected and offered for sale which are definitely agreed upon by both the seller and the buyer are said to be ascertained or specific goods. 

What are unascertained goods?

Example 2. Buell sold Hayes 300 bushels of potatoes to be delivered as soon as he can dig, sort, and bag that quantity ready for delivery. This is a sale of unascertained goods. No particular potatoes were selected, set aside or agreed upon by the parties at the time the contract was made. 

All this is to be done later. 

Goods that are not yet in existence or if they are in existence they have not been separated from other goods or actually selected, set aside, or specifically indicated are classed as unascertained goods. Goods such as corn, potatoes, wheat or any goods in mass are classed as fungible goods, and any portion of such goods less than the whole quantity offered for sale before being selected would be classed as unascertained goods. 

Had Buell purchased a ready-made overcoat from a tailor and left it with him to be altered slightly, this would be a sale of specific goods. The coat was seen and decided upon. But if Buell placed an order for an overcoat to be made from cloth selected by him, this would be a sale of unascertained goods. The coat will have to be made before it can be delivered.

When does the title pass in a sale of specific goods? 

It is important in every sale to know when the title to the goods actually passes from the seller to the buyer for the reason that the risk of loss follows the title. The Uniform Sales Act provides that in a contract to sell specific goods the title passes when the parties intend it shall pass, and states various rules for ascertaining intention. Only the owner or his authorized agent has a right to sell and transfer the title to the goods sold. 

The following rules apply to the passing of title in the sale of specific or ascertained goods:

Rule 1. When the contract is for the sale of goods in a deliverable state, the title passes when the contract is made, whether the time of payment, the time of delivery, or both, be postponed.

Example 3. King sold a ladder to Genter. The particular ladder is selected and paid for by Genter, who is to call for it the next day. This is a sale of specific goods and the title passes from King to Genter at the time the contract is made.

Rule 2. When the contract is for the sale of specific goods and the seller is bound to do something to the goods to put them in a deliverable state, title does not pass until such thing is done. 

Example 4. Reed, a dealer, sold a used automobile to Mead, and agreed to recondition the car and put it in good running order, ready for delivery within two weeks. Title to this automobile does not pass until Reed has put it in a deliverable state, and when this is done the title passes even before a delivery.

Rule 3. When the contract is to sell goods that are ready for delivery, but the seller is bound to measure, weigh, test or perform some other act for the purpose of determining the quality or quantity and the price, the title passes when the contract is made for the reason that such acts are not necessary to pass the title. 

Example 5. Wild sold Doty all the corn in a corn crib containing several hundred bushels. Wild had to measure the corn to ascertain how much 

Doty must pay at the price per bushel agreed upon. In this sale the title passed at the time the contract was made and if the corn is destroyed even before it is measured, Doty would have to bear the loss. 

Rule 4. When goods are sold and delivered by the seller to the buyer with the understanding that the buyer may return them, title passes to the buyer at the time of delivery, but he may pass it back to the seller by returning the goods within the time agreed upon or within a reasonable time. 

Example 6. Mrs. Bemish purchased a coat from the Hopewell Stores,

Inc. for $150. The agreement was that Mrs. Bemish might return the coat within 10 days if she decided to do so. The title to this coat passed to Mrs. 

Bemish at the time it was delivered to her, but she may transfer it back to the seller within the time fixed or if no time is fixed within a reasonable time.

Rule 5. When goods are sold and delivered to the buyer on approval or on trial, title remains in the seller until the buyer signifies his approval or keeps the goods beyond the time fixed by the contract, or if no time is mentioned, beyond a reasonable time; then the title is in the buyer.

Example 7. Wilson sold a piano to Hill. The agreement was that Hill should try the piano for 30 days with the privilege of returning it if it did not prove to be satisfactory to him. Title in this piano is in Wilson until the 30 days have passed or until, within that time, Wilson expressed his approval.

When does the title pass in the sale of unascertained goods? 

There are special rules that apply in determining when the title passes in the following cases: (a) fungible goods, (b) goods delivered to the buyer or to a carrier, (c) F.O.B. and C.O.D. shipments, (d) sale at auction, (e) bulk sales, and (f) goods sold by sample. 

Rule 1. Mass goods all of the same kind or variety such as coal, grain, oil, etc., which may be separated are known as fungible goods. Under the Uniform Sales Act and likewise under the laws of some states, a portion of mass goods may be sold and the title passes to the buyer immediately, and before such portion is separated or removed from the remainder or portion unsold. In many states, however, this rule does not apply, and the title to the portion does not pass until separated from the mass and ascertained by the parties to the sale.

Example 8. Etch bought 100 bushels of wheat stored in a bin containing about 1,000 bushels. The seller agreed to help measure out the 100 bushels when Etch should call to take his wheat the following day, which he agreed to do so. Should anything causing a loss happen to this bin of wheat, Etch would have to bear his proportionate share of the loss, as the title to the 100 bushels has already passed to him. This is the rule under the Uniform Sales Act and in many states, however, the laws of some states hold that the title to the 100 bushels of wheat does not pass until it has been actually separated from the whole quantity and consented to by the buyer. 

Rule 2. When a contract is made to sell unascertained or future goods; that is, goods which the seller must produce or do something to make them ready for delivery, the title passes to the buyer when goods answering the description in the contract are made ready for delivery and actually set apart, or are delivered to the buyer or to a carrier for transmission to him, depending upon the terms of the agreement. 

Example 9. Elrod purchased shoes from a manufacturer. The manu facturer agreed to pack the shoes in cases and deliver them to Elrod in

good order within 30 days. The title to these shoes is in the manufacturer until such time as they are delivered to Elrod, according to the contract, and the manufacturer must bear any loss resulting from any damage to the shoes before they are delivered.

Rule 3. When according to the contract the goods sold must be delivered to the buyer, or at a particular place, or the seller must pay the cost of transportation to a particular place, the title in the goods does not pass until they have been delivered to the buyer or reached the place designated. 

Example 10. The Birch Coal Company bought 5 cars of coal from the 

Lehigh Coal Co. of Scranton, Pa., to be delivered to the Birch Company at the Penn. R. R. Co.'s freight yard in Chicago. The title to this coal passes to the Birch Coal Company as soon as it reaches Chicago and they receive the necessary bills of lading so they may claim it. 

When does the title pass in f.o.b. shipments?

Where goods are shipped f.o.b. destination, the title to the goods does not pass to the buyer until they reach their destination, but where they are shipped f.o.b. shipping point, the title passes to the buyer as soon as the goods are delivered to the common carrier who is to transport the goods. 

When does the title pass in a c.o.d. shipment? 

The term c.o.d. (cash on delivery) indicates that the seller intends to withhold delivery until the goods are paid for. However, according to the Uniform Sales Act, the title is presumed to pass when the goods are delivered to the carrier. 

When does the title pass in a mail order? 

When goods are ordered by mail, title passes as soon as the seller selects the goods and they are delivered to the common carrier, who acts as agent for the buyer. The buyer has a right to reject any goods selected by the seller which are not according to agreement, unless this rule is changed by a special contract agreed to by the parties.

When does the title pass to goods sold at auction? 

The auctioneer acts as agent for the seller and when the hammer falls and the note or memorandum of the sale as required by the

Statute of Frauds is completed, the title passes to the buyer. The sale must be for cash unless the auctioneer is authorized by the seller to sell on credit or to accept certain negotiable paper in payment.

When does the buyer get title to goods sold in bulk? 

Under "Bulk-Sales Acts" which are in force in most of the states, the merchant or dealer who plans to sell out his entire stock is required to notify all his creditors some time before the sale takes place of his intention to sell. This is done so that the creditors may take action to protect their own interests if they see fit to do so. If the sale is not made in accordance with the Bulk-Sales Act in force in that particular state, the purchaser of an entire stock of goods does not get a good title thereto, as against the creditors. 

Example 11. Hapburn sold his entire stock of shoes to Thomas and retired from business. Hapburn owed the Banister Shoe Co. $486 at the time he made the sale and they were not notified. This being the case, Thomas does not get a good title to the stock of shoes as against the Banister Shoe Co., according to the Bulk-Sales Act in force in this particular state.

When does the title pass to goods sold by sample? 

Where goods are sold by sample, the title passes to the buyer as soon as the particular goods corresponding to the sample are selected under the agreement and both seller and buyer have assented to the transaction. Selecting the goods means to set them apart and label them to be delivered under the contract.

Example 12. Arden bought by sample, 2,000 yards of silk cloth from the 

Evans Silk Company. The cloth was selected and apportioned to the contract with consent of both parties. The title in this cloth has passed to 

Arden and should anything happen to it, he must bear the loss, even though it is still in the custody of the seller. In a sale by sample, the title does not pass, however, until the goods have been apportioned and both parties have consented to the transaction or the goods have been delivered to the buyer and accepted by him. 

Who bears the loss?

In a sale of goods, the rule is that the risk of loss follows the title. 

This means that when the title to the goods is transferred from the seller to the buyer, the risk of loss is on the buyer. This applies to

sales for cash and sales on credit, and it is not necessary that the goods actually pass to the buyer in order that the title may pass. 

Under the Uniform Conditional Sales Law, which is in force in most of the states, where goods are sold on a conditional sales contract, whereby the seller retains the title to them until the final payment is made, the risk of loss is on the buyer for the reason that he has possession of the goods. The New York Personal Property 

Law states specifically that where goods are sold on a conditional sales contract, whereby the seller retains title until the condition is fulfilled, the risk of loss is on the buyer.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 1. The risk of loss follows the title. 

2. The true owner or his authorized agent only can transfer the title to goods sold. 

3. In the sale of specific goods the intention of the parties is the principal factor considered by the court in determining whether or not the title has passed. 

4. When the intention of the parties cannot be definitely determined, certain rules are applied in determining whether or not the title has passed. 

5. In the application of the rules for the passing of title, goods are classified as specific or ascertained and unascertained. 

6. Goods not definitely selected and agreed upon by the parties to the sale are classed as unascertained goods. 

7. The title passes in a mail order purchase as soon as the goods are selected by the seller and delivered to the carrier who acts as agent for the buyer. 

8. When goods are sold at auction, title passes as soon as the auctioneer's hammer falls and the sales memorandum is completed. 9. A merchant cannot sell and convey a good title to his stock of goods unless he complies with the Bulk-Sales Act by notifying his creditors of his intention to sell some time before the sale takes place. 

10. The general rule is that the one who has the title to goods must bear the loss. 

11. The buyer under a conditional sales contract must generally bear the risk of loss.

SALES WARRANTIES TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Caveat Emptor. "Let the purchaser beware," meaning that the buyer under certain conditions buys at his own risk. 

Expression of Opinion. A statement of what one may think of or how one may regard an article offered for sale. 

General Warranty. An express or implied warranty that the goods sold are sound or fit for a definite purpose as compared with a particular warranty that warrants some one thing. 

Merchantable. Goods that are fit for sale or marketable. 

What is a sales warranty?

When the seller makes certain statements regarding the quality of the goods or represents in some way that the goods are of a particular kind and quality, and as a result the buyer is induced to purchase the goods, this amounts to a sales warranty. Anyone who offers goods for sale impliedly warrants that he is the owner or that he is authorized to sell them; and he may warrant the goods in one way or another in other respects. The two classes of warranty are (1) express, (2) implied. 

What is an express warranty?

Example 1. Hall bought an overcoat from a dealer. He was induced to make the purchase because the dealer said: "I warrant the material in this coat to be all wool and fast color." This amounts to an express warranty of quality, and if the coat is not all wool or the color fades more than might be expected normally, the seller is liable for a breach of warranty. 

An express warranty is a written or spoken statement made by the seller to the buyer regarding the kind, quantity, or quality of the goods or their fitness for a particular purpose. No special wording is necessary to create a warranty. Any statement made 371

with intention of creating a warranty will be considered in effect as a warranty. 

Example 2. Mrs. Gish purchased a sewing machine through a local salesman employed by the manufacturer of the machine. This salesman told Mrs. Gish that this particular make of machine is the best in the market. On the strength of this statement, she bought the machine, and it proved to be very unsatisfactory.

This statement by the salesman was a mere expression of his own opinion and did not amount to a warranty; therefore, Mrs. 

Gish has no redress. To state that a machine is in good running order is a warranty, but to state that no better machine can be purchased for the money, or that it is the best machine in the market is a mere expression of opinion. A warranty must be distinguished from a mere expression of opinion. 

Example 3. The written contract for the sale of an electric refrigerator stated that it was warranted against any mechanical defects resulting from poor material or workmanship for a period of 90 days. The salesman, in order to induce the purchaser to buy, stated orally that he would warrant the refrigerator against defects for one year.

The purchaser, after signing the written contract containing the 

90-day warranty, cannot hold the salesman or the manufacturer on the oral warranty. In an express warranty a written statement of warranty cannot be changed or supplemented by an oral statement of warranty. Therefore, the warranty should be written exactly as the contract is written. The safer plan is for the buyer to insist on the written warranty, in every case of an express warranty. The reliability of the dealer is a factor to consider in the purchase of any goods.

While an express warranty is generally binding upon the seller, statements about the goods or regarding the mechanism or quality must not be mistaken for a warranty. For example, to say that a certain article is made from carefully selected material, or has been thoroughly inspected for defects, or is carefully tested before being offered for sale does not amount to a warranty of character, quality or fitness of the goods, but if the statements were unintentionally false and the buyer relied on them to his injury, they probably would amount to fraud.

SALES WARRANTIES 

373 Under certain conditions an express warranty is understood to be given.

Example 4. The purchaser of a used automobile expressed doubt about the radiator being cracked and leaking. The seller assured him it was sound. This amounts to a warranty. If this radiator were leaking at the time the buyer examined the car and he failed to discover it, there would be no warranty on the part of the seller covering this defect. 

Should the buyer express any doubt after he has inspected the article and discovered defects, and should the seller thereupon state that the article is sound, this general warranty covers these defects. If the buyer has examined the goods, there is no warranty covering any defects which he should have discovered. 

What is an implied sales warranty?

Example 5. Case stored a wagon in Dow's barn. Dow sold it to Evarts. 

Case claimed the wagon. Evarts must give it up, as Dow had no title, but Dow is liable on an implied warranty that he had a right to sell it. 

An implied sales warranty is one that is understood from the nature of the transaction. No statement is made in writing or by word of mouth, but the transaction is such that a certain warranty is definitely implied. 

What are the principal implied warranties in a sales contract? 

1. That the seller can transfer a good title to the goods sold. 

2. That goods shall correspond with the description when they are sold in this manner. 

3. That goods sold by sample shall correspond with the sample from which they were selected. 

4. That goods purchased for a particular purpose shall be fit for that purpose. 

5. That the goods sold are merchantable and fit for use. 

What is an implied warranty of title? 

1. There is an implied warranty on the part of the seller that he is the owner or that he has authority to sell the goods, and in case of a contract to sell, that he will have a right to sell when the time comes to fulfill the contract and transfer a good title to the buyer. 

2. That the buyer shall have and enjoy quiet possession of the goods as against any lawful claims by others existing at the time of the sale. 

3. That the goods shall be free, at the time of the sale, from any claims,

charges, or incumbrances in favor of any third person, not declared or known to the buyer before or at the time the sales contract is made. 

4. These implied warranties of title do not apply to sales by a sheriff, auctioneer, mortgagee, or other person professing to sell by authority of law goods in which a third person has a legal or equitable interest. 

The purchaser of stolen goods will be forced to return the goods to their rightful owner, but he will have a right to recover the amount of his damages from the seller. 

Example 6. Ward bought a stolen car from Knight. The implied warranties in this sale are: (1) That Knight is the owner or has a lawful right to sell the car and transfer the title thereto; (2) That Ward shall enjoy quiet possession of the car; and (3) That the car is free from any encumbrance in favor of any third person. The real owner could recover the car from Ward, but Ward could recover from Knight the amount paid for the car, as damages for breach of implied warranty of title. 

What is the implied warranty in a sale by description or by sample? 

Example 7. Bower ordered 12 buff colored, best grade Holland window shades, 32" x 72", mounted on Excelso rollers. The dealer, who accepted this order, must furnish the shade according to the buyer's description, and should he attempt to furnish anything different, his implied warranty is broken. Had the buyer ordered the shade after the seller had described them to him, the same warranty rule would apply. 

In a contract to sell a specified article under a patent or trade name, there is no implied warranty that it is fit for a particular purpose. In Example 7, the rollers, under the trade name "Excelso" are not warranted. The dealer is not liable if he supplies the kind specified.

When goods are sold by description either the buyer describes the goods he wishes to buy and the seller furnishes them according to the description; or the seller describes the goods and the buyer orders them on the strength of the seller's description. In either case there is an implied warranty by the seller that the goods delivered are as described. Example 8. A producer showed a wholesale dealer a sample of potatoes priced in carload lots, f.o.b. shipping point, at $1.10 per bushel. The dealer ordered a carload of 700 bushels. There is an implied warranty on the part of the producer that the whole 700 bushels will correspond with the sample. The buyer should keep the sample so that he can make the comparison.

SALES WARRANTIES 

375 When goods are selected by the buyer from samples, there is an implied warranty on the part of the seller that they shall be like the sample or the same kind and quality as the sample. 

What are implied warranties of quality?

Example 9. Bayer bought a hoisting machine of 6,000 pounds capacity from the Donaldson Machine Co. In this sales contract there is an implied warranty that the machine is strong enough to hoist at least 6,000 pounds. 

Under the Uniform Sales Act implied warranties of quality are subject to the following regulations: 

1. Where the buyer makes known to the seller in some way the particular purpose for which the goods are required and it appears that the buyer relies on the seller's judgment, there is an implied warranty that the goods shall be reasonably fit for such purpose. 

2. Where the goods are bought by description from one who sells such goods, there is an implied warranty that the goods shall be of merchantable quality. 

3. An implied warranty or condition as to quality or fitness for a particular purpose may be annexed by the usage or trade. 

4. An express warranty or condition does not make an implied warranty inoperative unless inconsistent therewith. 

Example 10. The manager of a hotel ordered a case of cereal from a local dealer. When the cook opened the cereal he found it to be unfit for use. The dealer who sold this cereal impliedly warranted it to be fit for human consumption and he can be required to take it back, provided the defect was reported to him promptly. 

Although the Uniform Sales Act provides no regulation regarding warranties of food products; however, there is an implied warranty that when any kind of food is sold for human beings to consume, it shall be wholesome and fit to eat. 

What is the rule of "caveat emptor"?

Caveat emptor (a Latin phrase) means "Let the buyer beware." 

In effect it amounts to making the buyer who has had a chance to inspect the goods assume the risk of any defects, unless there is an express warranty. This very old rule is not recognized today to the same extent it was in the past. Where the buyer examines the goods and the seller who is also the producer of the goods has committed no fraud, or when there are defects which can easily be seen

and the buyer has a chance to inspect the goods, it is presumed that he relied upon his own judgment in making the purchase. 

Where the buyer selects and buys a particular article, there is no implied warranty on the part of the seller that it is suitable for any purpose the buyer may have in mind. Caveat emptor applies in such cases.

Example 11. Hurd bought a used electric refrigerator from King. 

Hurd inquired of King if the refrigerator was in good working order. King replied: "I have used it very little, and I am selling it just as it is." The rule of caveat emptor applies in this case. Had King stated that the refrigerator was in good working order, this warranty would not have covered any defect clearly visible, such as cracked enamel or surface mars. 

What liability in tort does the seller incur?

Example 12. A manufacturer of automobiles put on a car a wheel made of rotted wood and painted it so that it could not be discovered. The purchaser of the car met with a serious accident as a result of this wheel. The manufacturer was held liable in an action to recover damages. 

While the seller incurs a contractual liability to the buyer for a breach of an express or implied warranty, he may also in this connection incur liability in tort. (1) in case he is guilty of a fraudulent deception (2) for putting out articles which may endanger human life without notice or warning as to their dangerous character. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Every sale carries with it on the part of the seller certain express or implied warranties. 

2. An express warranty is a statement by the seller regarding the fitness, soundness, quality or quantity of the goods sold. 

3. A mere expression of opinion, sales talk, or "puffing" do not amount to a warranty. 

4. An implied warranty is inferred by law and arises out of conditions or circumstances connected with the sale. 

5. An implied warranty attaches to every sales contract: (1) That the seller can transfer a good title; (2) that the goods are merchantable, and if sold for food, that they are fit for human beings to eat; (3) that if the goods are sold by description, they will answer the description; (4) that if goods are sold by sample, they are equal to the

SALES WARRANTIES 

377 sample, and (5) that if goods are sold for a particular purpose made known to the seller by the buyer they will suit that purpose. 

6. An express warranty is a contract or undertaking by the seller, independent of the main sales contract. 

7. Implied warranties are as binding upon the seller as are express warranties. 

8. "Caveat emptor" applies only where the buyer has a chance to inspect the goods and relies on his own judgment. 

9. A seller may be liable in tort for fraud or for concealing the dangerous character of goods sold.

1. A dealer in used cars made this statement to Cook: "I will sell you this car for $450 and warrant it against all defects for 90 days." Cook purchased the car. (a) What kind of a warranty is this? (b) Who is responsible in this case and for what?

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Action in Replevin. Action at law to recover possession of goods wrongfully retained. 

Rescind. To cancel, make void, or set aside.

Recoupment. The right to keep back a sum due; to withhold a part of the price as damages.

Seller's Lien. A lien that an unpaid seller has on goods that have been sold and are still in his possession. 

Doing the particular thing contracted to be 

Specific Performance. done.

State of Insolvency. State of being unable to pay one's debts; liabilities exceed resources.

Transit. Act of moving goods from one place to another. 

What rights has the unpaid seller? 

Example 1. Hays bought a disk harrow from Wilbur on three months' credit. Hays left the harrow in Wilbur's possession for the three months and then sold it to Thomas, who demanded delivery from Wilbur. 

The fact that Wilbur is in possession of the harrow for which he has not been paid gives him a right of lien. The unpaid seller in possession of the goods has a right of lien against them, although the title has passed to the buyer. This is known as the "unpaid seller's lien," which means that the seller may keep possession of the goods sold for cash or without a stipulated term of credit until he gets his pay for them. This right is also available to an unpaid seller in possession of the goods after the term of credit has expired. 

This rule applies in a sale without any term of credit being mentioned, or in a sale in which the term of credit has expired, as in Example 1. It matters not that the title had passed to Hays and 379

he could have demanded delivery any time before the term of credit expired. But had no term of credit been mentioned, Wilbur would have a right of lien until he received his money. 

Example 2. Hedges sold a safe to Lakey on six months' credit. Before the safe was delivered to Lakey and within the six months he became insolvent. The circumstances in this case gives Hedges a right of lien against the safe.

If the buyer becomes insolvent before the goods which are still in the possession of the seller have been paid for, the seller may exercise his right of lien. 

How may the seller's right of lien be lost? (a) By delivering the goods to some one as bailee or agent for the buyer (usually a common carrier) without any reservation as to title or right of possession. (b) By the buyer or some one lawfully acting for him obtaining possession of the goods. (c) By the seller waiving his right to keep possession of the goods. 

The unpaid seller, who has shipped the goods, may, in case of insolvency of the buyer, who is the consignee, acquire possession of them at any time while they are in transit. This right is known as the right of stoppage in transit. 

To stop the delivery of goods while they are still in transit it is necessary for the seller to give reasonable notice to the carrier, and if a negotiable (order) bill of lading has been issued, it will have to be surrendered to the carrier for cancellation before he will be required to surrender the goods to the seller. 

When has the seller a right to stop goods in transit? (a) The goods must have been sold on account. (b) The buyer must be insolvent at the time the delivery of the goods is stopped. (c) The goods must be in the hands of the common carrier at the time the right of stoppage arises. According to the Uniform Sales Act a person who has ceased to pay his debts or cannot pay them as they become due, is insolvent regardless of whether or not he has committed an act of bankruptcy or is insolvent within the meaning of the federal bankruptcy law.

The seller who stops goods in transit does so at his own risk, and if the buyer is not insolvent, the seller will be required to make delivery and he may be liable to the buyer for damages. 

When are goods considered to be in transit? 

Example 3. Dort of New York sold goods on credit to Wall, who ordered them shipped via N.Y. C. and M. S. R.R. to Chicago. Should circumstances arise which would give Dort a right to stop the goods while in transit, he could exercise this right any time before they are delivered, by giving notice to the agent for the R.R. Company in Chicago not to deliver the goods to Wall. (a) Goods delivered to a carrier for transmission to the buyer are in transit until they are delivered to the buyer or to someone in his behalf. (b) Goods delivered to the buyer and rejected by him are still in transit so long as they are in possession of the carrier. 

No particular form of notice to the agent for the carrier is required. A notice similar to the following may be given. 

Michigan Southern Railroad Co. 

Chicago, Illinois Gentlemen:

Circumstances have arisen which give me a right to stop in transit all goods delivered by me to you on Dec. 2nd, 19-, for shipment to John C. Wall, 128 Dearborn St., Chicago, and you are hereby notified not to deliver these goods to the consignee, but to hold them subject to my orders. 

New York, December 9th, 19. 

Howard Dort.

NOTICE TO CARRIER 

The seller's right to stop goods in transit is barred if the buyer is in possession of the bill of lading and transfers it to a third person who in good faith paid value for it. The third person can hold the goods as against the unpaid seller. 

When is a shipment of goods no longer in transit? (a) Goods are considered to be no longer in transit if an order bill of lading was issued for them to the consignor, or to a third party and endorsed by him to the buyer. They could be stopped in transit in this case

only by the buyer surrendering the order bill of lading to the carrier for cancellation before the stoppage order is issued. (b) When the goods arrive at their destination and notice is sent by the carrier to the consignee, who is the buyer, that they are ready for delivery. 

After this notice is given, the goods are no longer in transit and a stoppage in transit would be of no avail. (c) After the carrier has wrongfully refused to deliver the goods to the buyer or his agent, they are no longer in transit. 

When part of the goods has been delivered to the buyer, the remainder may be stopped unless there is some agreement on the part of the carrier to deliver the remainder. 

Should the buyer sell the goods consigned to him before he receives them, this sale does not bar the seller from stopping the goods in transit.

When may an unpaid seller resell the goods? 

Goods that have been stopped in transit may be resold: (a) When the goods are perishable. (b) When the right of resale, in case of the buyer's failure to pay, was expressly provided for in the terms of the sale contract. (c) When the buyer has delayed paying for the goods for an unreasonable time, and then notice to the buyer of the seller's intention to sell is necessary. The seller is not required to notify the buyer of the time and place of the sale and he may resell at private or public sale.

When may the unpaid seller rescind the transfer of title? (a) When the right to rescind in case the buyer defaulted was expressly provided for in the sales contract. (b) When the buyer has been in default as to payment for an unreasonable length of time.

The seller who rescinds the transfer of title resumes the property in the goods; that is, the title reverts back to him. 

Example 4. Lane bought a chair for $50 from a dealer in antique furniture. Lane promised to pay for it within 10 days. The dealer heard nothing from him for over three months, so he rescinded the sale and put the chair back in stock.

The seller must make known to the buyer his intention to rescind and this he must do: 

1. By giving notice to the buyer, or

2. By some other act which will make known to the buyer that the transfer of title has been rescinded. 

Before the goods are delivered the seller may rescind by notifying the buyer to this effect. This he has a right to do: 

1. If the buyer has renounced his obligations under the sale or sales contract, or declared his inability to perform them; or 

2. If the buyer has committed a material breach of the sales contract. 

What rights of action has the unpaid seller? 

1. The seller has a right to bring action for the price where: (a) The title has passed to the buyer, but he refuses or has neglected to pay the price agreed upon; or (b) The price of the goods is payable on a certain day whether or not the title has passed or delivery made and the buyer has refused or neglected to pay according to the sales contract. (c) The goods cannot be resold for a reasonable price. The seller may attempt to deliver the goods, and if the buyer refuses to receive them, the seller may give notice to the buyer that he is holding the goods for him and subject to his orders. 

Example 5. Ashby, a builder of auto bodies, received an order from 

Wesley for a body to fit a particular truck. When the body was completed, Wesley for no reason refused to accept it. As this body cannot be readily resold to another person, Ashby may hold it ready for delivery and sue Wesley for the price. 

2. If the buyer wrongfully refuses or neglects to accept and pay for the goods, the seller may sue for the damages resulting directly and naturally from the buyer's breach of contract. 

The measure of damages is usually the difference between the contract price and the market price if there is an available market at the time when delivery was to have been made, or if no time for delivery was fixed, when the buyer refused to accept. 

Example 6. Bender contracted in writing to buy an apple orchard crop from Reed. Bender neglected to pick the apples and also refused to pay for them. Reed finally sold the apples for the market price and sued 

Bender for the difference between the contract price and the price at which he finally sold them. This he had a right to do. 

What rights has the buyer when the seller has defaulted? 

1. If the title to the goods has passed to the buyer and the seller wrongfully refuses to deliver them the buyer may bring

action in replevin and in this way get possession of the goods or he may sue the seller in tort for keeping the goods and in this way get their value in money.

Example 7. Lock sold his automobile to Murphy for $250 cash. When 

Murphy called for the automobile a few days later, Lock refused to deliver it, claiming he sold it too cheap, and he tried to get Murphy to take back the $250 paid. Murphy may bring suit in replevin if necessary and thus get possession of the automobile. 

2. In case the title to the goods has not passed, the buyer may sue the seller for damages resulting to the buyer from the seller's breach of the contract. 

Example 8. Adler sold to Wing for delivery on November 15th, 10,000 pounds of cotton at 9c a pound. When the time came to deliver, cotton had advanced to 12c per pound and Adler withheld delivery. Wing could sue in this case for $300 damages, or the difference in price between what he bought the cotton for and what he would have to pay for the same quantity and grade elsewhere. 

3. If the title to the goods has not passed to the buyer and the sales contract gives him the right to have them delivered, he may under certain conditions, in case the seller defaults, demand specific performance.

Specific performance is a remedy which will be granted by a court of equity when from the nature of the case money damages would not be an adequate remedy. Specific performance means fulfilling the contract according to its exact terms. 

Example 9. Eckert purchased a very old painting from Bass for which he paid $500. Bass refused to deliver this painting to Eckert and offered to refund to him the $500 paid. As this painting is not obtainable elsewhere, Eckert may bring suit in equity against Bass to compel him to deliver the painting. This remedy is called specific performance. 

What remedy has the buyer for the seller's breach of warranty?

When there has been a breach of warranty on the part of the seller: 

1. The buyer may accept or keep the goods and bring suit to enforce his right to damages or of recoupment. The right of recoupment gives the buyer a right to set up a complete or partial defense

to an action by the seller to enforce payment for the goods. The damage the buyer might properly claim would be the amount equal to the difference between the value of the goods as contracted for and the value of the goods as delivered. 

Example 10. Webb purchased 5,000 pounds of X grade wool from the 

Western Wool Company. Webb accepted the wool, but when he started to use it he found it to be of a much poorer grade than he contracted for. 

Webb may avail himself of his rights under Rule 1. He may keep the wool and sue for the amount of damage suffered; or be allowed to deduct the amount of the damage from the price he agreed to pay in case the seller takes action to enforce full payment for the wool. 

2. The buyer, upon discovering a breach of the express warranty, may refuse to accept the goods and if the title has not already passed, he may sue for damages resulting directly from the seller's breach of contract. If he has accepted the goods not knowing their condition, he may return them within a reasonable time after discovering the breach of warranty. He should notify the seller promptly. If the seller refuses to take back the goods, the buyer may hold them for him.

Example 11. Hake bought a fur coat from a dealer who warranted it in every respect. The first time Hake wore the coat he discovered the hair falling out, and spots in the coat showed signs of being moth eaten. Hake returned the coat and demanded the return of his money. In most states, under the Uniform Sales Act, the dealer will have to take back the coat and refund the entire price. 

3. The buyer may rescind the contract by refusing to receive the goods or offering to return them, or by bringing suit to recover what he has paid, and he may hold the goods to secure repayment of such amount.

The right to rescind is not available to the buyer: (a) If he knew of the breach of warranty when he accepted the goods, or (b) If he failed to notify the seller within a reasonable time that he is rescinding the contract, or (c) If he fails to offer to return the goods in as good condition, allowing for inevitable deterioration, as when they were received.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The unpaid seller has a lien on the goods sold until they are delivered to the buyer. 

2. The seller may lose his right of lien by delivering the goods; by the buyer lawfully acquiring possession of them; or by the seller waiving his right to retain possession of them. 

3. The unpaid seller may stop goods in transit before they are delivered to a buyer who is insolvent. 

4. If the seller refuses to deliver the goods to the buyer after title has passed, the buyer may sue for damages or he may recover the goods by replevin. 5. An unpaid seller may resell the goods when they are perishable; when the sales contract provides for resale; and when payment for the goods is delayed for an unreasonable reason or time. 

6. The unpaid seller, under certain conditions may rescind the transfer of title. He must make his intentions to rescind known to the buyer. 

7. In case of a breach of warranty, the buyer may accept the goods and sue for the amount of the damages; or, if he has not paid for the goods, he may deduct the loss from the payment; or he may return the goods and recover the amount paid; or refuse to accept the goods and sue, if necessary, to recover any amount paid, or the goods may be held to secure repayment.
