Buying and selling embrace the major part of our business activities today. They are carried on with such facility that hardly anyone thinks of them as subject to any rules of law, but rather as regulated by prevailing practice or custom. The preceding chapters show that every sales transaction is completely subject to legal rules, which are so generally followed that their legal nature is lost sight of. It is only in case of dispute that the law is invoked.

The activity of buying and selling brings people into close contact with each other, and develops between buyer and seller a relationship which calls for a high degree of integrity and good faith. The relationship that inspires mutual confidence in both parties to the sale results in real satisfaction.

The buyer and seller should deal fairly and honestly with each other, and each should use every precaution to safeguard his own interests in terms of what is right. The seller should stand back of his goods and the buyer should meet promptly every obligation which the transaction imposes upon him. Where this is done there is little likelihood that there will be any trouble resulting from the transaction that cannot be settled between the parties themselves without resorting to litigation. Nevertheless, it is inevitable that some controversies should arise from the great number of sales transactions that take place. The rules of law governing these controversies are of great interest and importance to every individual engaged in commerce. The general adoption of the Uniform Sales Law has removed many difficulties formerly existing because of different rules in different states. This law as previously explained should receive careful attention.

BAILMENTS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Mutual Benefit. Where all parties to the transaction receive some benefit. 

Prudent Person. One who is careful and watchful in all matters pertaining to his own property.

Tortious Bailee. One who willfully takes possession of another person's property and holds it unlawfully. 

What is a bailment?

Example 1. Bates borrowed a camping outfit from Deverman. The understanding was that Bates was to use this outfit when on his vacation and to return it as soon as his vacation was over. This is an example of a common form of bailment.

A bailment is a delivery of some article of personal property by one party, usually the owner, to another party to be held by him for some special purpose and to be returned or redelivered when that purpose has been accomplished. It amounts to a transfer of property without a change of ownership as in a sale. 

How is a bailment created?

A bailment is created by a contract between the owner or the one who controls the goods and who is known as the bailor and the party to whom the goods are delivered, who is known as the bailee. The purpose for which the bailment is created, together with all the terms and conditions of the bailment, should be specified in the contract, that the rights of the bailor and the bailee may be determined. Either party to a contract of bailment may act through an agent. A bailment may be created without intentional delivery by the owner. Example 2. Hodge found a sample case full of valuable samples that had fallen from a passing automobile. He took them into his home and in 392

BAILMENTS 

393 a short time the owner reclaimed them. In this incident a bailment was created without intentional delivery. 

How are bailments generally classified? 

There are two classes of bailments as follows: 

1. Bailments for the sole benefit of one of the parties, either the bailor or the bailee. 

2. Bailments for the benefit of both the bailor and the bailee, or mutual benefit bailments.

Bailments for mutual benefit are further classified as ordinary and exceptional. The bailments of innkeepers and common carriers, which are treated later, are exceptional, and all other mutual benefit bailments are ordinary. 

When is a bailment for the sole benefit of the bailor? 

Example 3. Mrs. Carr agreed to keep Mrs. Watts's pet dog during the latter's stay in Europe. This is a bailment for the sole benefit of Mrs. 

Watts, the bailor.

The most common bailments for the sole benefit of the bailor are those in which the bailee is to care for some property for the bailor without charge.

Any bailment in which the bailee agrees to do something to or about the property without compensation is a bailment for the bailor's benefit.

When is a bailment for the sole benefit of the bailee? 

Example 4. Wassen loaned Eberhard his fur coat to wear on an extensive motor trip. This is a bailment for the sole benefit of Eberhard, the bailee.

The most common bailments for the sole benefit of the bailee are those in which the bailor without any compensation allows the bailee the use of certain property belonging to him. 

When is a bailment for the mutual benefit of both the bailor and the bailee?

A mutual benefit bailment is one in which both the bailor and the bailee receive some benefit from the bailment. 

Example 5. Wemple hired a reaper for $25 from Hobbs to harvest his wheat. Both parties to this bailment receive benefit. Wemple received

the use of the reaper, which benefited him, and Hobbs received $25, which he could use for his benefit; therefore, this is a mutual benefit bailment. 

The different types of mutual benefit bailments are discussed later. 

What degrees of care are required of the bailee?

There are three degrees of care required of the bailee, depending upon who is benefited by the bailment; namely, slight, great, and ordinary.

Where the bailment is for the bailor's benefit, the bailee is required to use slight care only. What amounts to the proper degree of care depends on the purpose of the bailment and the nature of the thing bailed. In Example 3, even the duty of slight care would require Mrs. Carr to feed and look after the dog, as that was the purpose, and the subject of the bailment requires it. If Mrs. 

Watts had left a piece of furniture with Mrs. Carr, the only obligation would be to put it in a fairly safe place and give it some slight protection. Slight care is reasonable or acceptable care, depending upon the circumstances surrounding the bailment. 

Where the bailment is for the bailee's benefit, he is required to use great care. In Example 4, Eberhard only is benefited by the use of Wassen's coat; therefore, he is expected to take the best care possible of this coat, consistent with the use he is to make of it. 

Where the bailment is for the benefit of both parties, ordinary care is required of the bailee. This is the care a prudent workman or business man would take of his own property. In Example 5, Wemple would be expected to take the same care of Hobbs's reaper that he would of his own, and to return it to Hobbs in as good condition as when he received it, allowing for reasonable wear. 

What degrees of negligence render the bailee liable to the bailor for loss?

We have learned that there are three degrees of care required, depending upon conditions. There are likewise three degrees of negligence for which the bailee is liable to the bailor; namely, slight, gross, and ordinary. In a bailment for the bailor's benefit, which requires slight care of the bailee, the bailee is liable for gross negligence; that is, he would have to be careless and neglectful to become liable. This principle applies to Example 3. But in a bail-

BAILMENTS 

395 1 ment for the bailee's benefit, he would be liable for slight negligence, which means that he must take exceptionally good care of the bailor's property and failing to do so, he is negligent. This principle applies to Example 4. In a bailment for the mutual benefit of both parties' requiring the bailee to use ordinary care, he is liable to the bailor for ordinary negligence. This means that if the bailee fails to give the bailor's property the care a prudent man would give his own property he is guilty of negligence. This principle applies to Example 5.

What responsibility does a finder assume by taking the lost property into his possession?

The finder of lost property is not bound to take it into his possession, but if he does, he becomes a bailee for the owner. The bailment is one for the sole benefit of the owner, as bailor, and the finder, as bailee, need exercise only slight care toward the article and is liable only for gross negligence. The finder must make reasonable effort to discover the owner of the property and give him an opportunity to identify and reclaim it. Statutes in most states prescribe the nature and extent of such effort, and they usually provide that if the owner does not reclaim the goods within a certain time they shall belong absolutely to the finder. The finder may recover from the owner any expense he incurred in connection with the article found, before surrendering possession of it. 

The liability of the bailee may be varied by contract. 

The parties to a bailment may, by contract, make the liability greater or less than the regular rules provide, except that the law will not permit the bailee to be exempt from the consequences of his own willful misconduct.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. In a bailment, possession of property changes without a change of ownership. 

2. A bailment contract requires the consent of both parties. 

3. A person may become a bailee by taking possession of another person's property, and if he holds it unlawfully, he is a tortious bailee.

4. A bailment can result only where the bailee becomes possessed of the property either by delivery or otherwise and his acceptance is either expressed or implied. 

5. When the purpose of the bailment has been accomplished, the bailee must return the property bailed to the owner. 

6. The property bailed may be returned in a different state than when it was received if the contract calls for some service to be performed upon it. 

7. Gross negligence results when slight care has not been taken of the property; slight negligence results when great care has not been taken; and ordinary negligence results when ordinary care has not been taken. 1 8. The bailee is not permitted to escape the consequences of his own willful misconduct, even by contract.

BAILMENTS: SUMMARY OUTLINE 

A. Defined

B. How Created C. How Classified 

1. Benefit of bailor

BAILMENTS FOR THE SOLE BENEFIT OF THE BAILOR OR THE BAILEE TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Gratuitous Bailment. A bailment in which no charges are made by either party.

Great Care. The highest degree of care of the article bailed that might be reasonably expected of the bailee. 

Gross Negligence. That degree of negligence which results from failure to use even slight care. 

Inevitable Accident. Something that is unforeseen and therefore unavoidable.

Slight Care. The lowest degree of care permissible under any circumstances without becoming responsible for loss. 

How is a bailment for the sole benefit of the bailor created by contract?

Any bailment in which the bailee receives no benefit therefrom is a bailment for the bailor's sole benefit. It may be created (a) by contract, (b) by taking possession of lost property, or (c) by coming into possession of property belonging to another person without agreement.

Example 1. Coon agreed to care for Atkins's books and personal effects without charge for six months. This is a bailment created by contract for 

Atkins's sole benefit. The bailor and the bailee voluntarily assented to the bailment, and it becomes operative as soon as Atkins's property is delivered into Coon's possession. In this case, Coon might agree to perform some service in connection with Atkins's property. He might move it for Atkins or he might agree to make necessary repairs. If he agreed to do this gratuitously, the bailment would still be for the bailor's benefit. 398

Performing any service about the article gratuitously does not change the status of the bailment. 

Example 2. Small found a stray sheep wandering about the roadside and he took it into his pasture and cared for it. In this case Small voluntarily became a bailee, and the bailment created in this way is for the bailor's sole benefit.

Had this sheep strayed into Small's pasture, he would have become a bailee although he did not agree to care for the sheep, and regardless of what Small did with the sheep he would assume some responsibility. This is an obligation imposed by law for the benefit of the owner. In either case, the owner is entitled to recover his sheep, but he will have to reimburse Small for any expense he incurred in connection with the bailment. Should Small fail to find the owner after making reasonable effort to do so, he may have a right by statute to keep the sheep as his own. 

What are the bailor's duties in a bailment for his sole benefit? 

1. He must pay expense incurred by the bailee in caring for the property bailed.

Example 3. If the owner of a domestic animal delivered it to a friend to be cared for without charge, the owner is bound to reimburse the bailee for all expenses incurred in caring for the animal except those caused by the negligence or misconduct of the bailee. 

2. The bailor must make known to the bailee any traits or defect in the property bailed that would tend to make the risk greater. 

Example 4. Increased risk would occur in a case where a dog that was inclined to bite strangers was being cared for by a friend of the owner. The owner would be duty bound to tell his friend of the dog's trait so that he would watch him or keep him muzzled.

What are the bailee's duties in a bailment for the bailor's sole benefit?

A bailment for the bailor's sole benefit is a gratuitous undertaking on the part of the bailee, and since he is to receive no consideration, he is not bound to carry out the bailment. However, if he accepts the custody of the property and permits himself to be a party to a bailment contract, he is under certain obligations to the bailor.

1. He is expected to use slight care at least, and failing to do so, he is liable to the bailor for gross negligence. Example 5. Bowen agreed to keep without charge certain valuable papers in his safe for a friend of his. Instead of putting them in his safe he left them out on his desk and they were lost. This is a case of gross negligence and Bowen is liable. 

2. The bailee is expected to use the article bailed only when its proper care makes it necessary to use it. There are but few cases where moderate use of the article bailed would be considered necessary for its proper care, and should the bailee use it for any other purpose he would be liable for any injury resulting to the article even though he in no way was negligent. 

Example 6. Clark agreed to care for a pony belonging to Kruse for a few months without charge. The pony needed exercise and Clark allowed his young son to ride him moderately for this purpose. This he would have a right to do, but he would not be permitted to allow his son to ride the pony to school each day. 

3. The bailee must deliver back to the bailor the article bailed when the time comes to do so, together with all increase or profit derived therefrom. If the article has been damaged or lost, the bailee is liable only in case he is guilty of gross carelessness. 

4. Any one who attempts to perform any service about an article, even though he does it gratis, must use the skill required of a person doing such work, and failing to do so he is liable for the damages he may cause.

Example 7. Sims, for the purpose of advertising, volunteered to clean a valuable rug for Mrs. Hood without charge. She allowed him to clean the rug, and he tried a new cleaning fluid which caused the colors to run and the rug was practically ruined. Sims is liable to Mrs. Hood for the reasonable value of this rug. 

How is a bailment for the bailor's sole benefit terminated?

This class of bailments is terminated by: 

1. The purpose of the bailment being accomplished. When the bailment is for the purpose of accomplishing some act, as the delivery of an article from one place to another, the bailee who attempts to perform the act, must complete it with at least slight care, and when the act is completed the bailment is terminated.

2. The time agreed upon that the bailment shall continue having expired. If the parties to the bailment contract agree that the bailment shall terminate at a certain time, it terminates when that time arrives and the bailor takes the article bailed. 

3. Mutual agreement of the parties to the bailment. The parties may agree between themselves to terminate the bailment at any time. 

4. The express act of either party. The bailee may surrender the article bailed, and so terminate the bailment, or the bailor may make a demand and recover the article bailed. 

5. Death or insanity of either party. If, however, the surviving or sane party is obligated to the deceased or insane party, he must carry out his part of the agreement. In such cases termination is by operation of law.

Example 8. Alder allowed Wendel to store furniture in an attic room in his house. Wendel died, but his death does not cause Alder to be relieved from his responsibility as the bailee of Wendel's furniture until it can be removed. 

What bailments are for the sole benefit of the bailee?

This class of bailments include all loans of personal property for the exclusive use of the bailee (the borrower) or some one authorized by him to use the property and he is not to pay the bailor (the lender) for this use except that he must pay any expense attendant upon the use of the property. That is, if the article loaned is a power machine using fuel, he must supply the necessary fuel at his own expense. Should the machine need repairing while being used by the bailee, this item of expense would be chargeable to the bailor, unless the bailee agreed to keep the machine in repair while using it.

Example 9. Bantz borrowed a tractor from Green to plow a certain field. While Bantz was using the tractor a gear broke. Bantz must pay for the fuel used by him in operating the tractor but the cost of replacing the gear is chargeable to Green.

The loan of the property may be for a definite period of time, but the bailor, who receives no benefit from the bailment, may terminate it whenever he pleases.

What is the responsibility of the bailee? 

In any bailment for the bailee's sole benefit he is required to use the highest degree of care or great care; failing to do so he is liable for any loss to the bailor. In addition to this rigid requirement, the bailee is held strictly to the terms of the bailment contract, and should he deviate from these terms he is liable for resulting damage or loss.

Example 10. Prine borrowed a truck from Lawrence to take a load of fruit to market. While Prine had the truck he decided to haul a few loads of sand. While hauling the sand a tire blew out. Had this tire blown out while Prine was taking his fruit to market, he would be liable only in case he failed to use the required care, but as it blew out while he was hauling sand, he is liable for the damage regardless of the care he used, for the reason that he deviated from the terms of the agreement. 

The bailee who uses the property strictly according to the terms of the bailment contract is relieved from liability when by accident the property loaned is injured, or when fire accidentally destroys the property, or when an animal that was loaned dies from a natural cause.

The duties of the bailee may be specified in the contract itself, but when this is not done the following duties and responsibilities are always implied: ? 

1. The bailee must use the highest degree of care (great care). 

2. The bailee must use the property strictly in accordance with the terms of the contract. 

3. The bailee must use the property himself unless it is understood by the bailor that it is to be used by another person at the discretion of the bailee. 

4. The bailee must deliver back to the bailor the borrowed property, together with any increase or profits arising therefrom. 

How may a bailment for the bailee's sole benefit be terminated?

This class of bailments is terminated by: 

1. The expiration of the time, or the fulfillment of the purpose. 

When property was loaned for a definite item or for a definite purpose, the bailment may be terminated, when the time expires or the purpose is achieved, by the bailee returning the property to the bailor. 

2. The bailor recalling the property. The bailor may recall the

T property any time he chooses, regardless of the terms of the contract, and particularly so if the bailee violates any of his duties towards the property. 

3. The mutual agreement of the parties. Regardless of the terms or conditions specified in the contract the bailor and the bailee may agree between themselves to terminate the bailment at any time. 

4. The death of the bailee (borrower) or by his insanity. While death of the bailee or his insanity automatically terminates the bailment, death or insanity of the bailor (lender) does not terminate a bailment for a definite time if that time has not yet passed.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A bailment for the bailor's sole benefit may be created by contract, and also by the bailee voluntarily or involuntarily coming into possession of property belonging to the bailor. 

2. The bailor must pay expenses that result from taking proper care of the property. 

3. The bailor must tell the bailee of any thing about the property bailed that would cause an unusual risk. 

4. A gratuitous bailee is required to take only slight care of the property and he is liable only for gross negligence. 

5. A gratuitous bailee is permitted to use the article bailed only when necessary for its proper care. 

6. Every loan of personal property for the use of the bailee is a bailment for his sole benefit. 

7. The article loaned must be used personally by the borrower, unless circumstances indicate that someone else will use it, and it must be used for the purpose for which it was borrowed. 

8. Any bailee who deviates from the purpose of the bailment is responsible for all losses, except those caused by inevitable accident. 

9. The bailee in a bailment for his benefit, must pay any expense necessary in using the article. The bailor must pay for repairs that were to his benefit and any unusual expenses. 

10. The bailee in a bailment for his benefit, is required to use great care and he is liable for loss or damage resulting from his slight negligence.

BAILMENTS FOR THE SOLE BENEFIT OF EITHER THE BAILOR OR THE BAILEE: SUMMARY OUTLINE 

I. Bailments for Sole Benefit of Bailor

A. How Created 

B. Bailor's Duties

C. Bailee's Duties D. How Terminated II. Bailments for Sole Benefit of Bailee A. Responsibility of Bailee B. How Terminated

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Collateral Security. Stocks, bonds, or documents convertible into cash, pledged as security for a debt or the performance of some act. 

Mutual Benefit. All parties concerned receive some benefit from the transaction.

Pawnbroker. A person who makes a business of loaning money and accepting articles of personal property other than commercial paper as security.

Redeem. To recover pledged property by paying what is due on the pledge. 

What bailments are for mutual benefit?

Any bailment from which both the bailor and the bailee receive some benefit or profit is a mutual benefit bailment. Bailments in this class result from business transactions rather than from the friendly relations of the parties which prompts them to grant favors to each other.

Mutual benefit bailments may consist of: 

1. Bailment for hire (a) Hired service about some article (b) Hired use of some article 

2. Pledge or pawn (a) Personal property transferred to some one as security for a debt or the performance of an agreement. 

What is a bailment for hire?

Every business transaction in which service about some article or the use of some article is hired is a mutual benefit bailment for hire. When service about an article, such as repairs or custody, is hired, the bailor receives the benefit of the service and the bailee receives the compensation therefor. When the use of an article is 406

hired, the bailor receives the compensation and the bailee receives the use of the article. Therefore, in a bailment for hire both parties are benefited.

When an article is taken to someone to be repaired or goods are placed in storage or valuables are placed in a safety deposit vault, a mutual benefit bailment for hire is created in every case where a charge is made. 

How is a bailment for hire created?

Example 1. Havens took his automobile to Miller to be repaired. This is a bailment for hire; it begins as soon as the automobile is delivered to 

Miller and is accepted under the terms of the agreement between him and Havens. After the agreement is entered into, should either party default, there would be a breach of contract for which damages may be recovered. 

Should Miller start the job and fail to complete it, he is not entitled to pay for his services as a rule, but some courts will permit him to recover the value of his services less any damages suffered by the bailor. 

A bailment for hire is created only by contract. The bailor either pays or receives the compensation, and the bailee either performs the service on, or receives the use of, the article. 

What is the liability of the bailor?

Example 2. Barns hired a wagon from Woodman. It had a defective pole which Woodman knew about, but he failed to tell Barns. When 

Barns was driving down a steep hill the pole broke and the loaded wagon ran into the team and one horse was seriously injured. Woodman is liable to Barns for the damage.

The bailor is liable for a loss or injury to the bailee caused by defects in the article known to him and not easily discovered by the bailee. He is liable also if the bailee is disturbed in his possession of the article by some one who has a better title to it than the bailor has. The bailor is liable also to the bailee for any payment due to the bailee for services. 

What are the duties of the bailee?

In a bailment for service the bailee is required to use ordinary care and diligence and if he contracts to perform service which requires skill he must use such skill as a workman qualified to do this kind of work would be expected to use. Should the bailee fail in either particular, he is liable for ordinary negligence.

In a bailment for use the bailee must (a) pay the bailor for the use of the article, (b) return the article to the bailor when the bailment is terminated, and (c) in using the article, should he injure a third person, he must pay the damages. 

What are the rights of the bailee?

Example 3. Strand hired a mowing machine to use during July. While he was using this machine and before the time was up, the owner sold it and promised delivery at once. If Strand has complied thus far with the terms of the bailment contract, he can hold the machine for the full month of July.

The bailee, for hire, has the right to the exclusive use of the article for the period of the bailment. He is bound, however, to use the article only for the purpose for which it was hired, and according to the terms of the agreement. 

Example 4. Arnod put his automobile in Tait's paint shop to be painted. 

Tait did the painting and he can hold the automobile until Arnod pays the bill. This right of Tait's is lost as soon as he gives up possession of the car, or Arnod pays for the painting. 

The bailee for hire who has rendered service about an article has a right of lien against it for the price of the service so long as the article is in his possession. This right of lien is lost as soon as the bailor pays for the service, or the bailee gives up possession of the article. 

What is a pledge or a pawn?

Example 5. Harper needed some ready cash, so he deposited his watch with a pawnbroker as security for the loan of the cash he needed. The watch is the pledge, and the pawnbroker has the right to retain possession of it until the loan is paid. If Harper fails to pay the debt the pawnbroker may sell the watch and keep the proceeds of the sale up to the amount of the loan and costs. Any excess amount must be given to Harper. The pawnbroker makes a charge for the loan and his services, and Harper receives the use of the money. Both parties are benefited. A pledge, or a pawn, is a mutual benefit bailment in which personal property of some kind is deposited by the bailor in the custody of the bailee as security for the payment of some debt or the performance of some agreement. Stocks and bonds when pledged are called collateral security.

A pledge differs from a chattel mortgage in that the pledgee (the creditor) has the right to possession but no title, while the chattel mortgagee has title but usually not the right to possession. 

A pledge can be created only by contract. As in Example 5, any contract whereby one party bails personal property as security for a debt is a pledge. The person who borrows the money or agrees to perform some obligation and furnishes the security for the faithful performance of his agreement is the pledgor. The person who lends the money and receives the security is the pledgee. 

What are the pledgor's liabilities and rights?

The pledgor becomes a party to a contract which imposes certain liabilities upon him and also gives him certain rights: 

1. He obligates himself to pay the debt and should he default he forfeits his interest in the security pledged except for any amount realized from the sale of it in excess of the amount of the debt and costs. 

2. He impliedly warrants that his title in the article pledged is good. He is liable to the pledgee for a breach of this warranty whereby the pledgee suffers loss. 

Example 6. Hake stole a very valuable gun and borrowed $10 on it from a pawnbroker. The owner of the gun forced the pawnbroker to give it up. 

This act of the owner gives the pawnbroker a right of action against Hake for a breach of implied warranty. 

3. He has a right to transfer his interest in the article pledged to another any time before it is finally sold by the pledgee. 

Example 7. Long borrowed $25 on a valuable diamond set ring. Not being able to redeem the ring he sold and assigned his interest in it to Dodd for $50. Dodd may complete Long's agreement and acquire possession of the ring. 

4. The pledgor has a right to redeem the pledge on making payment of the debt. Any agreement between the pledgor and the pledgee annulling this right would not be lawful, for the reason that the pledgee might take advantage of the pledgor. Whether 

Long, in Example 7, would have a right to redeem the ring from Dodd would depend upon the agreement between them.

What are the pledgee's rights and duties? 

1. The pledgee has a right to assign or repledge to another his interest in the article pledged. The assignment, however, is subject to the original pledge.

Example 8. Moore pledged a silver cornet with Laky to secure a loan of $25. Laky assigned his interest in the pledge to Ward. This assignment gives Ward a right to collect the $25 from Moore, and Moore still has a right to redeem his cornet according to the original agreement. 

2. The pledgee has a right to use the article pledged only when it is of such a nature as to require use. Such cases are rare. 

3. The pledgee has a right to collect from the pledgor any expense incidental to the pledge. For instance, if an animal were pledged, the pledgor would have to pay for the food it consumed. 

4. The pledgee (or assignee) must keep the article pledged in his possession. Should he voluntarily surrender possession to the owner, his security for the pledge is lost. 

5. A pledge, being a mutual benefit bailment, the pledgee is required to give the article pledged ordinary care, and he is liable for ordinary negligence should the bailor suffer damage thereby. 

6. The pledgee is required to return to the pledgor the article pledged, together with all increase or profit belonging thereto, as soon as the debt secured by the pledge is paid in full. 

What are the rights of an unpaid pledgee? 

1. After the pledgor has defaulted in the payment of the debt secured by the pledge, the pledgee may sell the article pledged. The pledgee must give the pledgor reasonable notice of the time and place of the sale, and before giving notice he must demand payment. The sale must be by public auction, and to the highest bidder. Pawnbrokers who sell pledged articles are generally subject to special laws regulating the manner of selling. 

2. When collateral, such as notes, bills, or bonds, has been pledged, the pledgee may, if it matures soon, hold it until maturity and if possible collect it. The proceeds are applied on the debt. Any amount collected in excess of the debt, plus interest and necessary expenses incidental to the pledge, belongs to the pledgor. 

3. The pledgee may bring an action in the equity court to foreclose his claim upon the article pledged. This is the usual procedure when a large amount is involved. 

How is a pledge terminated?

A pledge is terminated by the pledgor paying the debt and the pledgee returning the article pledged. The pledgee must return the pledge to the pledgor as soon as the debt is paid. This is the usual

way of terminating a pledge, but should the pledgor default, the pledgee can terminate the pledge only by selling the article pledged. Although this is the proper and legal way to terminate the pledgor's interest in the pledge, most agreements, particularly with pawnbrokers, contain provisions terminating the pledgor's interest upon his default, permitting the pledgee to retain the pledge as his own or to sell it at public auction or private sale and retain the proceeds, without any duty to account to the pledgor for the surplus over the loan. 

Who is a warehouseman?

A warehouseman is one who operates a public storehouse for the storage of goods for hire. When goods are stored the usual warehouse receipt is given to the owner (See Sale of Personal Property, page 340). The receipt may be negotiable or nonnegotiable. If a nonnegotiable receipt is given for the goods they must be delivered back to the bailor only, unless they are held and finally sold for storage charges. A negotiable receipt makes it possible to transfer the title to the goods stored to another person by endorsing the receipt to him. The endorsee takes the place of the original owner in the bailment contract. 

What are the bailee's duties and rights? 

1. The bailee who accepts an article to repair or goods for storage must use ordinary care and the required skill, and he is liable for damage caused by his ordinary negligence. 

2. The bailee has a lien on the goods if the repair bill or storage charges are not paid by the bailor. This right of lien gives the bailee a right to sell the goods and the proceeds of the sale may be applied first towards the unpaid bill, and any sum left over goes to the bailor. 

The duties and rights of the bailee may be changed by agreement of the parties. 

Who must bear the loss if goods are destroyed?

The one who takes an article into his custody to repair or to store does not become an insurer of the article. He would be responsible for any loss only in case it was caused by his own carelessness. The owner of the article should insure it against fire and theft, if he desires protection. The bailee has an interest in

the article, which gives him a right to insure it. He also has a right of action against any one who damages the article or disturbs it while it is in his possession. 

Is a bank considered to be a bailee?

A bank, in performing its ordinary duties of receiving and paying out money, is not a bailee. The reason being that the bank is not expected to pay back to a depositor the same money it received from him on deposit. In a bailment the same article is returned that was received. There is a change of possession without a change of ownership. Any bank that accepts valuables from some one for safe-keeping is a bailee. 

Banks that operate safe deposit departments and rent safe deposit boxes to their customers are bailees, but their duties are somewhat different from those of the ordinary bailee. 

The bank gives the customer a key or keys to the box, and he alone is entitled to access to the box. To guard against unauthorized use of a key, the customer can open his box only in the presence and with the assistance of an officer of the bank, and the customer must be identified as the proper person to have access. 

Since the bank does not have immediate and actual possession of the property deposited, its duty to care for the property is different from that of the ordinary bailee for hire, but it is bound to use due diligence to protect the box and its contents and to permit only the customer to have access to it. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Both parties receive benefit if the bailment is for mutual benefit. 

2. In a mutual benefit bailment, ordinary or reasonable care is required of the bailee and he is liable for ordinary negligence. 

3. Bailments for service or custody and resulting from a pledge are mutual benefit bailments. 4. In a service bailment the bailee is liable if damage results from his failure to use the required skill. 

5. Serious defects in the article bailed known to the bailor but not easily discovered by the bailee may render the bailor liable for damages caused thereby.

6. The right of lien goes with the bailee's possession of the article until the bill for services about it is paid. 

7. The pledgor's right to redeem the pledge cannot be annulled by any agreement between the pledgor and the pledgee. 

8. Should a bailed article be stolen or destroyed by fire, the bailee is liable for the loss only in case he was unduly negligent.

INNKEEPERS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Accommodations. Lodging or food or both supplied by an innkeeper or boardinghouse keeper.

Acts of God. Lightning, flood, tornadoes, and earthquakes. 

Baggage. Wearing apparel and any articles necessary to personal convenience and comfort.

Public Enemy. An organized mob creating an insurrection or rebellion, or a country at war with this country. 

Transient. One who travels about and stays a short time in a place. 

One who is entertained at a hotel, but he is not regular or permanent.

What is the difference between an innkeeper and a boardinghouse keeper?

An innkeeper is one who operates an inn (hotel) for the lodging of guests for a compensation. He makes a business of giving accommodations and is bound to furnish them to all persons of good behavior not afflicted with a contagious disease or known to be otherwise obnoxious, who apply and offer to pay for their accommodation, unless he has no more room. 

An innkeeper is required by law to accept to the capacity of his available accommodations all persons not legally objectionable who apply and offer to pay. A boardinghouse keeper may accept or refuse to accept at will any person who applies for lodging or meals. In other words, he may choose his guests. The management of a restaurant has the same privilege. 

Improper conduct, certain physical afflictions (contagious disease, insanity), a criminal record, and no more room are reasons which ordinarily will be sustained by the law for rejecting a person as a guest. 415

Who is a guest?

A guest is one who engages accommodations (room or meals or both) at a hotel and pays the regular price for the accommodations he receives. He is a transient in the sense that he does not engage accommodations for any definite length of time. He may come and go as he pleases, but he is bound by an implied or express contract with the proprietor to comply with the enforceable regulations of the hotel and to pay the regular rates for the accommodations furnished him for the time he is a guest. 

Because of the unusual liability imposed on an innkeeper, it always is important to determine when rights as a guest begin and when they end. If the guest is actually received as such, as when he registers at the hotel and is assigned a room, the relationship has begun. But it may begin under other circumstances, as when his baggage is accepted by the hotel, he intending to secure a room later; or when he is served with food, although he is not lodging at the hotel. Using the public facilities of the hotel, such as the lobby or waiting room, without intent to pay and without being accepted by the innkeeper does not make one a guest. When the relation begins, is a question of fact in each case. 

A guest is not bound to stay for any particular time, and he may end his relation at any time by paying his bill and leaving. 

A temporary absence, with an intent to return and with an obligation to pay for his accommodations while he is away, does not terminate the relation. 

What other people furnish accommodations?

Example 1. Wade engaged a suite of rooms and meals for himself and family at the Esmond Hotel, for which he agreed to pay a special reduced rate of $150 per week. In this case Wade and the members of his family would be considered as boarders rather than guests, and in this transaction the proprietor of the hotel would be considered a boardinghouse keeper rather than a hotelkeeper or innkeeper. Lodginghouse keepers, steamship companies, and railroad companies operating sleeping cars and dining cars furnish much the same type of accommodations as innkeepers furnish, but they are not considered innkeepers, and therefore are not subject to the laws under which innkeepers are required to operate. A hotel-

INNKEEPERS 

417 keeper who takes roomers or boarders on a special contract on a weekly or monthly basis would be considered a lodginghouse or boardinghouse keeper in such transactions rather than a hotelkeeper.

What are the duties of an innkeeper? 

An innkeeper is subject to rather strict laws in the management of his inn (hotel) in most states, but in general his duties are: 

1. He must comply with all the local and state laws in force in his state affecting innkeepers. In general this means that he must comply with fire regulations, sanitation codes, and other safety requirements. 

2. He must furnish accommodations to all orderly persons who apply unless his reasons for rejecting anyone are sustainable at law.

Example 2. Hinds applied for accommodations at the Windsor Hotel. 

The proprietor of the Windsor must accommodate Hinds unless (a) he is known to be afflicted with a contagious disease; or (b) he does not conduct himself properly; or (c) the available accommodations have all been taken. 

3. He must insure the safety of his guests' baggage, except that he is not liable if loss results from causes over which he has no control, such as fire, acts of God, or acts of a public enemy. The innkeeper is permitted by statute in most states to limit his liability to a certain amount, and in the case of valuables to require that the guest leave them at the office where they may be put in the office safe; otherwise he will not be liable. To take advantage of this relief from the heavy responsibility imposed by the Common Law, the innkeeper must comply with statutory requirements as to posting notices, maintenance of a safe for the free use of his guests, and any other conditions. 

Example 3. Jordan, a guest at the Bradley Hotel, placed his billfold containing valuable securities under his pillow when he retired. The next morning he went out leaving it there, and later when he returned it was missing. The proprietor of the hotel had complied with the law by posting a notice in each room to the effect that he would not be responsible for a guest's valuables unless they were checked at the office where they might be put in the safe. As this case stands, Jordan cannot hold the proprietor of the Bradley Hotel liable.

The innkeeper's liability is limited to that of a bailee in a bailment for the bailor's benefit in case property is left in his custody by a guest who has checked out. 

4. He must provide sanitary and safe accommodations for his guests and give them the required protection from intruders. He is also responsible for the conduct of his employees in their relations with guests. 

Example 4. Grant, who was a guest at the Hampton Hotel, requested the proprietor not to allow any one other than the employees of the hotel access to his room. The proprietor is bound to respect Grant's request unless some one with authority of the law asks to see him. Should Grant be mistreated by an employee at the inn, he might hold the innkeeper responsible for the employee's act. 

What are the innkeeper's rights?

We have learned that the innkeeper has a right to refuse accommodations to persons who are in an unfit condition. He has certain other rights: 

1. He has a right to demand that a guest pay in advance for his accommodation.

When a guest arrives with baggage on which the innkeeper may assert a lien, payment in advance is rarely required, but it is customary to require it when the guest arrives without baggage. 

2. He has a right of lien on the baggage belonging to the guest for the amount of his unpaid bill. This gives him a right to hold the guest's baggage until he pays for his accommodation. 

The right to sell a guest's baggage to satisfy a lien is usually granted by statute law which regulates the manner of conducting the sale. Usually it is sold at public sale. 

What are the rights and liabilities of a boardinghouse keeper?

A boardinghouse keeper has a right to select his boarders, and in most states he has a right of lien against the baggage of a boarder who has not paid his bill if the baggage is still in possession of the boardinghouse keeper. Having the right of lien, he would also have a right to sell the baggage to satisfy his claim against the boarder. He is not an insurer of the baggage belonging to the boarder, as is an innkeeper. A boardinghouse keeper is required

INNKEEPERS 

419 to comply with local and state laws regarding safety and sanitation, and failing to do so he is liable. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. An innkeeper must accommodate all fit persons who apply, if he has room. 

2. Those who operate lodginghouses, passenger ships, or sleeping cars and dining cars are not considered to be innkeepers. 

3. The innkeeper is an insurer of his guests' personal effects. He is permitted by statute to limit his liability by posting notices to this effect where his guests can see them. 

4. A boardinghouse keeper is not an insurer of a boarder's personal effects. 

5. An innkeeper may not infringe his guests' exclusive rights to their rooms except for necessary reasons. 

6. The innkeeper has a right of lien on the baggage of a guest who has failed to pay his bill. He loses his lien by voluntarily surrendering possession of the baggage.

COMMON CARRIERS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Acts of God. Acts that result from natural causes, such as lightning, tornadoes, floods, and earthquakes.

Baggage. Wearing apparel and personal belongings needed by a traveler for his use and comfort while on a journey.

Carriage. Act of transporting goods by some means. 

Exceptional Bailee. A person, such as an innkeeper or common carrier, who is subject to special laws and regulations. 

Lawful Goods. Goods that are not being transported illegally.

Public-Service Commission. A commission, consisting of a certain number of members, who are appointed by the governor of the state, and charged with the duty of supervising and regulating the business of public-utility corporations operating in the state. 

Who is a common carrier of goods?

A common carrier is any individual or company engaged in the business of transporting personal property from one place to another, for a compensation, for all who need such service. In contrast with a private carrier who transports goods gratuitously or for hire in special cases, and who is an ordinary bailee, not subject to special rules, a common carrier is an exceptional bailee subject to laws and special rules, and he must transport all goods within the scope of his business and facilities for all who may choose to employ him.

Two things are necessary to constitute one a common carrier: 

1. There must be a continuous offer to the public to carry goods. 

2. A compensation must be charged for the service.

Express, railroad, steamship, and airplane transportation companies and all others engaged in transporting goods for hire from 421

place to place, by land or sea, are common carriers. Individuals or companies doing a trucking or moving-van business, or operating a parcel delivery, are also common carriers. 

Example 1. The Brady Trucking Company operates a fleet of autotrucks in a certain city and advertises to do all kinds of trucking, short haul or long distances. They are common carriers. If they do not hold themselves out as prepared to serve the public, but make private contracts to do the trucking for certain merchants or manufacturers, regardless of the number whom they serve, they are private carriers, for the reason that they do not make it their business to do trucking for all who apply. 

What are the duties of a common carrier?

The duties of a common carrier are as follows: 

1. He must accept all lawful goods offered to him for carriage, to the extent of his equipment, and within the terms of his holding out. 

2. He must provide such equipment as will insure the safe and proper handling of the goods he proposes to carry. 

3. He must deliver the goods to the consignee or the person to whom they are addressed, or to a connecting carrier according to the terms of the agreement. 

The term "goods" is taken to mean livestock, money, and all other personal property.

Example 2. The agent for the X Railroad Company delivered a shipment to the wrong party. The company is liable for the loss suffered by the shipper, unless his carelessness in addressing the shipment caused the mistake to be made by the agent. 

What are the rights of the common carrier?

While common carriers have certain rights, at the same time their business is controlled more or less by local, state, and federal laws, depending upon the nature and extent of their carrying business. 

1. They have a right to charge for their services, but in many cases the rates they may charge are fixed or must be approved by some authority under the law. The Interstate Commerce Commission created by Congressional enactment has authority to fix the rates that may be charged by common carriers whose business extends beyond the limits of a

COMMON CARRIERS 

423 single state, and in no case are carriers permitted to discriminate in their charges. They must charge all shippers alike. 

2. A carrier may refuse to transport goods for the following reasons: (a) When the charges are not paid or offered to be paid. (b) When the carriage is not within the carrier's facilities or conveyance. (c) When the carriage is not in the line of the carrier's vocation.

A carrier cannot be expected to accept goods to be transported when he has insufficient room or inadequate facilities for carrying them safely. Neither can he be expected to transport an article larger or heavier than he can handle with his equipment. That is, a carrier engaged in delivering parcels could not be expected to move a safe or a piano. 

3. They may refuse to receive goods to transport that may at the time be exposed to danger or hazard en route, or when the goods are not properly crated or packed. The dangers en route may be from natural causes such as floods or snow blockades or from riots or a state of war. 

4. The carrier may withhold delivery of goods carried by him until he is paid the carrying charges, and finally he may sell the goods to pay the charges. 

What is the Interstate Commerce Act? 

The Interstate Commerce Act was designed to regulate commerce between the states. It applies to all common carriers, either by land or water, who transport goods or property from one state to another. The principal provisions are as follows: 

1. There shall be no discrimination between large and small, or constant and occasional shippers. 

2. No charges shall be unjust or unreasonable, and proportionate charges shall be made for long and short distances. 

3. Adequate facilities to carry the goods necessary to meet the requirements by the community shall be provided. 

4. The schedule of rates shall be published and filed with the Interstate 

Commerce Commission, which has authority under the Act to regulate rates.

5. No common carrier engaged in interstate commerce is permitted to enter into agreement by which the continuous transportation of goods from one place to another shall be delayed or interrupted. 

What are the common carrier's liabilities?

The common carrier is liable for all loss or damage to the goods while they are in his custody, unless his liability is limited by statutory regulations or the loss or damage to the goods results from one of the following causes: 

1. Loss caused by an act of God. The carrier is not liable for losses resulting from causes which are beyond the control of man, such as floods, lightning, cyclones, earthquakes, snow, freezing, thawing, or sudden death. However, the carrier is expected to exercise prudence in caring for the goods, and failing to do so, he will be liable for losses from any of the causes mentioned. 

Example 3. The X Railroad Company accepted a quantity of oranges for shipment to a distant point. Freezing weather damaged the oranges while en route, so that they were unfit for sale. The railroad company's employees neglected to give the oranges proper attention; therefore, the company can be held for the loss. 

Loss by fire from any cause other than lightning does not excuse the carrier from liability unless by the terms of the contract he is excused. 

2. Loss caused by act of a public enemy. This is a loss caused by armed conflict between a foreign power and this country. Mob violence, riots, strikes, or any such disorders within the boundaries of this country do not make those who participate public enemies. 

Only in the case of loss caused by a public enemy is the common carrier relieved from liability. 

3. Loss caused by carelessness of shipper. When the shipper carelessly packs the goods and loss results, or should he incorrectly address the parcel so that it is lost or so much delayed that it is damaged, the common carrier is not liable in such cases. Example 4. Roberts shipped a parcel to a distant point. He wrapped the package so carelessly that the outside wrapper containing the address came off and delivery was not made before the contents spoiled. The carrier is not liable in this case and Roberts must lose unless the parcel

COMMON CARRIERS 

425 was insured. Common carriers will, as a rule, refuse to accept goods for shipment unless they are securely packed and properly addressed. 

Should the shipper make it appear that the goods are less valuable than they are or falsify the information about them, the carrier is relieved from responsibility for injury to them resulting from any cause.

Example 5. Darby shipped a set of glassware to a distant point. He was asked by the carrier if the package contained anything fragile and he replied, "No." If this glassware is broken in transit, Darby must stand the loss. A common carrier cannot, as a rule, be held liable for damage to a fragile article contained in a package which he accepted for shipment. unless it is marked "Glass," or "Fragile," or in some such way to indicate that it contains a fragile article. 

4. Loss arising from the nature of the goods. When the loss arises from the inherent nature of the goods, the carrier is not liable. This applies to the natural decay of perishable goods and also to the loss of animals arising from natural causes or their own viciousness. 

But the carrier who does not exercise proper prudence and foresight in caring for the shipment regardless of what it comprises, is not relieved from liability for loss. 

Example 6. One animal in a carload of livestock shipped from Des 

Moines to Chicago became vicious and killed two other animals in the car. 

The shipper cannot hold the carrier for the loss unless it can be shown that he did not use foresight and care in transporting these animals. 

5. Loss caused by intervention of public authority. When goods in transit are seized by an official acting under authority of law, the carrier is not liable to the shipper for any loss that may be caused by such seizure. Any unlawful goods such as smuggled goods, quarantined goods, goods that have been stolen, or goods that are being sold in violation of some law may be seized. 

Example 7. Small smuggled a consignment of woolen cloth into this country and shipped it to his firm in Chicago. The authorities served papers on the carrier and took possession of the cloth. Small cannot hold the carrier for any loss he may suffer on account of this seizure. 

How may the carrier limit his liability? 

The carrier may by special agreement limit his liability or stipulate the degree of his responsibility, unless forbidden by statute

to do so. He may specify that he will not be liable for loss caused by fire, robbery, or the hazards of navigation, provided he is not at fault; but he is not permitted by contract or otherwise to relieve himself from liability for loss caused by the fraud, misconduct, or neglect by himself or his employees in the service. Regardless of any agreement, the carrier may make with the shipper, he is still responsible as a mutual benefit bailee, and he must exercise ordinary care and diligence. 

Example 8. A common carrier who specified in his receipt for a shipment of goods that he would not be responsible for loss from any accident not caused by his negligence could not be held for loss resulting from an accident over which he had no control. 

The common carrier is allowed to state a reasonable amount for which he will be liable in case of loss, unless the shipper states the value of the goods at the time they are delivered to the carrier. 

Under the Interstate Commerce Act, the carrier is permitted to base his rates upon the valuations placed upon the goods by the shipper. Express companies generally limit the amount for which they will be liable to $50, and for any valuations in excess of this amount they charge a higher rate. The valuation the shipper placed upon the goods binds him, and should a loss occur, amount he could collect would be limited to this valuation. the 

Example 9. Carhart shipped an article valued at $250 by express.

When he was asked its value, he stated $100. This article was lost and 

Carhart tried to collect the full $250. He cannot succeed. The express company is liable for not more than $100. 

It generally has been held that a carrier is liable for damages due to the elements (rain, mud, or sun's rays) when the article is properly packed and protected by the shipper. The shipper is not required to pack his goods for shipment so that they are protected from rain, etc., and the carrier accepting them for carriage must protect them. 

What is a uniform bill of lading?

When a shipper delivers goods to a common carrier to be transported, he receives a receipt for them called a bill of lading. In the beginning each common carrier had his own particular form of re-

COMMON CARRIERS 

427 ceipt or bill of lading, and the stipulations in these different bills of lading varied considerably. These different stipulations and provisions often resulted in confusion when goods being transported had to pass over the separate lines or routes of two or three different carriers. With the rapid growth of transportation this lack of uniformity became more annoying to shippers and carriers alike. 

It was found that a uniform bill of lading would be an advantage to both shipper and carrier, and finally a uniform straight bill of lading and a uniform order bill of lading to be used for interstate shipments were approved by the Interstate Commerce Commission, and they are now in general use. When a straight bill of lading is used, the shipment is to be delivered to the consignee only. But when for any reason it may be desirable to have the shipment delivered to some person other than the consignee, an order bill of lading is used, which makes it possible for the consignee to endorse it to the one to whom he wishes the shipment delivered, as order bills of lading are generally negotiable. Now that bills of lading in general use are uniform, they all contain the same stipulations and provisions. This makes it possible to have but one bill of lading for each shipment, regardless of how many carriers handle it before it reaches its destination. 

How is the carrier's liability terminated? 

A common carrier assumes responsibility for the care and safety of the goods he accepts to transport, and this responsibility, and likewise his liability, ends: 

1. When the goods reach their destination and are delivered to the consignee. 

2. When goods must pass over the lines of two or more carriers to reach their destination the initial carrier usually contracts to carry them to that destination. In such a case it is liable for loss, whether it occurred on its lines or not. But if the initial carrier contracted only for transportation over its own lines, its contract is performed when the goods are delivered safely to the connecting carrier, and it is not liable for loss occurring thereafter. 

The Interstate Commerce Act provides that where an interstate shipment passes through the hands of two or more carriers before it reaches its

destination, the first carrier is liable to the shipper for any loss or damage, regardless of which carrier is at fault. 

3. When goods reach their destination and are placed in the freight house or otherwise are made available for delivery and the consignee is notified of their arrival. The exceptional liability of the carrier as such terminates after the expiration of a reasonable time, within which the consignee should remove the goods. Thereafter the carrier is liable only as a warehouseman or ordinary bailee. 

4. When, by custom, the carrier is required to make delivery to the consignee, as in the case of express companies, the exceptional liability of the carrier does not terminate until he has made reasonable effort to effect delivery. 

When is a shipment said to be delivered? 

A railroad company transports the shipment to its destination and delivers it at the depot or freight house. In case it is a carload lot, delivery is made in the freight yard. As soon as delivery is made in either way, the laws of most states provide that notice of the arrival of the shipment must be sent to the consignee at once, and the railroad company is liable as a common carrier until the consignee has had a reasonable time to remove the shipment. 

Shipments by water are delivered on the wharf where the boat docks, and notice must be sent to the consignee under the same rules that apply to shipments by rail.

A few states hold that a common carrier's liability as such ceases as soon as the shipment is delivered in the freight depot and thereafter he is liable only as a warehouseman. When it is the custom for the carrier to deliver the shipment to the consignee at his residence or place of business delivery at any other place would not be sufficient. This applies to shipments by express or parcel post where the destination is a place large enough to have a delivery service. Truckmen usually deliver according to special agreements with those whom they serve. Many railroad companies are conducting a "house-to-house" service whereby the shipment is delivered by truck from the freight yard to the consignee's residence or place of business.

COMMON CARRIERS 

429 

Who is a common carrier of passengers?

Any individual or company who transports persons from one place to another for hire is a common carrier of passengers. Many common carriers transport both goods and persons. The common carrier of passengers must receive and carry all persons who apply for carriage and are ready to pay for their transportation, subject to certain rules and regulations, explained following. 

A person who engages or accepts the facilities of a common carrier to convey him from one place to another, whether he pays his fare or is carried gratis, is a passenger. A person is considered a passenger from the time he enters upon the premises of the carrier with the intention of taking passage until he reaches his destination and leaves the carrier's premises. 

What are the duties of a common carrier of passengers? 

1. The carrier must provide the means and appliances suitable for the safe transportation of passengers, he must use reasonable effort to provide sufficient cars to accommodate all passengers who apply for transportation, and he must use all reasonable precautions for their safety. The fare charged must be reasonable. 

Fares quite generally are regulated by statute. 

2. The carrier must permit a passenger who has paid his fare to take with him on the journey certain baggage without an extra charge. 

3. The carrier must exercise the highest degree of care in transporting passengers and he is responsible for any injury to a passenger resulting from his carelessness or improper treatment on the part of himself or his employees in the service. 

Example 10. The conductor signaled the engineer to start the train before one passenger had time to alight, and he was thrown down and injured. In this case the railroad company was held liable for the injury which was attributed to the carelessness of the conductor. 

The carrier is not an insurer of the lives and safety of the passengers, but he is liable if injury results to a passenger even from his slight negligence. Most states do not permit the carrier to limit his liability for injury to the passengers, on the ground that it is contrary to public policy not to hold the carrier liable even

for slight negligence when the lives and safety of human beings are at stake. 

4. Should a passenger who has started upon a journey by railroad become too ill to travel, it is the duty of the carrier to remove him from the train and leave him until he is able to resume his journey. Large steamship companies carrying passengers usually provide nurse and medical attendants for any passenger who may be taken ill while on board. If this is the practice of the carrier, it becomes their duty to furnish this service. 

What are the rights of a common carrier of passengers? 

1. A carrier may refuse to take passengers when he has no more room, and he may refuse to take any passenger who for some good reason is objectionable. Drunken persons, notorious criminals, or a person infected with a contagious disease are considered objectionable. 

2. A carrier may prescribe reasonable rules regarding the purchase and showing of tickets, and he may require that the passenger pay his fare in advance.

There is some question about making a passenger give up his ticket if he cannot be furnished a seat. The decisions in such cases bear out the contention that if a passenger elects to ride in a crowded car he must pay his fare. 

3. Passengers must comply with the reasonable rules of the carrier as regards the safety and comfort of fellow passengers. 

Boisterous conduct, smoking in certain sections of cars, improper use of facilities, and molestation of other passengers are among the things which the carrier may regulate. 

What may be included as baggage?

Baggage which the passenger may take with him without charge and for which carriage must be furnished by the carrier includes such articles of personal necessity, convenience, and comfort that he may plan to use on his journey, including a reasonable amount of money which the passenger may need for his traveling expenses. 

A salesman's samples, presents for someone, or any articles which the passenger may wish to have transported cannot be classed as baggage in this sense. But a hunter's outfit taken with

COMMON CARRIERS 

431 him on a hunting trip would be classed as baggage. Much depends upon the circumstances, and no definite rule can be made to apply in every case. When sample cases are checked and a charge is made for excess baggage carriage, the carrier becomes liable as an insurer.

What is the carrier's liability for loss of the passenger's baggage? 

The carrier of baggage is liable in the same way that a common carrier of any goods is liable, and he becomes an insurer of baggage that is checked by him. He is excused from liability for losses resulting from causes over which he has no control, such as acts of God, a public enemy, etc., unless he failed to use the necessary precautions to protect the baggage.

The carrier may limit the amount for which he will be liable unless an extra charge is made. The amount is usually $50. The carrier may also limit the quantity of baggage which the passenger may take with him as such without an extra charge (excess baggage charge). The quantity is usually 150 pounds. The carrier may limit his liability for baggage by an agreement with the passenger. The passenger who signs a receipt for baggage containing a statement limiting liability thereby agrees to the limitation. The carrier is not liable for baggage kept by the passenger in his own possession, however he must give it necessary protection. The carrier, moreover, becomes an insurer of baggage checked by him. 

The carrier's liability for the baggage terminates as soon as the passenger has had a reasonable opportunity to take charge of it after it reaches its destination. If the baggage is not claimed after a reasonable time, the carrier may store it at a price for the storage, and then his liability as a carrier ceases and he becomes liable as a warehouseman. 

What is a public utility?

Any service or commodity furnished to the public under a permit granted and a right protected by some political division (town, city, county, state, or national) of our government is a public utility. 

Examples are railroads, gas, electricity, telephone, telegraph, and power of different kinds. The companies furnishing the different public utilities are public-utility companies. For the most part these public-utility companies or corporations are subject to special statutes, either state or national, for their control and regulation.

What is a public-utility commission?

Most states now have public-service or utility commissions which have charge of many matters affecting public-service corporations. 

The most important is the regulation of rates which public-utility corporations may charge for the service or commodity they furnish. Their principal duties are to see that reasonable rates are charged, that the service is uniformly good, and that the stockholders receive a fair return on their investments. 

State public-utility commissions have jurisdiction over utility corporations operating within the border of the particular state, and the Interstate Commerce Commission, created under Federal law, has jurisdiction over those whose operations extend beyond the boundaries of one or more states, such as railroad, telephone, and telegraph companies.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A common carrier is one which without discrimination publicly undertakes, for hire, to carry goods from one place to another for all who apply for carriage. 

2. A common carrier cannot be required to accept goods for carriage when his facilities are inadequate; or when he is not equipped to handle the kind of goods offered; or when the destination is not on his line or its connections. 

3. A common carrier may require that goods offered for carriage be properly packed and marked, that they be offered for carriage at the proper time and place, and that the charges be paid. 

4. A common carrier is an insurer of the goods he carries and he is liable for loss due to any cause except (1) act of God, (2) act of a public enemy, (3) carelessness of the shipper, (4) the inherent nature of the goods, (5) intervention of an authority. 

5. The business of common carriers is almost entirely regulated by statute. 6. Unless forbidden by statute, common carriers may by special agreement with the consignor limit their liability for loss due to any cause. 

7. The carrier may generally limit the amount for which he will be liable and may make an extra charge for assuming a liability beyond that amount.

COMMON CARRIERS 

433 8. A common carrier has a right of lien on the goods carried to secure the payment of charges. 

9. Carriers who do not undertake by contract or custom to deliver goods to the address of the consignee must send notice to him of their arrival, and after a reasonable time, if the goods are not removed, the carrier's liability becomes that of a warehouseman instead of a common carrier. 

10. The uniform bill of lading as approved by the Interstate Commerce Commission is in general use by railroad companies engaged in interstate transportation. 

11. A carrier of passengers is not an insurer of the safety of those whom he carries, but he is required to exercise the greatest possible care, and he is liable for injury caused by his slight negligence. 

12. The carrier is required to transport a reasonable amount of baggage for each passenger, and if the baggage is checked by him, he is liable as an insurer; but if the passenger keeps possession of his own baggage, the carrier is liable for its safety only when he fails to properly protect it.
