COMMENTS 

Bailments have such an important part in the experience of nearly everybody that the true significance of the bailment contract should be fully appreciated. When an article of personal property is lent or hired, or services about it are hired, or when care or custody of property or persons is arranged for or happens to come about in some way, either gratuitously or for hire, there is a bailment relation. Caring for, using, working upon, or doing something with the personal property of another are the most common forms of bailments. The relationship of the parties to a bailment contract calls for varying degrees of care and diligence, depending upon the class into which the bailment falls; and corresponding responsibility is imposed for varying degrees of negligence. This makes it fundamentally important for both the bailor and the bailee to respect the rights and interests of each other, and to show a high degree of fair-mindedness and good faith in such transactions. People generally are very sensitive regarding their personal and property rights. Poor workmanship, poor service, misuse, and improper care with regard to property regardless of whose it is, or whether it is privately or publicly owned, invariably results in waste and loss which must be borne by someone. This should be kept in mind by everybody who works upon or uses for any purpose the property belonging to another.

INSURANCE TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Beneficiary. The one named in the policy to receive the benefit from the insurance. Binder. A memorandum or oral agreement by which an agent binds his company in an insurance contract before the policy is issued. 

Cash Surrender Value. The amount payable to the insured in case he surrenders the policy to the company issuing it. 

Contingent Event. Some event that may possibly happen, such as an accident.

Estate. A person's interest in land or other forms of property. 

Indemnify. To protect a party from financial loss caused by the happening of some event.

Retroactive. Operating backward-applicable to contracts previously made or acts previously done. 

Rider. A provision or clause added to an insurance policy or for the pose of modifying some provision therein. pur- Vested Interest. That which becomes an established right, not to be denied or ignored. 

What is the meaning of insurance?

Insurance is the business of associations of individuals, or corporations, that agree to assume certain risks for others and to indemnify them for losses resulting from certain contingent events. 

It is a source of financial protection or security against losses. 

The insurance business had its beginning at an early period in a co-operative system by which merchants who shipped goods on the Mediterranean Sea made contributions to a common fund from which contributors were paid for ships or goods taken by pirates or lost at sea. This was the beginning of marine insurance, which is the oldest form of insurance. 438

INSURANCE 

439 Insurance of all kinds can be grouped under two main divisions, (a) that which relates to property and (b) that which relates to persons; or, property insurance and personal insurance. 

Kinds of property insurance. 

1. Insurance against loss or damage caused by fire, tornadoes, lightning, earthquakes, floods, explosions, invasion by a public enemy, riots, and other contingencies which may damage or destroy property. 

2. Marine insurance covers losses of property and ships at sea, and inland marine and transportation insurance, which covers losses resulting from any of the hazards of transportation by land or water within and outside the United States. 

3. Motor-vehicle insurance covers loss or damage caused by fire, lightning, transportation, or theft. 

4. Plate-glass insurance covers damage to plate glass, particularly plate-glass windows, due to any cause. 

5. Steam-boiler insurance covers loss caused by the explosion of a particular boiler whereby the property of the named insured or of another is damaged or another person is injured. 

6. Liability insurance covers loss or damage, due to any specific cause, to property of another for which the insured is liable, as in the case of warehousemen, common carriers, or of any other bailees who perform services on or about the property of another. 

7. Burglary or theft insurance covers loss of property by robbery or larceny. 

8. Title insurance covers loss to the purchaser resulting from a defective title to real property. 

9. Casualty insurance provides for indemnity against loss resulting from damage or destruction of a specific property caused by some catastrophe. 

10. Elevator insurance covers the risk from the use of an elevator, either the damage to the elevator itself or to persons or property injured in its use, one or all risks.

Other common kinds of insurance are, hail insurance, strike insurance, and crop insurance. Crops may be insured against damage from hail-

storms or against other destructive agencies. Manufacturers, contractors, and others, may insure against loss caused by a strike, riot, or civil commotion. 

Kinds of personal insurance. 

1. Life insurance provides for the insurer to pay a specific sum of money upon the death of a certain person, called the insured, to his estate, or to a person called the beneficiary. There are very many varieties of life insurance which are discussed later. See page 465.

Example 1. Havens insured his life for $5,000 with the National Life 

Insurance Company and agreed to pay $112.50 annual premium. His wife was named as beneficiary. When Havens dies, even if it is immediately after the first premium is paid, Mrs. Havens will be entitled to collect $5,000 from the Company. 

2. Accident insurance provides for the weekly or monthly payment of a stipulated sum of money to the insured during the time he is incapacitated because of personal injury he sustained from an accident, and additional sums for operations, hospital, and medical expenses made necessary by the accident. Most accident insurance contracts further provide for the payment of a fixed sum to the estate of the insured or to a named beneficiary in case of the accidental death of the insured. 

3. Health insurance provides for the payment to the insured of a certain sum at regular intervals, usually weekly or monthly during a period of illness not to exceed a definite time. 

4. Automobile liability insurance protects the insured from financial loss resulting from his legal liability for property damage, accidents, collisions, and loss of life or injury to others arising from his operation of an automobile. The extent and nature of the protection depends upon the stipulations in the policy. 

5. Guaranty and fidelity insurance protects employers against the dishonesty of employees, or one party to a contract against loss due to the failure of the other party to perform his part of the contract. 

6. Credit insurance protects merchants and tradesmen from loss through the insolvency or dishonesty of their customers. It is a guaranty against loss through bad debts.

INSURANCE 

441 1 7. Employer's liability insurance gives employers, engaged in manufacturing or in other activities, financial protection against loss resulting from liability for damages for personal injury to employees while on the job. In most states this is now replaced by workmen's compensation insurance, the carrying of which is compulsory. 

8. Rent insurance covers loss of rent or rental value during the time a building damaged by fire is being repaired and cannot be rented or used either in part or as a whole. 

9. Group insurance includes group accident insurance, group annuity insurance, group disability insurance, group life insurance. By this plan a large number of individuals may be insured against a specified risk without medical examination, in a blanket policy issued at a low rate of premium. The minimum number of individuals usually required is fifty. 

What is an insurance contract?

An insurance contract is one in which one party, usually an insurance company, for a consideration called the premium, agrees to indemnify another party called the insured for his losses due to fire or some other destructive agency, or due to the happening of some event causing loss or liability. An insurance contract contains all the essentials of a contract in general. No particular form' of contract is necessary other than to conform to some statute law. The insurance contract is called an insurance policy. 

What are the elements of the insurance contract? 

1. The possible occurrence of a loss must be contemplated. If a loss were not contemplated, there would not be sufficient reason for entering into a contract of insurance. 

2. The insured must have an interest in the subject covered by the contract. Unless the insured would suffer some loss by the occurrence of the contingency insured against, the insured would not have a sufficient interest to support an insurance contract. 

Insurable interest is discussed later on. 

3. The insurance contract must be specific as to the parties, terms, rates, amount, the property or person insured, and the risk insured against.

4. All clauses affecting the insurance contract which are agreed upon by the parties thereto must be fully stated in the contract itself. 

Who are the parties to an insurance contract?

The parties to an insurance contract are (a) the insurer, the one who assumes the risk, and (b) the insured, the one for whom the risk is assumed.

The insurer. There are two kinds of insurance companies-stock and mutual.

A stock insurance company is a private corporation organized and managed the same as any corporation. It assumes certain risks for its policyholders for which it charges a fixed premium. 

The fund accumulated in this way together with interest earned on accumulated surpluses and capital loaned or invested is used to pay fixed charges to operating costs, dividends, and policy losses. 

A mutual insurance company has no capital stock and no stockholders. Each policyholder becomes a member shareholder in the company for the amount of his policy. The policyholders assume to manage the business through officers whom they elect. The management of mutual companies does not differ much from that of stock companies. Their rates are the same, and they accumulate a reserve on an actuarial basis to meet losses. A mutual company divides its profits among its policyholders on a prorata basis, and these same policyholders are subject to an assessment for which they are liable should the company suffer losses it cannot meet or fail in business. In some states, mutual companies which meet certain requirements as to reserves and surpluses may issue nonassessable policies.

Co-operative insurance is a form of mutual insurance, usually operated among small groups in a neighborhood. 

Example 2. Two hundred farmers in a certain community organized an insurance association and agreed among themselves that each member of the association would pay an assessment each time a member's property covered by the association's policy is damaged or destroyed by fire. Each assessment is to be apportioned among the members according to the amount of insurance each one carries on his property. This is an example of co-operative association insurance. The officers of such an association

INSURANCE 

443 usually serve without pay except the one or two who collect the assessments and keep the records. Such an association is not, as a rule, subject to the laws governing insurance companies, but its members are bound in a contract which is enforceable.

There is in each state a department or bureau of insurance in charge of a commissioner or a superintendent, whose duty it is to see that the insurance companies comply with the laws of the particular state. 

What is an insurance policy?

An insurance policy is the contract of insurance. It is a written document containing the terms, description of the risk covered, the amount of insurance, which is the maximum for which the insurer may be liable, but is not necessarily the amount recoverable unless it is a "valued policy," and a number of provisions and restrictive clauses that relate to risk covered and to the rights and obligations of the parties to the contract. Insurance contracts are written, but an oral contract of insurance would be enforceable. 

What are the kinds of insurance policies? 

1. A valued policy is one by which a definite value of the subject matter insured is agreed upon by both parties at the time the policy is issued, rather than leaving it to be determined should a loss occur. In other words, the amount to be paid in case of a loss is determined by the contract itself. 

Example 3. Mrs. Bates insured a necklace for $1,500 against theft. The necklace was stolen and the insurance company paid the $1,500. The amount to be paid in this case was definitely agreed upon, after the necklace was appraised by the insurer; therefore, the policy was a valued policy. 

2. An open policy or nonvalued policy is one in which the value of the subject insured is not fixed or agreed in the policy, but is left to be determined in case of loss; and though a certain sum is written in the face of the policy, this is not the sum agreed on as the value of the policy, but as the maximum sum recoverable in case of destruction by the peril insured against. Therefore, as the policy contains no statement that the property is valued at or worth the sum insured, it will be regarded as an open, and not a valued policy.

Example 4. Jacobs insured his store building with the National Fire 

Insurance Company for $6,000. A fire damaged the building, and the 

Company sent out adjusters who appraised the loss at $1,500, the amount finally paid to Jacobs.

This was an open policy, as are most fire-insurance policies. Only a total loss would entitle Jacobs to collect the whole $6,000, and even then he could not collect $6,000 unless he could show that the amount of his actual loss was at least $6,000. 

3. A floating or floater policy is one which covers movable property or property changed from one location to another at times without mentioning any particular location. It is covered by the policy at the scene of the loss regardless of where it is located or whether or not it is in transit except while it is in the permanent residence of the insured, while in storage, or while in any public or private garage used by the insured. See inland marine and transportation insurance, page 458. 

4. A blanket policy (blanket form of policy) is used to cover risks that fluctuate or vary. It applies to a class of property rather than to any one thing, and the property may be in one or more stated locations. The policy names one amount on the whole risk regardless of the number of objects, classes or divisions of property insured. It is an open policy in that the amount of loss up to a certain maximum named in the policy must be determined after the event insured against has caused damage. 

Example 5. Dorsey insured his factory, the fixtures, and the machines therein for $45,000 with the Union Fire Insurance Co. They issued a blanket policy to cover this risk. Should a fire damage this property as insured, the amount of damage to all would have to be determined by appraisal, and the amount allowed would be named in one sum. 

5. The most common policies in life insurance are (a) ordinary or straight-life policies; (b) endowment policies; (c) limited-payment life (ten-, fifteen-, or twenty-payment policies); and (d) annuity policies and term policies, which are explained later under "Life Insurance." 

What is the premium?

The premium is the charge the insurance company makes for assuming the risk covered by the policy. It is paid by the insured

INSURANCE 

445 and may be paid for different periods of time either in advance or in installments depending upon the terms of the contract. 

The premium charged is fixed by the insurance company or underwriter and must conform to statutory regulations; it is determined by the nature of the risk. The risk is the contingency insured against. The greater the risk, the higher will be the rate of premium. 

The cost of insuring a fireproof building against damage from fire would be much less than the cost of insuring a wooden building. 

The premium rates for fire insurance are lower in places affording adequate protection against fires than are the rates in places affording poor protection.

The rates of premium that insurance companies charge are arrived at through actuarial statistics and calculations based on experience over long periods of time. They may be changed at any time, except that if they are regulated by law, the proper authority must authorize the change. 

Changes in rates are not retroactive, unless by agreement with the insured; therefore, new rates apply to new contracts and not to contracts already in force. The insured may cancel his policy at the old rate, on the short-term rate basis, and take out a new policy at the new rate, if it would pay him to do this.

When does an insurance policy become in force? 

An insurance policy like all contracts becomes effective when the offer by one party to the contract is accepted by the other party. 

The risk may be offered by the one who desires insurance, or the insurance may be offered to cover a certain risk by the agent for an insurance company, and when either offer is accepted by the other party an insurance contract becomes in force. 

Insurance companies conduct all their business through agents; therefore the party to be insured is either solicited by an agent or makes application through him for insurance to cover a certain risk. In all kinds of insurance except health insurance and life insurance, the agent usually has authority to accept the risk and close the contract according to the method employed by his company for handling its contracts. The agent usually has authority to put a binder on the risk which will protect the owner or insurer and bind his company in a contract to assume the risk pending the issuance of the policy. Some insurance contracts, particularly

those for health insurance and life insurance, do not bind the insurance company until its policy is actually issued and the first premium is paid.

An insurance underwriter is one who signs his name to a policy of insurance, thereby becoming liable as an insurer to reimburse the insured in case the contingency insured against should cause him loss or damage. 

An underwriter association is a group of insurers organized as an association for mutual benefit. 

What is an insurable interest?

An insured person's insurable interest is an interest of such a nature in the subject matter of the insurance contract that the occurrence of the contingency insured against would cause such an insured person financial loss or liability. If it were not provided that the person insured have an insurable interest in the subject insured, the object in taking out insurance might be a mere wager which would be unenforceable as against public policy. 

An insurable interest in insured property. 

A legal right or interest in the property is a sufficient insurable interest. Two or more parties may have an insurable interest in the same property.

Example 6. If a building is subject to a mortgage, two persons, the owner and the mortgagee, have an insurable interest in this building, for the reason that each would suffer some loss if the building were damaged or destroyed. A purchaser under contract to buy a building, a builder who is unpaid for material used in constructing a building, or a person who has a lien on a building, all have insurable interests in property. A stockholder has an insurable interest in the property of the corporation in which he owns stock.

The interest that the insured has in the property insured must continue to exist or be present at the time of the loss, but it does not have to be equal in value to the amount of the insurance. 

The amount of the loss is the most that will be paid. 

Example 7. Erhard insured his house against fire, and paid the premium for three years in advance. Six months later he sold the house to 

Warner for cash. Erhard no longer has an interest in this house, and should it be destroyed by fire, he could collect nothing. The policy should have been transferred to Warner at the time of the sale. As soon as

INSURANCE 

447 Warner contracted to buy this house he could have it fully insured to protect his interest in it, for the reason that after signing the contract he would have to pay the full contract price even if the house did burn down before the sale was completed. Warner could insure for a short period pending the completion of the sale and the transfer to him of the policy 

Erhard has on the house. 

An insurable interest in life insurance.

A person has an insurable interest in his own life and in the life of any other person whose death would cause him financial loss or a disadvantage. Close relationship by blood or affinity will generally create an insurable interest, particularly when there is involved the possibility of financial benefit, as of husband and wife, parent and child, sister and brother. More remote relationships as uncle and nephew, or cousins, do not alone create insurable interest. A partner has an insurable interest in the life of his copartner, and a creditor has an insurable interest in the life of his debtor.

If there was an insurable interest at the time the insurance was taken out, this interest may cease at any time without affecting the policy.

Example 8. Green took out insurance on the life of Wise, who owed him $1,000. Within three years, thereafter, Wise paid the debt. Green, who is named as a beneficiary in the policy, may continue to pay the premiums, and he is entitled to recover on the policy when it matures, or when Wise dies.

It is expected and in some states it is required by statute that the person who takes out insurance on the life of another shall get the consent of the one insured. The exceptions to this rule are mentioned under "Life Insurance," page 465. 

Are insurance policies assignable?

Life-insurance policies generally contain a specific provision that they are not assignable without the consent of the insurer (the insurance company). Fire-insurance policies are not generally assignable without the consent of the insurer. 

What are the rights of beneficiaries?

When a person is named as beneficiary in a policy on the life of another person, the interest of the beneficiary is considered to

be vested and irrevocable. Neither the insured nor anyone else, such as the insured's creditors, can defeat the rights of the beneficiary without his consent. The insured himself cannot surrender the policy and take its cash surrender value, nor cancel it and take a new policy naming another beneficiary, nor borrow on the policy, unless the beneficiary consents. Policies usually reserve to the insured the right to change the beneficiary without his consent. If the insured becomes bankrupt, his creditors can reach only the insured's interest in the policy, any cash surrender value payable to him. By statute in most states insurance policies, particularly those payable to the wife or children of the insured, are wholly or partially exempt from the claims of creditors. 

How is an insurance contract terminated?

A property insurance contract may be terminated, any time before a loss occurs, by either party giving notice in accordance with provisions in the policy. A life-insurance policy may be terminated by the insurer when the right to do so is reserved in the policy or is given by law. The insured may terminate a life policy at any time according to provisions in the policy, unless there is a named beneficiary with vested interests that must be respected. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Insurance is an indemnity contract whereby the insurer protects the insured against financial loss resulting from some peril or event. 

2. Insurance contracts relate to property or to persons. 

3. No one has a right to be the insured party to an insurance contract who does not contemplate a loss and have an insurable interest in the property insured or in the person on whose life he secures a policy. 

4. The insurance agent usually has authority to bind his company in a fire-insurance contract, but a life-insurance contract does not become effective until accepted by the company and the first premium is paid. 

5. The parties to an insurance contract are the insurer and the insured, and the contract is called an insurance policy.

INSURANCE 

449 6. In an open policy, the amount to be paid in case of a total or partial loss is not definitely fixed but must be determined after the loss has occurred. In a valued policy, the amount to be paid in case of a total loss is definitely fixed. 

7. An insurance company that authorizes its agents to issue binders is held in a contract as soon as a binder is issued or agreed to. 

Binders are not issued in life insurance. 

8. An insurable interest in property must be or continue to be present at the time of loss. There must be an insurable interest in a life at the time the insurance is taken out, and it may cease to exist thereafter without affecting the contract. 

9. Property insurance contracts are not assignable without the consent of the insurer. The insured may assign a life-insurance contract at will, unless the named beneficiary has a vested interest in the policy. The policy usually requires the consent of the insurer to an assignment. 

10. In property insurance either party may terminate the contract by giving notice. In life insurance, the insurer may terminate the contract if the right to do so is granted in the policy or by law. The insured may terminate the contract according to the terms in the policy unless a beneficiary has a vested interest.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Adjuster. One who examines the property insured after a loss to determine the amount to be paid under the policy. 

Appraised Value. Value placed on the damaged or lost property by the appraisers.

Arson. The malicious burning of property. 

Coinsurance Clause. A clause in an insurance policy which provides that the insured must keep his property insured up to a certain percentage of its value, usually 80%, and in case of his failure to do so he cannot collect the full amount of the loss. Full-Cover Risk. Insurance on the property equal to a certain percentage of its value according to the terms of the policy (usually 80%). 

Material Fact. Any fact which materially affects the risk assumed by the insurer.

Standard Policy. A uniform policy adopted in certain states for the use of all insurance companies operating in those states. 

Trust Deed. An instrument used to convey the property of the debtor to a third person called a trustee, who holds the property until the debt is paid. 

What is fire insurance?

Fire insurance may be defined as a contract whereby one party, the insurer, for a consideration, the premium, agrees to indemnify another party, the insured, for loss or damage to property caused by fire. 

What are the principal requisites of the fire-insurance contract? 

1. The contract must contain the names of the insurer and the insured and the other necessary requisites of a contract in general. 

The final contract is a fire-insurance policy. 452

2. The title or interest of the insured in the property must be clearly described. This interest must be an existing interest or lien, interest of lessee or a person who is under contract to purchase. 

Any person who would suffer a loss by reason of the property being damaged has an insurable interest, and this interest must exist at the time loss occurs; otherwise the insured could not claim the insurance. There may be a divided interest in the property; that is, two or more parties may have an insurable interest in the same property. 

3. The rate of premium and the amount to be paid must be stated. The premium is usually paid in advance in one sum or in installments for the term of the policy. 

4. The contract must contain the risk insured against. In fire insurance the risk includes fire and anything that causes damage in putting out the fire such as chemicals or water, or destruction of the building to prevent the spread of the fire, also loss due to removing the goods from the burning building to a place of safety. 

5. The contract must contain the term of duration of the insurance. Fire-insurance policies are usually issued for one year or for three years.

A property insurance policy is dated to run from 12 o'clock noon (standard time) on a certain date, until 12 o'clock noon on the date it expires. A renewal receipt in which the property insured is fully described serves to renew a fire-insurance policy; or a new policy may be issued. 

An oral contract of fire insurance is enforceable, but they are not used, so it is unnecessary to discuss them. The insurance contract, which is the policy, is always written. The standard form of policy is in general use.

Many states have passed statutes adopting a standard form of fire-insurance policy. These statutes provide for the use of a uniform contract and thus avoid possible conflict between different companies insuring the same property. Either the valued policy or the open policy may be used. 

In an open fire-insurance policy, which is the one generally used, the company pays the actual loss up to the amount named in the policy in a "fullcover" risk. 

When is a risk "full cover"?

Standard form policies and fire-insurance policies generally provide that the insured shall carry insurance on his property equal

to a certain per cent of its value, usually 80%. Therefore, a building valued at $10,000 should be insured for $8,000 ($10,000 x .80 = $8,000).

Example 1. If the building is insured for less than $8,000, and is damaged by fire, the insured can collect from the insurance company only that portion of the loss that the amount of the policy bears to the $8,000. 

That is, if a building worth $10,000 is insured for $6,000 instead of $8,000, and is damaged to the extent of $4,000, the company will have to pay only $3,000 ($6,000/$8,000 x $4,000). 

Example 2. If the building is insured for $8,000 (80% of its value), which is full cover, the company will have to pay the full adjusted loss up to the amount of the policy. This clause in a policy is called the coinsurance clause. In the New York standard policy it is the "average clause." 

The New York standard "average clause" provides that the insurance company shall not be liable for a greater portion of any loss or damage to the property insured than the sum for which it is insured bears to eighty per cent (80%) of the actual cash value of said property at the time such loss shall happen. The coinsurance clause is waived in the case of household furniture where the items insured do not exceed $2,500 in value. 

Example 3. Bliss insured a factory building valued at $150,000 for $100,000. The policy contained the 80% coinsurance clause which provided that the building should be insured for 80% of its value ($120,000). 

This building was damaged by fire to the extent of $60,000. According to the terms of the policy, Bliss can collect only $50,000 from the insurer ($100,000/$120,000 x $60,000). Had Bliss insured this building for $120,000, he could collect the full amount of loss from fire, up to the amount for which the policy was written. 

What is a representation in an insurance contract?

A representation is a statement of fact made by the insured regarding the property either at the time or before the contract of insurance is entered into. In most insurance transactions the insured is called upon to answer certain questions regarding the property. The insured should be careful to answer questions correctly for the reason that an incorrect answer might amount to a misrepresentation that would make it possible for the insurance company to avoid their contract, to the same extent as in life insurance. 

Example 4. Lynn, who insured a frame building with the Continental

Fire Insurance Company, was asked if it was near a railroad. He

answered: "It is not nearer than 700 feet." The building caught fire from a passing locomotive and was destroyed. The adjusters for the insurer found that the building was less than 200 feet from the railroad, and the company was not liable because of the misrepresentation by the insured. 

What is a warranty in an insurance contract?

A warranty is a statement of fact relating to the subject of insurance, a person, and certain property, made as a part of the insurance contract. The warranty is contained in the policy while the representation is not. In fire-insurance contracts, warranties relate to the use made of the property, to the keeping of explosives in or about the building, to the heating and lighting equipment, and to such other factors as might in some way increase the hazard insured against.

Example 5. A house heated by an oil-burning furnace was insured and a clause in the policy stated that the oil for fuel shall be stored in a metal tank of not over 275 gallons' capacity, unless located outside of the building. The 275-gallon tank was in the cellar and in addition to this, the owner of the house kept 50 gallons of oil in another tank in the cellar for emergency. Keeping this extra tank of oil in the cellar is in direct violation of a policy warranty. Should the house burn, regardless of how it got on fire, the facts in this case would make it possible for the insurer to avoid the contract. 

How does concealment affect an insurance contract?

Concealment, by the insured, of a fact which is material to the risk insured against may give the insurer a right to avoid the contract.

Example 6. Blynn owned a building which was rented to a clothing merchant. He insured this building, but failed to mention that the merchant operated a cleaning and pressing establishment in the rear of his store, and that his pressing machines were heated by gas and also that quantities of cleaning fluid were stored on the insured premises. The cleaning fluid ignited and fire damaged the building. The insurance company refused to pay the loss. In order to avoid their contract they would have to prove that Blynn was guilty of using bad faith in securing the insurance.

It is an accepted principle in insurance that even though the concealment or misrepresentation of a material fact may not cause the loss, the policy may, nevertheless, be avoided if the risk is different from that which the insurer accepted.

Example 7. A factory building was insured by the owner, who stated at the time he secured the policy that he operated a factory in the building on his own account. The facts were, that the building was leased to another, and the owner received a portion of the profits as rent. Such a misrepresentation, whether material to the loss or not, would give the insurer a right to avoid the contract. 

What does loss by fire include?

Loss by fire includes all loss resulting directly or indirectly from the fire. This includes loss or damage from water used in putting out the fire, and from exposure or theft. Fire caused by lightning is covered by the policy, but other damage resulting from lightning is not covered unless the policy contains a lightning clause. 

The insurance company is not liable on its contract if the insured has committed arson, but it is liable if fire is caused by an incendiary, by an act of the insured while insane, or by the carelessness of a third person. 

Changing location of insured property. 

A statement of the location of the property at the time it was insured is contained in the standard policy. If the insured property is removed to any other location without the consent of the insurer, the policy is no longer in effect. The reason for this rule is that the hazard is likely to vary in different locations, and the insurer has a right to know what risk he is assuming.

Example 8. Bliss insured his furniture while he was living in a singlefamily dwelling. Later he moved into an apartment in another locality without notifying the insurance company. Shortly after moving, his apartment caught fire and his furniture was badly damaged. The insurance company is not liable for the loss as the policy is no longer in effect. 

Can insurance be procured in more than one company?

A person who acts in good faith may insure his property in as many companies as he chooses; but in case of a loss, each company can be required to pay only its proportionate share of the total loss regardless of the amount of insurance on the property. There is nothing to gain, therefore, by insuring property for more than its true value. Most policies contain a clause prohibiting other insurance without consent.

Example 9. Brice insured his house valued at $10,000 in four different companies for $5,000 each. The house was destroyed by fire and the adjusters agreed that the loss was $10,000. Therefore, each company would have to pay only its proportion or $2,500, regardless of the amount of insurance on the house. 

May one company reinsure with other companies? 

When an insurance company finds that it is carrying a large amount of insurance on a single building, or in a particular neighborhood, so that a fire may cause a heavy loss, the company probably will reinsure all or part of its liabilities. That is, the company will contract with one or more other companies to assume part of the liability of the issuing company. In case of loss, the insured will collect on the policy, and the insuring company will call upon its reinsurers for their share of the loss. Some companies contract for automatic reinsurance of a specified percentage of every liability they assume.

The standard policy contains a number of clauses which the insured should study carefully before signing the contract. 

How is the amount of loss determined?

As soon as convenient after receiving notice of the loss, the company's adjusters examine the ruins and appraise the damage. The insured presents his claim and the company then offers a certain amount in settlement. If the offer is accepted by the insured, the account is closed. The standard policy provides that in case insured and the company fail to agree as to the amount of loss or damage, each party, on the written demand of either, selects an appraiser. The appraiser thus selected names an umpire. The appraisers then appraise the loss. If they fail to agree, they submit their differences only, to the umpire. An award, itemized in writing, of any two appraisers, when filed with the insurance company, shall determine the amount of loss or damage. The amount of loss agreed upon is payable within sixty days after proof of loss. 

What happens to the policy in case of a partial loss?

In case of a small loss paid by the company, the premium is adjusted at the time of paying the loss, and the original policy is thereby kept in force. If the loss is large or for more than one half

of the amount of the insurance, the old policy is canceled and the premium adjusted. A new policy is issued to cover the new risk when ready to be insured, while it is in the course of being repaired or when repaired. 

How is the mortgagee protected by insurance?

When mortgaged property is insured, it is the practice to attach a clause to the policy which provides that the insurance shall be paid to the mortgagee named to the extent of his interest, and the balance, if any, to the insured. In such cases the original policy is deposited with and held by the mortgagee as further security for his interest, and a certificate of the insurance is issued to the insured who has an equity interest in the property. 

What are the principal features of marine insurance?

A marine insurance contract provides that the insurer will indemnify the insured for losses which may result from certain perils or risks to which his ships, cargo, and profits are exposed during a certain trip or during a certain time. The regulations with regard to insurable interest, fraud, misrepresentation, and warranty that apply to fire insurance in general likewise apply to marine insurance. In addition to this there are certain other features peculiar to the marine policy, for instance, the general average clause. 

The general average clause, which has been featured in marine policies from very early times, provides that, where a portion of the cargo is thrown overboard to save the vessel from sinking, the owners of the goods allowed to remain on board and the owners of the vessel share proportionately the loss suffered by the owners whose goods were thrown overboard. 

What is inland marine or transportation insurance?

Inland marine or transportation insurance is a comparatively recent development in the field of insurance. Underwriters in this special field furnish coverage for the many risks to which property being handled, moved about, or transported in any way is exposed. 

Marine insurance contracts are more flexible and more easily adapted to these new requirements. This is the principal reason why risks that have nothing to do with water are insured under a marine policy.

The policies issued in inland marine or transportation insurance may cover, under certain specific conditions, the following: 

1. Imports on consignment may be covered wherever the property may be and without restriction as to time, provided the coverage of the issuing companies includes hazards of transportation. This also applies to shipments on consignment. These consignment risk policies are subject to many special provisions contained therein. 

2. Exports may be covered wherever the property may be without restrictions as to time, provided the coverage of the issuing companies includes hazards of transportation. 

3. Domestic shipments on consignment, provided the coverage of the issuing companies includes hazards of transportation, and also domestic shipments not on consignment, under the same provisions subject to the various stipulations in the policy regarding the time, purpose, and places not outside of the United States. 

4. Personal property floater risks cover individuals against loss from damage to personal effects while being moved, but exclude hazards while in a permanent residence of the insured. 

Example 10. King, who was giving exhibitions and sales demonstrations in the larger cities in a particular state, moved his exhibit from place to place by means of a truck owned and operated by his company. The company took out a "floater" policy for $2,500 to cover the exhibit and the truck against all hazards to which it may be exposed in transit or otherwise during the six months following, the period for these demonstrations. This is an example of inland marine and transportation coverage. 

What is public liability insurance?

Public liability insurance is protection against financial loss, furnished by insurance companies, to property owners, contractors, merchants, and others who are so situated that they may be held liable for damages for personal injuries to other people. 

Some workman about the place may fall and break an arm; a merchant may leave a trap door open causing someone to fall; or someone may fall on a slippery porch. Cases of this kind may result in an action against the property owner, or the one who contributed to the injury, for damages. 

How may a public liability insurance policy be terminated? 

1. By expiration of the time for which the policy was issued. 

2. By cancellation. Either party may cancel the policy according to the terms therein.

Example 11. Automobile public liability policies are usually written for the maximum amount for which the insured will be liable ($5,000— $10,000; $10,000-$20,000; $20,000-$40,000; etc.), which means that in case one person is injured or killed, the insurer is not liable for more than $5,000, $10,000, or $20,000, as the case may be, but if two or more persons are injured or killed in a single accident, the insurer's liability is limited to $10,000, $20,000, or $40,000. The policy continues in force for its full amount for the full time regardless of the number of casualties settled for or the amount paid by the insurer. Example 12. A $5,000-$10,000 policy may cost the insurer $40,000 if there are four or more accidents in which two or more persons were injured or killed during the time the policy is in force. However, the person with such a record for accidents would have trouble getting insurance, and it is probable that the company, after settling a large loss, would cancel the policy.

If the damage awarded is more than the insurance, judgment may be secured against the insured for the amount in excess of what the insurer pays. These rules in general apply to all liability insurance. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The insured is bound by all the provisions and clauses contained in his policy. 

2. A material misrepresentation may give the insurer a right to avoid the contract. 

3. A breach of a warranty contained in the policy gives the insurer a right to avoid the contract. 

4. Concealment of a material fact regarding the hazard to which the property is exposed gives the insurer a right to avoid the contract. 

5. Fire insurance covers loss or damage by fire and loss or damage incident to putting out the fire or removing the property from premises endangered by fire. 6. The insured has no right to increase the hazard or change the location of the insured property, without the consent in writing of the insurer. 

7. Property may be insured in one or more companies, and companies may reinsure in other companies. 

8. In fire insurance the insurable interest must exist at the time the loss occurs to give the insured a right to collect. 

9. Fire-insurance contracts are not assignable. The insurer may transfer the policy on application from the insured.

10. A fire-insurance contract may be terminated by expiration or cancellation. 

11. The regulations that apply to fire-insurance contracts likewise apply to marine insurance. 

12. A violation of any of the implied warranties in a marine insurance policy makes the contract voidable.

1. A building valued at $20,000 was insured for $12,000. The policy contained the standard form 80% average clause. The building was damaged by fire to the extent of $4,000. How much can the insurance company be required to pay? 

2. A gas-burning water heater exploded in the cellar of a house insured against fire. No fire ensued but the damage amounted to $200. The policy contained the usual "explosion clause." Is the insurance company liable? Explain. 3. A building contractor insured against loss by fire the building he was constructing. (a) Under what conditions would he have this right? (b) If the building burns down while his policy is still in force but after he has been paid in full for all claims against the building, could he collect the insurance? 

4. Edwards contracted to buy a house and lot for $4,000. He paid $500 at the time of signing the contract, which provided that the transfer of the title should take place on the 15th of the following month. He insured the house at once for $3,200 or 80% of the value of the house. Before the transfer of title took place, the house was destroyed by fire. (a) How much do you think Edwards could collect from the insurer? (b) On what do you base your opinion? 

5. Wilbur owned a store building valued at $50,000. He insured this building for $30,000 in each of two different companies. The building was totally destroyed by fire. How much insurance can Wilbur collect, if the policy contained the 80% coinsurance clause? 

6. King sold his house which was insured for $5,000, and the policy had two years to run. King filled out and signed the assignment form on the back of the policy and passed it to the purchaser, who put it in a safe place. 

Within a year, the house burned. (a) Is the insurer in this policy liable for the loss? (b) Explain. 7. Egan, who was heavily indebted, insured his house for its full value. 

He was not asked about his debts when he applied for the insurance and gave no information about them. Shortly thereafter the house was set on fire and totally destroyed. How can the company defeat Egan's claim for the insurance? 

8. A customer in a store caught her foot on a torn carpet on the stairs, fell, and sustained serious injury. (a) Is the owner of the store likely to be

held liable, if this customer takes action to recover damages? (b) What kind of insurance would protect the owner of the store against loss? (c) If the merchant carried insurance, could he be held liable in any way?

LIFE INSURANCE TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Annuity. A series of payments to be made periodically, either annually or at shorter intervals. 

Cash Surrender Value. The amount of cash the insurance company will pay the insured who surrenders his policy to them for any reason. 

Extended Insurance. Insurance extended to run a certain length of time in lieu of the cash settlement; sometimes called "automatic term insurance.'

Incontestable Policy. A policy which cannot be contested for any reason by the insurer after it has been in force a certain length of time. 

Loan Value. The amount the insurance company will loan on the policy issued by them when offered by the insured as security for the loan. 

Paid-up Insurance. The amount of insurance fully paid for by the insured; the amount for which the insurer is liable. 

Photostatic Copy. An exact copy of the questions and answers in the insured's application for insurance, reproduced by a device for making photographic copies. 

What is life insurance?

Life insurance is a contract whereby one party, usually an insurance company, for a consideration called the premium, agrees to pay the person whose life is insured a certain sum of money according to the terms in the contract, if he is living; or, when he dies, the company agrees to pay the amount of the policy to his estate unless some person is named therein to whom the insurance is to be paid. Insurance may be paid in one sum or as an annuity at fixed intervals over a period of time. 

Example 1. Hecker applied to the National Life Insurance Company, who issued an ordinary life policy to him in which his wife was named as beneficiary. Hecker agreed to pay the premiums on this policy at stated 464

LIFE INSURANCE 

465 intervals during his life, and upon his death the company will pay his widow the amount of the policy. This is a common form of life-insurance contract. 

Who has an insurable interest in a life?

Any person has an insurable interest in his own life, and any person who has a right to expect financial benefit from the continued life of another has an insurable interest in that life. See page 447. As a rule, and according to law in some states, one person is not permitted to insure the life of another unless he has the consent of the person insured. The exceptions to this rule are: (a) the wife, (b) the parent of a child under age, or a person who is liable for the support of a child, (c) and employers to insure employees collectively against accidents, sickness, or death. The insurable interest may cease to exist any time after the insurance on the life of another is taken out without affecting the policy. 

What are the principal kinds of life-insurance policies? 

1. The ordinary or straight life policy which provides for the payment of the premium quarterly, semiannually, or annually during the life of the insured and for the payment of the amount of the policy at the time of the death of the insured to his estate or to the beneficiary named in the policy. 

2. The limited payment policy provides for the payment of premiums during a term of years, usually ten, fifteen, twenty, twenty-five, or thirty years, and at the expiration of this time the policy is said to be "paid up." The insured, if he is living, may then elect to accept the cash surrender value of the policy or allow it to accumulate during his life to become payable at his death, at which time it will be paid to his estate or to the named beneficiary. 

Should the insured die before the insurance is fully paid up, the amount of the policy becomes payable at once to his estate or to the named beneficiary. This form of policy is attractive for the reason that it can be paid for during the time when the insured is most able to earn. 

3. The endowment policy provides for the payment of the premium in advance at regular intervals for a definite period of time,

usually ten, fifteen, twenty, or twenty-five years, and at the expiration of this time, for the payment of a certain definite sum named in the policy plus any dividends credited thereto to the insured, or he may elect to let the policy stand to be paid with accumulated earnings in full at his death. Should the insured die before completing the premium payments, the amount of the policy becomes fully payable at once to his estate or to the named beneficiary. This form of insurance serves as an investment and also as financial protection against the risk of premature death. 

4. An annuity policy provides for the payment of a certain sum of money by the insured to the insurance company at fixed intervals for a definite term of years, and that when the insured has reached a certain age, usually sixty or sixty-five years, the insurance company will pay him a fixed income monthly for the remainder of his life. This policy usually provides also that, in case the insured dies at any time, the face value of the policy shall be payable at once to the estate of the insured or to the named beneficiary. Such a policy is really an investment and sometimes it is bought with a single payment and the annuity payments begin at once. 

5. A term policy is taken for a fixed amount to cover a fixed term in days, months, or years. The maximum term is usually three or five years, at the end of which time the policy automatically expires without any return other than the protection it afforded while in force. But the term policy usually provides that it may be converted into any other form of policy written by the particular company at any time before it expires. This is a valuable privilege because rates are based on age of insured. The purpose of such a policy is to give maximum protection at a minimum cost. 

For the protection given, the premium rates in the term policy are much lower than in any of the other policies mentioned. 

Example 2. Faber, who was about to engage in a business venture, took out $10,000 insurance on his life for five years. He secured a term policy with the privilege of converting it into another kind of policy any time within the five years. A term policy may be made to protect the insured's creditors or dependents from financial loss, should the insured die during the time it is in force.

LIFE INSURANCE 

467 

How is life insurance secured?

Any person who desires insurance on his life must sign an application for the amount of insurance desired. The application form, which is usually filled out by the agent for the company, contains a number of questions to be answered by the applicant regarding his occupation, ancestors, health, and age. The answers given to these questions are written into the application and they amount to warranties. An applicant should answer all questions correctly and if he does not know the correct answers, he should say so. The answers to the questions may be attached to the policy as a part thereof. In addition to this, the applicant will be required to pass a physical examination given by a doctor employed by the insurance company before he will be accepted for insurance. 

How do misrepresentations and warranties affect life-insurance contracts?

Example 3. Ward, in his application for life insurance, stated as the answer to the question: "What is your occupation?" "I am a bank clerk."

The facts were that he was a brakeman employed on the railroad. This is a clear breach of a warranty which would give the insurance company a right to avoid the policy.

The answers given by the applicant to the questions in the application become a part of the policy, being attached to the policy by photostatic copy or otherwise, and amount to warranties. A breach of any warranty by the insured gives the insurance company a right to avoid the policy.

Example 4. Roe, in his application for insurance, stated his occupation as "sign painter," which was true. When asked by the insurance agent about his work, he represented that he painted small signs indoors. In fact, he was employed in dangerous work outdoors. This misrepresentation would justify the company in canceling the policy. 

The insurance company may avoid a policy on the life of a person who secured it by concealing a fact material to the risk. 

Example 5. An applicant for life insurance concealed the fact that he was going from Boston to Panama, where he would be employed indefinitely. The insurance company restricts its risks to residence within the 

United States and Canada. This act on the part of the insured released the insurance company from their contract unless they assented to his

change of location or accepted the premium payments knowing the facts. 

Some policies place no restrictions on travel or places of residence. 

Representation refers to matters not included in the application. 

They are not warranties and are not often questioned, but a misrepresentation of a material fact is ground for avoidance of a policy by the insurance company.

However, answering a question to the best of one's ability in good faith, even if information is not given, is not concealment. 

Example 6. An applicant for life insurance answered, "I do not know," to the question: "Did either of your parents die of tuberculosis?" Answering this question in this way or leaving it unanswered does not amount to a concealment, if the applicant has shown good faith. 

What are the rights of beneficiaries?

A person who insures his own life may name anyone whom he chooses as beneficiary, and he may reserve the right to change the one so named at will. If this right is not reserved in the policy, as it usually is, the beneficiary has a vested right of which he cannot be deprived without his consent. 

Any unchangeable beneficiary has a vested interest in the policy. The beneficiary who has a vested interest not subject to change by the insured, if he survives the insured, may collect the insurance unless the suicide clause is violated. Should the beneficiary die first, the insurance is payable to his estate as soon as the insured dies unless the policy contains a condition that the beneficiary shall survive the insured, which is a common condition. The beneficiary may claim the insurance to the exclusion of creditors of the insured, except where statutes limit this right so as to prevent creditors being defrauded. 

Proceeds of insurance policies are not subject to tax, except that their exemptions from estate taxes are limited in amount. 

May a person insure his life in two or more companies? 

A person may insure his life in any number of companies and for as much as he is willing and financially able to carry. Policies of $50,000 and $100,000 are not uncommon and a few wealthy men are known to carry insurance of a million dollars or more. In this respect life insurance differs from fire insurance, in which only the actual loss is recoverable regardless of the number of policies or the amount of insurance on the property.

LIFE INSURANCE 

469 

Is the insurer liable if the insured commits suicide?

If there is no clause in the policy stating that the insurance company will not be liable if the insured commits suicide, it must pay the amount of the insurance to the named beneficiary. But if the insured named himself as beneficiary and commits suicide, the insurer is not liable on the policy.

The law generally provides that the policy shall be incontestable after it has been in force a certain length of time, usually one or two years (two years in New York) unless the premiums are unpaid. This being the law, the policy contains a clause to the effect that the insurance company will not be liable if the insured commits suicide within two years. After the two years' period the insurance company is liable regardless of the cause of the death, unless by law it is relieved from liability, as is the case in some states if the insured is executed for a crime or is killed while committing a crime or resisting arrest. 

How may a life-insurance contract be terminated? 

1. Life-insurance contracts may be terminated by performance; that is, the insured has paid up all the premiums for the full time and elects to accept the cash surrender value of the policy. As soon as the policy is surrendered by the insured, and the company settles with him, the insurance is no longer in force. 

2. The policy may be terminated by the insurer if the insured defaults in the payment of the premiums. The insured is then entitled to the cash surrender value of the policy or to elect to accept paid-up insurance for a definite period of time according to the terms in the policy. If there is a beneficiary who has a prior right, the insured cannot cancel the policy without his consent. He may, however, refuse to pay the premium, and this gives the insurance company a right to cancel the policy subject to the paid-up insurance clause. When the insured dies, the beneficiary can collect the amount due on the policy if it can be found and surrendered to the company. 

3. Should the insured die while the policy is in force, it becomes payable immediately to his estate or to the beneficiary named in the policy, and as soon as the settlement is made, the policy is canceled. Before paying the insurance the company will require proof of the death of the insured. A copy of the burial permit issued by the proper authority to the undertaker and a statement from the attending physician, and from the undertaker, properly executed and witnessed will be accepted as proof of death. 

Insurance companies generally have printed forms for the doctor and undertaker to fill in and execute as a means of furnishing proof of the death of the insured.

What other purposes may life insurance be made to serve?

Most life-insurance policies specify a cash surrender and loan value after the policy has been in force for a certain length of time, usually two years and each year thereafter. This gives the insured the privilege of borrowing from the insurance company at a specified rate of interest the loan value of the policy or any amount less by depositing his policy with the company as security for the loan and executing the regular loan agreement. 

What is accident insurance?

Example 7. A mechanic working on an automobile accidentally cut his hand and blood poisoning caused his death. The mechanic had an accident policy, and it was held that the insurance company was liable as the death of the insured was the result of an accident. 

Accident insurance is a branch of life insurance whereby a person is insured against death or injury caused by accident. This form of insurance usually provides for the payment of a certain amount in case of accidental death, an amount weekly for either permanent or total disability caused by an accident, and a definite sum for injury resulting in loss of one or both hands, feet, or eyes. 

How do fire-insurance contracts compare with life-insurance contracts? 

1. Fire-insurance risks may be accepted by the insurer or by the agent who is authorized to issue a binder. A life-insurance risk must be accepted by the insurer before there is a binding contract. 

2. In fire insurance, the insurable interest must continue to the time of loss. In life insurance, an insurable interest at the time the contract is made is all that is necessary. 

3. In fire insurance the amount payable is determined by the loss. In life insurance the amount payable is specified in the policy. 

4. A fire-insurance policy may be assigned by the insured only with the consent of the insurer. A life-insurance policy may be assigned by the insured at will unless there is a beneficiary with a vested interest. The consent of the insurer is usually required by the policy.

LIFE INSURANCE 

471 5. A fire-insurance policy may be terminated by either party's giving notice at any time before a loss occurs. A life-insurance policy may be terminated by the insured at any time according to its terms unless there is a beneficiary with a vested interest, and by the insurer if given the right in the policy or by law. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Life insurance is a contract which obligates one party known as the insurer and another party known as the insured. 

2. One person can take out insurance on the life of another person only if he has an insurable interest in that person, and then, in most cases, the person to be insured must give his consent. 

3. Life-insurance companies, like fire- and other insurance companies, are subject to inspection and supervision of the department of insurance of the state in which they operate. 

4. Answers to questions on the application for life insurance amount to warranties which become a part of the policy contract. 

5. The insured may name himself as beneficiary and, if no beneficiary is named, the particular policy is payable to his estate; but he may name anyone he chooses as beneficiary. 

6. The insured who names a beneficiary without reserving the right to change the one so named at will, must get the consent of the named beneficiary to make any change in or use of the policy affecting the one named as beneficiary. 

7. There are no restrictions imposed on a person regarding the number of companies in which he may insure his life or the amount of insurance he may take. 

8. A life-insurance company may, as a rule, insert a clause in the policy whereby it is relieved from liability if the insured commits suicide within a fixed time, usually one or two years. 

9. Life-insurance contracts may be terminated by performance by both parties, by cancellation by the insured and settlement by the insurer, by default in the payment of premiums by the insured and settlement by the insurer's paying to the insured the cash surrender value of the policy or giving him a certain amount of "paid-up” insurance for a definite time. 

10. Accident insurance covers disabilities or afflictions of a person

caused by accident and it usually provides for the payment of a certain sum in case death results directly or indirectly from an injury sustained in an accident.
