COMMENTS 

Insurance in some of its many forms is a necessity for everybody. The hazards of modern life are so varied and the results so serious that no individual can afford to take the chance of having the loss fall entirely on himself. Insurance is the method of dividing the loss among a large number of persons similarly situated. Each one contributes a small sum regularly to a common fund out of which are paid the losses of any member of the group.

In such a relation it is obvious that honesty and good faith are essential to success. Fraud, sharp practice, or wrongdoing might secure a temporary advantage to one person, but ultimately the burden becomes heavier on all concerned and may result in the collapse of the enterprise. So the rules of law are designed to prevent the securing of such advantage and to punish the wrongdoer.

The law of insurance is principally a special form of the law of contracts and, in some of its phases, of the law of agency. A thorough knowledge of those two subjects will enable one to solve most of the legal questions that arise. The important and difficult feature of insurance is the great number of forms of insurance contracts, each form designed for a particular situation. There is hardly any conceivable hazard to which life, health, or property may be subject, against which insurance cannot be obtained. 

The scope of this book permits only a brief reference to some of the various forms of insurance. The main branches of insurance covering many risks are marine insurance, fire insurance, casualty insurance, guaranty and fidelity insurance, life insurance, health and accident insurance, and title insurance. The person seeking insurance should always take the advice of a reputable agent or broker as to the kind of contract suited to his needs, and should carefully study the contract offered to him to be sure that he will receive the protection he desires.

REAL ESTATE TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Eminent Domain. The right of a sovereign power to take private property for public purpose by paying a just compensation for it. 

Corporate Capacity. The capacity of a group of individuals organized under authority of law to act as one person. 

Ordinance. A rule or law enacted by a municipality (village or city) for the purpose of regulating certain acts of the people living therein. 

Rights of Discovery. Rights to property generally recognized as belonging to the one who made the discovery or under whose authority it was made.

Sovereignty. The power, right, or authority of a governmental unit, such as city, state, or nation. 

What was the source of all titles to land?

The "rights of discovery" have been recognized throughout the ages. When an expedition was sent out from a country to discover new land, the country, under whose flag the expedition set sail, claimed all the new land discovered. Following these discoveries, the country concerned fostered migration to the newly discovered lands, and as a result a number of different colonies were established by the different countries of Europe in what is now the United States. As a result of this colonization by the different countries, the system of land grants, landownerships, and land control used in the early periods was the same as that used in the country from which the settlers came, notably England, France, Netherlands (Holland), and Spain. 

Under the English common law, the King was the proprietor and the source of all titles to land within his dominion. After the United States won its independence, the title to all land in this country formerly possessed by the English Crown (King) passed to the people of the different 476

REAL ESTATE 

477 States wherein the land lay, except that full recognition was given to the rights and titles to land already granted by the King. 

Therefore, under the newly established government of the United States, the State, meaning the people, by virtue of the treaties made, succeeded the King in the ownership of all land that had not already been granted and the State became the source of all private title to land. When new territory was added to the country, not included in any state, the land was owned by the United States. Parts of it were transferred to private ownership by grants from the United States under Acts of Congress providing for homesteads, mining claims, railroad aid, and other purposes. 

As new states were created, the ownership of public land within their borders passed to the State. Now all property in continental United States is included within some state, which is now regarded as the ultimate owner and source of title. Whenever a person owning land dies without heirs, or when no owner of land can be found, the title passes to the state in its sovereign capacity. 

What is the primogeniture rule?

The primogeniture rule gives the oldest son the exclusive right to inherit land. It was practiced in England and other European countries and became the general rule of law in New York and in the Southern Colonies, but not in the New England Colonies with the exception of Rhode Island, nor in Pennsylvania. However, in New 

England and in Pennsylvania, the oldest son had a double portion. 

After the Revolution all primogeniture rules were abolished wherever they had been in force in the colonies. 

What was the source of our early land grants?

The settlers in New England and in certain sections of the South received their early land grants from the King of England. 

The settlers in New York and New Jersey received their early land grants from the King of the Netherlands, under what was known as the patroon system.

History records that Charles II, the King of England, had borrowed money from William Penn's father and to pay this debt he gave William Penn a grant of land which the King named Pennsylvania. 

France and Spain acquired by exploration and settlement, large sections of land in what is now the United States. After the colonies in this country won their independence from England and the government of the United States of America was finally established, it succeeded from time to time in purchasing from other countries all their possessions in this country. The title to all lands acquired in this way became vested in the

Federal government. As time went on, this new land was surveyed, territorial boundaries established, and one territory after another was opened up for settlement under the jurisdiction of the Department of the Interior at Washington, D. C. When a new territory was opened for settlement, new settlers acquired title to parcels (4 section or 160 acres) of this land through Federal grants by what is known as homestead, preemption, and tree claim rights, which are explained later. After the settlement in a particular territory had reached a certain development, the people of the particular territory, through their territorial legislature, would ask Congress to admit them as a State into the United States. When this petition was finally granted, all the property rights controlled by the Federal government were ceded to the particular State, which from that time became the source of all titles to real property not already granted. 

What does ownership of land mean?

Ownership of land means the right to use a certain parcel of land to the exclusion of any one else, subject to the powers vested in the State and Federal governments to take private property for public purposes, which is the right of eminent domain, and the right to levy taxes on property and sell it if necessary for taxes. 

The right of the owner to use his property is practically unlimited, except he is bound to refrain from using his property so as to injure others and is subject to all laws or restrictions affecting the property or that have to do with the use of it for certain purposes, such as the kind of building that may be erected thereon, the setback from street and property lines, forbidding the conduct of any business, and similar restrictions. These limitations may be imposed by restrictive covenants in a deed, in which case they may be enforced by the grantor or anybody claiming through or under him, or by zoning ordinances, in which case they are enforced by public authority. 

What is a zoning ordinance?

Many cities and villages have been authorized by the legislature of the particular state to pass ordinances regulating the kind of structure that may be erected on the land within the particular zone.

That is, the ordinance may restrict any area to single-family dwellings and forbid the erection of apartment houses or business buildings therein. 

It would establish other zones with less stringent restrictions and would leave some zones entirely unrestricted. Fire zones may be created under the same authority, whereby, on account of the close proximity of buildings, new buildings must be constructed of fireproof material.

REAL ESTATE 

479 Example 1. A certain section of a city was zoned for residence property, meaning single-family dwellings. A builder purchased a tract of this property and got out plans to erect a sixty-family apartment house thereon. Most cities require a permit before any building can be erected. 

In this case the permit would be refused and, if the builder tried to go ahead without a permit, the city would stop the work. 

What water rights has the owner of land?

The owner of land has the exclusive right to any body of water wholly upon the land because he owns the land under the water. 

He may use this water as he sees fit. He has the exclusive right of boating, bathing, and fishing. He may cut and sell the ice. He may use any or all of the water on his land or sell it for use elsewhere.

The owner's rights in a stream flowing through the land are less extensive. He may use a reasonable amount of the water on the land itself for domestic and farm purposes, but cannot divert water from the stream so as to lessen the flow. He has no right, by means of a dam or in other ways, to stop the flow of a stream of water on his neighbor's land or to change the course of the stream thereon. If a person owns land bordering on a body of water owned by the state, or navigable water, he has a right to use this water in common with other persons who care to use it. Should a stream or body of water divide the property of two owners, each owner may use the water and each owner owns the land under the water to the middle of the stream, unless provisions in the deeds of conveyance specify otherwise.

In some western states water is scarcer and consequently more valuable than in the East. In those states the common law as to water rights is not in force. Statutes usually permit the ownership of water rights, separate from the ownership of the land, and specified quantities of water are bought and sold as property. The student should inquire as to the nature of water rights in his own state. 

What fixtures are classed as real property?

Any fixtures which are permanently attached to the building or land, such as plumbing and bathroom fixtures, lighting fixtures, heating appliances, all machines intended to be used in connection with the building even though held in position by their weight only, and all other fixtures which are connected or used in such a way that they are considered a part of the realty are classed as real property. Such fixtures or articles as electric appliances, garden

hose, and tools, lawn mower, and any portable machines and articles, even though used on the property, would be classed as personal property. Fixtures are further discussed on page 524. 

What is an easement right?

An easement is a right one person may exercise over the property of another. The right is usually created in favor of the owner of the land against adjoining premises. 

Example 2. The owners of two adjoining lots in a congested district wished to build on their lots. To save space they agreed to build a single wall between the houses, half on one lot and half on the other, and agreed that each could use the wall as part of his house. Such a wall is called a party wall. The agreement creates an easement in favor of each lot owner. 

Other common examples are: a right of way for use on foot or in a vehicle, or for a pipe line, a railroad, or wires; a right to carry water across another's land to or from the owner's land; a right to use halls or stairways. 

An easement is an interest in land distinct from ownership of the land itself. It is real property, not personal, but is called incorporeal (intangible) real property as distinguished from corporeal (tangible) real property, which is the land itself and actual property appurtenant to it. Example 3. Hogan owned a wood lot adjacent to and back of Gerhard's property. Hogan found it convenient to cross Gerhard's land to reach his wood lot and he continued to avail himself of this privilege for more than twenty years. Finally Gerhard decided to sell his land and he tried to stop Hogan from using the right of way. Gerhard might have stopped Hogan any time before the twenty years passed, but now Hogan has a perpetual easement right to cross Gerhard's land. 

An easement may be created by grant or agreement between the owners of the two parcels of land, or it may be created in favor of one who has exercised the right continuously for a long period, usually twenty years. This is called an easement by prescription. 

The public may thus acquire an easement of way over a person's land.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Real estate is the land itself and whatever is considered as belonging with the land.

REAL ESTATE 

481 2. Ownership of land means the right to use the land subject to such restrictions as have been or may be lawfully imposed thereon. 

3. The original source of titles to land was some sovereign power. 

4. Fixtures permanently attached to the realty or intended to be permanently used therewith are considered a part of the realty. 

5. An easement right may be temporary or permanent, and it may be acquired in some states by continuous use of the property by one person for a period of time, usually twenty years.

COMMENTS 

In early days the only kind of property that was important was land. 

It was tangible, immovable, produced income for the owner, and was the basis of all property rights. Because of those qualities it was called real property.

During the centuries an immense body of real property law was developed. Certain things connected with the land were classed, according to their several natures, as real or personal property. Thus, buildings and other things permanently attached to the land; water on the land; trees and grass growing naturally without cultivation; coal, minerals, oil and gas under the land; were all classed as real property. Annual crops produced by cultivation and articles used with but not attached to the land are personal property. Different interests or estates in land were recognized, such as complete ownership called an estate in fee simple; ownership for life; rights in the property for a specified time, called an estate for years; interests to take effect in the future; and many others. Systems have been developed for recording instruments affecting real property, so that all of the various interests in any particular piece of land can be discovered by examining the records. This is called "searching the title." 

With so many complicated questions involved, the law of real property is technical and difficult and it should be handled by a trained expert. 

The value of land is determined by its availability for profitable use. Not long ago a plot ten feet square in New York City, was sold for one million dollars. Much larger tracts in undeveloped sections may have little or no value. Whether land has much or little value, the laws as to its ownership and control are the same and some knowledge of them is essential.

ESTATES IN LAND TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Curtesy. The estate or right the husband has in the realty owned by his deceased wife.

Devise. Act of disposing of real property by will. 

Dower. The estate or right the wife has in the realty owned by her deceased husband. 

Emblements. Crops of any kind produced by labor.

Freehold Estate. An estate in land that lasts during a particular life or indefinitely.

Fee Simple. A freehold estate that lasts forever; the largest estate in land usually equivalent to absolute and unconditional ownership. 

Feudal System. A system of land ownership in England after the Norman conquest (1066) from which our present law is derived. 

Homestead. A home and land used as a dwelling place. 

What is an estate in land?

An estate is an interest which one has in land, and it may be absolute ownership or it may be only a temporary or conditional ownership. The different estates in land may be described as 

A. Estate in fee simple.

This estate in land is sometimes referred to as a freehold estate. 

It is the nearest approach to absolute ownership of real property. 

This estate exists for a man during his life and, if not disposed of by him, descends to his heirs. Such an estate is subject only to the right of the state to take the owner's land for taxes or under the power of eminent domain, otherwise land owned in fee simple cannot be taken from the owner against his will except by creditors to pay his debts and then only by due process of law. 483

The term "fee" as applied to the ownership of land dates back to the time of the English feudal system. Under this system the absolute title to all real property was in the King. The land was granted by the King to others in return for various services rendered by them. Thus the King would grant large tracts to great nobles for their lives and they were required to furnish a prescribed number of knights or soldiers to fight for the King in his wars. This was known as tenure by knight service. These nobles would in turn grant part of their land to their followers in return for various kinds of services, such as services in war, supplying provisions and so on. Each of these holdings, or tenures, might again be divided in the same way until finally each part was in the possession of one who lived on the land and worked it. He was called the tenant in demesne. The interest or estate which each tenant had in the land was called a feud, fief, or fee. It was the largest interest obtainable under the feudal system and the word "fee" has come down to us as representing our largest interest in land, which is practically complete ownership.

The one who owns real property in fee simple may do as he sees fit with the property so long as he does not in its use interfere with the rights of others or become a public menace.

B. Life estates. 

A life estate is one held by a person during his own life or the life of someone else. Life estates may be created (1) by will or deed, and (2) by law. 

1. Life estates created by will or deed.

Example 1. Hobart willed his real property to his wife to be held by her during her life and upon her death it was to become the property of their only son John. Hobart died and his widow had a life estate by will in all real property owned by him at the time of his death. 

Mrs. Hobart is permitted to use this property and to take all the net income therefrom. She can sell her life estate, if she can find a buyer, but the buyer would get no better title than Mrs. Hobart has. She cannot sell all or any part of the property so as to make the buyer an owner in fee. 

At Mrs. Hobart's death the property will pass, under the will, to the son in fee simple. During her life tenancy, Mrs. Hobart cannot commit waste, meaning that she cannot remove or destroy any part of the freehold. 

Example 2. Mrs. Hobart during her use of the property cut down standing timber and sold it and also tore down a barn which was unsightly and which interfered with her convenient use of the premises. Mrs. Hobart is personally liable to her son for the damages to the estate caused by her acts. If the son had learned of her intentions, he could have secured an injunction against the waste. Had there been a coal mine or an oil well on

ESTATES IN LAND 

485 the property which was being worked at the time Mr. Hobart died, Mrs. 

Hobart, having a life estate, might continue working it and use the profits herself, but she could not open a new mine or oil well and sell the product therefrom without committing waste. 

Example 3. Wilson deeded a farm to his brother Harry with the stipulation that Harry should use it while he lived and upon his death, the farm should go to the City Boys Club, Inc. for an athletic field and recreation camp.

In Example 3, a life estate was created by deed. Wilson's brother Harry is to use this farm as his own during his life; he is entitled to all the profits therefrom, but he must not do anything that will depreciate its value. When he dies the farm passes to the 

City Boys Club, Inc., to be held by it in fee simple. 

Any crops on the farm which were planted but not harvested at the time of Harry's death may be gathered by his personal representative for his estate. The life tenant is entitled to the emblements when the estate is terminated without his fault, otherwise, proper tillage of the soil would be discouraged. Similarly, a lessee from a life tenant may recover crops he has planted before the termination of the estate. 

2. Life estates created by law. (a). Dower rights. The life interest which a widow has in the real property of her husband's from the time of his death is a dower interest. Under the common law this dower interest was a life interest in one third of the husband's realty.

This has been changed by statute in some states, and in many states dower has been abolished. Now, in some states, the wife is entitled to a life interest in one half of her husband's realty, while in some states she is given outright (in fee) a certain part of her husband's realty instead of a life interest in any portion. One should consult the laws of one's own state. 

Example 4. Reed, who owned considerable realty, died without leaving a will. He was survived by his wife and two adult children. 

In a state where the common law is in effect, the wife has a life interest or a dower right in one third of all her husband's realty. 

She may use this property or the income therefrom for her own benefit. The two children would inherit the two thirds not held

by the wife, and they would be entitled to the one third held by her upon her death. Usually the property is not actually divided between the widow and the other heirs. Instead, the income is collected and one third paid to the widow.

In order that a dower right may attach, there must have been a legal marriage; the husband must have owned the land some time after their marriage, and he must die before the wife. This dower interest ceases to attach in a case where the husband sells certain of his realty while living and his wife joins him in signing the deed of conveyance. 

In case there is a mortgage on the property that was on when the husband purchased it, or it is a purchase money mortgage, the wife's dower right is subject to this mortgage. In a few states the wife is not required to join her husband in a conveyance of realty, and in these states she takes dower only in the realty he owned at the time he died. The husband cannot defeat dower by deed or will, but he may make testamentary (by will) provisions in lieu of dower and then the widow must elect which she will take. (b). Curtesy rights. The estate the surviving husband has for life in the realty owned by his wife at the time of her death is an estate of curtesy. By common law, curtesy was a life estate in all property owned by the wife at her death, but unlike dower, it could be defeated by the wife's deeding the property during her lifetime. Curtesy was allowed only if there was born of the marriage a child capable of inheriting the property, but it was not necessary that the child survive the mother. 

The estate of curtesy has been abolished by statute in some of the states, while in others it exists only in case the wife dies without making a will disposing of her property. Both dower and curtesy have been abolished in 

New York, but property acquired by a married person before Sept. 1, 1930, is still subject to the old law. (c). Estates created by law. One example of such an estate is a homestead exemption, which is regarded in many states as an estate in land, but in others as a mere exemption. Statutes have been passed in many states creating a homestead law whereby certain realty is exempt from sale for debt, generally the home and a few acres of land not to exceed a certain value. This exemption is granted only to the head of a family or one whose duty it is to support dependents living with him.

ESTATES IN LAND 

487 Example 5. An unmarried man owned and maintained a home for his mother and a sister. They lived with him and he supported them. It was held in this particular state that his home, with a few acres of land, was exempt from sale for debts other than taxes. 

In some states a notice that the premises are claimed as a homestead must be recorded. The amount of land or the value of the homestead that may be claimed under the exemption right varies in the different states. 

As a rule the wife must join the husband in the transfer of a homestead estate, and if the husband dies, the homestead right passes to his widow or his minor children.

C. Estates in remainder and reversion. 

Such estates in realty are termed future estates. A life estate is sure to end and when it does some one must become the owner of the property. The one who becomes the owner may receive it under the terms of the original grant, in which case he has an estate in remainder. He takes it after the life tenant dies. The terms of the life tenancy may be such that when the tenant dies the property reverts back to the original owner or his heirs. Such an interest is an estate in reversion. (a) An estate in remainder is created by a will or a deed of conveyance and it does not take effect until the original estate (life estate) created thereby is terminated. 

Example 6. Hobbs deeded a parcel of realty to his invalid sister Mary for her support during her life and upon her death it was to pass to Hobbs' son James. The right James has in this property is an estate in remainder. 

Upon the death of his Aunt Mary he becomes possessed of this property in fee simple. (b) An estate in reversion may be created by will, by lease, or by deed, when the terms of the instrument used to convey the property are such that, after the estate granted terminates, the property conveyed reverts back to the grantor or his heirs. The interest the grantor or his heirs has in this property during the terms of the original grant is an estate in reversion. 

Example 7. Quinby, who owned a corner lot, leased it to the Gateway 

Oil Company for twenty years. The interest Quinby has in this property during the term of this lease is an estate in reversion. When this lease expires, full rights to this property will revert to Quinby, or to his heirs or assignees.

Either party, Quinby or the Gateway Oil Company, may sell and convey whatever interest he has in the property at any time subject to the rights of the other party, unless restricted by agreement. The purchaser will get the same rights the seller had. 

Had Quinby granted this property to the city to be used as a park, to revert on cessation of such use, his interest in it would also be an estate in reversion. 

D. Estates in severalty and joint estates. (a) An estate in severalty is one in which the ownership is in one person. 

Example 8. Carter bought a tract of land from the Homeland Development Company. The conveyance was made to Carter as the sole owner and as a result an estate in severalty was created. (b) Estates held by more than one person are classed as joint tenancies and tenancies in common. The distinction between the two is that if one of the tenants in a joint tenancy dies, his interest passes to the surviving tenant or tenants, while if a tenant in a tenancy in common dies, his interest passes to his heirs. 

Example 9. Howard and Case bought a tract of land. They took title to this tract as tenants in common. Each one owns an undivided half interest in this land, and if, during the period of their ownership, one dies, his share will go to his heirs or devises. (c) A grant to a husband and wife creates a particular form of joint tenancy called tenancy by the entirety. In case of the death of one spouse the property passes to the survivor. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Estates in land may be absolute or limited. 

2. An estate is a specific right or interest in realty. 

3. Fee simple means full ownership, free from all conditions, limitations or restrictions, except those agreed to or imposed by law. 

4. A freehold estate is an estate of indefinite duration, including estates in fee simple and life estates but not estates for years. 

5. All freehold estates, except life estates, are inheritance estates. 

6. A person who has a right to real property during his life or the life of another has a life estate.

ESTATES IN LAND 

489 7. Dower and curtesy are life estates by marriage created by law. 

Dower is the wife's right in her deceased husband's realty, and curtesy is the husband's right in his deceased wife's realty. The laws of the different states vary considerably as to these rights. 

8. Property deeded to husband and wife as tenants by the entirety, in case of the death of either one, passes to the survivor.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Covenant. A warranty or undertaking written into a deed of conveyance of real property.

Docketed. Entered in a docket or register; usually applied to a judgment 

Preemption. A prior right formerly offered to persons already settled on public lands to purchase them, under conditions prescribed by the statutes.

Section of Land. A parcel of 640 acres of land designated by government survey.

Survey. The result of measuring, staking, and mapping a parcel of land as a means of locating and identifying it. 

Title Insurance. Insurance against the risk of loss which the owner of real property may suffer on account of a defective title. 

Who may sell and convey real property?

Ownership is essential to the sale and conveyance of real property. The owner, or his authorized agent, may sell and convey a right or a title to real property. We have learned that ownership of land in this country was acquired in the beginning through grants from European monarchs. Some of the early settlers acquired their land by taking possession of it and asserting their rights of ownership. After a settler had held continuous possession of certain land for a period of time, his right to it was not denied. 

This is termed "acquiring title to land by prescription." 

After the government of the United States was established, acts of Congress made possible further land grants, from time to time, to individual settlers in new territories as they were opened up for settlement. The purpose of these acts was to aid and encourage the development of unoccupied land, thus adding to the resources 491

of the country. The settlers on this government land could acquire title to a quarter section or one hundred and sixty acres in one of three different ways: 

1. Homestead right. When new land was opened for settlement by Act of Congress, a person was given a right to select a particular quarter section and to settle on it under a permit from the Land Office. The settler was required to show his right to settle and state his intentions in good faith to improve and cultivate the land as a homestead. The permission to settle was entered in the Land Office records. This was called the homestead entry. Thereafter, the settler was required to reside on the land for a prescribed period (five years prior to 1912, and three years since 1912), make certain improvements, and cultivate the land. At the completion of the required term of residence and the performance of the conditions, the settler was entitled to a deed (called a patent) of the land from the United States upon payment of small fees. This is called a homestead right. 

2. Preemption right. When a person had settled on public lands and had made improvements thereon, without complying with the homestead laws, he was formerly given by statute a prior right to purchase the land at a minimum price. This was called a preemption right. The statute has been almost entirely repealed. 

3. Tree-claim right. When the prairie lands of the Northwest were opened up for settlement, the settlers were granted tree-claim rights in addition to the others mentioned. Under this grant a settler could take up a quarter section of land, live on it for five years, make certain improvements, and have a certain number of trees growing on a certain number of acres of the land. When all this was accomplished, the settler could file his claim and get his deed. 

It was possible in some territories for one settler to avail himself of all three rights and thereby secure deeds to three quarter sections or 480 acres. In large sections of the United States the first deeds to the land came from land offices operated by agents under authority of the National Government.

At the present time, desert lands in certain sections to be irrigated, may be bought from the government at low prices. In other sections, stone and timber lands may be had at low prices. 

What are the usual steps in a sale of real property? 

1. The survey. The particular land offered for sale should be surveyed, in order to establish the boundary lines and make it possible to describe the property in the sales contract. Civil engineers are employed, either by the owner of the land or by the government, to survey land as it is subdivided and prepare maps of each

subdivision. These maps may be filed in the county clerk's office in the county where the land is situated, and in most places in the tax department of the town, village, or city. 

It is advantageous to have such maps filed, as the boundary lines of the lots and roads may always be established by reference to the filed maps as a public record. Sometimes the purchaser, after signing the contract to buy, will have the property surveyed for his own satisfaction before taking title. 

2. The written sales contract. As soon as the sale has been negotiated, the written sales contract is prepared and signed by both the buyer and the seller. In some states the law requires that all documents necessary in the sale and conveyance of real property shall be prepared by a licensed attorney. In other places, it is quite generally the practice to employ an attorney in such transactions.

The usual sales contract contains (a) the names of the parties, (b) a description of the property to be conveyed, (c) the terms of the sale, (d) the date set for closing and the signatures of both buyer and seller. In some states the signatures must be witnessed. In case property owned jointly is sold, all having interest therein must sign the sales contract.

In those states allowing the wife a dower interest in her husband's realty, she may or may not sign the contract, but failing to sign the contract, there is nothing to keep her from refusing to sign the deed and defeating the sale. The same principle applies in case the wife sells her realty in a state where the husband has a curtesy interest in his wife's real property, which under local statutes, the wife cannot defeat by deed or will. 

3. Abstract of title. After the sale contract has been signed by the parties thereto, a period of time, one to three months, is usually allowed before the sale is closed and the title transferred. 

During this time the prospective purchaser will or should have a title search made to insure himself that the seller can transfer a clear title to the property. The one who makes this search, usually an attorney or a title company employed by the purchaser, will prepare an abstract of title from the records in the county clerk's office of the county where the land is situated. Any defects in

title, any limitations on the use of land, such as restrictive covenants or easements, and any liens against the land, such as mortgages, taxes and judgments, will be disclosed by the search and must be corrected or removed by the seller, unless the buyer agrees in the contract to take the land subject to them. As further protection against undiscovered defects, the title may be insured. 

4. The Torrens system of registering titles. In some states the 

Torrens system of registering titles to land is allowed by statute. 

Under this system anyone may have his title to land examined and registered by an official examiner of titles. If the title is found to be clear, the examiner issues to the owner a certificate of title. 

Subsequent transfers of the property are recorded on this certificate and thereafter, in searching the title to this property, it is necessary to examine the records only from the date of registration and official certification. 

5. The deed. The deed is the instrument used by the owner to convey his interest in certain real property to another party. The usual requirements of a deed are: (a) It must be in writing (printed form filled in on the typewriter may be used) and the parties thereto must be competent to contract. (b) The grantor and the grantee must be so identified that they may not be mistaken, and the property to be conveyed must be so described that there can be no doubt as to its identity. The description may include references to maps, markers, distances, or boundaries, and it often closes with the words, "with the appurtenances thereto belonging." The appurtenances are such rights as waterways, rights of way, rights to light and air, and unless they are expressly reserved they are all included in the grant under the general term "appurtenances.' 

At common law the owner of the land owned not only the surface, but everything under the land to the center of the earth and the air space over the land. The owner was entitled to prevent or recover damages for any trespass on his land, whether the trespass was committed going upon the surface, or by mining or boring into the earth below the surface, or by entering on the air space with wires or an overhanging building. Such is still the law except that by an act of Congress, the upper air space is free for air navigation and a trespass is not committed unless the airplane pilot

flies his plane below the limit prescribed by the Secretary of Commerce, which at this time is 500 feet over open spaces and 1,000 feet over settlements. (c) The conveyance clause contains the words sufficient to transfer the estate to the grantee. Such words as "do hereby grant, sell, and convey," are generally used. This clause also contains words defining the estate, as "unto the said party of the second part his heirs and assigns forever." These words show that an estate in fee is granted. Any exceptions or reservations must appear in the conveyance clause and be particularly described. 

Exceptions refer to outstanding rights of others in the property, such as easements, rights to take ore or oil or water from the land, and any interest in the land which the grantor cannot convey, such as a lease for years or a life estate. Reservations refer to any similar rights in the property which the grantor reserves to himself. 

The habendum is that part of the conveying clause which begins with the words "To have and to hold." It also designates the estate which is to pass. If it does not agree with the conveying clause, it is void. If the conveying clause designates the estate to pass, the habendum clause is unnecessary; however, it is generally used. (d) The deed must be properly executed; that is, it must be signed, sealed, witnessed, and acknowledged. These requirements vary in different states. The deed must be signed by the grantor or some one duly authorized to act for him, but the seal, that was required at common law, is not now required by a majority of the states; and, only a few of the states require that a deed must be witnessed. The deed must be acknowledged by the grantor before an officer authorized by law to take acknowledgments of deeds. 

If it is not duly acknowledged, it cannot be admitted to record. 

If a married man sells real property, his wife must join him in signing the deed in all states where she has a dower interest in the real property of which her husband is possessed in fee during their marriage, or in case they own the property jointly with the right of survivorship. In some states, if a married woman sells real property of her own, her husband must join her in signing the deed. This is done in order to release dower and curtesy rights. Anyone other than the grantor who has any kind of an

estate in land that is conveyed to another must sign a release which is recorded or join in signing the deed; otherwise, the title as transferred is subject to whatever interest he may have in the property. 

When the granting clause in a deed conveys the property to two or more persons with the added statement, "as joint tenants with the right of survivorship," or "as tenants by the entirety," should one of the owners die, his interest passes to the surviving owner or owners. Except as otherwise provided by statute, a conveyance of land to a husband and wife creates an estate by the entirety. (e) The deed must be delivered and accepted; otherwise, it does not become effective. It may be delivered to a third person to be delivered to the grantee when some stipulated condition has been fulfilled. This is called a delivery in escrow. In a valid delivery in escrow the grantor has no power to recall the deed. Death of the grantor before the deed is finally delivered, does not affect the delivery in escrow. The condition very often is that final delivery shall be made when the grantor dies. 

All states provide for the recording of deeds and other instruments affecting real property in some public office, usually the office of the county clerk. By recording these instruments notice is given to all people and those concerned may examine the records to see if the title to a particular property is clear or what is against it. In most states, as between the immediate parties, a deed is valid without recording. It is only against subsequent purchasers, lienors and others acquiring rights against the land in good faith and for a valuable consideration that unrecorded instruments are of no effect. 

What are the kinds of deeds?

The two principal kinds of deeds are quitclaim deeds and warranty deeds. A quitclaim deed. A quitclaim deed merely conveys to the grantee whatever interests the grantor has in the property and nothing more. It contains only one covenant and that is the covenant against the grantor, meaning that the grantor warrants that he has not done himself or permitted to be done anything that would affect the title to the property. 

A quitclaim deed is properly used when it is unfair to expect the grantor to warrant the title, as in the conveyance by an agent to his principal of

land held for the principal; or, in settling an estate, when several heirs holding land as tenants in common wish to transfer their interests to one of them; or, in clearing a title, when one wishes to release a possible or uncertain claim. 

A warranty deed. Warranty deeds are of two kinds, (1) simple warranty deeds and (2) full covenant warranty deeds. 

1. A simple warranty deed contains the following two covenants only: (a) Warranty of title. The grantor warrants that he has title to the property. (b) Warranty of quiet enjoyment. The grantor warrants that the grantee shall not be legally disturbed in his quiet and peaceable possession of the premises: 

2. A full covenant warranty deed contains the following covenants or warranties: (a) A seizin covenant warrants that the grantor is the sole owner of the property in fee simple and that he has a right to convey the same. (b) A quiet enjoyment covenant warrants that the grantee and his heirs and assignees shall not be legally disturbed in their quiet and peaceable possession of the premises. (c) An incumbrances covenant warrants that there are no outstanding rights in third parties to the land conveyed. 

An unsatisfied mortgage, an unexpired lease, an easement, unpaid taxes, or judgments against the property are all breaches of this covenant. (d) A further assurance warrant is an agreement by the grantor to perform any acts that may be necessary to perfect the grantee's title, including the execution of such further instruments as may be required for this purpose. (e) A warranty of title, the most important covenant, is the warranty of title, which is an agreement that the grantor warrants and will defend the title granted.

A breach of any of these covenants gives the grantee cause for action against the grantor for damages.

What is adverse possession of land?

A person may acquire ownership of land by holding open an exclusive possession of it in opposition to the rights of the true owner continuously for a period of time varying in the different states from ten to twenty-one years. His right of ownership may then be established by what is known as the right of adverse possession.

Living on the land, cultivating it, or making improvements on it-any one of these may be sufficient use to establish one's ownership by adverse possession. When one is in possession by agreement with the owner, or with his consent, he cannot acquire title no matter how long he remains, because his possession is not adverse. 

How may ownership be acquired through legal proceedings?

Title to real property may be transferred involuntarily or voluntarily. When property is seized according to law and sold at public auction to satisfy some claim against it, such as taxes, a mortgage, a judgment for debt, or a lien, title to it is transferred involuntarily, and it is said to be transferred by "involuntary alienation." The purchaser in such a transaction acquires a good title subject to legal regulations in force. That is, the owner may have a right, under the law, to redeem the property by fulfilling some condition. 

Another way of acquiring ownership of land by legal proceedings is by decree of specific performance of a contract to sell land. 

Example 1. The owner of a tract of land contracted to sell it for a factory site. When the time came to execute the deed and complete the sale he refused to complete his contract. A legal action against the seller for a breach of contract, would, in all probability, result in the court decreeing that he must comply with his agreement and complete the sale, thus the purchaser would acquire the land by decree of specific performance.

Ownership by voluntary alienation results when the owner willingly transfers the title during his lifetime. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The owner or his authorized agent may sell land. 

2. A survey is desirable to locate certain parcels of land and to establish boundary lines between different parcels.

3. The contract to sell land must be written and signed by the seller and the buyer. 

4. The abstract of title will show any unsatisfied claims against the property and any defects in the owner's title to it. 

5. The use of the Torrens system of registering titles to real property is permitted by law in a few states. 

6. Execution and delivery of the deed conveys the ownership of the property to another. 

7. The deed should be recorded promptly. An unrecorded deed does not protect the grantee against subsequent purchasers or encumbrancers from the original owner who acquire rights against the land in good faith and for a valuable consideration. 

8. The covenants in a deed amount to agreements between the grantor and the grantee. 

9. Ownership of land may be acquired by holding open and exclusive possession for the period fixed by the statutes. 

10. Rights in real property are acquired by adverse possession only when there is no agreement between the parties and the owner has not given his permission to use the property. 

11. The purchaser of real property sold through legal proceedings gets a good title thereto subject to legal regulations in force. 

12. The decree of specific performance will give the person under contract to purchase a tract of real property ownership through legal proceedings.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Descent. Transfer of the title to real estate by inheritance. 

Escheat. To revert.

Executor (Executrix). One named in a will to carry out its provisions. 

Intestate. Without making a will. 

Testate. Making and leaving a will; as, one dying testate. 

Testator. A man who makes a will. 

Testatrix. A woman who makes a will. 

What is a will?

A will is an instrument by which a person during his lifetime makes disposition of his property, both real and personal, to take effect after his death. Any owner of property who is of sound mind and legal age can make a valid will. The law of the state where the testator lives is controlling as to the execution and validity of a will, except that a will of real property is controlled by the law of the state where the property is situated. 

Several states, by statute, recognize as valid, a will executed according to the law of the testator's domicile (place of residence) or of the place of execution. Real property left to someone by will is said to be devised, and the one who so receives it takes it by devise. Personal property left by will is called a legacy or a bequest. The person who makes the will is called the testator or testatrix, and the one named in the will who is to receive some or all of the property is called a beneficiary or legatee (of personal property) or devisee (of real property). 

What are the requisites of a valid will?

Local statutes usually prescribe the requisites of a valid will; but, inasmuch as they vary considerably in the different states, one should consult an attorney when making one's will. Some of the requisites are: 502

1. Must be in writing. A will must be in writing-it may be handwritten, typewritten, or printed. It is common practice to use blank forms of wills, in which the formal and usual parts are printed and the blanks filled in writing. It may be executed under seal, making it formal, or it may be informal. A will written entirely in the handwriting of the testator, called a holographic will, does not have to be witnessed in some states, as it is considered improbable that such a will could be forged. 

There is one exception to the law that a will must be in writing. 

A soldier or a sailor, when in actual service, may make an oral statement to two witnesses, disposing of his property in case of his death, and such statement proved by the witnesses will be enforced as a will. This is called a nuncupative will. 

2. A will must be properly signed. No will is valid unless it is signed by the testator, and in many states it is required that it shall be signed at the end so as to preclude the possibility of additions by some person without authority. 

3. A will must be witnessed. The usual requirement is that there shall be at least two witnesses to a will; that the testator must actually sign in their presence or acknowledge his signature to them; that he must request them to sign as witnesses; and that each witness must sign in his presence. It is usual, although not essential, that the witnesses sign in the presence of each other. 

A person named in the will as a beneficiary should not sign it as a witness, because it tends to promote fraud. In such cases the validity of the will is not affected and the witness may be required to prove the will, but he loses his legacy. As a further safeguard, any apparent erasure or change made in the will should be initialed by each witness in such a way as to show that the change was made before the will was executed and that he saw it at the time of signing his name. Otherwise, someone might claim that the will was changed after it had been witnessed. 

What is a codicil?

A codicil is an addition to a will. After the testator has executed his will he may decide to change it in some particular without making a new will. This he may do by adding to his original will a supplement or codicil. This added supplement or codicil must be executed in the same manner as the original will.

Example 1. After Bliss had executed his will, he decided to bequeath $1,000 to the Waverly Home for Orphans, so he formally executed a codicil to his will making this bequest. This codicil is as valid and enforceable as any part of the original will. No partial change in a will can be made without a codicil. However, a will can be changed by making a new will, in which case the old will is revoked and should be destroyed. 

How may a will be revoked?

A will may be revoked by destroying it. However, if it is not destroyed and an entirely new will bearing a later date is made out and executed by the testator, the old will is automatically revoked. 

It is usual to include some such statement as the following in a will: "... do make, publish, and declare the following as and for my last will and testament, hereby revoking any and all will or wills made heretofore by me. "Such a statement in a will annuls all prior wills; but, even without such a statement the latter will supersedes the earlier one. The safer plan, however, is to destroy any prior will.

Wills sometimes are contested in court by a relative of the testator who was not remembered in the will and who would be entitled to a portion of the property if the will is invalid. Such contest is based on the invalidity of the will itself due to improper execution, forgery, or fraudulent alteration; or on the fact that the testator was incompetent to make a will because of unsound mind; or on the fact that he was subjected to undue influence and the will does not represent his own desires. It is exceedingly difficult for the contestant to establish the invalidity of a will, and success in will contests is very seldom attained. Should this dissatisfied relative win his case, the will is said to be broken. This amounts to annulling it, and the property will have to be handled the same as if the owner had died intestate. This is explained later. 

How are the provisions in a will finally carried out? 

The testator may name in the will one or more persons as executor or executrix. It is wise to secure the consent of the person named, as otherwise he might refuse the appointment and defeat the testator's plans. A relative or trusted friend usually is selected for this important office, but any adult may be named. A beneficiary under the will may act as executor. It is becoming more and more common to name a bank or trust company as executor, either alone or as a coexecutor with a relative or friend of the

testator. The testator also usually tells some trustworthy friend or member of his family where his will can be found after his death. At an appropriate time after the death of the testator his will is read and offered for probate. To probate a will means to prove that it was the last will of the deceased. This must be done in a court established for this purpose, a surrogate's, probate court, or some other county court, and here is where the witnesses will have to testify that they witnessed the will. After the will has been probated, the court will give any necessary orders to the executor or executrix who will carry out the provisions of the will. In some cases the executor is required, according to the will or by law, to furnish a bond, and the court must approve the bond furnished. The transfer of the testator's real property is effected by the will itself, and it is customary to record the will in the office of the clerk of the county where the property is situated as evidence of the transfer and to assist in searching the title. The executor will also distribute the personal property according to the provisions in the will. If any beneficiary under the will is a minor, a guardian must be appointed to receive the property and to manage it until this beneficiary becomes of age. Eighteen months is the time usually allowed to settle an estate. 

How is title to property acquired by inheritance? 

An heir is one who is entitled to, or has inherited, property. A person who dies without making a will is said to have died intestate. 

A state of intestacy also exists if a person makes a will and it is declared invalid after his death. In either case, if the deceased left real property and there are heirs who are entitled to receive it, they will inherit it by descent. That is, title to the property will pass to them according to the provisions of the law of the particular state. When the personal property is transferred in this way, title passes by what is called distribution of personal property. 

How is an intestate's property administered?

When a person possessed of property dies intestate, the court having jurisdiction in such cases, will appoint a person called an administrator who will take charge, under the supervision of the court, of the deceased person's property and business affairs. The

person appointed has nothing to do with the real property of the deceased, except that by court order he may sell it to pay debts when the personal property is insufficient. The title to the real property passes to the heirs under the statute without any action by the administrator or anybody else. The administrator will dispose of or distribute the personal property left after the debts are paid and he has closed up the other business affairs. 

Who may inherit property?

The persons entitled to inherit the property of decedent are determined by the statute laws of the state where the decedent lived. 

In most states there are different rules of descent as to real property and personal property, the principal difference being as to the rights of a surviving husband or wife. The persons who inherit real property are called heirs or heirs at law. Those who inherit personal property are called next of kin. In some states, including New York, the distinction between heirs and next of kin has been abolished and the same persons take the property in the same shares, regardless of whether it is real or personal property. 

In states where there are different rules of inheritance for real and personal property, the rights of a surviving husband or wife in decedent's real property are usually limited to the dower or curtesy allowed by the statute. These rights may be changed or increased by laws as to homestead rights and community property, and the local law must be consulted. After provision is made according to the law for the rights of the surviving spouse, the real property remaining is divided as follows, subject to variations in the statutes of different states: 

1. To the children of the intestate and the children of his deceased children (the intestate's grandchildren). 

2. If there are no children, grandchildren, or great-grandchildren to inherit the real property, it goes to the intestate's parents if living, otherwise to his brothers or sisters and to the children of a deceased brother or sister. 

3. If there are no surviving near relatives, other more distant relatives, such as uncles and aunts and their children and children's children, in order of descendancy, may claim a right to inherit the intestate's real property.

In states where the law of descent is the same for real and personal property, it is usual for the surviving spouse to inherit a specified part of all decedent's property, the remainder being divided between the children or other next of kin as provided by law. The law of New York is given as an example of this method of distribution: 

1. One third of the property goes to the surviving spouse and the residue in equal portions to the children or children of deceased children. 

2. If decedent leaves a surviving spouse and both parents, but no child or descendant, the spouse takes $5,000 and one half the residue and each parent takes half the balance; and if there be no spouse, each parent takes one half of the whole. 

3. If decedent leaves a surviving spouse and one parent, but no child or descendant, the spouse takes $5,000 and one half the residue and the parent takes the balance; and if there be no spouse, the parent takes the whole. 

4. If decedent leaves a surviving spouse, and no descendant, parent, brother or sister, nephew or niece, the spouse takes the whole estate; but, if there be a brother or sister, nephew or niece, the spouse takes $10,000 and half the residue and the balance is distributed among the brothers and sisters and their descendants. 

5. If there be no spouse, the whole estate shall descend to the children equally, or their descendants. 

6. If there be no spouse, no children or their descendants, and no parent, the whole estate shall descend to the next of kin of decedent, first to brothers and sisters of decedent and their descendants. 

When a person is entitled to share in an estate by representation, he takes per stirpes and not per capita; that is, he takes a fraction of the share his ancestor would have taken and not an equal share of the whole estate. 

Example 2. A died, leaving two children, B and C; two grandchildren,

L and M, who are children of D, a deceased son of A; and two greatgrandchildren, X and Y, who are children of N, a deceased son of D. 

Under this rule, the estate is divided: One third each to B and C; one ninth each to L and M; and one eighteenth each to X and Y. 

The probate court determines who is entitled to the decedent's real property under the statutes then in force, and the property descends to those persons accordingly. If there is no person entitled to inherit, the property escheats to the state.

If a person desires to have his property distributed in some other way than the law provides, he must make a will. It is prudent to make a will anyway, as the testator may divide his property as he wishes, usually giving his wife more than the law allows her, and he may select as executor the person he prefers to settle his estate. 

What disposition is made of an intestate's personal property? 

The personal property owned by one who dies intestate goes to his administrator who was appointed by the court and who is charged with the duty of paying the intestate's just debts, and distributing the balance of his personal property among the persons having the best right to it as designated by the statute. "Next of kin" is the usual designation. 

In some states the widow is given all the personal property remaining after the debts are paid. In other states, she receives a substantial portion of it. With the exception of the portion given to the widow, the descent of personal property is generally the same as that of real property. 

When property, real or personal, has been received by a person under a will, or by inheritance, it belongs to the recipient absolutely. In case of his death it passes to his heirs, not the heirs of the original owner, or as he may provide by will. 

What happens to the deceased's life insurance?

If a beneficiary was named in the policy, it is paid to him or her if he or she is living; otherwise, it is paid to the estate of the beneficiary named.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. Property may be disposed of by sale, by gift, by will, and by inheritance. 

2. A man who dies testate has disposed of his property by will which must go to probate and be carried out by the executor named therein. 

3. A man who dies intestate has not made a will, and the court must appoint an administrator to take over his property, close up his business affairs, and distribute his remaining property among the heirs. 

4. Real property is devised and personal property is bequeathed by will. 

5. A will must be in writing, properly signed and witnessed; and, it may be sealed.

6. A will may be revoked or annulled by destroying it, by a new will being made in its place, or by being declared invalid as a result of a court proceeding to contest it. 

7. The court having jurisdiction of wills and estates of deceased persons must act in all cases where property is disposed of by will or where property is left without a will having been made. 

8. Title to both real and personal property may be acquired by inheritance. 

9. The testator names the executor or the executors in his will; in case of intestacy the law provides who is entitled to administer the estate, and that person must be appointed by the court. 

10. The statutes of all states specify what relatives of the deceased person shall inherit his property in the absence of a will, and their several shares therein.
