TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Amortize. To pay a debt plus the interest in installments, at regular intervals, over a period of time, or to set up a fund to pay the debt within a certain time.

Deficiency Judgment. A judgment against the debtor awarded by the court in foreclosure proceedings where the mortgaged property does not sell for enough to pay the debt. 

Equity Interest. The interest the mortgagor has in the property over and above the mortgage.

Equity of Redemption. A privilege of the mortgagor to redeem his property before the sale in foreclosure proceedings, and in some states even after the sale.

Foreclosure Proceedings. Legal proceedings by which mortgaged property is taken from the mortgagor and sold at public sale to satisfy the mortgage. 

What is a real-estate mortgage?

A real-estate mortgage is an instrument by which in form the title to land or some interest in land is conditionally conveyed as security for a debt or obligation, the condition being that if the debt is paid or the obligation performed, the conveyance becomes void. At common law a mortgage was in fact as well as in form a conditional transfer of title and if the debt was not paid when due, the title of the mortgagee became absolute without further proceeding. In modern law a mortgage merely creates a lien against the property, and the lien must be enforced through foreclosure proceedings before the mortgagee can acquire any rights to the land. There are two parties to a mortgage: the mortgagor, the party giving the mortgage; and the mortgagee, the party to whom it is given. 511

Improved real estate which can readily be sold, particularly if it produces a regular income or is occupied by the owner, is considered good security for a loan. Mortgages are most commonly given as security in two kinds of transactions, although a mortgage may be security for the performance of any obligation: 

1. Security for a debt.

Example 1. Hood owned a building and land valued at $30,000. He borrowed $10,000 from a savings bank and secured the loan by a mortgage for three years on this property. By borrowing this money, Hood created a debt which he secured by a mortgage on his real property. If Hood is a married man and this property is in a state where the wife had dower rights, she would have to join him in signing this mortgage. 

2. A purchase-money mortgage.

Example 2. Waters purchased a house and lot from the Haden Building 

Company for $8,000. He paid $3,000 cash and executed a mortgage for $5,000 at 5% interest, both interest and principal to be completely amortized in ten years. This is a purchase-money mortgage, and if Waters has a wife, she will not have to join him in signing this mortgage, unless by the deed she is made a joint owner of the property. 

What are the requisites of a mortgage?

A mortgage must be in writing, must contain a description of the parties, the property mortgaged, and the debt secured, and must be signed by the mortgagor. A mortgage is commonly executed under seal and in some states a seal is required, but in many states it is unnecessary. If the mortgage is to be recorded, as it always should be for the protection of the mortgagee, it must be acknowledged and, in some states, witnessed. 

A mortgage on real property covers not only the land described in the mortgage, but also all appurtenances and fixtures that are connected with the land or used as part and parcel of it at the time it is mortgaged or that thereafter become connected with or attached to the land while the mortgage is on it. 

What are the usual clauses in a mortgage? 

1. The defeasance clause. This clause recites that the transfer of title to the grantee is on condition that, if the debt secured is duly paid, the transfer shall be defeated; i.e., it shall become void and of no effect. This clause distinguishes a mortgage from a deed.

2. The right of sale clause. This clause gives the mortgagee the right to sell the property in case the mortgagor defaults in the payment of the mortgage according to its terms or any part thereof; or fails to comply with other stipulations in the mortgage. In some states this clause is forbidden by statute and all sales must be in foreclosure proceedings. In other states, sales under this clause are subject to supervision and review by the courts. In others the clause gives the mortgagee full power to sell the property for the debt without foreclosure or other court proceedings. 

3. The insurance clause. This clause requires the mortgagor to protect the mortgagee's interest by keeping the building on the mortgaged premises insured. The insurance company must be notified of the mortgagee's interest, and it will issue a rider agreeing to pay the loss to the mortgagee as his interest may appear. Usually the original policy is deposited with the mortgagee and a certificate of insurance is issued to and held by the mortgagor. 

4. Interest and tax clause. This clause compels the mortgagor to pay the interest as it becomes due, the taxes, and all assessments against the property; and, should he default for a certain number of days, usually sixty or ninety days, the mortgagee may avail himself of his right to have the property sold to satisfy the mortgage and taxes. 

Can a second mortgage be taken on property?

A second mortgage, and even a third mortgage, is sometimes taken on property. If two or more mortgages are placed on property, they take precedence in the order in which they are recorded. 

Example 3. Marlo purchased a house and lot on which there was a fiveyear mortgage for $6,000 held by a bank. He paid $2,000 cash, and the seller took a mortgage for $2,000 to be amortized in five years. Such transactions as this are common. If the first mortgagee has to sell the property to satisfy his mortgage, the second mortgagee will lose unless the property sells for enough more than the first mortgage to satisfy the second, or the second mortgagee buys the property or bids it in at the sale to protect his interest. The second mortgagee may foreclose his mortgage if payment is defaulted, and the property will be sold subject to the first mortgage on the property. 

What is a trust deed?

A trust deed is an instrument by which the title to property is conveyed to one or more persons, in trust for a specified purpose. 

Such a deed is sometimes used in place of a mortgage and to accomplish the same purpose. The borrower of money conveys prop-

erty to trustees to hold it as security for the debt, giving the trustees power to sell the property in case of default in payment. If the debt is paid when due, the property is reconveyed to the owner. 

In case of default in payment the property is sold under the power of sale granted in the deed without the necessity of foreclosure proceedings which are required in a mortgage transaction. 

Trust deeds are frequently given by corporations to secure an issue of bonds sold to the public. In some states they are used generally instead of mortgages whenever real property is made security for a debt. 

What are the rights and duties of the mortgagor?

The mortgagor has a right to the possession of the property and he may use it freely for his own benefit, except that he must not destroy it or allow it to deteriorate for want of repairs. He may sell, assign, or lease the property and he may place a second mortgage on it, insure it, or make any alterations he wishes to make so long as the interests of the mortgagee are not affected thereby. 

Should the property be sold or assigned, the new owner holds the property subject to the lien of the mortgage. If the debt is not paid when due, the mortgagee may foreclose the mortgage and have the property sold to satisfy the debt secured thereby. 

When the mortgagee accepts a mortgage to secure a debt, he may require the mortgagor to accompany the mortgage with a note or a bond, whereby the mortgagor becomes personally liable for the debt, and in case he defaults in its payment and the mortgaged property does not sell for enough to pay it, he can be held on a deficiency judgment to pay the balance, except in those states where a deficiency judgment in such cases is not permitted. Where this is the law or when a note or bond is not given, the mortgagee's only right to collect his debt is out of the mortgaged property.

What is the liability of one who buys mortgaged property? 

When mortgaged property is sold, the buyer either assumes the mortgage or takes the property subject to it. If he assumes the mortgage, it means that he becomes personally liable for the debt and either he or the original debtor may be sued for the debt or held liable for any deficiency after foreclosure. If the original debtor is compelled to pay, he may recover the amount from the buyer who assumed the debt. If the buyer takes the property subject to the

mortgage, it means that the land is still security for the debt and may be sold on foreclosure, but the buyer is not liable for the debt or any deficiency. 

May a mortgage be assigned?

The mortgagee may sell, assign, or transfer the mortgage and the accompanying note or bond to a third party. The mortgage can be assigned only by a written instrument, and it should be recorded. It passes to the assignee all the rights of the assignor, but no additional rights. 

How is a mortgage foreclosed?

If the mortgagor defaults in the payment of the debt or any installment thereof or in complying with such stipulations in the mortgage as will give the mortgagee a right to foreclose, he may have the property sold to satisfy the debt. 

Foreclosure proceedings are started by the lawyer for the mortgagee searching the records to obtain the names of persons who have acquired interests in the property as purchasers, by inheritance, by filing liens or judgments against it or taking a second mortgage on it since the first mortgage was recorded. He will also make a tax search to see what taxes are unpaid. The owners of the property and all other persons who, according to the records, have acquired any interest in the property will be made parties to the action to foreclose, so that they can present their claims to the court if they desire. 

The mortgage takes priority over all interests except taxes created in the property since it was recorded. One reason for foreclosing a mortgage is to dispose of all such claims so that the purchaser at foreclosure sale may get a clear title. A tax or assessment lien against the property is not vacated by foreclosure of the mortgage. It must be paid or the property will be sold to satisfy it.

After the attorney for the mortgagee has made all preliminary arrangements for the foreclosure, he will petition the court for a hearing. The court will set a date when all parties interested may be heard, and if no good defense is offered, the court will issue an order authorizing the property to be sold at public auction to satisfy the debt, and appoint a referee who will take charge of the fore-

closure proceeding from that time on and report to the court the result of his actions. The referee sets a date for the sale and inserts the notice of it in the local paper as required by law. The mortgagor may redeem the property any time before the sale by paying the debt and all costs of foreclosure proceedings to date. If the property is finally sold and does not sell for enough to satisfy the debt, a deficiency judgment on the note or bond is taken against the mortgagor for the balance. 

A mortgagor who believes that the property will not sell for enough to pay the debt and costs of foreclosure may offer the mortgagee a deed to the property. If the mortgagee accepts the deed, the mortgage will be discharged and there will be no deficiency judgment against the mortgagor. 

In the great financial depression which began in 1929 mortgage foreclosures became very numerous, properties were sold on foreclosure at extremely low prices, and large deficiency judgments were regularly entered. This situation caused great hardship and loss to unfortunate homeowners and seriously affected the economic welfare of the country. In addition to several Federal agencies offering financial assistance to distressed mortgagors, many states passed statutes delaying or restricting the right of foreclosure. These were called moratorium laws and generally provided that the mortgagee could not foreclose his mortgage during the emergency, or until after a stated date, if the mortgagor complied with certain conditions, such as paying the taxes and interest on the mortgage, or paying to the mortgagee a sum equivalent to the reasonable rental of the property. Other statutes provided that, regardless of the amount for which the property was sold on foreclosure, no deficiency judgment could be entered against a debtor unless the amount of the debt exceeded the reasonable value of the property, and then only for the amount of such excess. Most of these statutes are in force at this writing, and any person holding a mortgage, or owning mortgaged property, should consult them as to his rights. 

Has the mortgagor the right of redemption?

Under the common law a mortgage was a conveyance of the title to the property to the mortgagee. This conveyance was subject to defeat by the mortgagor paying the debt, but in case payment was defaulted, the conveyance became absolute. Too often this worked an injustice because the property was mortgaged for much less than its value, and the equity courts recognizing this injustice to

the mortgagor would give him the right to redeem his property. 

This right was termed "equity of redemption." The right is now an inseparable part of every mortgage transaction. 

The mortgagor may always redeem his property up to the time of the foreclosure sale by paying the debt with interest and costs, and in some states he may redeem within a limited time after the sale. The right to redeem cannot be waived or surrendered by the mortgagor by any agreement in or contemporaneous with the mortgage, and any subsequent transfer of the property to the mortgagee or surrender of the equity of redemption is carefully scrutinized to be sure it is not unfair or oppressive. 

What is a satisfaction piece?

When a mortgage is paid, it is discharged. In order to cancel it on the records, an instrument called a satisfaction piece is executed by the mortgagee and given to the mortgagor, who will have it recorded. The mortgage continues to stand against the property until the satisfaction is recorded. 

What liens may be recorded against real property? 

A lien is a legal claim or charge against property as security for a debt, by virtue of which the creditor may force a sale of the property to satisfy the debt. State and Federal statutes provide that certain debts are liens on the debtor's property when the statutory requirements are complied with. These usually include the filing or recording of the claim in some public office, and a lien thus recorded is valid against every subsequent purchaser of the land. The following are the principal liens against real property. 

1. Mechanic's lien. Any unpaid mechanics who worked upon a building or furnished material for repairs or construction thereof, have a right to file a lien against the property for the amount due them. All liens, except tax liens, have priority in the order in which they are recorded. A mechanic's lien may be discharged by payment or by the owner or contractor who is involved bonding it, and thereby guaranteeing its payment. 

2. Judgment lien. A creditor who sues a debtor and is awarded a judgment by the court may have this judgment entered up or docketed against the debtor. As soon as it is docketed, it becomes a lien against any real property owned by the debtor or that he may thereafter own while the judgment is in force on the records. 

3. Tax lien. Amounts due a municipality, a state, or the United States for taxes or assessments against real property are secured by a lien on the

property, and this lien has priority over all other claims. Income and inheritance taxes are also liens on real property of the debtor or the estate. 

4. Vendor's lien. In some states a seller of real property has a lien on the property for any portion of the purchase price. This is an equitable lien, is not a matter of record, and is valid only against the buyer or a subsequent purchaser who took the property with the knowledge of the lien. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A mortgage creates a lien on real property in favor of a creditor as security for a debt. 

2. The bond or note accompanying the mortgage obligates the mortgagor to pay the debt, or the balance due, should the mortgage be foreclosed and the property not sell for enough to satisfy the debt. 

3. A mortgage must be executed the same as a deed and recorded. 

4. The mortgagor retains title and control of the property and may use it as his own, subject always to the rights of the mortgagee. 

5. The mortgagor is bound by the covenants against him in the mortgage. 

6. The mortgagee may sell or assign the mortgage to a third party without the mortgagor's consent, but the assignee gets no better title than the assignor had. 

7. The mortgagor who pays the mortgage can demand a satisfaction piece of the mortgagee. It must be recorded to clear the title. 

8. If the mortgagor defaults in his payments or his covenants, the mortgagee may bring foreclosure proceedings whereby the property will be sold at public auction to satisfy the debt. 

9. A deficiency judgment is awarded only when the mortgagor executed a bond or note to accompany the mortgage and the property did not sell for enough to satisfy the mortgage. 

10. Recorded mechanic's liens and judgment liens do not take priority over mortgages or other claims already recorded, and never over tax liens regardless of when they are recorded.

LEASES TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Copyright. A grant by the Federal government of the exclusive right to reproduce, publish, and sell literary or artistic work. 

Dispossess Notice. A notice to quit, served by a landlord on his tenant who has defaulted on his lease. 

Express Covenant. A promise on the part of either the landlord or the tenant fully stated in the lease. 

Implied Covenant. An agreement or promise not expressed in the lease, but understood from the nature of the agreement and the relations of the landlord and the tenant.

Patent Right. An exclusive right given by the Federal government to a person who has designed or created a new device or machine, to produce and sell the same.

Rights to Estovers. The right a tenant has to use the wood on the land for fuel, fences, and repairs to the building. 

Summary Proceeding. A court proceeding by which a tenant who has defaulted in performance of the lease may be forced to vacate the premises.

Tenantable. Fit to be used or inhabited for the purpose for which it was leased. 

What is a lease?

A lease is an agreement by which the right of possession of real property is transferred by the owner, called the lessor or landlord, to another party, called the lessee or tenant; for the use of which the lessee usually pays rent in money, goods, services, or otherwise. 

The estate or interest the lessee has in the property is called an estate for years or a leasehold. 

An estate may be created for a term of years, or months, or weeks. A leasehold interest in real property is classed as the tenant's personal prop- 521

erty unless otherwise provided by statute, but leased land is still the real property of the owner. 

When the owner of property grants it to another for a term measured by the life of the tenant, the owner, or another person, a legal life estate is created which is classed as real property. See p. 484. 

Example 1. Vance leased an apartment house from Harder for ten years with the privilege of renewal for another ten years. Vance's interest in this property is an estate for years. Had he leased this property either during his life or the life of Harder, his interest would have been a life estate. 

What are the requisites of a lease? 

1. Parties. There must be two competent parties named in the lease; one as owner or lessor, and the other as tenant or lessee. 

While it is not necessary to give the addresses of the parties in the lease, it is usually done as a means of identifying them. 

2. Form. Under the Statute of Frauds, in most states, a lease for a longer time than one year must be in writing. A lease for one year or less may be oral, and as to the Statute of Frauds, the time is computed from the beginning of the tenancy and not from the time when the lease is made. 

In a few states land may be leased for a limited number of years only, but the lease may be renewed, while in some states, long-term leases must be recorded. 

3. Property leased. That there may be no misunderstanding between owner and tenant, the lease should describe specifically the property leased. 

4. Terms and conditions. A lease should bear the date of making, state definitely when the tenant may have possession, and how long he may occupy the premises; as, from October 1, 19to 

September 30, 19-, inclusive. The amount of rent to be paid and the time and place of paying it should be agreed upon. Any conditions which the parties have agreed to should be specifically stated in the lease. 

The conditions most frequently inserted deal with: (a) the use which may be made of the property; (b) the respective duties of landlord and tenant as to repairs; (c) the tenant's right of renewal; (d) the tenant's obligation to pay water rents, which in most places are a lien on the land; (e) the landlord's right to put a "For Rent" sign on the premises and to

LEASES 

523 show them to prospective tenants before the expiration of the lease; (f) the tenant's obligation to obey all laws, ordinances, and regulations affecting the property. 

5. Execution. A written lease must be signed by both the lessor and the lessee, or by agents authorized to sign for them. A lease may be witnessed and it may be acknowledged before a notary public; but both are unnecessary unless required by law. Leases required to be recorded must be acknowledged. One should consult the laws of one's own state. 

What are the usual covenants in a lease?

A covenant in a lease is a legally binding promise or agreement, and it may be made by either the lessor or the lessee. The two kinds of covenants are express and implied.

The following are the usual covenants on the part of the lessee: 

1. To occupy the premises himself, and not to sublet the premises or assign the lease without the consent of the landlord. 

2. To use the premises as a dwelling or for the purpose stated in the lease. 

3. To pay the rent according to the terms of the lease. 

4. To surrender the premises at the expiration of the lease in as good condition, except the usual wear and tear, as when he took possession. 

The following are the usual covenants on the part of the lessor: 

1. That he will pay the taxes and assessments against the leased premises. However, the agreement between lessor and lessee may specify that the lessee shall pay all or a certain part of the taxes. 

2. That he will not interfere in any way with the possession and quiet enjoyment of the premises on the part of the lessee. 

3. In the absence of a covenant to repair, there is no duty on the landlord to repair the premises. In leases of residential property, particularly for short terms, it is customary for the landlord to make such covenant. 

4. In leases of space in apartment houses and office buildings, there is usually a covenant that the landlord will supply heat and elevator service. 

What are the duties and obligations of the tenant? 

1. Condition of premises. In the absence of any agreement to the contrary, the tenant is to take the premises as they are at the time he signs the lease. There is no implied covenant on the part of the landlord that

the premises are tenantable nor, in the absence of fraud or concealment by the landlord, is there an implied covenant that the premises are fit for their intended use. The landlord is liable only if damage results from a condition which the tenant could not have foreseen. 

Example 2. Lacy rented a store building. He opened up a music store, and displayed therein a number of musical instruments. He soon found that dampness in the building damaged the instruments and he tried to break his lease. It was held that the tenant must determine for himself the fitness of the premises he had had a chance to inspect. He was held on his lease. 

2. Repairs. Unless the lease contains a provision to the contrary, the tenant impliedly covenants to keep the premises in repair. In long-term leases of business or industrial property, the tenant usually makes an express covenant to repair; whereas in leases of residential property the obligation is usually assumed by the landlord. 

3. Use and care of premises. The tenant is entitled to exclusive use of the premises; he must take proper care of them, and he is liable for unnecessary waste. When a farm on which there is a wood lot rented, the tenant usually has the right to use the wood for fuel, fences, and repairs to the buildings. This is called "rights to estovers." 

4. Landlord's title. The tenant is estopped from denying his landlord's title to the premises. However, he may claim certain things of his own which are on the premises, and if his rights as a tenant are cut off without his fault, he may claim the emblements and have time to remove them even if he has to wait for them to ripen. 

What are the landlord's rights and obligations?

If the tenant has permanently annexed any fixtures, the removal of which would deface or injure the premises, the landlord may require him to leave them or pay damages; and, if the tenant surrenders possession without removing certain fixtures belonging to him and which he might have removed, the landlord may deny him the right to enter upon the premises later and take them. It is customary to include in a lease specific provisions as to fixtures and the right to remove them. The landlord may require that the tenant give up possession of the premises upon the expiration of the lease, and should the tenant, after signing the lease, refuse to comply with its terms, the landlord has a right to oust him from the premises and to recover damages. The landlord is obligated to comply with the terms of the lease, and should he default, the tenant has a right of action against him.

LEASES 

525 Has the tenant a right to assign his lease? 

The tenant may assign his lease unless it contains a provision prohibiting its assignment. If a lease is assigned, the landlord may look to either the original lessee or the assignee for the rent unless, by a provision in the lease or by agreement, the original lessee is released. The assignee is bound by the terms of the lease, and the lessor is obligated to him the same as to the original lessee, but this does not release the original lessee from his obligations to his lessor. 

Many leases contain a provision restricting the right to assign. 

The tenant is permitted to sublet the premises or any part of them unless the lease which he signed denies him this right. The tenant who sublets is still directly responsible to the lessor under the lease. 

What remedies has the lessor for nonpayment of rent? 

1. After the tenant has defaulted in paying his rent and there is an amount due, the landlord may take action against him to recover this amount. 

2. A lease usually contains a clause whereby the landlord has the right to take possession of the leased premises if the tenant failed to pay the rent. In any case, the landlord usually has a right to serve notice to vacate on a tenant who has defaulted in paying the rent, and he may have the tenant dispossessed. 

You, Charles R. Bassel, now a tenant in possession of my premises at 364 West 10th Street,

Mount Vernon, New York, are hereby notified to surrender possession of said premises on or before May 

1, 19-. On this day, I am taking possession of the premises. 

John C. Carmen 

Dated at Mount Vernon, N. Y. this first day of April, 19-.

DISPOSSESS NOTICE

A certain length of time, usually three days, after the landlord has served notice on the tenant to vacate he may be dispossessed on a court order by an officer of the law. This is usually a duty of the village or city marshal or the town constable, who will set the personal belongings of the tenant out on the street if necessary. 

A landlord who wishes to evict a tenant when the lease expires for default in paying rent, may obtain a process from some local court which is served upon the tenant, and if the court finds at the hearing that the landlord is entitled to possession of these premises, it will empower one of its officers to evict the tenant. This action is termed summary proceedings. 

3. In some states where land is leased for agricultural purposes, the landlord has a right of lien on the crops raised by the tenant who failed to pay his rent. 

4. Some states permit the landlord to seize any personal property belonging to the tenant which may be on the premises after he has defaulted in paying the rent. The property seized may be sold to satisfy the rent claim. This is called the landlord's right of distraint or distress. 

How may a lease be terminated?

A lease may be terminated in any one of the following ways: 

1. By expiration of time fixed in the lease. 

2. By the tenant's being released from his lease by the landlord and surrendering possession of the premises. 

3. By the tenant's failing to comply with the terms of the lease, thereby giving the landlord a right to terminate it and if necessary take action to have the tenant evicted. 

4. The lease is terminated by actual eviction if the landlord wrongfully deprives the tenant of the use of all or part of the premises; or by constructive eviction if the landlord creates conditions so obnoxious that the tenant vacates the premises. 

Examples of actual eviction are refusing the tenant access to the premises, or forcible possession by the landlord or by another with his consent. 

Examples of constructive eviction are creating a nuisance so intolerable as to make the premises untenantable; rendering the premises unsafe by excavation or demolition on or adjoining the property; continued failure to supply heat or water when obligated to do so. 

5. If a leased building is destroyed by fire, the lease terminates; and, in some cases, damage to the building due to any cause will

LEASES 

527 excuse the tenant from paying rent while it is being repaired, particularly if he cannot use it during this time. 

6. Should the landlord for any reason lose title to the leased premises, the lease terminates and the tenant has no redress. 

Examples would be where leased property was taken by a governmental unit under the right of eminent domain or where the property was sold under a mortgage or a judgment antedating the lease. Where the landlord voluntarily sells the leased premises or transfers title to another, the transfer is subject to the rights and interests of the tenant, and the lease is not necessarily terminated. 

In the absence of an agreement to the contrary, death of either party does not terminate a lease. It becomes binding upon the estate of the deceased. 

Who is entitled to the fixtures?

A fixture in this sense is an article actually or constructively annexed to the real property for use in connection therewith. 

Certain fixtures such as gas and water pipes, radiators, tubs, and basins, properly belong with the realty, and if the property is leased, such fixtures go with it. Certain other fixtures such as lights, window shades, stoves, and refrigerators when put in by the tenant are generally removable by him. 

As between the landlord and the tenant the assumption is that the tenant who puts in certain fixtures for his use in connection with the leased premises intends to remove them. The agreement, the mode of annexation, the use made of the fixtures, and the relation of the parties are factors in determining who is entitled to certain fixtures. 

The following rules are generally adhered to: 

1. If the fixture was annexed in such a way that its removal would deface or damage the premises, it may not be removed without the landlord's consent. The tenant who removes such fixtures lays himself liable for damages. 

2. When, by agreement with the landlord, the tenant is permitted to annex certain fixtures to the premises for his use as a tenant, he may remove them even if their removal does deface the property. 

3. A tenant who wishes to remove fixtures annexed by him must do so before giving up possession; otherwise he loses that right. 

4. When a building is rented for a particular purpose such as a store, and it is necessary to install certain equipment as shelves, it is understood that the tenant who installs such equipment may remove it.

What is a royalty?

A royalty is a percentage of the sales price or a price per unit paid by a publisher or a manufacturer to an author or a patentee for the privilege of producing and selling the publication or article protected by a copyright or patent. 

The term royalty is also applied to payments made to the owner of land for the privilege or taking therefrom oil, gas, or ores, the payments being based on the amount taken. It is not considered as rent although in some cases it may appear like rent. 

How are oil and mineral lands sometimes leased?

The owner of land on which a mineral or oil has been discovered may lease this land to a producer who will pay a certain sum per unit of weight or measure for the substance taken from the land and marketed. This sum paid is called royalty instead of rent. 

Example 3. Douglas leased his oil land to the West Oil Company for which they agreed to pay him sixty cents a barrel for all oil pumped from his land during a period of ten years with the privilege of renewing the lease for another period of ten years, at the current royalty prices for oil at the time. This is termed an oil lease. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A lease is a contract whereby one person acquires the use of property belonging to another person. 

2. Some leases must be written, others may be oral. 

3. A lease that does not conform with the law is void. 

4. A covenant in a lease is binding upon the one making it, either landlord or tenant. 

5. A tenant who continues to occupy the premises after his lease expires, except by special agreement, renews the lease by his act. 

6. The right to sublet or assign, if not to be permitted, must be specifically denied in the lease. 

7. A tenant can be evicted only on court order. 

8. A lease may be terminated by expiration of the agreement, eviction, destruction of premises, and taking of property by paramount title. 

9. There is no implied covenant of condition or fitness, and, in the absence of an express covenant, the tenant must take the premises as he finds them.

LEASES 

529 10. Without a special agreement, the landlord is not obligated to make repairs. 

11. Without a special agreement, the tenant has no right to remove fixtures he has attached to the premises. 

12. Royalties are sometimes paid in the place of rent for the use of copyrights, patents, or oil or mineral lands. 

13. All leaseholds and royalty rights are considered as personal property.

COMMENTS 

Acquiring interests in property, and controlling and disposing of these interests, are of much concern to many people. What we call real property is essential to our very existence. Under our economic system, it is acquired, controlled, and disposed of according to carefully formulated rules and laws which are the outgrowth of long years of experience. The most fundamental features of these rules and laws have been treated in the preceding chapter.

Comparatively few people are familiar enough with real-estate transactions to understand real property rights fully and how these rights should be administered and safeguarded. Every individual should possess a knowledge of the fundamentals of real-estate law, so that he may safeguard the interests of his own property. 

The time comes in the experience of nearly everyone when he must decide how a particular transaction shall be handled dealing with some real property rights, or when he shall engage a competent attorney to give the legal advice and the services required in connection with the transaction. 

Real-estate transactions frequently are complicated and the law regarding interest in real property is technical. It usually is better, therefore, to employ an attorney when real property rights are involved than to take any chances.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

And (or &) Company. Words indicating that other persons are associated in business with the one to whose name the words are added. 

Association. A union of individuals acting in concert for some definite purpose.

Co-owners. Two or more persons owning something together. 

Copartnership. Association of two or more persons in a firm. 

Limited Partnership. A partnership in which one partner's liability for the debts of the firm is limited to the amount he invested. 

Nontrading Partnership. A partnership not permitted to engage in buying and selling for profit making. 

Ostensible. Apparent, not real. Used to describe a person who is liable as a partner to persons dealing with the firm, but is not a partner in fact. 

Partnership by Estoppel. A partnership resulting from a person's acting so as to lead others to believe he is a partner. 

Trading Partnership. A partnership formed primarily for the purpose of buying and selling for profit. 

How may a partnership be defined?

A partnership may be defined as an association of two or more persons as co-owners and copartners in a business enterprise or venture for profit. Each member of the association is called a partner, and the partners together are often called a firm. The firm is usually described by the names of the partners, as "Hobart and Hines." When the number of partners is large, the word "Company" or "Co." may be used, unless forbidden by statute, with one or more names to indicate that other persons are associated with those named, as "J. W. Hobart and Company" or "Hobart, Hines &

Co." There is no limit by law to the number of partners in a firm. 534

How is a partnership usually formed?

Example 1. Two men, Baker and Earl, rented a store building together. 

Baker conducted a meat market on one side of the store, and Earl conducted a fruit and vegetable market on the other side. The lettering on the window read "Baker and Earl-Meats, Fruit, and Vegetables." They agreed that each should pay half the rent, that they should operate a delivery car in common, and that each should receive 10% of the other's business. This is a partnership by implication, whether the two men intended to create one or not. When a relation is established which legally is a partnership, the absence of an intent to be partners, or an actual intent not to be partners, will not prevent the necessary legal result. 

A partnership usually is formed whereby the contracting parties agree to combine their efforts, skills, knowledge, abilities, experience, and assets, or any of them, in some lawful business, and to share in some proportion the profits and losses arising therefrom. 

The contract of partnership may be oral or written, or it may result from implication.

When does a person become a partner by estoppel? 

Example 2. Chase was employed on a salary in Drake's store. Drake always consulted Chase on purchases of goods, loans, and other business, and, as a compliment, referred to Chase as "my partner" when they were talking with salesmen and other creditors. Chase is liable as a partner by estoppel to those who deal with Drake on the faith of his representation and not knowing the true relationship.

When a person, by words spoken or written, or by conduct, represents himself, or consents to another's representing him, as a partner in some business connection with another or others, he is liable as a partner to any person to whom such representation has been made, if such person acting on the faith of such representation, gave credit to the apparent partnership. There is no partnership relation between the partners themselves, but they are liable as partners to third persons.

The laws of the different states regulating partnerships vary considerably, except in states where the Uniform Partnership Law has been adopted. This law embodies the best features of the laws of the different states on partnerships, and it has been quite generally adopted. The discussion of partnership following is based on the Uniform Partnership Law.

Is the written contract of partnership necessary?

In most cases the written contract of partnership is not necessary. An oral contract or even an implied contract may be sufficient to bind the partners. But, every important contract of partnership should be written, and in most states, by the Statute of Frauds, a partnership contract for one year or more must be in writing. When the term of the partnership is measured by the life of any partner, or is indefinite, the contract need not be in writing, as the firm would be dissolved by law on the death of a partner. 

Some states, including New York, require a contract to be performed for a lifetime to be in writing. 

What are articles of copartnership?

The written partnership agreement which is executed by the partners is called articles of copartnership or partnership agreement. 

The partnership agreement, which must conform to contract requirements regarding competent parties, legal subject matter, agreement, and consideration, should contain all the agreements of the parties as to their relations to each other, their rights and duties in connection with the firm business and property, and their authority to represent the firm in dealing with third persons. 

What are the kinds of partners?

Partners may be designated as active, silent, secret, dormant, nominal, and limited. 

Active partner. An active partner is a partner in every sense; that is, he has a part in transacting the business of the partnership and he is known to third persons to be an active member of the firm. 

Silent partner. A silent partner is an actual partner in so far as the other partners or members of the firm are concerned, and he may be known to the outside world as a partner, but he takes no active part in the business itself. He assumes the role of partner without doing any of the work in connection with the business. 

He is liable the same as an active partner. 

Secret partner. A secret partner is one who takes an active part in the management of the business, but he conceals from the customers of the firm and from the public generally the fact that he

is in any way connected with the partnership. A secret partner is liable on firm debts, created by another partner in the firm business, even though the creditor did not know of the secret partner, or did not know that the debt was a firm obligation. As soon as the secret partner's connection with the firm is discovered, he may be sued on any obligation incurred while he was a partner. This is similar to the position of an undisclosed principal. 

Dormant partner. This is a term not exactly defined. It generally is the same as secret partner, but it sometimes is used as meaning silent partner.

Nominal partner. A nominal partner, sometimes called an ostensible partner, is one whose name appears as a member of the firm, with his own consent; and he is liable in every way as a partner, because he has allowed his name to be used. However, he has no interest whatever in the business, and as between the true owner of the business and himself there is no actual partnership. 

He is a partner in name only. 

Limited partner. A person may become a limited or special partner only in those states which have statutes providing for limited partnerships. The principal feature of a limited partnership is, that the one who is taken into the firm as a limited partner is permitted to contribute a certain amount of the capital and share in the profits without becoming liable in any way for the debts of the firm beyond the amount he contributed. A limited partner does not take part in the management of the business. 

The Uniform Limited Partnership Act requires the making and filing in a public office of a certificate setting forth all the particulars of the partnership, and the publication of a notice thereof in two newspapers in the county where the firm is to do business. Statutes in many states provide that "Ltd." shall follow the firm name to indicate that it is a limited partnership. Limited partnerships are not common in the United States, but in Canada they are numerous. 

What is the difference between a trading and a nontrading partnership?

The difference between a trading and a nontrading partnership is chiefly in the authority of a partner to bind the firm by contracts. 

In the trading firm any partner has implied authority to bind the

firm by contracts made in the scope of the firm's business, which is principally buying and selling for profit; such authority cannot be restricted by agreement between the partners. In a nontrading firm, as is created by lawyers for the practice of law, or by doctors for the practice of medicine, the doctrine of implied authority is presumed not to exist; such authority can result only from being conferred by the agreement of the partners, or by the usage of the business. In the former, the question of implied authority is a question of law; in the latter, a question of fact. 

What is a joint-stock company?

A joint-stock company is an association resembling a corporation, but in reality is a partnership. The capital in a joint-stock company is divided into shares, and the investment of each partner is represented by a certain number of shares. It operates the same as a corporation, but the reason it is not a corporation is that it does not receive a charter from the state under corporation laws, giving it a separate entity and the other attributes of a corporation; therefore, its shareholders are partners under the Uniform Partnership Law. Such companies are today quite generally regulated by statute. A comparison of joint-stock company, partnership, and corporations will be found on page 587. 

How is the existence of a partnership determined?

Authorities are not always in agreement on the rules for determining who are and who are not partners. The fact that they are to share the profits and losses is evidence that a partnership exists; however, this does not always create such a relation. The intention of the parties is a safe guide if it can be definitely determined.

The Uniform Partnership Law gives certain rules for determining the existence of a partnership. 

What are the advantages and disadvantages of a partnership? 

Some of the possible advantages resulting from a partnership are as follows: 

1. More working capital may be made available for developing and expanding the business.

2. The combining of the experiences, skills, and abilities of the different partners may result in greater efficiency. 

3. Division of responsibility and duties with greater personal interest. 

4. Increased business prestige and improved credit possibilities. 

5. More efficient management resulting in greater economy. 

6. Greater possibilities for enlarging the scope of the business. 

Some of the disadvantages resulting from a partnership are: 

1. Each partner as a general agent of the firm may bind the other partner in a contract. If he uses poor judgment, all must suffer. 

2. Partners must work together, and, if they cannot agree, the business usually suffers. 

3. Each partner is individually liable for all his firm's obligations, and his private property may be taken to pay firm debts. 

4. Although they may share equally in the profits, one partner may make a far greater contribution in the way of ability, time, effort, etc., to the business than the other partner or partners without any greater reward. 

5. A partner has freedom an employee does not enjoy, and he may abuse his privileges to the detriment of the other partners and the business generally.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. When two or more persons become associated together as coowners and operators of a business for profit, they become partners and a partnership exists. 

2. A partnership may be formed by a contract either oral or written, and any person who is competent to contract may become a partner. 

3. As a rule, persons who are not partners as between themselves are not partners as to third persons. The exception is the case of a person who represents himself, or allows himself to be represented, as a partner, which makes him liable to third persons by estoppel. 

4. Only limited partners are not liable individually for the debts of the partnership. 

5. Intention of the parties is the principal test in determining whether or not a partnership exists. An association of persons who do not share in the profits of a business is not a partnership. 

6. Sharing the profits does not of itself create a partnership. 

7. A person seeking to hold one liable as a partner by estoppel, must show that he entered into this transaction on the faith of the representations which create the estoppel.

8. A partnership is either a trading or a nontrading partnership, depending upon the purpose for which it is organized. 

9. Shareholders in a joint-stock company are in reality partners in a partnership. 

10. An active partner is a general agent for his firm and as such he may bind his copartners by the contracts he negotiates.

RIGHTS, DUTIES, AND LIABILITIES OF 

PARTNERS

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Confession of Judgment. Formal written consent by a debtor that judgment may be entered against him by the creditor without litigation. 

Course of the Business. Business that is normally and regularly transacted by the firm. 

Good Faith. Sincere, honest, and upright conduct towards another. 

Good Will. The value of an established business arising from its name, reputation, expectation of patronage, and similar intangible assets. 

Implied Powers. Powers not specified but understood to exist from circumstances or conditions. 

Property Rights. The rights of a person to use or dispose of property because he is the owner of, or has an interest in, it. 

What are the rights of a partner?

Each partner has certain rights as a member of the firm. Just what these rights are depends on the kind of partnership and the agreement entered into by the partners. In a regular partnership where the members are all active partners each partner has the following rights: 

1. Share in the management and the profits. A partner has a right to have a part in the management of the business and to share in the profits. Sharing in the profits implies a sharing of the losses. In the absence of a definite agreement, it is assumed that the partners shall share equally, both in the management of the business and in the profits and losses. 

2. A partner may buy and sell. Any one of the partners, as general agent for his firm, may buy any kind of property, the buying of which is clearly within the regular course of the partnership 542

RIGHTS, DUTIES, AND LIABILITIES OF PARTNERS 543 

business, and all the partners will be bound in the transaction. 

Likewise, each partner may sell the whole or any part of the partnership property if such sale comes clearly within the scope of the regular partnership business. A partner may not dispose of the business as a whole or of the good will of the business or real property belonging to the firm. In the conveyance of the firm's real property all the partners must sign the deed unless one partner has power of attorney to sign given to him by the other partners. 

Example 1. Linn and Brooks owned and operated a hardware store as active partners. One partner could sell the entire stock in the regular way, but not the store fixtures or the building, as such a transaction would not be in the regular course of the business. Both partners would have to be parties to a transaction involving the purchase or sale of any property outside of the regular course of the partnership business. 

3. Property rights. All property brought into the partnership originally by the partners and all property subsequently acquired by them with partnership funds is partnership property. Real property may be acquired in the firm name. All the partners must join in a deed of such property. 

4. Capital rights. The partnership capital consists of the properties, including cash, contributed by the partners at the beginning of business or that may be contributed later. No partner may claim as his own any particular article of property belonging to the partnership. The partners are owners "in common" of all partnership property. This does not keep a partner from using his own property in connection with the partnership, either for hire or otherwise, and as it is his own he may do as he wills with it. 

Example 2. Hall and Roberts, two master painters, joined forces in a partnership. The ladders, tackle, scaffolding, and tools formerly owned by each partner became the property of the new firm. Roberts owned an automobile which he used in the business for which it was agreed he should charge the firm 6¢ a mile while in its service. Roberts may do as he wills with this car in or out of the service. 

5. Right to indemnity. A partner who pays out of his own funds some item of expense in connection with the partnership, or pays more than his share of the expenses or debts, has a right to demand indemnity from the other partners for their share.

6. Compensation rights. The partnership agreement usually contains a clause specifying that each partner shall have a drawing account of a certain amount or a certain salary payable weekly or monthly. In the absence of a special agreement, a partner who does extra work or more than his share of the work, or works overtime is not entitled to extra compensation, and he may not claim it. 

Example 3. Harder and Devoe were partners in the grocery business. 

Harder was ill for two months during which time Devoe worked extra hard and overtime, but he is not entitled to any extra compensation himself unless Harder agrees to it. 

7. Right to receive and pay money and to issue and endorse negotiable paper. A partner may receive money on account from customers, make settlements with them, and give receipts. He may also give out the firm's money in the payment of the firm's debts. If the partnership funds are deposited in a bank, some plan must be agreed upon by the partners for handling the bank account and for drawing and signing partnership checks. 

Example 4. Wolsey and Horton are engaged as copartners in farming. 

Wolsey bought a corn harvester and gave a ninety-day note in payment. 

He signed the note "Wolsey and Horton per J. C. Wolsey." As theirs is a nontrading partnership, Wolsey had no right to give this note. Instead both partners should have signed the note. In a trading partnership, Wolsey would have this right. 

In a trading partnership a partner may issue, accept, and endorse negotiable paper in the name of the firm, and he may borrow money on the credit of the firm, and mortgage the firm's property to secure the loan. 

In a nontrading partnership a partner is without this implied power. 

8. A partner may retire from the firm or sell his interest. A partner may retire from the firm, or sell his interest, at any time. 

Even if the partnership articles provide that the partnership shall continue for a stated time, a partner may retire or sell out before that time, although he would be liable to the other partner for breach of contract. If no term of duration is specified, a partner may retire without liability to his partners. In some states, where the Uniform Law is not in force, a partner may not retire or sell out in violation of the partnership articles. 

The retirement of a partner or a sale of his interest in the firm, either to another partner or to a third person, effects a dissolution of the firm. The

RIGHTS, DUTIES, AND LIABILITIES OF PARTNERS 545 

purchaser of a partner's interest does not acquire the right to be taken into the firm as a partner, since partners have an absolute right to choose their copartners. The purchaser acquires only the right to receive his vendor's share of the firm's assets after firm debts are paid. If the purchaser is admitted to partnership by the other members of the firm, it is not a continuation of the firm but the creation of a new one. 

What are the duties of a partner? 

1. Good faith. The partner must show good faith in his relations with the other partners. The reason for this is obvious when one realizes that each partner acts as agent in the transacting of the firm's business, and that all the partners are bound by the acts of each partner in matters pertaining to the business. 

Example 5. Morley and Waldo were partners in the building business. 

They had agreed that all bids should be made and contracts signed by both partners. Morley alone contracted to build a house for a friend of his at a low price and the firm lost $600 on the work. The contract was binding on the firm, as Morley had apparent authority to make it, but the loss should fall on Morley alone, as he has acted in bad faith and in violation of the partnership agreement. 

2. Records of transactions must be kept. The firm must keep books of account, and it is the duty of each partner to enter all his transactions for the firm or to see that they are entered upon these books. This is necessary that each partner may know of all the transactions in the business. A partner may examine the records of the firm or demand an accounting for a given period at any time. 

3. A partner must account for profit. Each partner must account to the other partners for any profits resulting directly or indirectly from any business which he transacted for his firm. 

Example 6. Wendel, a partner in the firm of Wendel, Heath, and Co., dealers in automobile supplies, while on his vacation, purchased in his own name a quantity of tires. When he returned, tires showed a marked increase in price and he turned those he had purchased over to his firm at the increased price. Heath and the other partners may require Wendel to account to them for any profits he made from this transaction. 

4. A partner must devote his time to the business. In the absence of an agreement to the contrary, each partner must devote his full time to the business of the partnership; and he must not

have other interests in conflict with or detrimental to the business of the partnership. 

5. Partners must be kept informed. It is the duty of each partner to inform the other members of the firm regarding matters affecting the business of the partnership that he alone may know about, and particularly for the reason that notice by a third party to one partner is notice to all partners. 

What are some things a partner may not do?

There are certain things one partner may not do without the consent of his copartners: 

1. One partner may not bind his firm in any contract of guaranty, either to pay his personal debts or the debt of another, and should he make such a guaranty, he alone is liable. 

2. One partner has no power to bind his firm in an agreement to submit a claim or dispute to arbitration, or in a confession of judgment. All partners must act together in such matters. 

Example 7. Sanders, a partner in the firm of Welch, Sanders, & Co., confessed judgment in the name of his firm to R. D. Lord for a questionable claim of $500 Lord had against Sanders's firm. Neither the firm nor the partners are bound by this judgment, which is worthless. 

3. One partner has no power to assign all the property of the firm to pay the firm's debts, unless the other partners cannot be reached, and an emergency exists. 

Example 8. Havens and Young were partners in the drug business, and 

Havens mysteriously disappeared and nothing was heard of him. Creditors of the firm threatened bankruptcy proceedings, and Young settled their claims by assigning to them all the partnership property, which under the circumstances he had a right to do. 

What is the liability of a partner?

Each partner in a regular partnership, regardless of whether he is an active, a silent, a secret, or a nominal partner, is liable for all the debts of the partnership. This means that if the partnership property is not sufficient to meet partnership debts, the individual partner's property may be taken to pay them, and the partner who has property of his own may have all the partnership debts to pay.

RIGHTS, DUTIES, AND LIABILITIES OF PARTNERS 547 

However, he is entitled to indemnity from his copartners if he can. collect from them. The only exception to this rule is in case of a limited partner. See page 537. 

What is the liability of an incoming partner?

The Uniform Partnership Law provides that a person admitted as a partner into an existing partnership is liable for the obligations of the partnership arising before his admission, except that his liability in such cases is limited to partnership property; that is, his private property cannot be taken to pay such obligations. 

However, the new partner is individually liable for all the debts incurred after he became a member of the firm. 

What is the liability of a retiring partner?

A retiring partner remains liable for debts of the firm contracted while he was a partner, even though the continuing partners or the purchaser of the retiring partner's interest may have agreed to assume and be responsible for such debts. As between themselves the assumption is valid, and, if the retiring partner has to pay the debts, he is entitled to reimbursement; but, as to creditors, the assumption does not relieve the retiring partner from liability. 

What is the effect of notice on liability of partners? 

Neither the individual partners nor the firm will be liable for any particular act of a partner, if fair notice that such acts are forbidden is given by the copartners to the person with whom the partner deals. This notice must be given before the partner acts. 

Are partners liable for the fraud of copartner?

The partners are liable for the fraud and the false representation of one partner when they are made in the course of the firm's business. One partner cannot be held for the wrongful acts of another partner unless they were done within the proper scope of the business of the partnership, or were authorized or adopted by him. The partnership is liable for civil torts of a partner and of an agent employed by the partnership when committed in the course of the firm's business.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A partner, as agent, may bind his firm in transactions in the course of the business. 

2. The firm is not bound in a transaction in which the third person knew that the partner had exceeded his authority. 

3. In a regular partnership each partner may transact any partnership business and share in the profits therefrom. 

4. A partner, who pays from his own funds the expenses or debts of the firm, may claim indemnity from his copartners. 

5. In the absence of an agreement with his copartners, one partner may not claim extra compensation for extra work. He may hire extra help for which his firm will have to pay. 

6. In a trading partnership, one partner may buy and sell, collect and pay bills, borrow money, sign or endorse negotiable instruments within the course of the business. 

7. In a nontrading partnership, one partner has no implied authority to bind the firm in any business outside of the purposes for which the partnership was formed. All partners must authorize, ratify, or join in such transactions. 

8. Partners are duty bound to act in good faith towards each other. 

9. A notice to one partner of a firm is notice to all partners. 

10. Records of partnership transactions must be kept, and any partner may examine them or demand an accounting at any time. 

11. A partner cannot make a secret personal profit out of any partnership transaction, nor can he engage in a business which competes with the partnership. Any profits so received must be accounted for to the other partners. 

12. A regular partner must devote his full time to the business, and have no outside interest that conflicts with the interest of his firm. 

13. The partners are not bound by the acts of one partner when he guarantees the payment of his own or a third party's debt; submits a partnership matter to arbitration; or gives a confession of judgment for a claim against his firm. 

14. One partner has the power to assign all the partnership property to pay the firm's debts when an emergency exists and the other partners cannot be reached.

RIGHTS, DUTIES, AND LIABILITIES OF PARTNERS 549 

15. Each partner in a regular partnership is liable for all partnership debts. 

16. Partners are liable for the acts of a copartner within the course of the business, unless notice is given to third persons prohibiting the partner's right to act. 

17. The partnership is liable for fraud or torts of a partner or agent acting within the scope of the business.

TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Dissolution of Partnership. The breaking up of the partnership and a discontinuance of the business. 

Firm Debts. Debts owed by a partnership firm. 

Individual Debts. Debts owed by a partner on his personal or individual account.

Mutual Consent. Consent or agreement of all the partners to some plan or proposition.

Retiring Partner. A partner who discontinues as a member of the firm. 

Statutory Regulations. Regulations or rules prescribed by a statute law. 

Surviving Partner. The partner left in the firm to close up its affairs after the death of a copartner. 

How may a partnership be dissolved?

The articles of copartnership usually state how long the partnership shall continue. There are many circumstances, however, which may operate to terminate the partnership created by these articles before the time set therein for its duration has expired. 

When this happens the partnership is said to be dissolved. 

A partnership may be dissolved in any one of the following ways: 

1. By provisions in the articles of copartnership. When the time for which the partnership was formed has expired, it is automatically dissolved, unless the partners agree to continue it. 

When a partnership is formed for a definite purpose, it terminates and is dissolved when that purpose is accomplished. When a partnership is formed for no definite period or for no definite purpose, any partner may terminate it at any time by giving notice to the other partners of his intention to do so. 

2. By mutual consent of all the partners. The partners may 552

agree among themselves to dissolve the partnership at any time, regardless of whether or not the period for which it was formed has elapsed. This agreement will usually carry with it a plan for closing up all partnership affairs, meeting the obligations, and distributing among the partners what remains of the partnership property. 

3. By the act of one or more of the partners. When one partner makes an assignment of his interest in the partnership for the benefit of his creditors, or becomes a bankrupt, or his creditors take his property to pay his debts, or in any case when his property passes beyond his control, he is no longer a partner and the partnership is dissolved. Under such circumstances as these this partner is not liable to the other partners for a breach of any provisions in the partnership agreement. 

Example 1. Three partners were engaged in a manufacturing business. 

One partner, after continuing in the firm for two years, went away and later wrote the other partners to do as they pleased with the business, he was through. The other two partners continued the business, but this act of one partner caused a dissolution of the old partnership, and by the other partners continuing a new partnership was formed. 

4. By a change in the partnership. When a partner withdraws from the firm, or transfers his interests to a third party, such an act dissolves the partnership. Should one partner sell his interest to a third party whom the remaining members of the firm accept as a partner, the old partnership is dissolved and a new one formed. 

5. By the decree of a court of equity. The court will decree a dissolution of a partnership for good cause upon the application of one or more of the partners.

The usual causes for which the court will decree a dissolution are: (a) when the partnership was entered into through fraud or for illegal purposes; (b) when the conduct of one of the partners is such as to jeopardize materially the business of the partnership; (c) when one of the partners becomes insane or mentally unfit to transact partnership business; (d) when one of the partners becomes physically unfit to do his part as a partner; (e) when the undertaking for which the partnership was created. failed; or (f) according to the Uniform Partnership Law, "when a partner willfully or persistently commits a breach of the partnership agreement, or

otherwise so conducts himself in matters relating to the partnership business that it is not reasonably practical to carry on the business in partnership with him." 

6. By operation of law. A partnership is dissolved by operation of law when either the partnership itself or one of the partners becomes bankrupt. In case the partnership becomes bankrupt, the trustee in bankruptcy appointed by the court will take over the property and the business of the partnership and close up its affairs according to law. Should a partner become bankrupt, he loses control of his property and he is no longer a partner. 

A partnership is also dissolved by operation of law if one of the partners dies. Title to the firm's property remains in control of the surviving partners for the purpose of settling the affairs of the partnership. After the firm's debts are paid, what remains of the deceased partner's share of the property goes to his estate, and dissolution is complete. The articles of copartnership may provide how the surviving partner shall close out the business, and when such provision is made, it must be followed. 

A partnership is dissolved by operation of law when the business in which it is engaged, though lawful when the partnership was formed, later became unlawful as a result of a new law being passed. 

Example 2. Wendel and King were partners in the distribution of loose milk to eating places. A law was passed prohibiting the distribution of loose milk for any purpose. As the purpose for which the partnership was formed became illegal, the partnership is dissolved by operation of law. 

When is a notice of dissolution necessary? 

A partner who retires from a business that is to be continued by a new firm must, for his own protection, see that notice is given, either orally or in writing, to those who have had dealings with the old firm. This notice is necessary to protect him against further liability. By giving this notice he is not relieved from his liability for the debts and contracts of the old firm, but he is relieved from any obligations incurred by the new firm. 

How should notice of dissolution be given?

The usual way of giving notice to customers of the firm or to those with whom the firm have dealt is to have a regular notice

printed and mail copies of it to all concerned. If a customer has actual knowledge of a partner's retiring, it is not necessary to send notice to him. Notice to the general public is given through a newspaper of general circulation in the community where the firm is located. This notice may read as follows:

Notice is hereby given that the partnership heretofore existing between James C. Wilson, Horace E. Crane, and Wilbur Grant, under the name of Wilson, Crane, & Co., has been dissolved by the retirement of James C. Wilson from the firm. The business will be continued as usual under the firm name of H. E. Crane & Co. All old accounts are payable to or by the new firm, which will also complete all unfinished contracts.

How are the affairs of a dissolved partnership settled? 

When a partnership business is for any reason discontinued, the partner or partners who take charge of winding up the business should notify all people who have dealt with the firm that its dissolution has taken place and that concluding the business is in process. The business is usually wound up by disposing of all existing contracts, collecting outstanding accounts, converting all assets, so far as possible, into cash, paying all claims against the firm, and finally making a distribution of profits among the partners. 

After all this has been done, each partner's investment or such portion of it as remains is returned to him, and the business is finally closed. If the final settlement shows that firm assets are insufficient to pay firm debts, the deficit must be made up by the partners out of their individual property, the liability being divided according to their several interests in the firm. 

What are the usual remedies against a partnership?

The law considers a partnership to be a collection of individuals; and, in the absence of special statutory regulations, it must be sued not in the firm name, but in the name of the persons composing it. Some states permit partnerships to be sued in the firm name. In states where this is not permitted, any legal action to

collect a debt is taken against the members of a partnership the same as against an individual.

When there are firm creditors and creditors of the individual partners, the law provides that firm property shall be taken first to pay firm debts and any surplus remaining may be claimed by the creditors of the individual partners; but, if there is not sufficient property to satisfy the firm creditors, and there is a surplus of individual property after the individual creditors have been satisfied, this surplus of individual property may be taken to pay firm debts. In case there are no partnership assets, the firm creditors and the individual creditors may share equally in the individual assets of any partner. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A partnership may be dissolved: a. By provision in the articles of copartnership b. By the mutual consent of all the partners c. By the acts of one or more of the partners d. By a change in the partnership e. By the decree of a court of equity: 

1. Fraudulent or illegal partnership 

2. Wrongful conduct of a partner 

3. A partner becoming insane 

4. A partner becoming physically unfit 

5. When the partnership undertaking fails f. By operation of law: 

1. Bankruptcy of the partnership or of a partner 

2. Death of a partner 

3. The business becoming unlawful 

2. When a partnership is dissolved, the affairs of the partnership are wound up, and the business is discontinued, or a new partnership may continue the business. 

3. A partner who retires or withdraws from a partnership is still liable for the debts due creditors of the firm. 

4. Notice of dissolution should be given to all who have had dealings with the firm, and a notice to the general public should be published in a newspaper as a means of protecting the retiring partner from further liability and future creditors against possible loss.

5. A partnership business is wound up by certain of the partners disposing of existing contracts, reducing the assets to cash, collecting and paying all bills, distributing the profits among the partners, and finally returning to each partner his portion of the remaining investment. When a partnership is dissolved and firm assets are insufficient to pay firm debts, the deficit must be made up by the partners individually. 

6. Partnership property is liable for firm debts, and the individual partner's property is liable for his individual debts. The remaining property in either case is liable for the debts still unpaid. 

7. A partnership must be sued in the names of the partners, unless the law permits it to be sued in the firm name.
