COMMENTS An individual who owns and operates his own business may conduct it about as he wishes, so long as he complies with the law. This type of ownership is called sole proprietorship. In all transactions pertaining to this particular business he is accountable to no one and he obligates no one other than himself.

Some of the reasons for conducting business under a partnership type of organization are that an individual owner may associate others with him in a plan for business expansion which requires additional capital; or that persons of different abilities, skills, or experience may be brought together in a partnership for some purpose to their mutual advantage; or that an overworked owner of a business may wish to share his responsibilities with a trusted employee whom he will associate with him as a partner. There are other reasons why persons become associated in partnerships, and as a result there are many partnerships in operation. 

The particular business relationship of persons who become associated as partners in some undertaking calls for a very definite understanding on the part of those who are thus associated, regarding their duties and obligations to each other and to third parties, and also regarding their rights as partners. It is pertaining to all these matters as well as to the business dealings of the partnership firm, that rules and laws are necessary for the guidance and protection of the partners and of those with whom they deal. 

Partnerships still have a prominent place in our business life, but anyone who has studied this type of business organization must have been impressed with some of the objections to partnership management and control of a business, such as the complexity of the law of partnership, the heavy liability of a partner for the acts of his copartners, and the personal liability for debts of the firm. It is only when conditions are ideal that this type of business organization will prove to be entirely advantageous to the partners. Now it is becoming common to incorporate even a small business instead of doing business as partners. All of these matters should be considered seriously by anyone who contemplates becoming a partner in a business enterprise.

CORPORATIONS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Certificate of Incorporation. A document setting out the name of a proposed corporation, its incorporators, its powers, its stock structure, and other details, which, when accepted and approved by proper state authority, becomes the charter of the corporation. 

Charter. Broadly, the power conferred by the state on a group of individuals to become and act as a corporation. Specifically, the document, approved by the state, showing the name, powers, and other information regarding a corporation. 

Incorporators. Persons who are instrumental in organizing a corporation and who become members thereof. 

Par Value. The amount specified on the face of a certificate of stock as the value of each share. 

Stock Certificate. A document representing a member's interest in a corporation showing the names of the corporation and the stockholder, the number and class of shares owned, and any other necessary information. It is issued by the corporation under its seal and signed by corporate officials, usually the president and secretary. 

What is a corporation?

A corporation is an organization of individuals, called stockholders, who are united by authority of law into one body, under a special name for a definite purpose. A corporation has the power of continuous existence, and of acting in all its business transactions as an individual. 

How may a corporation be formed?

A corporation may be formed by a number of persons agreeing among themselves on a plan and a purpose of forming an organization for some specific purpose. The law requires that a certain part 562

CORPORATIONS 

563 of this number, usually two thirds, be residents of the state in which the organization is to operate. The minimum number of persons making application for such an organization differs in the various states, usually three or five. Any person who has the capacity to enter into a binding contract may be an incorporator. 

The laws of the different states vary somewhat in the requirements and in the manner of procedure in forming a corporation, but as a rule, after all preliminary plans have been made, the next step is to send an application for a charter to the secretary or other designated official of the state in which the corporation is to be chartered. If the application is granted and the corporation is chartered, a duplicate copy of the charter is required to be filed with some county officer, usually the county clerk, in the county in which the corporation has its main office. 

What does the application for a charter include?

The usual method of making application for a charter is to have an attorney prepare a proposed certificate of incorporation, which is executed and sent to the proper state official to be filed. The request for filing is the application for the charter. If the certificate is approved and filed, the charter is granted. 

The certificate must be signed by the incorporators, acknowledged before a notary public, and, with the necessary fee, sent to the proper state official. If approved and filed, the certificate is the charter of the corporation.

Amendment of the charter. 

When a certificate of incorporation has been approved and filed, it can be amended only by proceedings similar to those taken at the original incorporation. The proposed amendments must be prepared, must be approved by the directors and stockholders, and a certificate thereof sent to a state official, whose approval is necessary before the amendments can become effective. 

Can a corporation exist without securing a charter from the state? 

When a corporation is organized in full compliance with all statutory requirements, it is a corporation de jure (legally). The powers, rights and duties of the corporation itself and of its stockholders are those provided by law or by the charter. When a bona fide attempt has been made to organize a corporation under the

laws and when the legal requirements have been generally or substantially complied with, but the organization is defective in some particulars, the actual exercise of the supposed corporate powers creates a corporation de facto (in fact). Such a corporation is subject to attack by the state and its existence may be terminated; but in the absence of such attack, it is a corporation for practical purposes. However, one or more individuals cannot adopt a corporate form of organization and do business under a corporate name, without any attempt to comply with legal requirements, and thereby create a corporation de facto. Such an organization is not a corporation of any kind, and the members are liable for their acts and contracts, either as partners or on principles of agency. 

What are the principal features of a corporation?

The following features make the corporate form of business organization so attractive that not only large enterprises but many small ones also are operated as corporations. 

1. A corporation has the power of continuous existence. That is, a change in the membership of a corporation does not dissolve it. 

2. Any stockholder may sell or transfer his stock to another without affecting the organization. 

3. A stockholder is not personally liable for the debts of the corporation. If he has paid in full for his stock, he cannot be called upon for further payments; although, if the corporation is insolvent, he will lose whatever he has invested.

What are the different kinds of corporations? 

There are two principal kinds of corporations: (1) public and (2) private. 

1. Public corporations, sometimes called municipal corporations, are created for the purpose of operating and managing public or governmental business. Counties, cities, towns, villages, and school districts are examples of public corporations. Public corporations have authority under the laws of the state to manage public affairs within their jurisdiction. They may take and hold property and may sue and be sued in their corporate name. A public corporation receives its charter from the state the same as a private corporation. It has no stock or stockholders, and does not operate for profit.

CORPORATIONS 

565 2. Private corporations are created for the purpose of conducting affairs in which the members are interested as private parties. Private corporations are either (a) stock, or (b) nonstock corporations. (a) A stock corporation is formed primarily for profit making. It has a capital stock divided into a certain number of parts called shares of stock, and membership in the corporation is acquired by the purchase of some of these shares. Printed stock certificates issued to each stockholder are used to represent the number of shares he owns. This certificate can be transferred from one party to another without the consent of the officers or other members of the corporation, but so far as the corporation is concerned, the transferee is not the owner until the old certificate is surrendered to the corporation, the transfer is entered on the books of the corporation, and a new certificate issued. (b) A nonstock corporation is not organized for profit making, but instead, it is organized for social, religious, educational, charitable, or mutual benefit purposes. Examples are clubs, churches, hospitals, historical societies, library associations, alumni organizations and similar associations for public or mutual benefit. A person becomes a member by being admitted to the organization upon the consent of the other members or of the organizers.

Another kind of private corporation is called a quasipublic corporation. 

Utility companies such as electric light and power companies, gas companies, telephone and telegraph companies, and transportation companies are examples of quasipublic corporations. They are private because they are operated for profit for the benefit of their stockholders, but they are quasipublic because they are subject to regulation by the state. They must receive permission from the state to conduct their business, usually within a specified territory, and their rates and methods of doing business are controlled by the state because of the public service they render. 

Corporations are further classified as domestic and foreign. In the state where a corporation has its home office it is a domestic corporation, but in all other states where it transacts business it is a foreign corporation. 

What is a stock certificate?

When a person buys stock in a corporation, a certificate is issued or transferred to him showing the number of shares he has and such other data as will serve to identify the stock. Each certificate is signed by the president and secretary or treasurer of the corporation and sealed with the corporate seal.

What is the difference between par-value and no-par-value stock? 

Par-value stock shows a specific value on the certificate as the face or par-value of each share. For example, 10 shares-par

value $100 each. A certificate for no-par-value stock simply shows the number of shares without mentioning any par value. 

Example 1. The X Corporation was organized with a capital stock of $100,000 divided into 1,000 shares of $100 each. Therefore, the par value of each share is $100. 

Example 2. The Y Corporation was organized and 5,000 shares of nopar-value stock were subscribed for at $10 per share. The first price at which this stock was sold was $10 per share, but after the first sale, its value will depend on the market price. The certificate itself shows no value whatever.

The purchaser of stock should remember that the par value stated in the certificate is no indication of the real value. The market value of a stock is what it will sell for on a stock exchange. The book value is the amount each share would be worth if all the corporate assets were sold for cash, all debts paid, and the surplus divided pro rata among the stockholders. The par value bears no relation to these.

Example 3. The Z Corporation was organized with a capital stock of $50,000 divided into 500 shares of the par value of $100 per share. It had assets of the value of $40,000 and debts of $15,000. The book value of the shares of Z Corporation is $50 per share. The same would be true if the stock had been issued with no par value. 

What is the difference between common and preferred stock? 

Common stock. The capital stock of a corporation may be divided between common stock and preferred stock, or only one kind of stock may be issued, in which case it is called common stock or capital stock. Except as otherwise provided in the charter, common stockholders are entitled to all the rights of stockholders, including the right to vote and to act as directors, and are entitled to share in all the profits of the corporation without limit as to amount.

Preferred stock. Preferred stock, as the term implies, entitles the holder to a preference in some particular, usually in the division of the profits or in the distribution of assets in case the corporation discontinues and its assets are liquidated. 

The different kinds of preferred stock are: (a) straight preferred,

CORPORATIONS 567 (b) cumulative preferred, (c) participating and nonparticipating preferred, and (d) convertible preferred. (a) Straight preferred stock has a preferred claim to dividends up to the rate specified before a dividend can be paid on common stock.

Example 4. A holder of $5 preferred stock is entitled to receive a dividend of $5 a share in one fiscal year, before anything can be paid on the common stock. The preferred stock is entitled to dividends up to the agreed amount and no more. All profits over that amount may be paid to common stockholders. (b) Cumulative preferred stock is entitled to full dividend payment before any dividend may be paid on the common stock; that is, if the net earnings of the corporation during any period are insufficient to pay the full dividend on this stock, the unpaid dividends are allowed to accumulate and must be paid in full before the common stock is entitled to any dividend. (c) Participating preferred stock may share in the profits with the common stock after the preferred dividends are fully paid, and a common stock dividend equal to the preferred dividend has been paid. What remains of the net profits may be divided between the two classes of stock, unless the charter limits the dividends that may be paid on the preferred stock. Preferred stock that does not share in the remaining net profits after all regular dividends are paid is called nonparticipating preferred stock. It may also be preferred in the distribution of the assets after liquidation. (d) Convertible preferred stock may be exchanged for common stock, if the stockholder so desires, on such basis as the charter provides. The conversion privilege is attractive to investors, as it permits them to enjoy the preference of preferred stock so long as it is to their interest; but, if the corporation is prosperous, they may exchange all or part of their stock for common stock and share in the prosperity. 

What is treasury stock?

Treasury stock is stock that has been authorized but not sold, or that has been bought in by the corporation and held in reserve. 

The directors of the corporation may market it at such time as the

corporation has need for additional capital. While this stock is held in reserve, it is not entitled to a dividend and has no vote. A corporation usually has the power to buy in and hold, or retire its own stock.

What are some advantages and disadvantages of the corporation? 

There are certain rather outstanding advantages of the business corporation which should be noted. 

1. The stockholders' liability is limited to the amount of stock he owns. That is, there is no personal liability beyond the amount a stockholder has paid or agreed to pay for his stock. 

2. A large amount of capital may be more easily obtained because the type of organization makes it possible to interest more people. 

3. A corporation is said to have the power of perpetual succession, or the power to exist indefinitely, independent of its stockholders. 

4. Shares of stock in a corporation may be transferred any time without the consent of other members of the organization or without affecting the organization. 

5. The stockholders elect the directors who in turn select the officers. 

The most efficient officers may be selected and should any of them prove to be inefficient a change may be made. 

There are also certain disadvantages that a corporation may have. 

1. A corporation, often referred to as an "artificial person," is considered rather impersonal and as a result it is shown little consideration or sympathy in our social order. 

2. A corporation is a creature of the law and as such it is held under rigid governmental control. 

3. Large fees and taxes create a real problem for corporation management. 

4. The plan of corporation organization and management is unwieldy and cannot be as easily adjusted to changing conditions as can a single proprietorship or a partnership.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. A corporation is an organization of individuals created under authority of the law for a certain purpose. 

2. A corporation is composed of a group of persons known as stockholders.

CORPORATIONS 

569 3. A person becomes a member of a business corporation by becoming the owner of shares of stock. 

4. A corporation is formed according to the laws of the state wherein it establishes its home office. 

5. A corporation exists legally only after it receives its charter from the state wherein it is located. 

6. A corporation's activities are limited to those specified in its charter or implied therefrom. 

7. Corporations are either public or private, and private corporations are either stock or nonstock corporations. 

8. Par-value stock has a face value which may not be the same as its market value. No-par-value stock has only a market value. 

9. The advantages of a corporation are: Limited liability of stockholders, easier to obtain necessary capital, continuous existence, change in membership does not dissolve company, and more efficient management. 

10. The principal disadvantages are: Lack of popular favor, rigid governmental control, large fees and taxes, and lack of flexibility.

POWERS AND LIABILITIES OF CORPORATIONS TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Artificial Person. A title ascribed to a group of persons organized into one body under authority of law to act in all business matters as a natural person.

Bylaws. A code of regulations and rules adopted by the members of an organization for the purpose of guiding them in their deliberations and actions as a body.

Corporate Name. The name under which a corporation is chartered and operates its business. 

Corporate Powers. Those powers expressly or impliedly granted to a corporation by its charter; the things it may do. 

Corporate Seal. The seal selected by a corporation for its own use on such documents as it may desire or is required by law to execute under seal. 

What are the powers of a corporation?

A corporation has only the powers that are granted to it by its charter. Certain of these powers are definitely stated in its charter or articles of incorporation, and other powers which it has may be implied either because they are incidental to the business of the corporation, or because the exercise of its expressly granted powers makes certain implied powers necessary. 

Practically all private stock corporations have the following powers: 

1. To have continuous succession. This means that the corporation is not dissolved as a result of the death, withdrawal, or insolvency of a stockholder. When the charter specifies how long the corporation shall continue, it exists continuously for that time; otherwise, it may exist indefinitely. 572

POWERS AND LIABILITIES OF CORPORATIONS 

573 2. To buy, sell, and hold real property unless restricted by its charter. A corporation, therefore, may buy the property necessary to carry on its business, but doing so is not essential to its existence. 

It may lease the necessary property. 

3. To borrow money and mortgage its property for the purposes of its business, and to issue notes, bonds, or other evidences of indebtedness. Statutes generally require special authority from stockholders to issue a mortgage on real property. When a corporation desires to borrow a large amount of money for a long term it is usual to issue bonds, secured by a mortgage, in amounts of $1,000 or $500, which are offered to the general public. 

4. To enter into contracts in conducting the kind of business that is clearly stated in the articles of incorporation. 

5. To issue, accept, and endorse negotiable paper in the usual or proper course of its business as a means of accomplishing the results for which it was created. It may not, however, enter into a contract of suretyship or endorse an instrument for the accommodation of another, unless specifically empowered by its charter, for such acts might call for improper use of the stockholders' funds. 

6. To sue and be sued in the corporate name. This "artificial person" created by law may deal and be dealt with the same as a natural person; therefore, this artificial person may sue and be sued in its own name the same as a natural person. 

7. To have a corporate seal for use when required by law. Corporate bonds, stocks, and mortgages bear the corporate seal. 

8. To appoint officers and agents who shall represent it in its business transactions. 

9. To make and amend bylaws for its own regulation and control. The charter might contain all the details necessary to regulate the operations of the corporation, but as the charter cannot be readily changed or amended to meet new situations, most of the details regarding the management are embodied in the bylaws which the corporation has implied power to make and to amend so long as they do not conflict with the provisions of the charter or of general laws.

The bylaws are generally adopted by a majority vote of the stockholders, and when once adopted all the stockholders are

bound thereby. The bylaws, when once adopted, may be amended according to the provisions for amending them contained therein. 

They usually contain the following provisions: 

1. Where and how the meetings of the stockholders shall be held. 

2. How the stockholders shall vote. 

3. When and where the directors shall meet and what powers they shall exercise. 

4. The officers of the corporation and how they shall be chosen. 

5. The way the stock certificates shall be issued and recorded. 

6. How the funds of the corporation shall be handled. 

7. How the bylaws shall be amended.

What are ultra vires acts? 

A corporation has a right to perform all acts expressly specified in its articles of incorporation and its charter and all acts impliedly necessary to carry out the purpose for which the corporation was formed. But, when a corporation performs acts not within its expressed or implied powers, such acts are said to be ultra vires. An ultra vires contract is not binding on the corporation and cannot be enforced by or against it; but a claim of ultra vires will not be sustained when it will procure an advantage for the corporation at the expense of others.

Example 1. The Fort Auto Corporation was chartered to deal in motor cars. It bought on credit from Adams a number of vacuum cleaners which it had no power to do. When sued by Adams for the purchase price of the cleaners the corporation pleaded that the purchase was ultra vires. Although the plea is legally correct the corporation will not be allowed to use it as a means of escaping its just obligation and Adams may recover. 

What are the liabilities of a private corporation?

Private corporations are liable on their contracts and for their debts, the same as an individual. A private corporation may be sued and a judgment entered up against it in its corporate name. 

In case it commits an offense against the law, it can be fined, but not imprisoned.

A corporation is liable for the frauds and wrongs of its agents and other employees, committed in the course of their employment. 

What rights have creditors of a corporation?

Creditors have the same rights against a corporation as they would have against an individual. A creditor, who sues a corpora-

POWERS AND LIABILITIES OF CORPORATIONS 

575 tion to collect damages or a debt and secures a judgment, may enter it up against the corporation's property. While the general rule is that a stockholder is not individually liable for the debts of the corporation, there are cases in which the creditor may look to the stockholder for the payment of the corporation's debts. 

What is the liability of stockholders? 

If a person subscribes for a certain number of shares of stock at the time the corporation is formed and he does not fully pay for it, he is liable to the corporation itself and to its creditors for the amount remaining unpaid. His liability in this case is limited to the par value or subscription price of his stock.

A stockholder who received any part of the capital assets of the corporation that were unlawfully distributed or paid out to him is liable to the creditors of the corporation for the amount he received. In order to defeat creditors' claims the officers of the corporation may distribute funds as dividends, or divide any surplus funds among the stockholders. Where this is done, the stockholders who received such funds may be compelled to return, for the benefit of the creditors, the amount so received. 

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The powers of a corporation are expressly granted by its charter or implied because they are necessary to its existence. 

2. Corporations are managed according to regulations and rules found either in the charter or in the bylaws. 

3. A corporation may perform any act within the scope of the purpose for which it was created. Acts beyond the scope of its powers are ultra vires acts. 

4. An ultra vires contract made by a corporation is unenforceable but if such a contract is executed, it may be allowed to stand. 

5. Corporations are liable on contracts and for debts the same as natural persons. 

6. A corporation is liable for the acts of its agents and other employees committed during the course of their employment. 

7. Creditors may take action against a corporation in its corporate name to collect damages or a debt.

8. A stockholder, as a rule, is not personally liable for any part of the debts of the corporation unless his stock is not fully paid for, or the full capital stock is not paid in, or he has been a party to fraudulent acts to defeat the creditors' claims.

ADMINISTRATION AND DISSOLUTION OF A CORPORATION TERMS DEFINED AS USED 

Board of Directors. Members of a corporation elected by the stockholders to manage the business affairs of the company. 

Capital. The actual assets or property owned by a corporation. 

Capital Stock. The amount of stock a corporation is allowed to issue. 

Power of Substitution. The right of the person who was named to perform an act to name another to act for him. 

Proxy Vote. A vote cast by a person authorized in writing to vote in the place of another who has voting privileges. 

Surplus Fund. A fund reserved out of earnings by the directors of a corporation for emergencies or a special purpose. 

Who is a promoter?

A promoter is a person who conceives the idea of organizing a corporation. His usual plan is to get the formation of the corporation under way and then interest others in the idea, having in mind selling out to them at a profit. When this is done, the purchasers of the stock become the stockholders and they may vote to take over all the promoter's contracts and obligations. Or, as in many cases, the promoter has no idea of selling out, but instead he becomes the principal stockholder, director, and officer in the corporation.

When several persons subscribe for stock in a corporation thereafter to be formed, each subscription is a binding contract as soon as the corporation is formed. The delivery of the stock certificate is merely evidence of the ownership of the shares, and is not necessary to make the subscriber a stockholder. For further discussion of the stock certificate, see pages 562 and 565. 578

CORPORATIONS-ADMINISTRATION, DISSOLUTION 579 

Who owns and manages a corporation?

A corporation is owned by its stockholders. Any party (individual, society, or firm) by acquiring ownership of one or more shares of the capital stock of a private stock corporation becomes a stockholder. This stock may be acquired by subscribing for it before or after the corporation is chartered, or by purchasing it either from the corporation or from a former purchaser. While the stockholders own and control the corporation, as a rule, they have little part in its direct management. However, stockholders do have certain rights as holders of the common stock. 

What rights have stockholders? 

1. Each holder of voting stock may vote on all matters within the jurisdiction of the stockholders which come before them for action. Meetings of the stockholders are held at regular intervals, usually annually or semiannually. They may be held at other times by a special call issued according to the provisions in the bylaws, or the board of directors may vote to call a meeting of the stockholders. The stockholders may be called upon to decide many things by their votes, such as general business policies, amending bylaws, amending the charter, and other general questions. A vote of a majority of the stockholders binds each stockholder, provided the subject voted upon is within the scope of the powers conferred by the charter. A majority of the stockholders. cannot bind the minority in any transaction not within their expressed or implied powers.

The principal duty of the stockholders is to elect directors in whom the management of the corporation, in most cases, is vested. The directors are elected by the stockholders usually at their annual meeting. Vacancies in the board of directors may be filled at any regular meeting of stockholders, or at a special meeting called for that purpose. Bylaws usually authorize the directors to fill a vacancy for the unexpired term. 

2. Each stockholder is entitled to notification of all stockholders' meetings.

Notice of the time and place of the stockholders' meetings must be given to each stockholder unless the charter or the bylaws state definitely when and where the meetings shall be held, and each stockholder knows of this provision.

The notice is usually given by mail. Some such printed form, properly filled in, may be used, as shown below. 

GENERAL OFFICE PACIFIC FRUITS COMPANY 

Oakland, California, June 5, 19..

Notice to Stockholders:

NOTICE OF STOCKHOLDERS' MEETING 

3. Each stockholder is entitled to share proportionately in all dividends declared on the class of stock which he owns. 

The directors of the corporation may vote a dividend to be paid out of surplus funds or out of the net profits. The dividend may be declared at so much per share, as in the case of no-par stock; or at a certain per cent of the capital stock. (The par value of the stock in the hands of the stockholders.)

Dividends on the preferred stock must be paid before dividends on the common stock, and according to the terms under which the stock was issued and sold. If there is an outstanding issue of cumulative preferred stock, no dividend may be paid on other stock until the full dividend on this stock, including all arrears, has been paid. 

Dividends can be paid only from earnings or accumulated surplus and if neither is available, dividends must be passed even on preferred stocks. 

The directors are not obliged to declare dividends even though earnings or surplus are available. If they determine, in good faith, that the corporation earnings should be reserved for future corporate purposes they may pass a dividend and the stockholders can not compel its payment. 

4. Each stockholder has a right to share proportionately in the net assets in case the corporation is dissolved and the assets liqui-

CORPORATIONS-ADMINISTRATION, DISSOLUTION 581 

dated, subject to any preferences given in the charter to particular shares of stock. 

5. Each stockholder, regardless of the number of shares he owns, may inspect the books and accounts of the corporation. 

6. Each stockholder has a right to sell and transfer any stock which he owns without the consent of the corporation or any one connected with it. 

The owners of preferred stock have the same rights as the owners of the common stock, except as their rights may be enlarged or restricted by the conditions under which the stock was issued. 

How is stock transferred?

Shares of stock are permitted to change hands freely. The transfer from one holder to another usually is made in the form of an assignment which is written or partly printed and filled in upon the back of the certificate of stock. This assignment reads some what as follows: 

For value received I hereby sell, assign, and transfer unto L. W. 

West fifty shares of the capital stock represented by the within certificate, and do hereby appoint C. R. Ross my attorney to transfer the said stock on the books of the within named corporation, with full power of substitution in the premises. 

The secretary of the company is generally named as the attorney with full power of substitution.

When stock is sold by one person to another, the certificate is endorsed and delivered to the purchaser. He should surrender it to the corporation, which will enter him as a stockholder, cancel the old certificate and issue to him a new one in its place. Many corporations whose stock is bought and sold in large quantities in stock exchanges maintain transfer agents in New York City or other active trading centers to facilitate transfers in the books of the corporation.

All transfers of stock must be recorded in the books of the corporation and a new certificate issued by the transferee before he is legally a stockholder and entitled to voting privileges or dividends.

As between himself and the one from whom he received the stock, he is entitled to all benefits therefrom. 

It is customary to declare dividends "payable to stockholders of record” on a fixed date. To be certain that all pending transfers of stock are completed and the new owners duly recorded as stockholders, many large corporations close the transfer books for a short period just preceding the dividend date. During that period no stock will be accepted for transfer. 

The sale and transfer of stock is subject to legal regulations, both Federal and State, which must be complied with. There is a Federal tax at a certain rate per share that must be paid by the seller on all transfers of stock. Many states also impose a transfer tax. 

How are stockholders' meetings conducted?

The stockholders are notified of the meeting, or the charter specifies when stockholders' meetings shall be held. Usually notice is sent out by the secretary of the company. As a rule a majority of the voting shares must be represented at the meeting either by the stockholders personally or by proxy, to constitute a quorum to do business. The meeting may be presided over by the chairman of the board of directors or by the president of the company, depending upon the provisions in the bylaws. 

Each stockholder has one vote for each share of voting stock he owns. He may vote in person or he may authorize another to vote in his place. Provision may be made in a certificate of incorporation for cumulative voting for election of directors. Under this method of voting each stockholder is entitled to as many votes as equals the number of shares of stock he owns, multiplied by the number of directors to be elected, and he may cast all the votes for one director or divide them among the candidates as he may choose.

Example 1. If there are five directors to be voted, and a stockholder has fifty shares of stock he is entitled to 250 (5 x 50) votes, and he may cast 50 votes for each of the five different individuals for directors, or he may cast 250 votes for one person as director, or he may distribute the votes otherwise. The purpose of this method of voting is to permit minority stockholders to elect representatives to the board of directors. 

Stockholders may exercise the right to vote through trustees. A voting trust is a device to secure unified control and continuity of policy of the corporation, and to avoid factional disputes among

CORPORATIONS-ADMINISTRATION, DISSOLUTION 583 

stockholders which may imperil the success of the enterprise. The procedure is that stockholders make an agreement that their stock shall be voted by certain designated voting trustees for a given period. They deposit their stock certificates with the trustees and receive therefor voting-trust certificates which entitle the holders to all the rights of stockholders, including the right to dividends, except the right to vote. These certificates may be sold like other stock and the purchaser receives the same rights but is subject to the voting trust agreement. 

What is a proxy?

A proxy is a person who represents another in some capacity, or a written statement authorizing another to act as his representative. A stockholder's proxy is a written statement by which a stockholder authorizes his proxy to vote in his place at a meeting of the stockholders of a corporation. 

Know all men by these presents, that I, John W. Hines, the undersigned stockholder in the Weston Electric Co., Inc., do hereby constitute and appoint D. W. Harmon and E. L. James, or either of them, my true and lawful attorney and agent for me and in my name, place and stead, to vote as my proxy at the Annual Meeting of the stockholders of said company, to be held on the 

20th day of June, 19.., or at any adjournment thereof, for the election of directors and for the transaction of any business which may legally come before said meeting, and for me and in my name to act as fully as I could do if personally present. 

Witness my hand and seal this second day of June, 19—. 

In the presence of 

Howard Kester

John W. Hines (L.S.) A PROXY 

A proxy is usually given for a specific meeting and its adjournments. In some states by statute a proxy is not valid after the expiration of a certain time, usually a year or less. A proxy may be revoked at any time by the stockholder, and is revoked by his attendance at the meeting, or by giving a subsequent proxy.

What are the duties of the board of directors?

The directors of a corporation are charged with directing and controlling its affairs. The active management of the corporation is in their hands. They are required to act in person and can not vote by proxy. They occupy a position of trust and confidence and. must deal honestly, faithfully, and impartially with the property and business of the corporation and the rights of the stockholders. 

At their first meeting following their election by the stockholders, they elect the officers of the company, including a chairman of the board, who is usually the President, and a secretary. Either one or both may or may not be from among their number. However, the chairman of the board is usually a director. The charter or the bylaws usually specify the requirements and limitations imposed on officers, election, appointments, etc. The number of directors may vary from three to any number, depending upon the size of the corporation. The number usually ranges from 3 to 21. 

The directors manage the financial policies of the corporation, declare dividends, authorize the purchase of property, and new construction together with many other transactions, but among their most important duties is the appointing of the officers of the corporation. 

What officers are usually elected?

The following officers usually are elected: (a) a president, (b) as many vice-presidents as are needed, (c) a secretary, and (d) a treasurer. Assistants to the regular officers may be appointed. 

The board of directors may determine the powers and duties of the officers or they may be fixed by the bylaws. 

The President. The president of a corporation is its chief executive officer and while his powers are limited he is practically a general agent. He is usually one of the directors and he may act as chairman of the board of directors. He usually has authority to sign all contracts for the company.

The Vice-President. The vice-president is usually charged with special duties or he may have charge of a special department, for which he is responsible, such as purchases, sales, or advertising. 

He takes the place of the president during his absence. In larger

CORPORATIONS-ADMINISTRATION, DISSOLUTION 585 

corporations there may be two or more vice-presidents, each of whom will be in charge of some department or branch of the work. 

The Secretary. The secretary records the minutes of the meetings of the stockholders and of the board of directors. He usually has many special duties to perform, and much correspondence in connection with his office. He is the custodian of the corporate seal. 

The Treasurer. The treasurer is the company's financial officer. 

He has charge of the financial operations of the company and its current funds. 

Other rights of stockholders.

A stockholder may deal with the corporation in which he owns stock the same as he would deal with any other party. He may sue the corporation as an individual and he may be sued by it. 

A stockholder may bring court action to compel the directors who have withheld dividends unlawfully to pay past due dividends. 

Dividends may be paid in cash, in property, or in stock of the corporation (stock dividend).

Should the capital stock of the corporation be increased, the present stockholders must be given the first chance to buy this stock.

A stockholder who loses his certificate of stock should report his loss to the secretary of the company at once. A new certificate will be issued to take the place of the lost certificate, but before it is issued the stockholder may be required to furnish a bond to protect the company against loss. 

Corporations are required to file reports. 

Statutes generally provide that corporations shall file reports at regular intervals, usually annually, with the secretary of state or some designated state official. These reports have to do primarily with the amount of capital stock, the volume of business transacted, the assets, the debts, the operating expenses, the net profit, and the dividends of the corporations. These reports when filed may be inspected by any one. 

How may a private corporation be dissolved? 

1. By the expiration of its charter. When a corporation is chartered for a definite period of time, 10, 25, or 50 years, it is automatically terminated when this time expires and must be dis-

solved, unless the time is extended or a new charter is secured. 

When a charter expires, the stockholders may demand that the assets be liquidated and the net assets distributed among the stockholders of record. A receiver may be appointed by the court to close up the corporation's affairs. 

2. By the surrender of its charter with the consent of the state. 

The stockholders may agree among themselves to dissolve the corporation and surrender its charter to the state. The law generally provides that this can be done only with the consent of the state. 

3. By a decree of the court. The state reserves the right at the time of granting the charter to repeal it at any time for cause. To repeal a charter the state must take action in the court, and if it is proven that the corporation has abused its powers or acted illegally the court may decree a dissolution. 

4. By the state for nonuser. State laws generally require that the company receiving its charter shall begin to exercise its corporate powers within a certain time after incorporation or forfeit its charter. In New York State the law provides that if a corporation does not organize and commence the transaction of its business within two years from the date of its incorporation, its corporate powers shall cease. 

What is a merger?

Sometimes conditions are such that two or more corporations find it to their mutual advantage to merge into one company. 

Before this may be done, the stockholders of the corporations affected must agree to the merger and the state must give its consent. If it so happens that any of the corporations has outstanding bonds, the bondholders must also consent to the merger. 

What is a holding company?

Another method of combining several corporations under a single management is to create a parent or holding corporation with one or more subsidiary corporations. 

Example 2. An iron mining company might find it desirable to operate a railroad, a fleet of boats, a blast furnace, a steel plant, and a sales organization, all in connection with the same general enterprise. Each branch of the industry would be operated by a separate corporation and the stock

CORPORATIONS-ADMINISTRATION, DISSOLUTION 587 

of all the corporations would be owned by a single corporation. In the example given, if all the stock were owned by the mining corporation, it would be called the parent corporation and the others subsidiary corporations. In some cases the stock of all the operating units is owned by a separate corporation called a holding company, which does no business except to direct generally the affairs of its subsidiaries, and receive and distribute dividends. 

When is a receiver appointed?

When a corporation becomes insolvent, either the directors of the corporation or its creditors may petition the court to appoint a receiver. If the court grants the petition after the hearing, the judge will appoint a receiver to take over the assets of the corporation and administer its affairs in the interest of the creditors and stockholders.

If a majority of the stockholders feel that the company's affairs are being poorly managed, and that its assets are being wasted, they may petition the court to appoint a receiver to administer its affairs in the interest of all the stockholders.

FUNDAMENTAL PRINCIPLES 

1. The promoters of a corporation are bound by all contracts they make while organizing the corporation, even though they sell out to stockholders. 

2. A person who subscribes for shares of the capital of a corporation is bound by his subscription if the corporation is formed. 

3. A subscriber to articles of incorporation becomes a stockholder as soon as the corporation is formed, even though he has not received a stock certificate. 

4. The corporation is owned by the stockholders and managed by the directors and officers whom they elect. 

5. No holder of voting stock may be denied the right to vote at stockholders' meetings. The vote of the majority binds the minority. 

6. Common stock is usually issued without special privileges or restrictions. 

7. The capital stock is represented by the amount of stock the corporation is authorized by its charter to issue. 

8. The capital of a corporation is its actual assets or property. 

9. The person who owns the stock is entitled to the dividend, but the corporation will pay it to the one in whose name it is recorded on the books. 

10. Cumulative voting, although generally permitted, usually must be provided for in the certificate of incorporation.

CORPORATIONS-ADMINISTRATION, DISSOLUTION 589 

11. A majority vote means a majority of the shares of stock and not of the stockholders. 

12. The directors of a corporation control its management, appoint the officers, and declare the dividends. 

13. Only those who have a right to vote are entitled to attend stockholders' meetings. 

14. The bylaws usually specify the time and place of holding meetings, and whether or not notice of any meeting is required depends upon the provisions therein. 

15. Notice of any special meeting is always required. 

16. A corporation may be dissolved by expiration of its charter, by action of the state for cause, and by the stockholders with the approval of the state. 

17. Two or more corporations may be merged into one company only after all the stockholders agree to it, the state grants permission, and the bondholders approve. 

18. Two or more corporations may also be combined by the holding company device. The holding company achieves control of the subsidiary companies through ownership of the voting stock of the subsidiaries.
