COMMENTS 

Our economic development has been such that individual ownership and management and also partnership ownership and management were found inadequate to meet the requirements of business, particularly "big business." Therefore, the necessity for developing a new type of business organization became apparent, and as a result the corporation was brought into existence. This type of business organization has developed and increased in this country to such an extent that today the major part of our business throughout the United States is transacted either through or by corporations.

Corporate ownership and management make it possible to procure more capital through increased membership in the organization than could be procured otherwise. The large enterprises, such as railroads, steamship lines, banks, manufacturers, and insurance companies require large amounts of capital for their operations. Such enterprises also require a stability in management and a continuity of existence that only the corporate form of organization makes possible. 

Statutes affecting corporations differ considerably in their provisions for the organization and control of corporations, the rights and liabilities of stockholders and directors and other matters pertaining to the corporate structure. In a book of this kind it is impossible to discuss statutory provisions. The study of corporations here is confined, therefore, to the funda-

mental rules and laws applicable to the organization, management and control of corporations. The student is referred to the statutes of his own state for specific regulations.

The corporation, as a type of business organization, holds such a prominent place in our social, religious, educational, political, and industrial activities that it is today, more than ever before, a potent factor in our social and economic development and stability. Corporate bodies are so numerous in every kind of endeavor where organized and concerted effort is essential to achieve some purpose, that everybody has some interest in common with one or more of these organizations. Our political subdivisions such as towns, villages, and cities, our churches, our charitable organizations, our hospitals, our schools and colleges, and all our numerous chartered business organizations such as insurance companies, public utility companies, banks, manufacturing and merchandising establishments, etc., are all examples of corporations of one kind or another. The influence of these different corporate bodies is so far reaching that in one way or another the lives of practically everyone are influenced by them. 

Therefore, a study of how corporations are created, and of their powers, limitations, and operations is essential to an understanding of the social and economic environment in which we live.

What Acts are involved? 

In the years of business depression following 1929, the Congress of the United States passed a number of Acts designed to promote business recovery and to relieve and improve social conditions. 

Most of these Acts extended the legislative power of the Federal Congress considerably into fields which were formerly regulated exclusively by the several states. Not all of the Acts were able to withstand attacks on their constitutionality, as in the following cases.

The National Industrial Recovery Act (Act of June 16, 1933) was declared unconstitutional in Schechter Poultry Corp. v. United States, 295 U. S. 495, 55 S. Ct. 837, 79 L. Ed. 1570, as an unwarranted attempt to regulate intrastate commerce.

The Agricultural Adjustment Act (Act of May 12, 1933) was held to be invalid in United States v. Butler, 297 U. S. 1, 56 S. Ct. 312, 80 L. Ed. 477, as being a regulation of agricultural production, which field of legislation is reserved exclusively to the states. 

However, two Acts of great importance to business, industry, and private citizens have been sustained and are now in operation. 

These are the National Labor Relations Act (Act of July 5, 1935), and the Social Security Act (Act of August 14, 1935). A summary of the provisions of these Acts follows. 

What is the National Labor Relations Act? 

This Act, popularly called the "Wagner Act," was designed to increase the income of wage earners by securing and protecting for them a bargaining power similar to that enjoyed by employers. 

The essential features of the Act are the provisions for collective bargaining and the protection afforded to employees against unfair labor practices.

State and Federal employees and agricultural workers are excluded from the operation of the Act. 

The Act is an exercise of the power of Congress to regulate inter- 595

state commerce. It recites that "the denial by employers of the right of employees to organize and the refusal by employers to accept the procedure of collective bargaining lead to strikes and other forms of industrial strife or unrest which have the intent and the necessary effect of burdening or obstructing commerce," and that the policy of the United States is "to eliminate the causes of certain substantial obstructions to the free flow of commerce." 

The Act applies not only to any business directly engaged in interstate commerce but to any industry so related to interstate commerce that an interruption of its activities by labor troubles would obstruct the free flow of commerce. The following are examples of businesses to which the Act has been held to apply: 

Example 1. A steel plant operating within a given state received its raw materials from out of the state and shipped its finished product out of the state.

National Labor Relations Board v. Jones & Laughlin Corp. 

301 U. S. 1, 57 S. Ct. 615, 81 L. Ed. 893 

Example 2. A fruit packing plant received fruit from points within the state and delivered the package to buyers within the state, but a large part of the packages were finally shipped out of the state. 

Santa Cruz Packing Co. v. Labor Board 

303 U. S. 453, 58 S. Ct. 656, 82 L. Ed. 954. 

Example 3. A Corporation supplied gas and electricity wholly within a state. None was sold for resale out of the state, but the corporation supplied certain interstate railroads, steamship lines, telephone and telegraph companies, and other interstate agencies. 

Consolidated Edison Co. v. Labor Board 

305 U. S. 197, 59 S. Ct. 206, 83 L. Ed. 126. Very few businesses would be outside the scope of the Act as thus construed. 

What are unfair labor practices?

The Act prohibits practices by employers which tend to thwart or weaken labor organizations, and forces employers to consent to the principle of collective bargaining. Enforcement of the Act is delegated to the National Labor Relations Board. 

"Unfair labor practices" are dealt with in five specific provisions of the Act.

The first is a general prohibition of interference with the rights guaranteed.

The second deals with the company union situation. Theoretically, a union formed within a single plant is an adequate representative of its members, but in practice it is generally without sufficient power to afford proper protection to employee interests. 

It is claimed that this lack of power is due to the employer dominating the company union and that it thus isolates the company union from the rest of the industry. These conditions tend to make an effective strike impossible. The Act permits company unions, however, but makes it an unfair labor practice for the employer to control or interfere with the formation or administration of any labor organization, or to contribute financial or other support to it. In practice it has proven almost impossible to establish a company union which will escape these prohibitions. 

The third unfair labor practice is discrimination against an employee because of union activities. It is a violation of this provision to discharge, demote, or penalize in any way, an employee on account of his acts in promotion of union interests. Cases under this provision involve a determination of the motives of the employer-an admittedly difficult question-but the Labor Relations Board has generally afforded adequate protection to employees. 

The fourth provision prohibits the discharge of or discrimination against an employee because he has given testimony in any proceeding under the Act.

The fifth provision prohibits refusal on the part of an employer to bargain collectively with representatives of his employees. What is a sufficient compliance with this provision depends upon the facts of each case. The employer is not compelled to accede to the demands of his employees. On the other hand, he cannot legalize a flat refusal of such demands merely by a conference with employee representatives. There is required a reasonable and bona fide. attempt to come to an agreement through conference and, if possible, mutual concessions. 

The representatives with whom the employer is under a duty to bargain may be any individual or labor organization, not necessarily his own employees. When selected by a majority of the

employees, such representatives are the exclusive bargaining representatives of all the workers. A dispute as to the proper representatives is settled by the Board, usually through an election. 

When an employer is charged with unfair labor practices, the National Labor Relations Board or its agents may serve upon him a complaint with notice of hearing. If a violation is found after hearing, the Board must make findings of fact, issue a "cease and desist" order, and require appropriate action by the employer, including reinstatement of a discharged employee with or without back pay. Such orders may be enforced by a Federal court upon petition by the Board. Provision is made for judicial review of the orders, but serious questions exist as to the scope of the review, the finality of the Board's findings of the fact, the applicability of rules of evidence, and other matters, which have not yet received final answers. 

THE SOCIAL SECURITY ACT 

In the early history of this country towns or counties assumed the whole responsibility of taking care of their needy and those who could not care for themselves. As the burden became too heavy for a community alone to handle, the State furnished at least part of the required funds. With the growing demands upon the various 

States they one by one sought assistance from the Federal government. Under the Social Security Act, passed in 1935 and greatly improved and broadened by amendments in August 1939, the Federal government is now prepared to assist each State in serving its own deserving people.

How does the Social Security Act function? 

Using as a basis the past experiences of the various States in administering the public-assistance program, the Federal government set up a Federal pattern that is designed to be an improvement upon the earlier methods practiced by communities and States. Every 

State makes its own program for administering assistance, but it must follow the Federal pattern in order to be eligible for the Federal grant. Each State decides who shall get aid and how much shall be

paid to each person; hence the requirements for getting aid are not the same in all States. However, the Act requires that aid shall be given in relation to the actual need in each case, but the State determines what is necessary to be eligible for assistance; it fixes the amount to be paid each person receiving aid; it makes the payment to the recipient; it decides the amount of its own State and local money that shall be used for this social undertaking, and it is responsible for the actions of the State agency appointed to carry out this program. 

Provisions of the Social Security Act. 

The Social Security Act contains various provisions relating to social welfare. It is divided into eleven "Titles," as follows: 

I. Grants to States for Old-Age Assistance II. Federal Old-Age Benefits III. Grants to States for Unemployment Compensation Ad ministration 

IV. Grants to States for Aid to Dependent Children 

V.

Grants to States for Maternal and Child Welfare 

VI. Public Health Work VII. Social Security Board VIII. Taxes with Respect to Employment 

IX. Tax on Employers of Eight or More 

X. Grants to States for Aid to the Blind

XI. General Provisions Titles VI and VII contain general administrative provisions, and Title XI contains definitions, grant of power to make rules, and similar provisions of general application. The provisions that have to do with old-age insurance and unemployment insurance are of greatest interest and importance to employees and employers. 

TITLE I. OLD-AGE ASSISTANCE 

The title old-age assistance should not be confused with the title 

Federal old-age benefits.

Old-age benefits or insurance is administered entirely by the Federal Government. The Government pays insurance benefits

directly to the individual on the basis of past wages regardless of what other income or property a person may have, Old-age assistance is administered by the States under a plan that is approved by the Social Security Board. The Federal Govern ment makes grants to the States which have approved plans, and the States pay monthly cash allowances to men and women over 65 years of age on the basis of their needs. Each State decides who shall get aid and how much shall be paid to each person; hence the requirements for getting assistance are not the same in all States. 

The Federal Government will contribute a sum equal to one half of whatever the State pays, not counting payments to any individual exceeding $40 per month, plus 5 % of such sum to be used for the cost of administering the State plan, or for old-age assistance, or for both. The State may pay more or less than $40 a month, but it will not receive Federal aid for any payment in ex cess of $40 a month. For a discussion of Title II and Title III see pages 601-608.

TITLE IV. AID TO DEPENDENT CHILDREN 

For several years States have provided for children who are in need because they have no parent to support them. This assistance was formerly administered by many States under Mother's Aid laws, but now the Social Security Act provides that the Federal Government contribute one half of whatever the State decides shall be paid toward assisting its dependent children, on the basis of allowing the first dependent child of a family up to $18 a month and a second child of the same family up to $12 a month. A State may contribute more than these maximum amounts on its own responsibility.

To receive assistance from the Federal Government a child must live with a relative-mother, father, brother, sister, grandparent, aunt, or uncle. All States give assistance to dependent children at least up to age 16. Many States provide assistance up to age 18 if the child is still in school; the Federal Government will continue to share the cost under similar conditions. No State can require more than one year of residence in order to obtain assistance and

no child may be denied aid because he has not lived long enough in a given town or county.

TITLE V. MATERNAL AND CHILD WELFARE The Social Security Act designates the Children's Bureau of the 

United States Department of Labor as the administering Agency for maternal and child-health services, child-welfare services, and services for crippled children. Payments are made to States having plans for such services which meet the requirements of the Federal Act.

The financial participation by the Federal Government in this program does not require a State to match the fund dollar for dollar as in the old-age assistance program. 

TITLE VI. PUBLIC HEALTH WORK 

The Social Security Act provides that funds be alloted to the States for the general strengthening of public health. The money is available through the Surgeon General of the United States Public Health Service, according to the population of each State, its health problems, and its financial needs. 

Under U. S. Code, Title 29 ("Labor") §§ 31-45, the Federal 

Government shares with the States any cost connected with the service known as Vocational Rehabilitation of Persons. Injured in

Industry. The Federal Security Agency administers the funds made available to the States for this program. 

UNEMPLOYMENT COMPENSATION 

Title III authorizes appropriations for unemployment compensation. Title VIII levies an income tax on employees and employers. 

Title IX levies an excise tax on employers. This separation of the appropriation and the corresponding tax was probably to avoid the objection that the tax is for an object not within the constitutional powers of Congress. The Agricultural Adjustment Act was held unconstitutional on this ground. (See United States v. Butler, ante, p. 595).

Appropriations under Title III are made to States having unem-

ployment compensation laws which are approved by the Social Security Board, on the basis of population, number of unemployed, and other relevant factors. Among other requirements, the State laws must provide for the payment of all money received in the unemployment fund of the State into the Federal Unemployment Trust Fund, and the expenditure of all money received by the State from such Fund in the payment of unemployment compensation.

Title VIII levied an income tax on employees, based on wages received, and an excise tax on employers, based on wages paid. 

Insofar as the Title related exclusively to internal revenue, it was repealed and incorporated in U. S. Code, Title 26 (“Internal 

Revenue"), §§ 1400 et seq. 

Title IX levies an excise tax on employers who have had on each of twenty days during the taxable year a total of eight or more employees, the tax being based on the total wages payable by him during the year. The initial rate was 1%, increased to 3% in 1938 and subsequent years. Against the tax so levied the employer is allowed a credit of the amount of contributions paid by him into an unemployment fund under a State law approved by the Social Security Board, the total credit not to exceed 90% of the tax against which it is credited. Most State laws, therefore, impose rates equivalent to 90% of the Federal tax, or 2.7%. This makes taxes payable to the State for unemployment purposes 2.7% and to the Federal Government .3% of the pay roll, or a total of 3% to both. Except in a few states, employees are not taxed to help make up this fund.

Under this plan, the funds necessary to make payments under State unemployment compensation laws are actually furnished by the Federal Government from the Unemployment Trust Fund, from which the funds are withdrawn as requisitioned by the States. 

Besides paying benefits to unemployed workers, each State provides a service by registering unemployed workers so that they may be directed to suitable jobs. The Wagner-Peyser Act of 1933 authorized grants to the States to maintain a system of employment offices and now these same offices administer the unemployment insurance program in each State.

As soon as an employee loses his job, he should file a claim at the nearest State employment office. At the same time he should register for work at that office so that he can be directed properly in finding another job. 

TITLE II. FEDERAL OLD-AGE INSURANCE 

It has been explained how the Federal Government co-operates with the States in providing benefits for insured wage earners who became temporarily unemployed. We shall now consider the 

Federal old-age insurance program that has been established by the Social Security Act. This program provides a regular income for workers in commercial and industrial jobs when they reach the age of 65 years and stop working. It includes also supplementary benefits and survivors' benefits. In the former case the benefits for temporarily unemployed persons are administered by the States. with the aid of contributions by the Federal Government; in the latter case the benefits are administered solely by the Federal Government and are paid by the Government each month. 

Attention is again called to the fact that old-age assistance is administered by the States with the aid of the Federal Government and is granted on the basis of need, but old-age insurance is administered solely by the Federal Government and is granted on the basis of past wages. The Social Security Board determines the amount of insurance due each individual and furnishes the information to the Treasury Department, whereupon a government check is sent to each individual named in the report. 

What is "covered employment "?

Work for wages in factories, mines, stores, shops, or other industrial or commercial establishments may be considered covered employment. The following employments are not covered: agricultural labor, domestic service in a private home, casual labor not in the course of the employer's trade or business, service performed in the employ of any Federal, State or local government, service performed in the employ of certain organizations having religious, charitable, scientific, educational, or humane purposes.

How are funds provided?

To provide funds for carrying out the old-age insurance program, each employer and each employee in covered employment must pay to the Federal Government under the Federal Insurance Con tribution Act (U. S. Code, Title 26, §§ 1400-1432), taxes as follows: 

From 1937 to 1942 inclusive From 1943 to 1945 inclusive From 1946 to 1948 inclusive 

From 1949 and thereafter 

1% of total wages paid 

2% of total wages paid 

24% of total wages paid 

3% of total wages paid

Wages in excess of $3,000 from any one employer may not be . counted.

The employer is required by law to deduct from the wages of the employees the amount of tax each employee has to pay, and to forward it with a like amount paid by himself to the United States Treasury. This fund, called the Federal Old-Age and Survivors 

Insurance Trust Fund, is managed by a Board of Trustees composed of the Secretary of the Treasury, the Secretary of Labor, and the Chairman of the Social Security Board. 

What is the worker's "social security account "?

The Social Security Board keeps a social security account for every worker who earns wages under "covered employment." To this account are credited all wages that the worker has earned, as reported by his employer; and upon this record the worker depends for the amount of monthly payment he will receive. 

A social security card showing the worker's name and the number of his account is issued to each wage earner. The employer also must keep a record of the name and account number of each employee and enter them on the quarterly tax report submitted to the Government. It is important that a worker file his card in some place for safe-keeping and ready reference. Workers frequently carry with them a separate record of their account number. 

QUALIFICATIONS FOR MONTHLY BENEFITS 

The Federal old-age insurance program provides for three kinds of payments-monthly benefits, single cash benefits, and lump-sum death payments.

The system went into effect January 1, 1937, and the payment of monthly benefits began January 1, 1942. 

In general, for monthly benefits a worker must qualify as follows: 

1. A worker must be at least 65 years of age. 

2. A worker must retire from "covered employment" in order to be entitled to monthly benefits, except that his wages do not exceed $15 a month. However, if a worker at age 65 is not eligible to receive monthly benefits, he may become eligible by working after he is 65. 

3. A worker must be fully insured. To be fully insured the worker must earn $50 or more a quarter year in at least half the quarter years between January 1, 1937 and the quarter year in which he becomes 65. 

Example 1. A worker became 65 years of age in January, 1940.

During the years 1937, 1938, and 1939 he was employed not less than 6 quarters and received not less than $50 in wages each quarter. He is "fully insured" and eligible to receive monthly benefits the rest of his life.

Example 2. A worker earning $125 a month from 1937 to 1947 inclusive is then incapacitated and unable to work again. He becomes 

65 years of age in 1965. He is "fully insured" because he has worked at least 40 quarters. When a worker once becomes qualified for benefits, subsequent unemployment will not disqualify him.

Example 3. A worker is steadily employed at $150 a month from 

1937 to 1945 inclusive and is then taken ill and is not able to work again. He becomes 65 years of age in 1956. This worker is not "fully insured," because he was not employed one half of the quarters from 

1937 to 1956, nor has he 40 quarters of coverage. 

Determining the monthly benefit payments.

The monthly benefit payment is based on the average monthly wage of the worker. The average monthly wage is found by dividing the total wages from covered employment by the number of months in which the worker could have earned such wages, i.e., 3 times the number of quarters from the time he began work after 1936 and before the quarter in which he became eligible to receive the benefits.

Supplementary monthly benefits.

In addition to the monthly benefit payment that a retired worker receives, he may also receive supplementary benefits as follows: (1) for his wife at age 65 or over, he may receive his monthly benefit (unless the wife has in her own right a monthly benefit equal to or greater than this supplement); (2) for each unmarried child under 18 years of age his monthly benefit. But in no case may the total benefits paid exceed twice the worker's primary benefit. 

Survivors' benefits.

In case a worker who is either "fully insured" or "currently insured" dies, the Act provides survivors' benefits as follows: (1) A surviving widow 65 years old receives of the worker's benefit rate. (2) A widow less than 65 years of age who has dependent children receives of the worker's benefit rate. (3) For each unmarried dependent child under 18 years of age the widow will receive the worker's benefit rate. Except that in no case will the total amount received be more than double the worker's benefit rate. (4) If a deceased worker leaves no widow or dependent children, each dependent parent of his is entitled to receive of the worker's monthly benefit rate.

LUMP-SUM DEATH PAYMENTS 

Upon the death of a fully or currently insured individual, leaving no surviving widow, child, or parent who would be entitled to monthly benefits, a lump sum equal to six times a monthly insurance benefit, as previously described, shall be paid to the surviving spouse, if any; or if no spouse, to the surviving children, if any; or, if no spouse and no children, to the parents; or, if none of such persons be living, such amount shall be paid to any person or persons, equitably entitled thereto, to the extent and in the proportions that he or they shall have paid the expenses of burial of the deceased.

SOLDIERS' AND SAILORS' RELIEF ACT 

607 

SOLDIERS' AND SAILORS' CIVIL RELIEF ACT OF 1940 The Soldiers' and Sailors' Civil Relief Act of 1940 repealed the 

Selective Training and Service Act of 1940 and the National Guard Act which were temporary in nature. 

In order to understand properly the provision of this Act, it must be remembered that Congress by this legislation was anxious to assure men in military service that they and their dependents would be protected against enforcement of civil debts and obligations that they were unable to meet by reason of their military service.

It must also be recalled that the Act does not create a general mandatory moratorium on all debts and other civil obligations of soldiers and sailors. The relief which was given by this Act is to be granted only when the court was of the opinion that the ability of the man in service to prosecute or defend actions or to meet his obligations was materially affected by reason of his military service. In the exercise of this provision, courts must take into consideration that by reason of the increased pay and allowances to the man in the service and his dependents many men in military service are now in a better financial position to meet their obligations than they were in civilian life. 

Persons protected.

The provisions of this Act extend to all persons on active duty or in training for active duty in the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Coast Guard and members of the Public Health Service detailed for duty with the Army and Navy; members of the 

WAACS; members of the WAVES; members of the SPARS; persons who are citizens of the United States and are serving with the military forces of our allies. 

The Act expires on May 15, 1945 or six months after the termination of the war, whichever date is later. 

Relief to servicemen. 

1. Judgment upon default. The act prohibits the entry of a judgment upon default in appearance by the defendant without an order of court unless the plaintiff files an affidavit showing that the defendant is not in military service.

2. Fines and penalties. Whenever action for compliance with any contract is stayed pursuant to the provisions of the Act, no fine or penalty shall accrue during the period of such stay by reason of failure to comply with the terms of the contract. 

3. Statute of limitations. The law extends the running of the 

Statute of Limitations in favor of or against a person in military service during the period of such service. 

4. Leases, termination, and eviction. The wife, children, and other dependents of a man in the service shall not be evicted from a dwelling if the rent does not exceed $80 per month without a court order and such proceedings may be stayed for not more than three months. 

5. Taxes. No sale of property to enforce collection of any taxes may be made without an order of the court. 

Relief to nonservicemen; landlords.

Where a stay of eviction has been granted, the owner of the rented premises may apply to the court for relief similar to that granted to the men in service with respect to contracts, mortgages, and taxes and the court may grant relief to such extent and for such period as it may deem just.

STATUTORY CHANGES 

609 

STATUTORY CHANGES 

The discussion on the following pages relates to recent changes in the statutes of New York. They represent a considerable range of statutes that affect the business world and the general public. It is believed that these statutory changes are indicative of a trend toward similar legislation in other states. Students should be encouraged to read the changes given on the following pages and compare them with corresponding statutes of their own states. 

The page references shown at the beginning of each topic refer to the text page on which the same general topic has previously been discussed.

CONTRACTS 

Infants' contracts (pp. 44-47). An infant may not disaffirm on the ground of infancy a contract made by him after he became eighteen years of age, where the contract was made in connection with a business in which the infant was engaged and which was reasonable and provident when made. The burden is upon the person seeking to enforce the contract, to establish that it was made in connection with a business in which the infant was engaged, and also that it was reason able and prudent. (Debtor & Creditor Law § 260, added by L. 1941, ch. 327) 

How can an offer be kept open (p. 64)? When a written offer, signed by the offeror, states that the offer is irrevocable for a stated period, it shall not be revocable during such period because of the absence of consideration for the assurance of irrevocability. When the writing states that the offer is irrevocable but does not state any time, the offer shall be irrevocable for a reasonable time. (Real Prop. Law § 279, subd. 4; Pers. Prop. Law § 33, subd. 5, added by L. 1941, ch. 328)

Note. These sections do away with the necessity for consideration for an option. It is no longer necessary that the offeree pay anything for the promise to keep the offer open. It is required only that the offer be in writing, signed by the offeror, and state that it shall be irrevocable. 

Remedies for fraud (p. 78). The courts of New York have decided that the remedy of rescission of contract on the ground of fraud, in which the injured party seeks to abrogate the contract, to return what he has received and to recover what he has parted with, is inconsistent with the remedy of damages for fraud, in which the injured party

affirms the contract, retains what he has received and seeks as damages the amount by which its value was less than represented. (See 

Merry Realty Co. vs. Shamokin Co., 230 N. Y. 316; Weigel vs. Cook, 237 N. Y. 136.) This doctrine has been changed by Civil Prac. Act, § 112-e, added by L. 1941, ch. 315, which provides that a party aggrieved by fraud or misrepresentation may obtain complete relief in one action, including rescission, restitution of benefits conferred by him, and damages, but there shall be no duplication of items of recovery.

Past consideration (p. 99). A promise in writing, signed by the promisor, shall not be denied effect as a valid obligation on the ground that the consideration for the promise is past or executed, if the consideration is expressed in the writing, is proved to have been given or performed, and would be valid consideration but for the time when it was given or performed. (Real Prop. Law, § 279, subd. 2; Pers. 

Prop. Law § 33, subd. 3, added by L. 1941, ch. 331)

Note. These sections do away with the Common Law requirement that consideration be given in present exchange for the promise. In 

Example 10, if Morrow had written and signed his promise to pay Borden $50, reciting that it was in consideration of the services rendered, the promise would be enforceable under these statutes. 

Seals (pp. 101, 117). Except as otherwise expressly provided by statute, the presence or absence of a seal upon a written instrument executed after Sept. 1, 1941, is without legal effect. (Civil Prac. Act, § 342, added by L. 1941, ch. 329)

Statute of limitations (p. 118). An action upon a sealed instrument must be commenced within six years from the time when the cause of action accrued. If a cause of action on a sealed instrument accrued before Sept. 1, 1941, and would not be barred under the former statute for more than six years after that date, the period is shortened to six years. If less than six years remains under the former statute, the time is not extended. (Civil Prac. Act, § 47, amended by L. 1941, ch. 329)

Accord and satisfaction (p. 108). An executory accord is an agreement to give and accept at a future time a stipulated performance in satisfaction of an existing obligation. Such accord is a defense to an action brought by the creditor before the time for its performance has arrived. If the debtor tenders the agreed performance, the creditor is bound to accept it. If the debtor fails to render the performance as agreed, the creditor may sue on the accord or on the original obliga tion. (Real Prop. Law, §§ 280, 281; Pers. Prop. Law, § 33, subds. a, b, added by L. 1937, ch. 77)

STATUTORY CHANGES 

611 Note. At Common Law an accord was ineffective unless followed by full satisfaction, made and accepted. The creditor could disregard the accord and sue to enforce the original obligation, even though the debtor offered to perform the accord and even though he had partly performed it. The statute does away with that highly technical rule and actual performance of the compromise agreement is not necessary to give it legal effect.

Release (pp. 109, 153). A written instrument which purports to be a total or partial release of all claims, or any particular claim, or of a mortgage or other lien on property, real or personal, shall not be invalid because of the absence of consideration or of a seal. (Debtor & 

Creditor Law, § 243, added by L. 1936, ch. 222) 

Note. One objection to the abolition of the legal effect of a seal was that it prevented the giving of a release without consideration that would be binding upon the creditor. This statute makes such release effective if it is in writing.

Extension of time (p. 109). An agreement to change or modify, or to discharge in whole or in part, any contract, obligation, lease, mortgage or other security interest in real or personal property, shall not be invalid because of the absence of consideration, provided such agreement be in writing and signed by the party against whom it is sought to be enforced. (Real Prop. Law, § 279; Pers. Prop. Law, § 33, subd. 2, added by L. 1936, ch. 281)

Note. At Common Law an existing agreement could not be changed so that one party assumed a new obligation unless the other party gave a new consideration for such new obligation; e.g., the promise of an employer to pay an employee additional wages over the amount fixed by a contract between them, in consideration of the performance of his contract by the employee, was not enforceable. (See "Promise to do what one is bound to do," p. 100.) Similarly, an agreement by a creditor to extend the time for the payment of a debt, or a promise by a mortgagee to accept a lower rate of interest, would not be enforceable. 

The statute makes all such agreements enforceable if in writing. 

Assignments (p. 125). An assignment in writing and signed by the assignor irrevocably transfers the assignor's rights, even in the absence of consideration therefor. (Pers. Prop. Law, § 33, subd. 4, added by 

L. 1941, ch. 330)

Wage assignments. No wage assignment securing an indebtedness of $1,000 or less shall be valid for any purpose unless contained in a separate, written instrument, prominently entitled, specifically describing

the transaction, personally executed by the assignor and a copy of the instrument delivered to him, and unless the wages exceed $15 per week in a city of 250,000 population or more, and $12 per week elsewhere. 

Not more than 10% of the wages assigned shall be collectible from the assignor's employer, and payments on assignments or executions against wages shall be made in the order in which such assignments are filed with the employer, not more than one 10% deduction to be made. Wage assignments must be filed and indexed in the County 

Clerk's Office before being filed with the employer, and shall be refiled after two years. (Pers. Prop. Law, § 46, amended by L. 1942, ch. 508, §§ 47 to 47-e, added by L. 1941, ch. 867)

Bankruptcy (pp. 164-169). The Bankruptcy Act was drastically amended by Act of June 22, 1930, known as the "Chandler Act."

Several new chapters were added, under which certain classes of debtors may arrange a composition with their creditors and procure an extension of time to pay their debts; and corporations may be reorganized and their debt structures altered, all under the supervision and control of the Federal Court and with its consent and approval. 

There are separate chapters providing for compositions and extensions by farmers, taxing agencies, and wage earners; for arrangements by individuals as to ordinary debts and those secured by real property; and for reorganization of railroads and other corporations. 

The new proceedings have been used extensively, particularly in corporate reorganization, as they are much more flexible than regular bankruptcy. They permit the debtor to hold his property and continue to conduct his business, instead of being forced to sell all his assets, usually at sacrifice prices, as must be done in a bankruptcy proceeding. 

Statute of limitations (p. 182). With the abolition of the legal effect of a seal by the new § 342 of the Civil Practice Act (see ante, p. 610), the period of limitation on an action to enforce a sealed instrument has been reduced from twenty years to six years. (Civil Prac. Act, § 47, amended by L. 1941, ch. 329)

Garnishment (p. 190). An execution against wages, salary, or income from trust funds may be obtained, if the debtor is entitled to more than $15 per week in a city of 250,000 population or more, or $12 per week in any other case. (Civil Prac. Act, § 684, amended by 

L. 1941, ch. 865)

TORTS 

Negligence (p. 26). Claims for damages for negligence arising out of motor vehicle accidents are very numerous. The amount of losses from bodily injury or death, and from property damage, is tremendous and a serious economic question is presented. In many cases the guilty

STATUTORY CHANGES 

613 party is financially irresponsible and the loss falls on the innocent party or his family, often with tragic results. Various solutions have been proposed. One solution is to place the burden on all motorists through a statute based on the same theory as the workmen's compensation law (see text, p. 237), but the difficulties involved have so far proved to be insuperable and no such statute has been exacted. Some statesnotably Massachusetts-have statutes requiring compulsory liability insurance for all motorists. 

New York adopted in 1941 a statute entitled "Financial Responsi bility for Operation of Motor Vehicles." (Vehicle & Traffic Law, Art. 

6A, §§ 94 to 94 nn)

Under this statute an operator's license may be revoked and the registration certificate and plates of any motor vehicle registered in his name may be suspended, upon proof of his conviction of any offense under the Vehicle & Traffic Law, or of his conviction in another state or in Canada; or upon proof of his failure for fifteen days to satisfy a judgment in excess of $25 for property damage, or any judgment for damages for bodily injury to or death of any person arising out of the ownership or operation of any motor vehicle.

A judgment is deemed to be satisfied when paid in full; or if $5,000 be paid on account of a judgment in excess of that sum for injury to one person; or when $10,000 has been paid on account of a judgment in excess of that sum for injury to more than one person in one accident; or when $1,000 has been paid on account of a judgment in excess of that sum for property damage.

The statute permits the suspension of the driving privileges of a nonresident under the same circumstances. 

A license revoked, and a registration certificate and plates suspended, will not be reissued or renewed in the name of the person whose license and/or registration certificate was suspended, or in any other name where the commissioner has reasonable grounds to believe that such registration will have the effect of defeating the purpose of the statute, and no other motor vehicle shall be registered in the name of such person nor any new license issued to him, unless the operator or owner gives proof of financial ability to satisfy any judgment resulting from an accident, and proof of financial responsibility in the future. This requirement is met by proof of a bond with sufficient surety, or an automobile liability insurance policy, with limits of $5,000 for injury to one person, $10,000 for injury to two or more persons, and $1,000 for property damage; or by proof of the deposit of $11,000 in cash or securities. with the Department of Taxation. This means that an operator can not drive, nor can a registered car be used or sold, until the required proof is furnished.

A license or registration revoked or suspended shall be restored upon

satisfaction of any judgment obtained, or upon the judgment debtor obtaining an order of the court permitting payment of the judgment in installments, or upon the written consent of the judgment creditor that the license or registration may be restored notwithstanding nonpayment of the judgment; and in all such cases with proof of financial responsibility in the future. Provided, however, that any person whose license or registration has been suspended, whether or not he has furnished security or proof of financial responsibility, shall be relieved from furnishing or maintaining proof of financial responsibility if one year has elapsed since the accident, and he has not paid anything for damages resulting from such accident and no suit because thereof has been brought against him, or if a suit has been brought it has resulted in his favor. In such case the fact of having been involved in such accident shall not bar the issuance of license or registration to such person. (Last sentence, § 94-h as amended by L. 1942, ch. 720) 

A discharge in bankruptcy following the rendition of a judgment shall not relieve the judgment debtor from the requirements of the statute.

Note. This statute makes it practically obligatory for every motorist to carry automobile liability insurance, at least sufficient to satisfy the minimum requirements of the statute. In addition to furnishing protection under the statute, such insurance offers many other advantages to the policy holder. It is suggested that an agent or broker who writes such insurance be asked to address the class on the subject. 

AGENCY 

Appointment under seal (p. 210). The abolition of the legal effect of a seal by § 342 of the Civil Prac. Act (ante, p. 610), renders it unnecessary that the agent's appointment be sealed.

The relations between employer and employee have been materially affected by recent Federal legislation, particularly the National Labor 

Relations Act, the Wages and Hours Act, and the Social Security Act, which are explained on pp. 595–604, ante, and which should be discussed in connection with this topic. 

New York statutes also contain provisions for unemployment insurance (Labor Law, §§ 500 to 539), and for social security (Social Welfare Law), which are similar to the Federal legislation in scope and purpose. 

Employers are required to keep records of wages paid to employees in connection with the administration of the Unemployment Insurance 

Fund (Labor Law, § 521), the Workmen's Compensation Law (Workmen's Comp. Law, § 112), and the Income Tax Law (Tax Law, § 366).

NEGOTIABLE INSTRUMENTS Interest and usury (p. 276). General Business Law, § 370, provides that the legal rate of interest is 6%. § 371 provides that the taking of any greater sum in money or property, directly or indirectly, for the loan or forbearance of money is usury. § 373 provides that all instruments or contracts by which any greater sum shall be secured, reserved, or taken, shall be void and the same may be ordered to be surrendered and canceled.

Pawnbrokers may charge as interest: on loans not over $100, 3% per month for the first six months and 2% per month thereafter; and on loans over $100, 2% per month for the first six months and 1% per month thereafter. (General Business Law, § 46) 

The business of making small loans, as conducted by so-called "small loan companies" and "personal finance companies," has been the subject of much discussion and investigation in recent years, Such loans are usually sought by needy borrowers who have not sufficient credit or resources to satisfy the requirements of a commercial bank. The amounts loaned are small and the risk of loss to the lender is supposedly great, so that the legal rate of interest is an inadequate return. The problem is how to allow the lender to charge enough to induce him to make such loans, thereby meeting the needs of the borrower, and at the same time to protect the borrower from exorbitant and unconscionable charges and demands. 99 In New York the business of making such loans is regulated by the 

Banking Law, Art. IX, §§ 340 to 365, entitled "Licensed Lenders,' 

adopted in its present form in 1932 and last amended by L. 1941, ch. 524.

Under this statute no person shall engage in the business of making loans of $300 or less and charge therefor more than the legal rate of interest without first obtaining a license from the superintendent of banks. A careful investigation is made of the financial responsibility, experience, character and fitness of the applicant for license, and his qualities must be such as to command the confidence of the community and to warrant belief that the business will be operated honestly, fairly and efficiently. (§§ 340, 343) 

A licensed lender may loan not exceeding $300 and charge as interest not over 21% per month on any unpaid balance of the loan not exceeding $100, and 2% per month on the remainder of the unpaid balance. 

The lender can not induce the borrower to split up his loans (so that each is under the limit, but the total exceeds the limit), nor can a borrower, or a husband and wife together or separately, be indebted to a lender on more than one loan at the same time. Interest shall not be deducted in advance or compounded, and shall be computed on unpaid

balances. In addition to the maximum rate, no other charge whatsoever for any purpose shall be made or received, except lawful fees actually paid for filing or recording any instrument securing the loan. 

If any interest or charge in excess of that allowed is charged or made, the loan shall be void and the lender shall have no right to collect any principal, interest or charge whatsoever. (§ 352) 

Note. The matter relating to small loans is affected by L. 1942, ch. 

605. This chapter amends Banking Law § 352. After forbidding the compounding of interest, the new provision says that, when a new loan includes the unpaid balance of a prior loan, the unpaid interest on such prior loan which accrued within sixty days before the making of the new loan may be included in the new loan as interest-bearing principal. 

The lender is required: to deliver to the borrower when the loan is made a complete statement of the details of the loan and a copy of § 352 of the statute; to give a receipt for all payments made, showing the amount applied to principal and interest and stating the unpaid balance; to permit payment in advance; and, upon final payment, to return the obligation marked "paid” and to release any and all security given by the borrower. The lender shall not take a confession of judgment or power of attorney. (§ 353) 

Note. Chapter 605 also amends § 353, which requires that a receipt be given for each payment made by the borrower, showing the amount applied to interest and principal, by providing that an unitemized receipt may be given temporarily and replaced by an itemized receipt within ten days.

A lender can not charge more than the legal rate of interest on any loan in excess of $300, which applies when a person is directly or contingently liable, as borrower, indorser, guarantor, or surety, to the lender at any time for more than $300. (§ 354) 

Forgery (p. 296). If a bank pays a check on which the signature of the depositor is forged, and charges the check against the account, the depositor may recover the money so paid, provided he notifies the bank of the forgery within one year after the return to him of the forged check. (Negot. Inst. Law § 326) 

A depositor may recover from his bank money paid on a forged or unauthorized indorsement, provided he notifies the bank of the forgery within two years after the return of the voucher. (Id. § 43, added by 

L. 1941, ch. 87)

SALE OF PERSONAL PROPERTY 

Conditional sales (p. 353). The Uniform Conditional Sales Law was adopted in New York in 1922 and is Art. 4, §§ 60 to 81, of the Personal

STATUTORY CHANGES 

617 Property Law. In general, the text explanation and discussion is in accord with the Uniform Law. Some of the detailed provisions and certain amendments are as follows.

Form and contents of contract. The printed portion of any conditional sales contract for $1,500 or less for non-commercial use shall be in eight point type; shall be prominently entitled "Conditional Sales 

Contract"; shall contain an itemized statement of the transaction, with the insurance charge, if any, and the credit service charge separately stated; and an executed copy of the contract shall be delivered to the buyer at the time of its execution. (§ 64-a, added by L. 1941, ch. 866)

Insurance and service charges. If the buyer's interest in the goods is insured, the contract shall state the type of coverage and whether the insurance is to be procured by the buyer or the seller. The buyer shall receive a copy of the policy. The credit service charge may be expressed in dollars or as a simple interest charge on unpaid balances payable in installments. (§ 64-a)

Filing of contract (p. 355). The reservation of title to the conditional seller is void as against a purchaser from or a creditor of the buyer, who without notice of the reservation purchased or acquired a lien on the goods before the contract is filed, unless it is filed within ten days after making the conditional sale (§ 65). Contracts for conditional sale of canal craft must be filed in the Office of the Superintendent of Public Works. Other such contracts, except those for fixtures, must be filed in the office of the city or town clerk where the buyer resides or, if he is a non-resident, where he keeps the goods for use (§ 66). Conditional sales contracts for fixtures (see text, p. 527) must be filed in the office where a deed would be recorded to affect the real estate (§ 67). Conditional sales contracts for goods sold for resale are valid whether filed or not, but the reservation of title is void against a bona fide purchaser from the buyer (§ 69). The filing officer is required to mark the contract with the date and hour of filing and to keep a separate book or card index, showing the names of both seller and buyer indexed alphabetically, date of filing and date of cancelation (§ 70, as amended by L. 1939, ch. 634). Filing is valid for three years and may be extended for successive additional periods of one year each by re-filing within thirty days next preceding expiration of the period, with a statement signed by the seller that the contract is in force and showing the amount remaining unpaid (§ 71). Upon the payment of the amount due, the seller must execute and file a certificate of satisfaction and the filing officer shall note the cancelation of the contract on the record. (§ 72, as amended by L. 1940, ch. 741) 

Removal or sale of goods. Unless prohibited by the contract, the buyer may remove the goods from the filing district, or sell his interest

in them, but only upon written notice to the seller. If the buyer fails to give such notice, the seller may retake the goods (§ 73). In case of removal to another filing district within the state, or the removal from another state into this state, the reservation of title shall be void unless the contract is filed in the district to which the goods are removed within ten days after the seller has received notice of the filing district to which the goods have been removed. (§ 74) 

Retaking possession. When the buyer is in default under the contract the seller may retake possession of the goods (§ 76). Not more than forty nor less than twenty days prior to retaking, the seller may serve on the buyer notice of intention to retake, stating the default, the time when the goods will be retaken, and the buyer's rights (§ 77). 

If such notice be not given, the seller must retain goods retaken for at least ten days, during which period the buyer may redeem them and recover possession upon payment of the amount or performance of the duty in default and upon payment of the seller's expenses in retaking and storing the goods. (§ 78 as amended by L. 1941, ch. 859) 

Resale. If the buyer does not redeem the goods, and if he has paid at least 50% of the purchase price, the seller must sell the goods at public auction within thirty days after the retaking, upon notice to the buyer and public notice of the sale (§ 79). If the buyer has paid less than 50% of the purchase price, he may demand a resale (§ 80). The proceeds of resale shall be applied to payment of the expenses and the balance due under the contract, any surplus being payable to the buyer (§ 80-a, as amended by L. 1941, ch. 861). If the proceeds of resale are not sufficient to pay the expenses and the balance due, the seller may recover the deficiency from the buyer, provided that, if the price of the goods was $1,500 or less and the goods were for non-commercial use: (1) the buyer may have the reasonable value of the goods determined and shall be credited with the sales price or the reasonable value, whichever is higher; or (2) if the buyer has paid 80% or more of the purchase price and has surrendered the goods at the seller's request, the seller must elect to retain the goods and release the buyer from further obligation, or to return the goods to the buyer and be limited to an action to recover the balance due (§ 80-b, as amended by L. 1941, ch. 860). If there is no resale, the seller may retain the goods as his own and the buyer shall be discharged of all obligation (§ 80-c). If the seller fails to comply with the statutory requirements after retaking the goods, the buyer may recover from the seller his actual damages, and in no event less than one-fourth of all payments made under the contract, with interest. (§ 80-e)

Confession of judgment. A confession of judgment, executed by the buyer before default under a conditional sales contract for $1,500 or less for non-commercial use, is invalid and a judgment entered

STATUTORY CHANGES 

619 thereon is void. (Civil Prac. Act § 543, subd. 2, added by L. 1941, ch. 864)

Additional purchases. Where a buyer makes additional purchases on conditional sales contract or chattel mortgage from a seller to whom he is indebted on previous conditional sales contracts, and the total purchases are $1,500 or less, the contract or mortgage may provide that the goods first purchased shall be security for the price of the later purchases. Payments on the several contracts may be allocated as provided in the statute. (§ 81, added by L. 1941, ch. 862)

Guarantee by wage assignment. No guarantee to a seller under a conditional sales contract for the amount of $1,500 or less, secured by an assignment of wages to be earned, shall be valid unless it identifies and fully describes the transaction secured. If the guarantee includes subsequent transactions, the liability of the guarantor shall be limited to transactions within two years and the maximum amount of liability shall be stated. (Pers. Prop. Law, § 48, added by L. 1941, ch. 859) 

Federal regulations. In May, 1942, the Federal Government promulgated regulations governing instalment purchases, limiting the term of credit, requiring larger down payments, and making other provisions, designed to prevent inflationary buying. 

Implied warranty (p. 373). An express warranty does not negative a warranty implied under the Act unless inconsistent therewith. (Pers. 

Prop. Law, § 96, subd. 6, amended by L. 1941, ch. 47)

(P. 358). The statutes relating to chattel mortgages (Lien Law, §§ 230 to 238) were amended by L. 1941, ch. 94, 642, which added § 230-b relating to mortgages on agricultural crops and those given by motor vehicle dealers, and by L. 1941, ch. 856, which added §§ 239 to

PARTNERSHIP 

Firm name (p. 534). The use of a firm name may be continued: (1) where the business of the firm continues to be conducted by some or any of the partners or their assignees, appointees, or successors in interest; (2) where a new partnership is formed to carry on the business of a firm that has dissolved and a majority of the members of

the old firm shall be members of the new firm. (Partnership Law, § 80, amended by L. 1938, ch. 129)

Where a firm name continues to be so used, the persons using it shall sign a certificate, giving their names and addresses, and file it in the office of the clerk of the county where the principal place of business of the firm is located, and publish a copy in a newspaper in the city or town where the principal place of business is located. (Partnership 

Law § 81, amended by L. 1939, ch. 580)
